title: Test-Input Generation for Tensor Programs: What Actually Finds Kernel Bugs
comment: 8 pages, 1 figure, LNCS format. Companion paper: arXiv:2606.20128 (P1). Additional companions (P2, P4) to follow on arXiv this week; IDs will be added in a v2 replace
summary: Test-input generation for tensor kernels is folkloric. Most projects pick a representative shape and dtype, run a fixed-shape allclose-style check, and ship. We make the choices explicit and measure them. Using the gpuemu op-schema-aware seeded fuzzer (arXiv:2606.20128), we evaluate seven test-generation strategies across a 26-op corpus (16 correct controls and 10 LLM-style buggy variants seeded with documented transcription patterns) on an RTX 3060 GPU instance. Strategies vary the shape candidate set, the dtype mix, and the input value distribution. We report each strategy on two axes: bug recall and control false-positive (FP) rate. Boundary-only shape sampling is the operationally safe winner: 78% recall on the 10 buggy kernels with 0% FP on the 16 controls. Adversarial value sampling reaches higher recall (99%) but inflates control FP to 94% because the strategy injects NaN and Inf inputs and the validator's NaN check fires on every kernel that propagates them, not only on buggy kernels. On the two softmax tail-mask bugs the "regular" strategy (no boundary shapes) catches 0%, while boundary raises recall to 100% and 62% respectively. That gap is the clearest single signal in the data. The corpus result is about which seeded bug patterns each strategy catches, not about the bug rate of any specific deployed LLM.

AI.tldr: A systematic evaluation of test-input generation strategies for GPU tensor kernels reveals that boundary-only shape sampling achieves 78% bug recall with 0% false positives, while adversarial value sampling boosts recall to 99% but causes 94% false-positive rate due to NaN/Inf propagation. The largest performance gap appears in softmax tail-mask bugs, where boundary sampling catches 100% vs. 0% for regular strategies.
AI.motivation: Tensor kernel testing lacks systematic evaluation of input generation strategies. Most projects use ad-hoc representative shapes and dtypes without measuring the trade-offs between different strategies in terms of bug detection and false-positive rates.
AI.method: Using the gpuemu op-schema-aware seeded fuzzer, seven test-generation strategies were evaluated across a 26-op corpus (16 correct controls, 10 LLM-style buggy variants) on an RTX 3060 GPU. Strategies varied shape candidate sets, dtype mixes, and input value distributions. Each strategy was assessed on bug recall and control false-positive rate.
AI.result: Boundary-only shape sampling: 78% recall, 0% FP. Adversarial value sampling: 99% recall, 94% FP (NaN/Inf injection causes validator false positives). For softmax tail-mask bugs specifically, regular strategy catches 0%, boundary sampling achieves 100% and 62% recall respectively.
AI.conclusion: Boundary-only shape sampling is the operationally safe winner, offering strong bug detection without false positives. The study's contribution is about which seeded bug patterns each strategy catches, not about LLM bug rates in deployment.

title: Implementing GenAI-Supported Learning in Software Engineering and Computer Science Education using Bloom's Taxonomy
summary:
Context: Generative AI adoption in software engineering education raises opportunities for learning support alongside concerns about superficial learning and academic integrity.
  Objective: This study investigates how explicit instructional guidance aligned with Bloom's taxonomy supports responsible GenAI use in SE/CS education, exploring student and instructor perceptions of GenAI-supported learning.
  Method: We designed a Bloom-aligned GenAI framework that articulated appropriate GenAI roles at different cognitive levels. The framework was embedded in course instructions, labs, and assessment across multiple SE/CS courses at Queen's University Belfast and Azerbaijan Technical University. Data were collected via anonymous questionnaires and learning artifacts, analyzed using thematic analysis with Bloom's taxonomy as an analytic lens.
  Results: Students perceived GenAI as most valuable for higher-order cognitive activities (analysis, evaluation, reflection) and less suitable for foundational learning. Explicit Bloom-level guidance influenced students to use GenAI reflectively, with delayed or intentional non-use when independent thinking was prioritized. Both students and instructors reported pedagogical benefits alongside challenges in cognitive effort and instructional design workload.
  Conclusion: GenAI's educational value lies in intentional alignment between cognitive learning goals, instructional guidance, and learner self-regulation. Bloom's taxonomy provides a scalable, pedagogy-driven framework for responsible GenAI use in SE/CS education, offering a practical alternative to enforcement-focused responses.

AI.tldr: A study across two universities developed and tested a Bloom's taxonomy-aligned framework for guiding responsible GenAI use in software engineering education, finding that explicit cognitive-level guidance encourages reflective, intentional use — particularly for higher-order tasks — while surfacing tensions around cognitive effort and instructor workload.
AI.motivation: Generative AI tools are rapidly entering software engineering and computer science education, creating a dual challenge: leveraging their pedagogical potential while preventing superficial learning and academic integrity violations. Existing responses tend toward enforcement (bans, detection) rather than pedagogical integration. The authors sought a principled, pedagogy-driven alternative that aligns GenAI use with specific cognitive learning goals.
AI.method: The researchers constructed a Bloom-aligned GenAI framework that prescribes appropriate GenAI roles for each level of Bloom's taxonomy (remembering, understanding, applying, analyzing, evaluating, creating). This framework was embedded into course instructions, lab activities, and assessments across multiple SE/CS courses at Queen's University Belfast and Azerbaijan Technical University. Data were gathered through anonymous student questionnaires and learning artifacts, then analyzed via thematic analysis using Bloom's taxonomy as the analytic lens.
AI.result: Students perceived GenAI as most valuable for higher-order cognitive activities (analysis, evaluation, reflection) and less suitable for foundational knowledge acquisition. Explicit Bloom-level guidance prompted more reflective GenAI use, including deliberate delay or non-use when independent thinking was prioritized. Both students and instructors acknowledged pedagogical benefits but also reported challenges: students faced increased cognitive effort in metacognitive decision-making about when/how to use GenAI, and instructors experienced added workload in instructional design to effectively scaffold the framework.
AI.conclusion: The educational value of GenAI depends on intentional alignment among cognitive learning goals, instructional guidance, and learner self-regulation. Bloom's taxonomy offers a scalable, pedagogy-grounded framework for responsible GenAI integration in SE/CS education, presenting a practical, educationally sound alternative to purely enforcement-based approaches.

title: Formal Grammars in Business Process Management: A Systematic Literature Review
summary: Business Process Management (BPM) is concerned with the systematic design, execution, monitoring, and improvement of business processes. Formal grammars have emerged as a particularly fruitful formalism for BPM, offering generative, declarative, and analytical capabilities that are uniquely well-suited to process-oriented concerns. This paper presents a systematic literature review of 34 primary studies at the intersection of formal grammars and BPM. We identify seven research streams: (i) process grammars for organizational process design; (ii) process modeling languages evaluated as grammars under the Bunge-Wand-Weber ontological framework; (iii) production-rule grammars for process structural specification and variant management; (iv) attribute grammars for the declarative specification and distributed execution of workflows; (v) graph grammars for the transformation, generation, and semantic analysis of process models; (vi) grammatical inference for process mining and discovery; and (vii) process algebras as grammar-like compositional frameworks for behavioral specification and verification. For each stream, we synthesize contributions, formalisms employed, and limitations. The review reveals that formal grammars have influenced BPM across every lifecycle phase (from organizational design to formal verification and data-driven discovery) yet the seven streams have developed largely in parallel, without cross-stream synthesis. We identify five corpus-grounded open challenges and argue that a deeper, unified exploitation of grammatical theory holds significant promise for advancing the state of the art in BPM.

AI.tldr: A systematic literature review of 34 studies identifying seven distinct research streams where formal grammars have been applied to Business Process Management, revealing parallel development without cross-stream synthesis and presenting five open challenges for unified grammatical approaches.
AI.motivation: Formal grammars offer generative, declarative, and analytical capabilities well-suited to BPM, yet no comprehensive synthesis existed mapping how grammatical formalisms have been applied across all BPM lifecycle phases. The authors aim to consolidate this fragmented landscape.
AI.method: Systematic literature review of 34 primary studies at the intersection of formal grammars and BPM. Studies were categorized into seven emergent research streams. For each stream, contributions, formalisms, and limitations were synthesized.
AI.result: Seven research streams identified: (1) process grammars for organizational design, (2) Bunge-Wand-Weber ontological evaluation of modeling languages, (3) production-rule grammars for process structure and variants, (4) attribute grammars for declarative workflow specification, (5) graph grammars for model transformation and analysis, (6) grammatical inference for process mining, and (7) process algebras for compositional behavioral verification. These streams have developed largely in parallel.
AI.conclusion: Formal grammars have influenced every BPM lifecycle phase, but the seven streams remain siloed. Five open challenges are identified, and a deeper, unified exploitation of grammatical theory is argued to hold significant promise for advancing BPM.

title: Recall Before Rerank: Benchmarking Deep Learning Models for Large-Scale Code-to-Code Retrieval
summary: Semantic code search and clone detection are essential for software development, maintenance, and reuse. This paper evaluates the effectiveness, efficiency, and scalability of contemporary deep learning models for first-stage recall in large-scale code-to-code search engines. Benchmarking across multiple programming languages and datasets reveals critical limits in the precision and scalability of these models on Terabyte-scale source-code collections. We present LLM-based code normalisation and query-rewriting schemes that yield significant gains in precision for lower-performing models. Our results question the sustainability of resource-constrained deployment and the assumed robustness of current code-specialised LLMs across datasets. We conclude with actionable insights for building scalable, efficient code-retrieval systems.

AI.tldr: Evaluates deep learning models for large-scale code-to-code search, revealing precision and scalability limits at terabyte scale. Proposes LLM-based code normalization and query rewriting to improve recall, and questions the robustness and sustainability of current code-specialized LLMs across diverse datasets.
AI.motivation: Code search and clone detection are critical for software engineering, yet the effectiveness of contemporary deep learning models at terabyte-scale, multi-language code retrieval remains poorly understood. The authors aim to benchmark these models rigorously and identify where they fail.
AI.method: Benchmarking of deep learning code-retrieval models across multiple programming languages and datasets at terabyte scale, measuring precision, efficiency, and scalability. Introduction of LLM-based code normalization and query-rewriting schemes to boost recall for underperforming models.
AI.result: Contemporary models exhibit critical precision and scalability limits on terabyte-scale collections. LLM-based normalization and query rewriting yield significant precision gains, particularly for lower-performing models. Results reveal that resource-constrained deployment is unsustainable and that current code-specialized LLMs lack robustness across datasets.
AI.conclusion: Current deep learning models for code search are not yet robust or scalable enough for terabyte-scale deployment. LLM-based query rewriting and normalization offer practical remedies. The authors provide actionable guidance for building scalable, efficient code-retrieval systems.

title: SidConArena: An Environment Evaluating Agents in Open-Ended,Positive-Sum Bargaining Game
summary: Evaluating LLM agents requires dynamic environments that go beyond static reasoning and zero-sum games. Real-world economic interaction is often open-ended and mixed-motive: agents must negotiate, create positive-sum surplus, compete for scarce assets, and plan under delayed returns. We introduce SidConArena, a new benchmark framework for evaluating LLM agents in open-ended, positive-sum bargaining. SidConArena formalizes a multi-player economy as a finite-horizon partially observable stochastic game with three coupled phases: natural-language negotiation with binding trades, deterministic converter-based production, and sealed-bid auctions for long-term assets. The framework combines structured observations, phase-aware agent dispatching, a neural-symbolic action interface, and asynchronous execution, enabling free-form interaction while preserving rule-grounded evaluation. Across homogeneous and heterogeneous tournaments, stronger frontier models achieve higher economic outcomes, yet agents still misvalue resources, bargain passively, and remain limited in long-horizon investment planning.

AI.tldr: SidConArena is a benchmark for evaluating LLM agents in open-ended, positive-sum bargaining economies featuring negotiation, production, and auctions; frontier models perform better but still exhibit strategic limitations.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agent evaluations rely on static reasoning or zero-sum games, failing to capture the open-ended, mixed-motive nature of real-world economic interactions where agents must negotiate, cooperate for mutual gain, compete for scarce resources, and plan under delayed returns.
AI.method: SidConArena formalizes a multi-player economy as a finite-horizon partially observable stochastic game with three coupled phases: (1) natural-language negotiation with binding trades, (2) deterministic converter-based production, and (3) sealed-bid auctions for long-term assets. The framework integrates structured observations, phase-aware agent dispatching, a neural-symbolic action interface, and asynchronous execution to enable free-form interaction under rule-grounded evaluation.
AI.result: In homogeneous and heterogeneous tournaments, stronger frontier LLMs achieve higher economic outcomes. However, agents consistently misvalue resources, bargain passively, and demonstrate limited long-horizon investment planning capabilities.
AI.conclusion: SidConArena provides a challenging testbed that reveals significant gaps in LLM agents' strategic economic reasoning, particularly in resource valuation, active negotiation, and long-term planning, despite frontier models showing relative gains.

title: HandMade: Spatial Prompting for Generative 3D Creation with Part-Labeled VR Sketches
summary: Text-to-3D generation lowers the barrier to 3D content creation, but text alone is a weak interface for specifying spatial intent: where parts should be placed, how they relate, and how an object should be organized in 3D. We present HandMade, a workflow that combines VR 3D sketching and language for open-domain 3D asset generation. HandMade treats coarse, part-labeled 3D sketches not as incomplete geometry to reconstruct directly, but as spatial prompts for existing generative models. It converts segmented VR strokes into multi-view part guidance and structured prompts, allowing users to specify object layout and part relationships through 3D sketching while using language for identity, material, style, and local details. A technical evaluation shows that HandMade better preserves user-authored spatial scaffolds than text-only and sketch-based baselines on 20 varied examples. A user study with eight participants characterizes how users make use of 3D sketching for spatial layout and language for identity, materials, and details across initial authoring and subsequent revision. HandMade contributes an interaction paradigm and interface-to-generation pipeline for spatially guided 3D creation.

AI.tldr: HandMade introduces a VR-based workflow that combines 3D sketching with language prompts for spatial-guided text-to-3D generation, treating coarse part-labeled sketches as spatial prompts rather than geometry to reconstruct, and demonstrates improved preservation of user-authored spatial structure over baselines.
AI.motivation: Text-to-3D generation democratizes 3D content creation, but language alone is a weak interface for specifying spatial intent — where parts go, their relationships, and overall 3D organization. There is a need for an interaction paradigm that lets users directly express spatial layout while still leveraging language for appearance, style, and identity.
AI.method: HandMade is a workflow integrating VR 3D sketching with generative models. Users create coarse, part-labeled 3D sketches in VR. These segmented strokes are converted into multi-view part guidance and structured text prompts — sketches serve as spatial scaffolds (layout, part relationships), while language specifies identity, material, style, and local details. The pipeline feeds both modalities into existing text-to-3D generation models.
AI.result: A technical evaluation on 20 diverse examples shows HandMade better preserves user-authored spatial scaffolds compared to text-only and sketch-based baselines. A user study with eight participants characterizes usage patterns: 3D sketching for spatial layout and language for identity, materials, and details — across both initial authoring and revision workflows.
AI.conclusion: HandMade contributes a novel interaction paradigm and an interface-to-generation pipeline that leverages complementary strengths of 3D sketching (spatial intent) and language (appearance/identity), enabling spatially guided, open-domain 3D asset creation.

title: When the Aggregator Cheats: Data-Free Backdoors in Federated LLM-based QA Systems
comment: Accepted at the 35th USENIX Security Symposium (USENIX Security 2026)
summary: Large Language Model (LLM)-based question-answering (QA) systems are increasingly deployed in sensitive domains such as healthcare, mental health counseling, and legal consultation. Federated learning (FL) enables collaborative training without sharing raw client data, for which locally trained models are aggregated at a central server (i.e., a cloud service provider) to obtain a global model. In this paper, we explore the potential vulnerability where a malicious aggregator, who may collude with a third-party vendor, stealthily implants advertisement-type backdoors into federated QA models, without ever accessing client data. The attacker's goals are twofold: (1) preserve clean QA fidelity (i.e., the poisoned model behaves like a clean model on non-triggered queries); and (2) generate highly natural, contextually relevant responses with target advertisements when a trigger appears. Achieving these two goals simultaneously is highly challenging, as naive backdoor injection without knowledge about private data may degrade model's clean performance or fail to inject the target. Motivated by this, we propose to leverage clients' uploaded gradients during training, and develop a two-stage framework for data-free and stealthy poisoning: (1) recover representative training samples from client gradients, and (2) construct poisoning datasets utilizing recovered samples and trigger phrases to inject backdoors into the global model. Experiments across representative QA datasets and LLM families under full fine-tuning and LoRA settings demonstrate that, our method achieves nearly 100% Attack Success Rate (ASR) while incurring negligible degradation on clean tasks. Crucially, reconstructing only 5-20% of gradients suffices to mount a reliable attack, exposing a practical blind spot in the pipeline of federated training of QA LLMs.

AI.tldr: A malicious FL aggregator can implant advertisement backdoors into federated QA LLMs without accessing client data by reconstructing training samples from client gradients and crafting poisoned data, achieving ~100% ASR with negligible clean performance degradation.
AI.motivation: Federated QA LLMs in sensitive domains are susceptible to supply-chain attacks from a malicious aggregator. Existing backdoor attacks require either data access or cause clean performance degradation. The key challenge is simultaneously preserving QA fidelity on clean queries while injecting targeted advertisements on triggered queries — without any client data access.
AI.method: A two-stage data-free poisoning framework: (1) Gradient-based data reconstruction — recover representative training samples from uploaded client gradients using gradient inversion techniques; only 5–20% of gradients are needed. (2) Poisoning dataset construction — splice recovered samples with trigger phrases and target advertisement responses to create poisoned training pairs, then inject backdoors during aggregation. Evaluated under both full fine-tuning and LoRA settings.
AI.result: Nearly 100% Attack Success Rate (ASR) with negligible degradation on clean QA tasks. Reconstructing only 5–20% of client gradients suffices for a reliable attack. Validated across multiple representative QA datasets and LLM families.
AI.conclusion: Federated training of QA LLMs harbors a critical blind spot: a malicious aggregator can stealthily implant contextually natural advertisement backdoors without data access, using only a fraction of client gradients. This exposes a practical vulnerability in federated QA pipelines.

title: Formalizing Latent Thoughts: Four Axioms of Thought Representation in LLMs
summary: We introduce an axiomatic evaluation framework for latent thought representations in LLMs, comprising metrics that are independent of downstream benchmark scores and reveal representational failures that benchmark accuracy masks. Existing evaluations conflate representation quality with model capacity. Therefore, failures cannot be attributed to the representation rather than to the model that processes it. We formalize four functional axioms (Causality, Minimality, Separability, and Stability) and define a quantitative measure for each, computed directly on the representation independently of downstream accuracy. We audit open-weight LLMs across 23 reasoning tasks (e.g., Spatial Reasoning, Factual QA). We find that no candidate satisfies all four axioms simultaneously, that the representations distinguish task type reliably but cannot distinguish between two questions within the same task, and that the representations encode little information beyond what is already present in the input embedding. The failure is consistent across dense, reasoning-distilled, and RL-trained model families, indicating that the gap is structural rather than a property of model size or training procedure.

AI.tldr: Proposes an axiomatic framework to evaluate LLM latent thought representations independently of downstream benchmarks. Defines four axioms (Causality, Minimality, Separability, Stability) with quantitative measures. Auditing 23 reasoning tasks across multiple model families reveals that no representation satisfies all axioms, representations distinguish tasks but not individual questions within tasks, and encode little beyond input embeddings—a structural failure across model types.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM latent representations conflate representation quality with downstream model capacity, making it impossible to determine whether failures stem from the representation itself or the model processing it. The authors aim to isolate and directly measure representational quality using axiomatic criteria independent of benchmark scores.
AI.method: The authors formalize four functional axioms—Causality (representation causes correct output), Minimality (representation contains no task-irrelevant information), Separability (distinct questions yield distinct representations), and Stability (same-question paraphrases yield similar representations). For each, they define a quantitative metric computed directly on the representation without downstream evaluation. They then audit open-weight LLMs across 23 reasoning tasks (Spatial Reasoning, Factual QA, etc.), spanning dense, reasoning-distilled, and RL-trained model families.
AI.result: No candidate LLM satisfies all four axioms simultaneously. Representations reliably distinguish between task types but fail to distinguish between two distinct questions within the same task. Representations encode minimal information beyond what is already present in the input embedding. These failures are consistent across dense, reasoning-distilled, and RL-trained models, indicating a structural gap rather than one attributable to model size or training procedure.
AI.conclusion: The axiomatic gap in latent thought representations is structural and pervasive across diverse LLM families. Current representations function as task-type classifiers but lack the granularity to disambiguate individual reasoning instances, highlighting a fundamental limitation in how LLMs internally represent reasoning that downstream benchmark accuracy obscures.

title: OverFlowLight: Real-Time Gridlock Prevention and Traffic Signal Optimization for Urban Intersections
summary: Queue overflow, a severe consequence of urban traffic congestion, occurs when vehicle queues exceed intersection capacity, obstructing upstream traffic and triggering cascading gridlocks. Prevailing traffic signal control (TSC) algorithms, primarily optimized for throughput, often fail to address overflow during peak hours, exacerbating congestion and creating safety hazards. We propose OverFlowLight, a real-time framework designed to preemptively resolve overflow and enhance overall TSC performance. It first introduces a mechanism to accurately detect overflow in real-time by leveraging multi-modal sensing from cameras and radars. Upon detection, it dynamically generates and inserts dedicated overflow phases into the signal cycle to clear the blocking queues. This is orchestrated by a hybrid control design that combines rapid rule-based overflow intervention with controller back ends such as reinforcement learning (RL) for longer-horizon efficiency. We conducted extensive real-world deployments of OverFlowLight across 43 intersections in three major cities. The framework demonstrates seamless integration with existing RL-based TSC agents, highlighting its modularity and practical applicability. Empirical results show that OverFlowLight reduces overflow incidents by 60.4% and increases network throughput by 18.2% compared to deployed baselines. Furthermore, it substantially diminishes the need for manual intervention common with expert-tuned signal plans. This work presents the first practical, scalable, and data-driven framework for actively preventing traffic gridlock, offering a crucial component for building resilient and efficient urban transportation systems. Our demonstration videos, codes and datasets are available at the anonymous URL, https://anonymous.4open.science/r/OverFlowLight-FBF9.

AI.tldr: OverFlowLight is a real-time traffic signal control framework that uses multi-modal sensing (cameras/radars) to detect queue overflow, then dynamically inserts dedicated overflow phases via a hybrid rule-based + reinforcement learning controller. Deployed across 43 intersections in three cities, it reduced overflow incidents by 60.4% and increased throughput by 18.2%.
AI.motivation: Existing traffic signal control algorithms optimize for throughput but fail to address queue overflow during peak hours, where vehicle queues exceed intersection capacity and block upstream traffic, triggering cascading gridlocks. This creates both severe congestion and safety hazards that current systems cannot adequately handle.
AI.method: OverFlowLight comprises three core components: (1) real-time overflow detection using multi-modal sensing from cameras and radars; (2) dynamic generation and insertion of dedicated overflow phases into the signal cycle to clear blocking queues; and (3) a hybrid control architecture combining rapid rule-based overflow intervention with reinforcement learning backends for longer-horizon efficiency optimization.
AI.result: In real-world deployments across 43 intersections in three major cities, OverFlowLight achieved a 60.4% reduction in overflow incidents and an 18.2% increase in network throughput compared to deployed baselines. It also substantially reduced the need for manual expert intervention in signal plan tuning and demonstrated seamless integration with existing RL-based TSC agents.
AI.conclusion: This work presents the first practical, scalable, data-driven framework for actively preventing traffic gridlock, providing a crucial component for building resilient and efficient urban transportation systems. Its modular design and demonstrated real-world efficacy mark a significant advance over throughput-only TSC approaches.

title: AI-Model Network: Concept, Current State and Future
summary: While the primary function of computers lies in computation and processing, the core value of the Internet is rooted in sharing and collaboration. Computers create the Internet, and the Internet empowers the value of computers. The rapid development of the Internet, cloud computing, and big data is pushing artificial intelligence into the era of large models (LMs). However, the practical application of LMs is currently hindered by high training costs and deployment complexities, driving a shift toward lightweight, private, and domain-specific models. With the rapid proliferation and wide distribution of heterogeneous models, enabling effective interaction and collaboration among them has emerged as a critical bottleneck that urgently needs to be addressed in LM development. Drawing inspiration from the development of the Internet, this paper proposes the concept, vision, and system architecture of world wide AI-model network (AI-ModelNet). It is a novel paradigm that achieves interconnection, capability sharing, and collaborative reasoning by establishing pathways between models. We first briefly review the current state of single-model and multi-model research. Subsequently, the systemic vision and hierarchical architecture of AI-ModelNet are articulated, followed by validation of the framework's feasibility through a prototype system and diverse application cases. Finally, key directions for future research are discussed preliminarily.

AI.tldr: Proposes AI-ModelNet, a novel paradigm inspired by the Internet that interconnects heterogeneous AI models for capability sharing and collaborative reasoning, addressing the bottleneck of isolated domain-specific models.
AI.motivation: Large models face high training costs and deployment complexity, driving adoption of lightweight, private, domain-specific models. However, these heterogeneous models operate in isolation, creating an urgent need for effective interconnection and collaboration mechanisms.
AI.method: The paper proposes AI-ModelNet with a hierarchical architecture enabling model-to-model pathways for interconnection, capability sharing, and collaborative reasoning. Validation is conducted via a prototype system and diverse application cases.
AI.result: The prototype system and application cases demonstrate the feasibility of the AI-ModelNet framework for connecting heterogeneous models and enabling collaborative intelligence.
AI.conclusion: AI-ModelNet represents a promising paradigm shift toward networked AI, with the paper outlining key future research directions for realizing a world-wide network of collaborating AI models.

title: A Sensitivity-Aware Test Collection for Search Among Personal Information
summary: Traditional search tasks aim to satisfy user information needs by returning a subset of a collection of documents, ranked by the documents' relevance to a user query. However, some collections that contain useful information also contain sensitive personal information. Recently, there has been increasing interest in the development of Sensitivity-Aware Search (SAS) retrieval models to provide users with effective retrieval results without revealing such sensitive information. To develop such systems, test collections containing both sensitive and non-sensitive information, a set of queries, and query-document relevance assessments are required. The Enron email corpus contains real business-related emails, where some emails also contain sensitive personal information. However, the original Enron collection does not contain queries or query-relevance assessments. To this end, we crowdsource 150 query formulations for 50 different topics and 11,471 query-relevance assessments for a subset of the Enron documents that have been manually labelled for sensitivity. We follow best practices for using large language models (LLMs) in Information Retrieval evaluation to extend the collection further with additional LLM judged query-relevance assessments and sensitivity labels. We present baseline performances for relevance, sensitivity classification, and sensitivity-aware search on the collection. We make the collection available, including through the popular ir_datasets package, and provide pre-built sparse and dense indices on Huggingface to facilitate easy experimentation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a new test collection for Sensitivity-Aware Search (SAS) built on the Enron email corpus, featuring crowdsourced queries, manual sensitivity labels, relevance judgments, and LLM-extended annotations, along with baseline results and publicly available resources.
AI.motivation: Sensitivity-Aware Search (SAS) aims to retrieve relevant documents while suppressing those containing sensitive personal information. Despite growing interest, no suitable test collection existed with both relevance judgments and sensitivity labels. The Enron corpus naturally contains both business and sensitive personal content, making it ideal — but it lacked queries and relevance assessments.
AI.method: The authors crowdsourced 150 queries across 50 topics and 11,471 query-document relevance assessments on manually sensitivity-labeled Enron documents. They then employed LLMs following IR evaluation best practices to generate additional relevance judgments and sensitivity labels at scale. The collection was packaged with sparse and dense indices, made available via ir_datasets and Huggingface.
AI.result: Baseline performances are reported for three tasks: relevance ranking, sensitivity classification, and sensitivity-aware search. The collection comprises real emails with both crowdsourced and LLM-generated query-relevance assessments, plus manual and LLM-generated sensitivity labels, providing a foundation for SAS research.
AI.conclusion: The paper delivers the first publicly available, reusable test collection for Sensitivity-Aware Search, lowering the barrier to entry for researchers through standardized data formats, pre-built indices, and integration with popular IR infrastructure like ir_datasets and Huggingface.

title: Towards Evaluation of Implicit Software World Models in Coding LLMs
comment: Accepted to DL4Code workshop at ICML 2026
summary: Software engineering, whether performed by humans or by AI agents, requires reasoning about how software behaves. We call the internal model that supports such reasoning the software world model, and view current code-execution benchmarks as covering one well-studied slice of it -- control flow. In this paper, we take a step toward a broader evaluation by shifting the observable axis to execution resources: alongside test outcome and exception class, we predict peak memory, wall-clock time, and ranked profiler outputs at method and line granularity. We use SWE-bench Verified as the source of data to hold the test close to real-world software engineering tasks. All tested models, frontier ones included, show modest performance and brittle behaviour, suggesting a notable lack of understanding of how software is executed, as opposed to how its source code is written.

AI.tldr: This paper broadens the evaluation of software world models beyond control flow to include execution resource prediction (peak memory, wall-clock time, profiler outputs). Using SWE-bench Verified, even frontier models perform poorly, revealing a gap in understanding software execution as opposed to source code.
AI.motivation: Current code-execution benchmarks focus narrowly on control flow (test outcomes, exceptions). The authors argue that a true "software world model" — the internal representation enabling reasoning about software behavior — must also encompass execution resources. They aim to expose whether models truly understand runtime behavior, not just static code structure.
AI.method: The authors shift the evaluation axis from control flow to execution resources. Using SWE-bench Verified as a data source to ensure real-world relevance, they task models with predicting: (1) peak memory usage, (2) wall-clock execution time, and (3) ranked profiler outputs at both method-level and line-level granularity, alongside traditional test outcomes and exception classes.
AI.result: All tested models — including frontier models — exhibit only modest performance and brittle behavior on execution resource prediction tasks, indicating a substantial deficiency in understanding how software executes at runtime.
AI.conclusion: There is a notable gap between models' ability to reason about source code syntax/structure and their ability to reason about runtime execution behavior. Broadening benchmarks to include execution resource prediction is a necessary step toward developing more robust software world models in AI systems.

title: Delayed Verification Destabilizes Multi-Agent LLM Belief: Instability Thresholds and Optimal Corrector Placement
comment: 20 pages, 5 figures, 1 table. Code and data: https://github.com/YehudaItkin/delayed-verification-llm
summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) systems often rely on verifier and critic agents to suppress hallucinations, but verification is delayed. During this delay, false claims can propagate through the agent network. We model this process as delayed consensus on a graph with grounded corrector nodes. Spectral decomposition by the grounded Laplacian yields a closed-form stability threshold for the verification dose: correction that is too strong or too delayed can turn consensus into oscillation. The most unstable regime occurs when the communication and verification delays coincide; for delay two, the threshold is the inverse golden ratio. The same framework gives a supermodular placement objective and a greedy (1-1/e)-approximation rule for assigning a limited corrector budget to influential nodes. Experiments across five open models confirm the predicted dose-delay oscillations. By contrast, grounded factual answering makes truth an absorbing boundary and eliminates the effect, suggesting that the instability is specific to signed-belief tasks while grounded verification remains stabilizing

AI.tldr: The paper models multi-agent LLM verification as delayed consensus on a graph with grounded corrector nodes. Using spectral analysis of the grounded Laplacian, it derives a closed-form stability threshold where overly strong or delayed correction induces oscillation rather than consensus. The worst instability occurs when communication and verification delays coincide (for delay two, the threshold is the inverse golden ratio). A supermodular placement objective yields a greedy (1-1/e)-approximation for assigning correctors. Experiments confirm predicted dose-delay oscillations, while grounded factual answering eliminates the effect, suggesting instability is specific to signed-belief tasks.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems use verifier/critic agents to suppress hallucinations, but verification is inherently delayed. During this delay, false claims can propagate through the agent network, creating a tension between correction strength and timing. The paper aims to formally characterize when delayed verification destabilizes consensus rather than reinforcing it.
AI.method: The authors model the multi-agent system as delayed consensus dynamics on a graph, where grounded corrector nodes inject correction signals. They apply spectral decomposition using the grounded Laplacian to derive a closed-form stability threshold relating correction strength to delay magnitude. For corrector placement, they formulate a supermodular objective and prove a greedy (1-1/e)-approximation guarantee. Experiments validate predictions across five open-source LLMs on signed-belief and grounded factual answering tasks.
AI.result: A closed-form stability threshold emerges: correction that is too strong or too delayed turns consensus into oscillation. The most unstable regime occurs when communication and verification delays coincide; for delay two, the threshold equals the inverse golden ratio (≈0.618). The greedy placement algorithm achieves a (1-1/e)-approximation. Experiments across five open models confirm the predicted dose-delay oscillations. Grounded factual answering makes truth an absorbing boundary and eliminates instability, indicating the phenomenon is specific to signed-belief tasks.
AI.conclusion: Delayed verification in multi-agent LLM systems exhibits a fundamental stability trade-off governed by the grounded Laplacian spectrum. The instability is specific to signed-belief deliberation; grounded factual verification remains stabilizing regardless of delay. The supermodular placement framework provides practical guidance for deploying limited corrector resources to maximally influential nodes.

title: Context-Aware Explanations for Spatialized Document Layouts
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures, accepted to Graphics Interface 2026 (GI 2026)
summary: Spatialized document layouts are widely used for exploratory analysis of text corpora, but interpreting the spatial organization of documents and the relationships between regions remains challenging. Existing approaches primarily summarize document content or explain how layouts are generated, providing limited support for understanding spatial relationships within the layout itself. We present CAPE, a context-aware explanation framework that generates natural-language explanations grounded in both document semantics and layout-derived spatial context. CAPE identifies salient spatial patterns (e.g., clusters, subgroups, outliers, and bridging documents) and constructs multi-level contextual representations to guide LLM-based explanation generation. It supports both AI-guided overview and user-driven exploration, with explanations available at multiple levels of detail. We demonstrate CAPE on news and scholarly document layouts and evaluate it in a controlled user study against keyword-based and content-only LLM baselines. Our results suggest that spatially grounded explanations are perceived as more helpful than content-only baselines for interpreting the spatial organization of document layouts.

AI.tldr: CAPE is a framework that generates natural-language explanations for spatialized document layouts by combining document semantics with spatial context, identifying clusters, subgroups, outliers, and bridging documents, and was shown in a user study to be more helpful than content-only baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches to interpreting spatialized document layouts focus on summarizing document content or explaining layout generation algorithms, but fail to support understanding of spatial relationships (e.g., why documents are positioned near or far from each other) within the layout itself.
AI.method: CAPE identifies salient spatial patterns (clusters, subgroups, outliers, bridging documents) and constructs multi-level contextual representations that combine document semantics with layout-derived spatial context. These representations guide an LLM to generate explanations at multiple levels of detail, supporting both AI-guided overview and user-driven interactive exploration.
AI.result: In a controlled user study on news and scholarly document layouts, CAPE's spatially grounded explanations were perceived as significantly more helpful than keyword-based and content-only LLM baselines for interpreting spatial organization.
AI.conclusion: Spatially grounded natural-language explanations that integrate both document semantics and spatial context improve users' ability to interpret the spatial organization of document layouts compared to content-only approaches.

title: On the Inseparability of Instructions and Data in Shared-Embedding Sequence Models
summary:
Prompt injection is the top security risk for LLM-integrated applications, yet every defense proposed so far has been broken. We prove this is not a coincidence: in shared-embedding architectures that lack enforced control-data separation, perfect prompt-injection prevention is mathematically impossible. We formalize prompted systems as Prompted Action Models whose outputs include control-authoritative actions: refusal decisions, tool authorization, policy routing, and memory writes. We define Semantic-Faithful Control (SFC), the property that such behavior depends only on the meaning of untrusted input, not on how it is encoded. We then prove SFC is unachievable within the shared pipeline, via three results: a provenance-recovery impossibility (shared representations make trusted and untrusted content statistically inseparable, bounded by total variation distance); control-path exposure (untrusted tokens enter control-relevant computation through the same attention value-aggregation that determines outputs); and a finite-coverage invariance gap (finite training cannot certify invariance over infinite semantic-equivalence classes). We ground each quantity in measurements on production tokenizers and models.
  The result is structural, not a gap in current defenses. It mirrors the code-data confusion in Von Neumann machines that gives rise to buffer overflows, a vulnerability class that took decades of layered defenses (DEP, Write-XOR-Execute, ASLR, stack canaries, and ultimately memory-safe languages) to contain, because no single mechanism sufficed. The implication is the same: prompt injection cannot be eliminated by better in-pipeline classification or alignment alone. It requires architectural separation of instruction and data channels. We identify the root cause and the class of solution it demands.

AI.tldr: The paper proves that perfect prompt-injection prevention is mathematically impossible in shared-embedding LLM architectures lacking enforced control-data separation. Using a formal framework called Prompted Action Models, the authors define Semantic-Faithful Control (SFC) and prove its unattainability through three impossibility results. The structural flaw mirrors Von Neumann code-data confusion, implying architectural separation of instruction and data channels is required — not merely better in-pipeline defenses.
AI.motivation: Every proposed defense against prompt injection in LLM-integrated applications has been broken. The authors aim to demonstrate that this repeated failure is not coincidental but rather a structural inevitability arising from the shared-embedding architecture itself, analogous to buffer overflow vulnerabilities in Von Neumann machines.
AI.method: The paper formalizes prompted systems as Prompted Action Models where outputs include control-authoritative actions (refusal, tool authorization, policy routing, memory writes). It defines Semantic-Faithful Control (SFC) as the property that control behavior depends only on the meaning — not encoding — of untrusted input. Three impossibility proofs are provided: (1) provenance-recovery impossibility via total variation distance bounds; (2) control-path exposure through shared attention value-aggregation; and (3) a finite-coverage invariance gap showing finite training cannot certify invariance over infinite semantic-equivalence classes. Quantitative measurements ground these theoretical results.
AI.result: All three proof lines converge on the same conclusion: in shared-embedding architectures, trusted and untrusted content are statistically inseparable; untrusted tokens influence control-relevant computation through the same attention mechanisms that determine outputs; and finite training data cannot cover infinite semantic-equivalence classes. Measurements on production tokenizers and models confirm the practical relevance of these theoretical bounds.
AI.conclusion: Prompt injection cannot be eliminated by better in-pipeline classification or alignment alone. The vulnerability is structural, rooted in the shared representation of instructions and data — directly analogous to code-data confusion in Von Neumann architectures that enabled buffer overflows. The solution requires architectural separation of instruction and data channels, mirroring how memory-safe languages and hardware protections ultimately contained buffer overflow exploits.

title: Position: The Term "Machine Unlearning" Is Overused in LLMs
comment: 13 pages; ICML 2026 Position Paper Track. Sangyeon Yoon and Yeachan Jun contributed equally
summary: Large language models increasingly face demands to "forget" training data, knowledge, or behaviors due to regulatory deletion obligations, copyright/licensing disputes, and safety or product-policy requirements. This position paper argues that machine unlearning is overused as a term in LLM research and should be reserved for dataset-defined deletion: removing the training influence of a precisely specified forget set such that the resulting model is approximately indistinguishable from retraining without that data. We contend that many tasks currently labeled "unlearning" (e.g., refusal for harmful requests, entity/knowledge removal, or targeted suppression) pursue different, often policy-dependent objectives and therefore require different terminology and baselines (e.g., alignment, suppression, editing, obfuscation). We further argue that this confusion is not cosmetic: because papers make different implicit guarantees under the same label, metrics and benchmarks are frequently reused outside their intended scope, rewarding surface-level non-disclosure (e.g., low ROUGE/forget accuracy) even when retraining-equivalence is not tested and derived capabilities remain. We conclude by calling for stricter terminology tied to explicit guarantees and reference models, and for evaluations that match the claimed objective.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that "machine unlearning" is misused as a catch-all term in LLM research; it should be reserved strictly for dataset-defined deletion where the model approximates retraining without the forget set. Other tasks (refusal, knowledge removal, suppression) require distinct terminology and evaluation baselines to avoid cross-purpose metric misuse.
AI.motivation: LLMs face growing demands to delete data for regulatory, legal, and safety reasons, but the research community conflates fundamentally different objectives under the single label "unlearning," leading to mismatched metrics, invalid comparisons, and surface-level solutions that fail to achieve true retraining-equivalence.
AI.method: This is a position paper that presents a conceptual analysis and taxonomy. The authors distinguish dataset-defined deletion (true unlearning) from policy-driven tasks (alignment, suppression, editing, obfuscation), analyze how each carries different implicit guarantees, and critique how benchmarks like ROUGE/forget accuracy are inappropriately reused across these distinct tasks without testing for retraining-equivalence or residual capabilities.
AI.result: The analysis reveals that conflating distinct objectives under "unlearning" leads to systematic evaluation failures: metrics designed for one task reward superficial non-disclosure in another, and derived capabilities often persist even when surface metrics improve. This undermines the validity of claimed unlearning results.
AI.conclusion: The field needs stricter, guarantee-tied terminology: "unlearning" should be reserved for dataset-level deletion with retraining-equivalence guarantees, while other objectives (alignment, suppression, editing, obfuscation) should be named and evaluated according to their actual goals and baselines.

title: RANSAC Scoring Done Right
summary: The most widely used RANSAC variants score candidate models by counting inliers or summing per-point scores that saturate beyond a residual threshold. Every such score requires a user-supplied parameter that is a function of the inlier scale, which must itself be estimated from contaminated data. We remove this dependence by reversing the usual order of inference: rather than estimating the scale and then scoring against it, we marginalize the inlier scale analytically in closed form under a conjugate Inverse-Gamma prior for a fixed inlier partition, then optimize over partitions. A single closed-form expression spans the non-informative Jeffreys limit and informative empirical-Bayes priors, so the same score adapts across data-rich and data-scarce regimes without any change to the algorithm. The proposed RANSAC score is the first in which the inlier scale is genuinely absent from the formula. The score admits O(N log N ) computation via sort-and-sweep. On a benchmark of nearly 70 000 image pairs spanning different two-view estimation problems and both engineered and learned feature pipelines, the proposed score exceeds the state of the art (RANSAC, MSAC, GaU, MAGSAC): it stays nearly flat under threshold miscalibration where baselines degrade, reaches near-optimal accuracy from as few as two validation pairs where baselines need ont he order of 100 times more,. and tightens its prior regularization as validation data grows scarce.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel RANSAC scoring function that eliminates the need for an inlier-scale parameter by analytically marginalizing over the scale under a conjugate Inverse-Gamma prior, yielding a closed-form, scale-free score that adapts across data regimes, achieves O(N log N) computation, and outperforms state-of-the-art variants (RANSAC, MSAC, GaU, MAGSAC) on nearly 70,000 image pairs.
AI.motivation: All widely used RANSAC variants require a user-supplied inlier threshold (or score-saturation parameter) that depends on the unknown inlier scale, which must be estimated from contaminated data. This introduces fragility: threshold miscalibration degrades performance, and reliable scale estimation requires substantial validation data. The authors aim to eliminate this dependence entirely by reversing the inference order.
AI.method: The authors reverse the standard RANSAC inference pipeline: instead of estimating the inlier scale and then scoring models against it, they fix an inlier partition, place a conjugate Inverse-Gamma prior over the unknown scale, and analytically marginalize it in closed form. This yields a single expression spanning the non-informative Jeffreys prior and informative empirical-Bayes priors, adapting automatically to data-rich and data-scarce regimes. The resulting score requires only O(N log N) computation via sort-and-sweep and contains no explicit scale parameter.
AI.result: On a benchmark of ~70,000 image pairs across different two-view estimation problems with both engineered and learned features, the proposed score surpasses RANSAC, MSAC, GaU, and MAGSAC. It remains nearly flat under threshold miscalibration (where baselines degrade), reaches near-optimal accuracy with as few as 2 validation pairs (vs. ~100x more for baselines), and automatically tightens prior regularization when validation data is scarce.
AI.conclusion: The proposed scale-free RANSAC score is the first to genuinely eliminate the inlier-scale parameter from the scoring formula. By marginalizing rather than estimating the scale, it achieves robustness to miscalibration, sample-efficient adaptation, and state-of-the-art accuracy, making it broadly applicable without manual threshold tuning.

title: When Does Personality Composition Matter for Multi-Agent LLM Teams?
summary: Personality prompting shapes how large language models communicate, yet whether these behavioral shifts affect objective task outcomes remains under-explored. Prior work shows that agents prompted with low agreeableness produce adversarial language, while those prompted with high agreeableness become cooperative, but the relationship between communication style and task performance has not been systematically examined across multiple domains. In this work, we investigate whether personality composition matters for multi-agent team performance by manipulating personality traits across frontier LLMs on three task domains: structured coding, open-ended research collaboration, and competitive bargaining. We find that personality effects depend critically on task structure. In coding tasks, low agreeableness leads to large communication shifts that have little effect on milestone completion. In open-ended collaboration and bargaining, the same manipulation substantially degrades performance. We discuss implications for multi-agent system design and the limits of personality manipulation.

AI.tldr: Personality prompting in LLMs alters communication style but its impact on task performance is task-dependent: low agreeableness harms open-ended collaboration and bargaining but has negligible effect on structured coding tasks.
AI.motivation: Prior work establishes that personality prompting shifts LLM communication behavior, but whether these shifts translate to changes in objective task outcomes across domains remains unexplored. The authors aim to systematically examine the relationship between personality composition and multi-agent team performance.
AI.method: The authors manipulate personality traits (specifically agreeableness) across frontier LLMs deployed in multi-agent teams, testing performance on three distinct task domains: structured coding (well-defined milestones), open-ended research collaboration, and competitive bargaining.
AI.result: Low agreeableness prompts produce substantial communication shifts (more adversarial language) across all domains. However, task performance effects diverge: in structured coding, milestone completion is largely unaffected; in open-ended collaboration and bargaining, performance degrades substantially.
AI.conclusion: Personality composition matters for multi-agent systems, but its effects are mediated by task structure. Designers should account for domain characteristics when applying personality prompting, as behavioral shifts do not uniformly translate to performance changes.

title: Intuition-Guided Latent Reasoning for LLM-Based Recommendation
summary:
Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive reasoning capabilities in complex problem-solving tasks, motivating their use for preference reasoning in recommender systems. Latent reasoning, which operates in continuous hidden spaces rather than discrete tokens, has recently emerged as a promising paradigm for LLM-based recommendation. However, existing methods often start from unconstrained reasoning points, where hidden representations are misaligned with target item embeddings, leading to suboptimal reasoning trajectories.
  Inspired by cognitive neuroscience, which suggests that human multi-step reasoning is guided by intuition as a latent prior, we propose \emph{IntuRec}, a two-stage framework that anchors latent reasoning with \emph{recommendation intuition}. In the extraction stage, the LLM-based recommender generates a top-$K$ candidate set based on users' histories as the source of intuition. In the injection stage, the candidate set is transformed into a preference-aligned intuition embedding using self- and cross-attention mechanisms, which initializes the reasoning start point and guides subsequent latent reasoning. By providing a semantically grounded starting point, IntuRec efficiently explores the preference space along more accurate reasoning trajectories. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that IntuRec consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. We release our code at https://github.com/Ten-Mao/IntuRec.

AI.tldr: IntuRec is a two-stage framework that anchors LLM-based latent reasoning with a "recommendation intuition" — a top-K candidate set generated from user history — which is transformed into an embedding that initializes and guides the reasoning trajectory, outperforming state-of-the-art baselines on real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing latent reasoning methods for LLM-based recommendation start from unconstrained reasoning points, causing hidden representations to misalign with target item embeddings and leading to suboptimal reasoning trajectories. The authors draw inspiration from cognitive neuroscience, where human multi-step reasoning is guided by intuition as a latent prior.
AI.method: IntuRec operates in two stages: (1) Extraction — the LLM-based recommender generates a top-K candidate set from user interaction history, serving as the source of intuition; (2) Injection — this candidate set is converted into a preference-aligned intuition embedding via self- and cross-attention mechanisms, which initializes the reasoning starting point and guides subsequent latent reasoning in continuous hidden space.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that IntuRec consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines.
AI.conclusion: By anchoring latent reasoning with a semantically grounded intuition embedding, IntuRec enables more accurate exploration of the preference space along better-aligned reasoning trajectories, validating the effectiveness of recommendation intuition as a guiding prior for LLM-based recommender systems.

title: Speculative Refinement: A Hybrid Autoregressive Diffusion Decoding Strategy and Its Behavior Across Benchmarks
summary: How should we evaluate generation systems that combine autoregressive (AR) and diffusion decoding? We study this question through Speculative Refinement (SpecRef), a training-free hybrid method that warm-starts a masked diffusion language model from an AR draft using entropy-guided selective masking. Evaluating SpecRef across six benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, BBH, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag) with three distinct evaluation protocols (execution-based pass@1, exact-match, log-likelihood scoring), we surface several findings relevant beyond our specific system: (1) code benchmarks conflate structural discovery with logical correctness: providing a syntactic scaffold lifts accuracy from near zero to over 20% without changing the model, indicating that much of the baseline failure is structural; (2) a refinement tension phenomenon where multi-stage correction degrades already-correct tokens, exposing benchmark saturation ceilings invisible to single-model evaluation; (3) log-likelihood and generative evaluation produce different model rankings for the same model pair, suggesting they measure different capabilities; (4) standard Python post-processing silently breaks code evaluation for non-AR generators. These observations apply to any multi-stage or non-autoregressive generation pipeline and point toward more diagnostic evaluation practices.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how to evaluate hybrid AR-diffusion generation systems using SpecRef, a training-free method that warm-starts masked diffusion from AR drafts. Through extensive benchmarking, it surfaces four key findings: code benchmarks conflate structure with logic, refinement can degrade correct tokens, log-likelihood and generative evaluation rank models differently, and standard Python post-processing breaks non-AR evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluation practices were designed for autoregressive models. As hybrid AR-diffusion generation systems emerge, it is unclear whether standard evaluation protocols remain valid, comparable, or diagnostic. The authors aim to systematically surface evaluation pitfalls and methodological tensions that arise when multi-stage or non-autoregressive generation pipelines are assessed using conventional benchmarks and metrics.
AI.method: The authors propose Speculative Refinement (SpecRef): a training-free hybrid decoding method that uses an AR model to generate a draft, then applies entropy-guided selective masking to identify low-confidence tokens, and finally warm-starts a masked diffusion language model (MDLM) to refine only those masked positions. Evaluation spans six benchmarks (HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, BBH, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag) using three protocols: execution-based pass@1, exact-match, and log-likelihood scoring. They systematically compare AR-only, diffusion-only, and SpecRef configurations to isolate evaluation artifacts.
AI.result: Four major findings: (1) On code benchmarks, providing a syntactic scaffold (via AR draft) lifts accuracy from near 0% to over 20% without changing the diffusion model, revealing that structural errors dominate baseline failures. (2) A "refinement tension" effect: multi-stage correction degrades already-correct tokens, exposing benchmark saturation ceilings invisible in single-model evaluation. (3) Log-likelihood and generative evaluation produce contradictory model rankings, indicating they measure distinct capabilities. (4) Standard Python post-processing (e.g., stopping at newlines) silently breaks evaluation for non-AR generators that produce different output formats.
AI.conclusion: The findings argue that multi-stage and non-AR generation systems require more diagnostic evaluation practices. Code benchmarks should disentangle structural and logical correctness. Refinement tension implies saturation-aware metrics are needed. Log-likelihood is not a reliable proxy for generation quality in hybrid systems. Post-processing pipelines must be validated across generator types. These insights generalize beyond SpecRef to any pipeline combining AR and diffusion decoding.

title: Glite ARF: Verifier-Driven Research with Parallel LLM Coding Agents
comment: 13 pages, 6 figures, 7 tables. Open-source framework (Apache-2.0) and a public demo project at https://github.com/GliteTech/glite-arf and https://github.com/GliteTech/research-ace-cefr
summary: LLM coding agents make it tempting to automate empirical research by delegating experiments to them directly, but naive delegation does not scale to large projects: low-rate instruction lapses compound into broken, irreproducible artefacts. To address this problem, we present Glite ARF, an open-source Python framework for running many LLM coding agents in parallel on a research repository without sacrificing reproducibility or auditability. The framework defines a three-role stack: a human researcher chooses which hypotheses to test, coding agents (Claude Code, Codex CLI) implement individual tasks under a fixed structure, and deterministic Python verifier scripts enforce task isolation, immutability of completed work, a corrections overlay, and a materialised project overview. We call this verifier-driven research: the rules of the research process live in code that fails loudly when violated, not in prose that agents are merely asked to follow. Using Glite ARF, we developed our submission to the BEA 2026 vocabulary-difficulty shared task, placing first in the closed track and second in the open track on all three target languages (Spanish, German, Mandarin) and reducing the official baseline RMSE by 29.9% (closed) and 35.9% (open). The campaign comprised 273 tracked tasks (146 experiment runs) across 129 feature sets, run by up to twelve parallel agents orchestrated from a single laptop - with some model training on rented A100s - at approximately \$450 in LLM API spend (\$498 total third-party cost), and structured per-fold provenance let us catch and strip four target-leaking feature sets, correcting an implausible 0.609 RMSE to 0.802. Across three campaigns in three domains, the framework's structural machinery adds only about 1% of wall-clock time. Framework and a public demo project accompany this paper.

AI.tldr: Glite ARF is an open-source framework that enables parallel, verifier-driven LLM coding agents for empirical research. It uses a three-role architecture (human, coding agents, verifier scripts) to enforce reproducibility. Applied to the BEA 2026 shared task, it achieved first place (closed) and second place (open) with 29.9% and 35.9% RMSE reductions, operating 12 parallel agents for ~$450 in API costs.
AI.motivation: Naive delegation of empirical research to LLM coding agents fails at scale: compounding instruction lapses produce broken, irreproducible artifacts. There is a need for a structured framework that enables parallel agent execution while maintaining reproducibility and auditability.
AI.method: A three-role stack: (1) a human researcher selects hypotheses; (2) coding agents (Claude Code, Codex CLI) implement individual tasks under fixed structure; (3) deterministic Python verifier scripts enforce task isolation, immutability of completed work, a corrections overlay, and a materialized project overview. This "verifier-driven research" encodes process rules in code that fails loudly rather than prose instructions. The framework runs agents in parallel with structured per-fold provenance tracking.
AI.result: On the BEA 2026 vocabulary-difficulty shared task: first place in closed track, second in open track across Spanish, German, and Mandarin. Reduced official baseline RMSE by 29.9% (closed) and 35.9% (open). Campaign comprised 273 tracked tasks (146 experiment runs) across 129 feature sets, using up to 12 parallel agents from a single laptop. Total cost: ~$450 LLM API spend ($498 total). Provenance tracking caught 4 target-leaking feature sets, correcting RMSE from 0.609 to 0.802. Framework overhead adds only ~1% wall-clock time across three domain campaigns.
AI.conclusion: Verifier-driven research, where process rules are enforced by code rather than prose instructions, enables scalable, reproducible, and auditable LLM agent-based empirical research. Glite ARF demonstrates this approach can produce state-of-the-art results at modest cost with minimal overhead.

title: Typing Behavior in Human-LLM Interaction: Keystroke Dynamics Reveal Cognitive Effort During Prompting
summary: As Large Language Models (LLMs) become increasingly integrated into daily routines, understanding how users interact with these systems is crucial for effective human-AI collaboration. This work investigates keystroke dynamics as a behavioral measure of user mental effort and perceived output usefulness in human-LLM interaction. We conducted a user study (N = 36) to examine how task difficulty (easy vs. hard) and device type (desktop vs. mobile) influence typing behavior and workload (NASA-TLX) during interactions. Our results indicate that hard tasks led to significantly more keystrokes, slower typing, increased pauses, and higher self-reported workload. Device type had weaker effects, with mobile use slightly reducing input length and typing speed. While keystrokes captured differences in cognitive effort, they did not predict perceived LLM output usefulness. These findings highlight the potential of keystroke dynamics as real-time indicators of cognitive effort during LLM prompting, while also showing their limitations in capturing perceived collaboration success.

AI.tldr: A user study (N=36) shows keystroke dynamics (typing speed, pauses, keystroke count) reliably reflect cognitive effort during LLM interactions — harder tasks increase keystrokes and slow typing — but fail to predict perceived output usefulness, with device type (desktop vs. mobile) having only weak effects.
AI.motivation: As LLMs become integrated into daily life, there is a need for real-time, unobtrusive behavioral measures of user cognitive states during human-AI collaboration. Keystroke dynamics offer a potential passive indicator of mental effort and interaction quality without interrupting the user.
AI.method: A within-subjects user study with 36 participants crossing two factors: task difficulty (easy vs. hard) and device type (desktop vs. mobile). Keystroke dynamics (keystroke count, inter-key intervals, pause frequency, typing speed) were logged, and subjective measures (NASA-TLX for workload, perceived usefulness of LLM output) were collected via post-task questionnaires.
AI.result: Hard tasks significantly increased keystrokes, slowed typing speed, and increased pause frequency, alongside higher NASA-TLX scores. Device type showed weaker effects: mobile slightly reduced input length and typing speed. Critically, keystroke dynamics did not predict perceived LLM output usefulness.
AI.conclusion: Keystroke dynamics serve as promising real-time, non-intrusive indicators of cognitive effort during LLM prompting but are insufficient for capturing perceived collaboration success (output usefulness). Future adaptive systems could leverage typing behavior for cognitive load sensing but would need complementary signals to assess interaction quality.

title: AdvScan: Black-Box Adversarial Example Detection at Runtime through Power Analysis
comment: 15 pages, 10 figures. Published in IEEE Transactions on Information Forensics and Security
summary: TinyML models deployed on edge devices are increasingly adopted in safety/security-critical applications, making them a prime target for adversarial example (AE) attacks where inputs are modified to cause misclassifications. However, existing AE detection methods either require white-box model access, which is often unavailable in licensed black-box deployments, or rely on input pre-processing stages that add non-trivial latency and resource overhead, often exceeding what mission-critical applications can afford on their inference path. To address these challenges, we propose AdvScan, a runtime power analysis-based methodology for AE detection that operates in a black-box scenario while inducing minimal latency. AdvScan is based on the observation that AEs produce anomalous neuron activations, which in turn generate distinctive power-consumption signatures. The algorithm initially constructs a baseline distribution of power signatures from known benign inputs; then, at runtime, it applies a one-sample t-test to determine whether a test input's power signature significantly deviates from this baseline, thereby detecting AEs. We evaluated AdvScan using three adversarial example generation algorithms: Fast Gradient Sign Method (FGSM), Projected Gradient Descent (PGD), and Carlini-Wagner (C&W), on three MLPerf Tiny benchmark models implemented on two target devices: the STM32F303RC (ARM Cortex-M4) and STM32L562RE (ARM Cortex-M33) microcontrollers. Across 318,400 total test inputs, AdvScan detects 99.984% of AEs with only 40 false negatives and zero false positives. These results demonstrate the viability of power-based AE detection for secure, accuracy-critical TinyML deployments in black-box environments.

AI.tldr: AdvScan proposes a black-box adversarial example detection method for TinyML edge devices using runtime power analysis. By observing that adversarial inputs cause anomalous neuron activations with distinct power signatures, it applies a one-sample t-test against a benign baseline to detect attacks, achieving 99.984% detection with zero false positives across 318,400 test inputs on ARM Cortex-M4/M33 microcontrollers.
AI.motivation: TinyML models in safety/security-critical edge applications are vulnerable to adversarial example attacks, but existing detection methods either require white-box access (unavailable in black-box deployments) or impose prohibitive latency and resource overhead through input preprocessing. A lightweight, black-box, minimal-latency detection approach is needed for mission-critical TinyML inference paths.
AI.method: AdvScan constructs a baseline distribution of power-consumption signatures from benign inputs. At runtime, a one-sample t-test determines whether a test input's power signature statistically deviates from this baseline, leveraging the observation that adversarial examples trigger anomalous neuron activations producing distinctive power signatures. The method is evaluated using FGSM, PGD, and C&W attack algorithms on three MLPerf Tiny benchmarks across STM32F303RC (Cortex-M4) and STM32L562RE (Cortex-M33) microcontrollers.
AI.result: Across 318,400 total test inputs, AdvScan detected 99.984% of adversarial examples with only 40 false negatives and zero false positives, demonstrating robust detection performance on both target microcontroller platforms.
AI.conclusion: Power-analysis-based adversarial example detection is viable for secure, accuracy-critical TinyML deployments in black-box environments, offering a practical solution that requires no model access and introduces minimal inference-path latency.

title: A Survey of Automated Presentation Coaching: Systems, Methods, and Open Challenges
comment: accepted into the BEA 2026 workshop at ACL
summary: Automated coaching for oral presentations sits at the intersection of computer-assisted pronunciation training (CAPT), prosody modeling, and speech synthesis, yet no prior work has systematically surveyed and compared existing systems along these dimensions. This survey reviews and categorizes automated presentation coaching systems, spanning pronunciation tutors, fluency and prosody coaches, multimodal trainers, and conference Q&A practice tools. We introduce a five-dimensional task taxonomy - covering segmental pronunciation, lexical stress, suprasegmental prosody, pacing, and content faithfulness - and explicitly map surveyed systems onto it to reveal coverage gaps. We further review the core technical methods these systems employ: TTS-based exemplar generation and diagnostic methods for pronunciation, prosody, and fluency assessment. Key open challenges include the scarcity of annotated presentation corpora, achieving accent-fair feedback across diverse L1 backgrounds, and delivering low-latency diagnostics for real-time rehearsal.
