AI.tldr: This survey systematically reviews and categorizes automated oral presentation coaching systems along a novel five-dimensional taxonomy—segmental pronunciation, lexical stress, suprasegmental prosody, pacing, and content faithfulness—mapping existing tools onto it to identify coverage gaps and discussing core technical methods (TTS-based exemplar generation, diagnostic assessment), alongside open challenges like data scarcity, accent fairness, and real-time latency.
AI.motivation: No prior work has systematically surveyed and compared automated presentation coaching systems across the intersecting dimensions of CAPT, prosody modeling, and speech synthesis, leaving a gap in understanding system coverage and unmet technical needs.
AI.method: The authors conduct a literature survey and propose a five-dimensional task taxonomy (segmental pronunciation, lexical stress, suprasegmental prosody, pacing, content faithfulness). They categorize existing systems onto this taxonomy, then review the underlying technical methods (TTS-based exemplar generation and diagnostic techniques for pronunciation, prosody, and fluency assessment).
AI.result: The survey reveals coverage gaps in existing systems across the five taxonomy dimensions and identifies key open challenges: scarcity of annotated presentation corpora, difficulty of providing accent-fair feedback for diverse L1 speakers, and the need for low-latency diagnostics for real-time rehearsal scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Automated presentation coaching remains fragmented across CAPT, prosody, and synthesis domains; future work must address corpus annotation, accent fairness, and real-time performance to close the identified functional gaps and improve system robustness.

title: Unified Zero-Shot Time Series Forecasting: A Darts Foundation
summary: Since its initial release in 2020, Darts has become a widely used open-source Python library for time series analysis. A series of foundation models have recently claimed accuracy improvements in zero-shot forecasting, promising a paradigm shift from training custom models to harnessing pre-trained general-purpose forecasters. Foundation models, however, are often released as isolated packages with fragmented interfaces and limited interoperability with common tooling, making joint evaluation and integration within complete pipelines difficult. In Darts, we developed a unified $\texttt{FoundationModel}$ class collection (Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5, TiRex, PatchTST-FM) that provides standardized, full-cycle forecasting interfaces with minimal external dependencies for integrating foundation models into the ecosystem. Existing Darts pipelines can now use foundation models with only a name change; new pipelines can use them for zero-shot or fine-tuned forecasting, uncertainty estimation, and backtesting, combined with data processing and evaluation tooling, all within a unified framework.

AI.tldr: Darts has integrated a unified FoundationModel class for four pre-trained forecasting models (Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5, TiRex, PatchTST-FM), enabling zero-shot and fine-tuned forecasting with standardized interfaces, minimal dependencies, and full compatibility with existing Darts pipelines including uncertainty estimation, backtesting, and evaluation.
AI.motivation: Foundation models for time series forecasting are released as isolated packages with fragmented interfaces and limited interoperability, hindering joint evaluation and integration into complete analytical pipelines.
AI.method: The authors developed a unified `FoundationModel` class collection in Darts that wraps Chronos-2, TimesFM 2.5, TiRex, and PatchTST-FM under standardized, full-cycle forecasting interfaces with minimal external dependencies.
AI.result: Existing Darts pipelines can leverage foundation models via a simple name change; new pipelines benefit from zero-shot or fine-tuned forecasting, uncertainty estimation, backtesting, data processing, and evaluation — all within a unified framework.
AI.conclusion: A unified interface for heterogeneous foundation models addresses the fragmentation problem, facilitating broader adoption, reproducible benchmarking, and streamlined integration of pre-trained forecasters into production time series workflows.

title: Internalizing the Future: A Unified Agentic Training Paradigm for World Model Planning
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents have demonstrated strong capability in sequential decision-making, yet they remains fundamentally reactive in long-horizon tasks. Unlike humans who employ "what-if" reasoning to evaluate potential plans before commitment, standard agents lack an internal world model to simulate future outcomes. Therefore, we propose to internalize future-aware planning by training a single autoregressive model to verbalize both a prospective state rollout and a plan-conditioned success estimate-a textual analogue of the Q-value. Crucially, we identify a format-capability gap: simply fine-tuning agents on look-ahead traces during post-training leads to superficial mimicry of foresight without genuine predictive grounding. To bridge this gap, we introduce a three-stage training paradigm: (i) World Model Agentic Mid-Training (WM-AMT) to inject latent predictive capabilities into the policy; (ii) Format-Eliciting SFT (FE-SFT) to structure this injected capability; and (iii) Foresight-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (FC-RL) to refine the calibration and utility of the generated simulations. Evaluated on search and mathematical reasoning tasks, our approach consistently outperforms other training baselines. Our results demonstrate that effective internal world modeling in LLM agents requires a capability-first training pipeline to achieve grounded and calibrated foresight.

AI.tldr: Standard LLM agents lack internal world models for "what-if" planning. The authors propose training a single model to verbalize state rollouts and success estimates (textual Q-values). They identify a "format-capability gap" where naive fine-tuning yields superficial foresight, and address it with a three-stage pipeline: World Model Agentic Mid-Training (WM-AMT), Format-Eliciting SFT (FE-SFT), and Foresight-Conditioned RL (FC-RL). The approach outperforms baselines on search and math reasoning tasks.
AI.motivation: LLM agents excel at sequential decision-making but remain reactive — they lack the human capacity for "what-if" reasoning to simulate and evaluate future plans before acting. Standard post-training on look-ahead traces yields only superficial mimicry of foresight rather than genuine predictive grounding, a phenomenon the authors term the "format-capability gap."
AI.method: The paper proposes training a single autoregressive model to generate both a prospective state rollout and a plan-conditioned success estimate (a textual analogue of Q-values). The core contribution is a three-stage training paradigm: (i) **WM-AMT**: World Model Agentic Mid-Training that first injects latent predictive capabilities into the policy model; (ii) **FE-SFT**: Format-Eliciting Supervised Fine-Tuning that structures the injected capability into proper verbalized foresight formats; (iii) **FC-RL**: Foresight-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning that refines the calibration and downstream utility of generated simulations via reward signals.
AI.result: Evaluated on search and mathematical reasoning tasks, the proposed approach consistently outperforms alternative training baselines, demonstrating that grounded and calibrated foresight requires the capability-first training pipeline rather than naive fine-tuning on look-ahead traces.
AI.conclusion: Effective internal world modeling in LLM agents cannot be achieved through superficial training on foresight formats alone. A capability-first pipeline — injecting predictive capacity before structuring and refining it — is essential for achieving grounded, calibrated, and practically useful future-aware planning.

title: Bifocal Diffusion Language Models: Asymmetric Bidirectional Context for Parallel Generation
summary: Discrete diffusion language models (dLLMs) recover masked tokens in parallel, offering significant speedups over autoregressive (AR) generation. However, such promising frameworks face a fundamental architectural design dilemma: \ding{182} Adopting bidirectional attention achieves strong generation quality by allowing each position to access the full context, but is inherently incompatible with KV caching, limiting inference throughput in batch-serving scenarios; \ding{183} Conversely, causal attention enables efficient cached inference but loses all right-side context, substantially degrading generation quality. This paper introduces Bifocal dLLMs, a new paradigm that resolves this dilemma through \emph{asymmetric bidirectional context}. Analogous to bifocal lenses, we instantiate the paradigm as \textbf{R2LM} (Right-to-Left Mamba), which combines two complementary mechanisms: $a$) standard causal attention providing precise left-context with full KV cache compatibility, while $b$) a lightweight reverse Mamba SSM sidecar supplying compressed right-side context without breaking cacheability. Comprehensive experiments on continued pretraining of Qwen3-1.7B with 60B tokens demonstrate that R2LM achieves $2.4\times$ to $12.9\times$ higher throughput than bidirectional dLLMs and $1.9\times$ to $2.9\times$ speedup over AR baselines in batch serving through parallel decoding with KV caching, while exceeding the causal baseline on most benchmarks and surpassing the bidirectional dLLM on average.

AI.tldr: Bifocal dLLMs (R2LM) combine causal attention with a lightweight reverse Mamba SSM sidecar to provide asymmetric bidirectional context, achieving both high-quality generation and KV-cache-compatible parallel decoding, yielding 2.4–12.9× throughput gains over bidirectional dLLMs and 1.9–2.9× over AR baselines.
AI.motivation: Discrete diffusion language models face a fundamental architectural dilemma: bidirectional attention yields strong generation quality but breaks KV caching (harming throughput), while causal attention enables efficient cached inference but loses right-side context (degrading quality). No existing architecture simultaneously delivers both.
AI.method: The authors propose Bifocal dLLMs, instantiated as R2LM (Right-to-Left Mamba), which pairs: (a) standard causal attention for precise left-side context with full KV cache compatibility, and (b) a lightweight reverse Mamba SSM sidecar that provides a compressed representation of right-side context without breaking cacheability. This asymmetric bidirectional context is analogous to bifocal lenses.
AI.result: On continued pretraining of Qwen3-1.7B with 60B tokens, R2LM achieves 2.4× to 12.9× higher throughput than bidirectional dLLMs and 1.9× to 2.9× speedup over autoregressive baselines in batch serving via parallel decoding with KV caching. It exceeds the causal baseline on most benchmarks and surpasses the bidirectional dLLM on average.
AI.conclusion: The Bifocal dLLM paradigm successfully resolves the quality–efficiency dilemma in discrete diffusion language models, enabling both strong generation quality and high-throughput cached inference through asymmetric bidirectional context.

title: Contextual Associations Between Webpage Elements for Web Accessibility: An Empirical Study
comment: 11 pages, 2 Figures, 1 Table, submitted to ESEIW 2026 ESEM - Registered Reports Track
summary: [Context] Screen reader users navigating webpages by element list often encounter accessible names such as "Read more" that are valid under the W3C Accessible Name and Description Computation specification but uninterpretable in isolation. The surrounding elements that would make these names meaningful exist in the page but are not linked to the target by any mechanism. No prior work has empirically studied how to select which surrounding elements are contextually relevant to a given target. [Objective] This registered report investigates whether human-perceived contextual associations between webpage elements can be recovered from the accessibility tree using link prediction, and whether the learned associations generalize across websites. [Method] We will construct a dataset of human-annotated contextual associations on 35 websites, stratified across the Tranco top-million list, with three independent annotators per page. Each page is represented as a graph derived from its accessibility tree, augmented with spatial and semantic features from the DOM and CSS. We compare four machine learning models (MLP, GCN, GAT, and SEAL) against two heuristic baselines under leave-one-site-out cross-validation with a pre-registered statistical framework, using Hit@K and MRR. [Results] We have conducted a five-site author-annotated pilot study to establish the pipelines and parameterize the power simulation, with pilot Hit@10 ranging from 0.16 to 0.85 across four learned models and 0.08 to 0.30 across two heuristic baselines. The final results will be reported after the planned experiments and analyses are completed. [Conclusion] The study contributes a human-annotated dataset of contextual associations on webpages, an empirical evaluation of link prediction for context selection on accessibility-tree graphs, and a cross-site generalization analysis.

AI.tldr: This registered report proposes using link prediction on accessibility-tree graphs to recover human-perceived contextual associations between webpage elements, aiming to resolve uninterpretable accessible names (e.g., "Read more") encountered by screen reader users. A human-annotated dataset across 35 websites will be used to evaluate four ML models against heuristic baselines under cross-site validation.
AI.motivation: Screen reader users navigating by element lists often encounter accessible names like "Read more" that are technically valid per W3C specifications but semantically meaningless in isolation. Surrounding webpage elements that provide disambiguating context are not linked to the target by any existing mechanism. No prior work has empirically studied how to identify contextually relevant surrounding elements for a given target.
AI.method: The study constructs a human-annotated dataset of contextual associations across 35 websites (stratified from the Tranco top-million list), with three annotators per page. Each webpage is represented as a graph from its accessibility tree, augmented with spatial and semantic features from the DOM and CSS. Four machine learning models (MLP, GCN, GAT, and SEAL) are compared against two heuristic baselines under leave-one-site-out cross-validation, using Hit@K and MRR metrics within a pre-registered statistical framework. A five-site pilot study established pipelines and parameterized the power simulation.
AI.result: Pilot study results (five sites, author-annotated) show Hit@10 ranging from 0.16–0.85 across the four learned models and 0.08–0.30 across the two heuristic baselines. Final results are pending planned experiments.
AI.conclusion: The study contributes a novel human-annotated dataset of contextual associations on webpages, an empirical evaluation of link prediction for accessibility context selection, and a cross-site generalization analysis, advancing accessible web navigation for screen reader users.

title: QueenBee Planner: Skill-Evolving Communication Topologies for Token-Efficient LLM Multi-Agent Systems
summary: Large language model (LLM) multi-agent systems increasingly depend not only on how individual agents reason, but also on how agents are connected. This paper introduces QueenBee Planner, a framework that treats inter-agent communication topology as a retrievable and self-improving design skill. A pool of worker agents, the task adapter, and the scoring function are frozen; only an outer LLM planner learns to generate temporal communication DAGs specifying who sends information to whom, in which round, who merges messages, and who emits the final answer. Execution traces are distilled into evidence-backed design rules with three actions: \emph{Preserve}, \emph{Modify}, and \emph{Avoid}. To prevent self-evolution from turning lucky runs or plausible but false explanations into policy, QueenBee uses held-out acceptance gates, variance-aware credit, motif-level attribution, transfer trust, insight falsification, and structural deduplication. We evaluate the method on Count-Frequency aggregation and Silo-Bench-style distributed coordination tasks. With fixed workers, self-evolved graph generation produces communication structures that improve over fixed topologies and cold generation. In the CF fulltest setting, the best generated graph reduces RMSE from 12.53 for the strongest fixed topology to 7.87 while also reducing messages, model calls, and token cost; Silo-style results show the same direction of improvement over cold and fixed-topology baselines. These results suggest that multi-agent systems can learn reusable architectural design knowledge rather than merely memorizing task answers.

AI.tldr: QueenBee Planner is a framework that treats inter-agent communication topology as a retrievable and self-improving design skill. An outer LLM planner learns to generate temporal DAGs specifying agent communication, distills execution traces into design rules (Preserve, Modify, Avoid), and uses multiple safeguards to prevent overfitting to spurious patterns. Evaluated on aggregation and coordination tasks, self-evolved graphs outperform fixed topologies and cold generation while reducing costs.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems depend critically on communication topology, yet designing optimal topologies is non-trivial and typically hand-crafted. The authors aim to automate this by treating topology design as a learnable, transferable skill that improves over time through evidence-backed self-evolution.
AI.method: QueenBee uses an outer LLM planner that generates temporal communication DAGs (who talks to whom, when, who merges, who outputs). Worker agents, task adapters, and scoring functions are frozen. Execution traces are distilled into design rules via three actions: Preserve, Modify, Avoid. Self-evolution is governed by held-out acceptance gates, variance-aware credit assignment, motif-level attribution, transfer trust, insight falsification, and structural deduplication to ensure robust policy learning.
AI.result: On Count-Frequency aggregation (CF fulltest), the best self-evolved graph reduced RMSE from 12.53 (strongest fixed topology) to 7.87, while also reducing messages, model calls, and token cost. Silo-Bench-style coordination tasks showed consistent improvements over both cold generation and fixed-topology baselines.
AI.conclusion: Multi-agent LLM systems can learn reusable architectural design knowledge—specifically communication topologies—rather than merely memorizing task-specific answers, enabling more efficient and effective agent coordination.

title: Functional outcomes and naturalistic engagement with a purpose-built conversational AI for mental health (Ash)
summary:
Background: Conversational AI chatbots designed for mental health may offer an accessible, scalable avenue for supporting psychological well-being, yet prior evaluations have largely focused on clinical symptom reduction rather than broader indicators of day-to-day functioning, and have rarely monitored for potential harms such as inflated self-perception.
  Objective: We examined within-person change in psychological functioning indicators among real-world users of Ash, a purpose-built conversational AI for mental health support, over the first four weeks of use, and whether these changes were associated with engagement metrics.
  Methods: In this single-arm observational cohort study, new users (n = 1,284) completed in-app single-item measures of psychological functioning (life satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, sleep quality, behavioral activation), working alliance, and grandiosity (inflated self-perception), at baseline and Week 4. Paired-sample t-tests examined within-person change; ANCOVAs tested engagement-outcome associations at Week 4, controlling for baseline.
  Results: At baseline, participants reported below-average life satisfaction and fair sleep quality. Significant within-person improvements emerged across all functioning indicators and working alliance (ps < .001; d = 0.14-0.26), with no change in grandiosity. Active days, total sessions, and total minutes consistently predicted Week 4 psychological functioning and working alliance (ps <= .006; partial R^2 range: 0.58-2.15%; controlling for baseline), whereas user message volume did not.
  Conclusion: Findings provide preliminary data for the potential of evidence-based conversational AI to extend mental health support for broad psychological functioning, extending the existing literature beyond symptom-based outcomes.

AI.tldr: A 4-week observational study of 1,284 users of a mental health chatbot (Ash) found significant small-to-moderate improvements in life satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, sleep quality, behavioral activation, and working alliance, with no increase in grandiosity. Engagement metrics (active days, sessions, minutes) modestly predicted outcomes.
AI.motivation: Prior evaluations of mental health chatbots have focused narrowly on clinical symptom reduction rather than broader psychological functioning indicators, and have rarely monitored for potential adverse effects such as inflated self-perception (grandiosity). The authors aimed to fill this gap by examining real-world, within-person changes in day-to-day functioning.
AI.method: Single-arm observational cohort study. New users (n=1,284) of the Ash chatbot completed in-app single-item measures at baseline and Week 4, covering life satisfaction, relationship satisfaction, sleep quality, behavioral activation, working alliance, and grandiosity. Within-person change was assessed via paired-sample t-tests; engagement-outcome associations were tested with ANCOVAs controlling for baseline scores.
AI.result: All functioning indicators and working alliance showed significant within-person improvements (p<.001; Cohen's d=0.14–0.26). Grandiosity showed no significant change. Active days, total sessions, and total minutes significantly predicted Week 4 outcomes (p≤.006; partial R²=0.58–2.15%), while user message volume did not.
AI.conclusion: Evidence-based conversational AI shows preliminary potential for supporting broad psychological functioning beyond symptom reduction, without evidence of inflated self-perception as a harm. Engagement frequency and duration, rather than verbosity, appear to drive benefits.

title: Reliable Homomorphic Matching for Fuzzy Labeled PSI at Scale
summary: Fuzzy Labeled Private Set Intersection (FLPSI) lets a receiver learn the labels of enrolled records similar to its query, and nothing else. Constructions based on a set-threshold reduction reach practical performance: a query matches a record when the two agree on a threshold number of components, and the private matching is delegated to an inner set-threshold kernel. We study its homomorphic form, which combines leveled-BFV homomorphic encryption (HE), a garbled circuit, and secret sharing to decide the match under encryption and release the record's label. We identify a composition gap in this kernel: efficiency is bought with a per-trial false-accept probability, but one query runs a trial for every record, so the error compounds with the database size into the kernel's realization soundness error (RSE), the rate at which it accepts a query the plaintext matcher would reject. The RSE is a reliability property of the cryptographic matching layer, not the matcher's accuracy, and a sound kernel must contribute zero or negligible RSE of its own. We formalize this as a composable security property, give a closed-form bound on the receiver's advantage, and close the gap with CSTPSI, a kernel that runs independent token rounds and raises the per-trial bound to a matching power. We prove CSTPSI secure in the semi-honest model. The bound sets the round count: two token rounds suffice for million-scale databases and three for billion-scale at the $10^{-6}$ engineering threshold. Our evaluation confirms this: at a million records the baseline kernel's RSE reaches 100% while CSTPSI holds it at 0 in every measured configuration. For large labels at small to moderate scale CSTPSI is more than 20x faster than the baseline, with up to 93% less communication, converging to the baseline only at million-scale. Our implementation, with a one-command reproducibility harness, is publicly available.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a critical flaw in homomorphic Fuzzy Labeled Private Set Intersection (FLPSI) where per-trial false-accept errors compound across database records, yielding a realization soundness error (RSE) that grows with database size. The authors formalize RSE as a composable security property, provide a closed-form bound on the receiver's advantage, and propose CSTPSI — a kernel using independent token rounds that raises the per-trial bound to a matching power, effectively eliminating RSE. Experiments show CSTPSI holds RSE at zero while the baseline reaches 100% at million-scale.
AI.motivation: Existing FLPSI constructions using set-threshold reduction with homomorphic encryption suffer from a composition gap: the per-trial false-accept probability, accepted as negligible in single-trial analysis, compounds across all database records during a query. This produces a realization soundness error (RSE) where the cryptographic matching layer accepts queries that the plaintext matcher would reject, undermining the protocol's reliability at scale.
AI.method: The authors formalize RSE as a composable security property in the semi-honest model and derive a closed-form bound on the receiver's advantage. They propose CSTPSI, a kernel that runs independent token rounds per record and raises the per-trial false-accept bound to a matching power, making the compounded error negligible. The construction combines leveled-BFV homomorphic encryption, garbled circuits, and secret sharing. The round count is set analytically: two rounds for million-scale databases, three for billion-scale at a 10⁻⁶ engineering threshold.
AI.result: At one million records, the baseline kernel's RSE reaches 100% while CSTPSI maintains it at 0 in all measured configurations. For large labels at small to moderate scale, CSTPSI is over 20× faster than the baseline with up to 93% less communication, converging to baseline performance only at million-scale. The analytical bound confirms two token rounds suffice for million-scale and three for billion-scale databases.
AI.conclusion: CSTPSI closes the composition gap in homomorphic FLPSI by providing a sound kernel with negligible RSE, proven secure in the semi-honest model. The work demonstrates that careful cryptographic design accounting for database-scale error compounding is essential for practical, reliable private set intersection with fuzzy matching. An open-source implementation with reproducibility harness is provided.

title: Causal Connections: Leveraging Multilingual Fine-Tuning for Financial QA@FinCausal 2026
summary: This paper describes team HSA_CORAL's submission to the FinCausal 2026 shared task on extracting cause-effect relations from financial narratives via extractive question answering in English and Spanish. We compare three modeling families: (i) encoder-only token tagging with multilingual BERT, (ii) encoder-decoder generation with multilingual BART, and (iii) decoder-only LLMs (Llama 3.1 and GPT variants) using prompt refinement, few-shot demonstrations, and supervised fine-tuning. Across settings, prompting and few-shot examples yield competitive performance, while supervised fine-tuning provides the largest gains. Our best system, GPT-4.1 Mini fine-tuned on combined English and Spanish training data, achieves a tied highest score on the English subtask (score 4.8140) and ranks third on Spanish (score 4.7753) under the shared task's LLM-as-a-judge metric. Overall, the results highlight the value of task-specific adaptation and multilingual fine-tuning for cross-lingual transfer in financial causality QA.

AI.tldr: Team HSA_CORAL's submission to FinCausal 2026 compares encoder-only, encoder-decoder, and decoder-only LLM approaches for extracting cause-effect relations from financial texts. Their best system—a fine-tuned GPT-4.1 Mini trained on combined English and Spanish data—tied for first on English and ranked third on Spanish, demonstrating the effectiveness of multilingual fine-tuning for financial causality QA.
AI.motivation: Financial narrative understanding requires accurate extraction of cause-effect relationships, yet cross-lingual transfer in this domain remains challenging. The shared task setting (English and Spanish) provides a testbed for evaluating whether modern LLMs, particularly through fine-tuning and multilingual training, can bridge the performance gap across languages in specialized financial causality extraction.
AI.method: The authors compare three model families for extractive QA on cause-effect relations: (1) encoder-only token tagging with multilingual BERT, (2) encoder-decoder generation with multilingual BART, and (3) decoder-only LLMs (Llama 3.1 and GPT variants). For LLMs, they explore prompt refinement, few-shot demonstrations, and supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Their best configuration fine-tunes GPT-4.1 Mini on combined English and Spanish training data. Evaluation uses the shared task's LLM-as-a-judge metric.
AI.result: Prompting and few-shot demonstrations yield competitive baseline results, but supervised fine-tuning produces the largest performance gains. The best system—GPT-4.1 Mini fine-tuned on combined bilingual data—achieves a tied highest score of 4.8140 on the English subtask and ranks third on the Spanish subtask (score 4.7753).
AI.conclusion: Task-specific supervised fine-tuning substantially outperforms prompting-based approaches for financial causality QA. Multilingual fine-tuning on combined English and Spanish data enables effective cross-lingual transfer, suggesting that shared representations across languages benefit domain-specific causal extraction tasks.

title: PairSAE: Mechanistic Interpretability from Pair Representations in Protein Co-Folding
comment: Accepted at the Machine Learning in Structural Biology (MLSB) 2025 workshop
summary:
Foundation models for structural biology have achieved remarkable performance in predicting biomolecular structure and show promise for the design of proteins and small molecules. Yet understanding which internal features drive their outputs remains challenging. Standard sparse autoencoders (SAEs), effective on transformer-style sequence embeddings, do not transfer cleanly to pairformer-like architectures: naively operating on pairwise representations yields a quadratic blow-up of features and obscures concepts distributed jointly across sequence and pair representations.
  We introduce PairSAE, which summarizes pairwise tensors via an N-mode SVD into token-wise interaction roles, then uses a sparse autoencoder to learn a shared set of token-level features that decode into both sequence and pair representations. Evaluated on Boltz-2 activations for PLINDER protein-ligand complexes, PairSAE yields interpretable features that align with UniProt annotations and predict Boltz-2 affinity values. These results indicate that PairSAE links the latent space of foundation models for structural biology to interpretable structural concepts, clarifying what the model "knows" while avoiding pairformer-induced pitfalls that limit conventional SAEs.

AI.tldr: PairSAE introduces an N-mode SVD to compress pairwise representations into token-wise interaction roles, then applies sparse autoencoders to learn interpretable features bridging sequence and pair representations in structural biology foundation models, avoiding the quadratic blow-up that naïve SAEs suffer on pairformer architectures.
AI.motivation: Standard sparse autoencoders (SAEs) work well on transformer sequence embeddings but fail on pairformer-like architectures because applying them directly to pairwise representations causes a quadratic explosion of features and fails to capture concepts distributed jointly across both sequence and pair representations. There is a need for interpretability tools tailored to structural biology models like Boltz-2.
AI.method: PairSAE decomposes the pairwise tensor using an N-mode SVD into token-wise interaction roles (compressing the quadratic structure into a linear, per-token form), then trains a sparse autoencoder to learn a shared set of token-level latent features that decode into both sequence and pair representations simultaneously.
AI.result: Evaluated on Boltz-2 activations for PLINDER protein-ligand complexes, PairSAE yields interpretable features that align with UniProt annotations and can predict Boltz-2 affinity values.
AI.conclusion: PairSAE successfully links the latent space of structural biology foundation models to interpretable structural concepts, clarifying model knowledge while avoiding the pairformer-induced pitfalls that limit conventional SAEs.

title: Odyssey: Constructing Verifiable Local Truth-Preserving Foundation Models
summary: We introduce a categorical framework called ODYSSEY for constructing verifiable, local truth-preserving foundation models as compositions of foundries: building-block architectural components that specify a cover of local contexts, local representation families, restriction maps, gluing rules, obstruction policies, update obligations, and human-facing views. A foundry is an organized sheaf of knowledge that carries within it an argumentation component. Concrete foundries are built from generic foundries such as evidence/argument, operational decision, institutional/financial, market meaning, scientific challenge, research-program, assistant-build, and evaluation-harness foundries. Universal Foundry Learning (UFL) formalizes foundry construction as a composition of left and right Kan extensions, with left Kan extension rolling local artifacts into candidate foundries and right Kan extension enforcing the restriction, gluing, obstruction, and argumentation conditions required for promotion. Foundry SQL (FSQL) is a small typed query surface for slicing maintained foundry artifacts that uses TICKET (Topos Integration using Causal Kan Extension Transformers) certification for admitting external or pre-built models into durable ODYSSEY state. ODYSSEY is fully implemented and tested across a wide spectrum of concrete foundries, showing that the same categorical machinery supports domain construction, artifact replay, sheaf diagnostics, grounded Toulmin/local-LLM scrutiny, residual-obstruction ledgers, and optimized TICKET-compatible causal-claim extraction across heterogeneous sources. This paper is to be presented as a 2.5 hour tutorial at ICML 2026. The tutorial home page is at https://bit.ly/4ajS0nA.

AI.tldr: ODYSSEY is a categorical framework for building verifiable, truth-preserving AI foundation models by composing modular "foundries" — sheaf-like components that encode local knowledge, argumentation, and consistency rules — using Kan extensions and a typed query language (FSQL) with TICKET certification for model integration.
AI.motivation: Current foundation models lack verifiable local truth preservation, compositional structure, and transparent argumentation. The authors aim to provide a principled categorical framework that ensures consistency, traceability, and certifiable reasoning across heterogeneous knowledge sources.
AI.method: The framework uses sheaf-theoretic foundries as building blocks, each specifying local contexts, representation families, restriction maps, gluing rules, obstruction policies, update obligations, and human-facing views. Universal Foundry Learning (UFL) formalizes construction via left Kan extensions (rolling up local artifacts) and right Kan extensions (enforcing structural conditions). Foundry SQL (FSQL) provides a typed query interface, and TICKET (Topos Integration using Causal Kan Extension Transformers) certifies external models for integration.
AI.result: The system is fully implemented and tested across diverse foundry types (evidence/argument, operational decision, market meaning, scientific challenge, etc.), demonstrating support for domain construction, artifact replay, sheaf diagnostics, Toulmin-style LLM scrutiny, residual-obstruction ledgers, and causal-claim extraction from heterogeneous sources.
AI.conclusion: ODYSSEY demonstrates that a unified categorical sheaf-theoretic machinery can underpin verifiable, composable foundation model construction across diverse domains, with the work to be presented as a tutorial at ICML 2026.

title: End-to-End Dynamic Sparsity for Resource-Adaptive LLM Inference
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) inference is typically deployed under a static resource assumption, where models execute a fixed computational graph regardless of the runtime environment. However, real-world cloud infrastructure is inherently dynamic, characterized by fluctuating availability (e.g., spot instance preemption) and tiered Quality-of-Service requirements. In such volatile settings, static models are inflexible: they either crash under resource constraints or waste compute on redundant operations. To bridge this gap, we propose Learning to Allocate (L2A), an end-to-end framework for resource-adaptive inference. Unlike prior methods that condition only on input difficulty, we formulate inference as a constrained allocation problem conditioned on both the input and the runtime resource budget itself. We introduce lightweight, budget-conditioned and input-aware gating networks integrated into the LLM. These gates are trained via a unified objective that jointly optimizes task performance, logical consistency, and resource costs along three axes matching how real-world dynamics manifest: layer skipping for memory and depth pressure, head pruning for throughput contention, and reasoning-token reduction for latency tightening. This lets the model learn a budget-aware policy beyond input difficulty alone: it adaptively configures its computational footprint with respect to real-time resource dynamics, maximizing reasoning depth when resources permit while enforcing strict frugality when budgets tighten. A single L2A model traces the entire compute-accuracy Pareto frontier on Llama-3-8B and Qwen-3-4B: at up to 34% realized layer sparsity, it stays within 0.6% of the dense baseline on GSM8K, with the same gap holding zero-shot on out-of-distribution tasks, while every static or heuristic baseline requires a separately tuned model and still drops by 5-10% at comparable inference time.

AI.tldr: L2A is a resource-adaptive LLM inference framework that trains lightweight gating networks conditioned on both input difficulty and runtime resource budgets, enabling a single model to trace the full compute-accuracy Pareto frontier across layer skipping, head pruning, and reasoning-token reduction.
AI.motivation: Static LLM inference assumes fixed computational graphs, but real-world cloud infrastructure is dynamic with fluctuating resource availability (e.g., spot instance preemption) and tiered QoS. Static models are inflexible—they crash under constraints or waste compute on redundant operations. Existing adaptive methods condition only on input difficulty, ignoring runtime resource budgets.
AI.method: L2A formulates inference as a constrained allocation problem conditioned on both input and runtime resource budget. It integrates lightweight, budget-conditioned and input-aware gating networks into the LLM, trained via a unified objective that jointly optimizes task performance, logical consistency, and resource costs across three axes: (1) layer skipping for memory/depth pressure, (2) head pruning for throughput contention, and (3) reasoning-token reduction for latency tightening. This enables a single model to learn a budget-aware policy that adapts its computational footprint to real-time resource dynamics.
AI.result: A single L2A model on Llama-3-8B and Qwen-3-4B traces the entire compute-accuracy Pareto frontier. At up to 34% realized layer sparsity, it stays within 0.6% of the dense baseline on GSM8K, with the same gap holding zero-shot on out-of-distribution tasks. In contrast, every static or heuristic baseline requires a separately tuned model and drops by 5–10% at comparable inference time.
AI.conclusion: L2A demonstrates that a single, jointly trained model can dynamically reconfigure its computational graph along multiple axes in response to real-time resource budgets, achieving near-dense accuracy under significant sparsity while generalizing zero-shot to OOD tasks—something no static or heuristic baseline can match without separate per-budget tuning.

title: Test Case Selection for Deep Neural Networks: A Replication Study on LLMs for Code
comment: Accepted at ISSTA 2026, the 35th ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis
summary: Recently, test case selection (TCS) techniques have been explored to support the operational evaluation of deep neural networks (DNNs) under limited testing budgets, where labeling cost is a primary concern and uncovering model failures early is a key objective. Although prior studies report promising results, existing empirical evaluations focus almost exclusively on vision-based DNNs and datasets, leaving it unclear whether prior findings generalize to LLM code models. This paper presents a large-scale replication study of TCS techniques in the context of LLM code models. We re-examine established TCS strategies originally proposed for DNNs and complement them with statistical sampling strategies not previously evaluated for TCS. We assess their effectiveness on three code-related classification tasks: clone detection, vulnerability detection, and technical debt prediction. The study spans 17 task-specific fine-tuned model instances, 7 predictive features, and 13 selection strategies, including 12 feature-aware strategies and simple random sampling (SRS) as a feature-agnostic baseline. We evaluate performance along two dimensions: accuracy estimation and early failure discovery. The results indicate that only a subset of findings reported for vision-based DNNs generalize when TCS is applied to LLMs for code. In particular, uncertainty-based features are effective for early failure discovery, while representation-based features are more robust for accuracy estimation. At the same time, performance varies substantially across tasks and models, indicating that TCS effectiveness is context-dependent. Overall, this study provides empirical evidence on the replicability of TCS techniques beyond vision-based deep learning and offers insights into their use for the operational evaluation of LLMs for code.

AI.tldr: A large-scale replication study evaluating test case selection (TCS) techniques for LLM code models across three tasks (clone detection, vulnerability detection, technical debt prediction), finding that prior vision-based DNN findings only partially generalize — uncertainty-based features aid early failure discovery, while representation-based features better support accuracy estimation, with substantial context-dependent variability.
AI.motivation: Existing TCS research focuses almost exclusively on vision-based DNNs, leaving unclear whether findings generalize to the increasingly important domain of LLMs for code, where labeling costs are high and early failure discovery is critical for operational evaluation.
AI.method: The authors conduct a replication study across 17 fine-tuned model instances on three code classification tasks (clone detection, vulnerability detection, technical debt prediction). They evaluate 13 selection strategies (12 feature-aware + random sampling baseline) using 7 predictive features, measuring performance via accuracy estimation and early failure discovery metrics.
AI.result: Only a subset of prior vision-based DNN findings generalize. Uncertainty-based features prove effective for early failure discovery, while representation-based features are more robust for accuracy estimation. Performance varies substantially across tasks and models, indicating that TCS effectiveness is highly context-dependent.
AI.conclusion: TCS techniques for DNNs do not uniformly transfer to LLMs for code; practitioners should select strategies based on the specific evaluation goal (accuracy estimation vs. failure discovery) and account for task/model-specific variability. The study provides empirical evidence on cross-domain replicability of TCS.

title: GenWorld: Empirically Grounded Urban Simulation Infrastructure for Scalable LLM-Agent Studies
comment: 27 pages, 24 figures. Code: https://github.com/Perseus1993/genworld. Project page: https://genworld1993.netlify.app/
summary: LLM-agent simulation faces a joint grounding and scaling problem: agents should act in environments that reflect real urban constraints, yet direct online LLM calls for city-scale populations are computationally prohibitive. We present GenWorld, an empirically grounded urban simulation infrastructure that combines a building-level synthetic city, a structured agent-environment interface, and offline compilation of LLM-derived decision signals into lookup policies for scalable rollout. In a reference instantiation for Higashihiroshima, Japan, GenWorld grounds 196,608 synthetic residents in census and geospatial data, validates demographic consistency against census tabulations, and uses YJMob100K mobile-phone data as a commuting-distance diagnostic. We demonstrate the infrastructure through three reproducible cases: a full-city weekday rollout, a weekday-weekend behavioral contrast, and a warning-response perturbation with auditable replanning traces. These cases support GenWorld as a reproducible platform for grounded and scalable LLM-agent studies, while calibrated forecasting for traffic, evacuation, or policy outcomes remains future work.

AI.tldr: GenWorld is a scalable urban simulation platform that uses offline-compiled LLM decision policies to simulate city-scale populations (196,608 agents) grounded in real geospatial and census data, validated against demographic and mobility ground truth.
AI.motivation: LLM-agent urban simulations face a dual challenge: agents must operate in realistic urban environments (grounding), but making live LLM calls for hundreds of thousands of agents is computationally prohibitive (scaling). Existing approaches cannot satisfy both requirements simultaneously.
AI.method: GenWorld combines three components: (1) a building-level synthetic city model grounded in census and geospatial data, (2) a structured agent-environment interface, and (3) offline compilation of LLM-derived decision signals into lookup policies that enable scalable rollout without online LLM calls. The Higashihiroshima instantiation uses 196,608 synthetic residents validated against census tabulations and YJMob100K mobile-phone data for commuting diagnostics.
AI.result: The platform is demonstrated through three reproducible cases: a full-city weekday rollout, a weekday-weekend behavioral contrast, and a warning-response perturbation with auditable replanning traces. Demographic consistency is validated against census tabulations, and commuting distances are benchmarked against mobile-phone data.
AI.conclusion: GenWorld provides a reproducible infrastructure for grounded, scalable LLM-agent urban studies. Calibrated forecasting for traffic, evacuation, and policy outcomes is identified as future work, positioning the platform as a foundational tool rather than a predictive system.

title: DysLexLens: A Low-Resource LLM Framework for Analysing Dyslexic Learners Insights from Online Forums
summary: Dyslexic learners increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) tools to support reading, writing, organisation, and study-related tasks. However, their lived experiences with these tools remain largely underexamined. This paper proposes DysLexLens, a low-resource LLM framework, designed to analyse dyslexic learners experience with AI through online forum discussions. DysLexLens is designed as an end-to-end, evidence-traceable architecture which transforms noisy social media posts into a dictionary-driven corpora, provides knowledge-graph (KG)-based question reasoning, generates verifiable query responses, and enables response evaluation through quantitative and human-grounded assessment. DysLexLens has four key features. First, it employs a dictionary-driven filtering method to construct a more focused Reddit corpus on dyslexia and AI, filtering out noisy and weakly related posts to improve the relevance of data collected from low-resource forum contexts. Second, it integrates LLM-assisted semantic analysis with KG-based query reasoning to uncover meaningful patterns. Third, it has quantitative evaluation metrics (RAGAS and Query Robustness) to measure LLM-generated response performance. Fourth, it provides structured qualitative validation guidelines for assessing response quality, with a specific focus on hallucination and evidence alignment. We demonstrate the effectiveness of DysLexLens using dyslexia-related Reddit forum data and 30 questions. The results show its potential generalisability to other low-resource forum data contexts. DysLexLens, sample data, questions and evaluation results are available at Github to support reproducibility.

AI.tldr: DysLexLens is a low-resource LLM framework that transforms noisy social media posts into structured, verifiable analyses of dyslexic learners' experiences with AI tools, combining dictionary-driven filtering, knowledge-graph reasoning, and multi-metric evaluation.
AI.motivation: Dyslexic learners are increasingly adopting AI tools, yet their lived experiences remain underexplored. Existing methods lack systematic, traceable approaches for extracting meaningful insights from low-resource, noisy forum contexts like Reddit.
AI.method: DysLexLens employs a four-stage end-to-end architecture: (1) dictionary-driven filtering to construct focused corpora from noisy social media; (2) LLM-assisted semantic analysis integrated with KG-based query reasoning; (3) quantitative evaluation via RAGAS and Query Robustness metrics; and (4) structured qualitative validation guidelines targeting hallucination and evidence alignment.
AI.result: The framework was validated using dyslexia-related Reddit data and 30 questions, demonstrating effective filtering of weakly related posts, meaningful pattern discovery, and robust response generation with measurable quality.
AI.conclusion: DysLexLens demonstrates potential generalizability to other low-resource forum contexts and provides a reproducible, evidence-traceable pipeline, with all artifacts (code, data, questions, results) publicly available on GitHub.

title: Exploring and Exploiting Synchrony Limitations of Time-Triggered Network-Agnostic Guardians
comment: Presented at the "29th International Symposium on Real-Time Distributed Computing" ISORC 2026
summary: Time-triggered communication protocols rely on trusted components known as guardians to enforce adherence to predetermined network schedules. Network-agnostic guardians offer an efficient and scalable distributed solution with reduced implementation cost and complexity compared to network-aware alternatives. However, this efficiency is based on the guardian's dependence on the controlled node for clock synchronization, which introduces a vulnerability: a malicious node can exploit this dependency to launch timing attacks against its guardian and eventually interfere with messages from other nodes on the network. In this paper, we establish a theoretical lower bound on the attainable clock synchronization precision between a node and its network-agnostic guardian. Building on this result, we introduce a timing attack that leverages the unavoidably imperfect clock synchrony to cause controlled and undetected de-synchronization of the guardian. The attack enables a malicious node to cause collisions with targeted critical network messages. We evaluate the effectiveness of the attack using a FlexRay field bus network model implemented in the OMNeT++ simulation framework. Our results show that the attack is able to remain undetected with 100% success and disrupts the transmission of the critical messages of the target node by causing collisions with them with 100% success.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals a fundamental vulnerability in network-agnostic guardians: a malicious node can exploit unavoidable clock synchronization imprecision to launch undetected timing attacks that cause 100% successful message collisions, and the authors prove a theoretical lower bound on achievable synchronization precision.
AI.motivation: Network-agnostic guardians are an efficient, scalable, and cost-effective alternative to network-aware guardians for enforcing time-triggered communication schedules. However, their reliance on the controlled node for clock synchronization introduces a security vulnerability. The authors aim to rigorously characterize this vulnerability and demonstrate its exploitability.
AI.method: The authors first derive a theoretical lower bound on the clock synchronization precision between a node and its network-agnostic guardian. Using this bound, they design a timing attack that leverages the inherent imperfect synchrony to gradually and undetectably de-synchronize the guardian. The attack is implemented and evaluated using a FlexRay network model within the OMNeT++ simulation framework.
AI.result: The simulation results demonstrate that the attack achieves 100% success in remaining undetected and causes collisions with the target node's critical messages with 100% success rate.
AI.conclusion: The dependency of network-agnostic guardians on their controlled nodes for clock synchronization constitutes a critical and exploitable vulnerability. The proven lower bound on synchronization precision implies that complete protection is theoretically impossible, necessitating a re-evaluation of network-agnostic guardian designs in safety-critical time-triggered systems like FlexRay.

title: Developmental approach reveals the statistical learning of Neural Language Models: Transformers generalize from the most abstract statistical patterns
comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, oral presentation at Interdisciplinary Advances in Statistical Learning
summary: In this study, we use a developmental approach to investigate the statistical learning and mental representation of neural language models (NLM). A series of Generative Transformer models are trained on a synthetic grammar. The model states are saved at multiple stages in the course of training. Through analyzing how the internal representations of these models change in the developmental path, we found that NLMs acquire the most abstract global statistical knowledge at the beginning of learning and later acquire the relatively local statistical dependencies. This learning path contains many over-generalizations from the very beginning and these over-generalizations are gradually constrained in the later stage of learning. Based on this observation, we propose a new framework to explain the statistical learning and language cognition of NLMs.

AI.tldr: Neural language models exhibit a developmental learning trajectory where abstract global statistical patterns are acquired early, followed by local dependencies, with initial over-generalizations gradually constrained over time.
AI.motivation: To understand how neural language models (NLMs) acquire and internally represent statistical knowledge during training, using a developmental perspective akin to cognitive language acquisition.
AI.method: A series of Generative Transformer models were trained on a synthetic grammar. Model states were saved at multiple stages during training, and the evolution of internal representations was analyzed to track how statistical dependencies are acquired over developmental time.
AI.result: NLMs first acquire abstract global statistical knowledge at the onset of learning, later acquiring more local statistical dependencies. Early learning is characterized by over-generalizations that are progressively constrained in later training stages.
AI.conclusion: A new framework is proposed to explain statistical learning and language cognition in NLMs, grounded in the observed developmental trajectory of global-to-local acquisition and progressive constraint of over-generalizations.

title: Learning in Markovian bandits with non-observable states and constrained decision epochs
summary: This paper studies the problem of regret minimization in Markovian bandits with \emph{non-observable states} and possibly \emph{constrained} decision epochs. The focus is restricted to a ``pure'' regret benchmark, that compares the performance of the learning algorithm to the best \emph{pure policy} which -- akin to optimal policies of stochastic bandits -- picks the optimal arm from start to finish without ever switching. We introduce a generalization of rested Markovian bandits, \emph{self-degrading Markovian bandits}, for which pure policies are always asymptotically optimal.We show that without prior knowledge on the underlying bandit, the regret of algorithms that switch arms rarely necessarily scales super-logarithmically for every bandit, i.e., as $ω(\log(T))$, where $T$ is the learning horizon. Despite the unreachability of the logarithmic regime, we design UCB-NOM, an optimistic algorithm inspired by UCB, of which the regret is nearly logarithmic. Lastly, we show that given prior knowledge on the Markovian bandit in the form of a bound on the bias functions of its arm, a proper instantiation of UCB-NOM achieves $O(\log(T))$ regret. We further show that this prior knowledge allows for a $O(\sqrt{T \log(T)})$ worst-case regret bound for UCB-NOM. Notably, our regret bounds do not depend on the number of states of the underlying Markov chains. Our findings suggest that the non-observability of states is a mild inconvenience in self-degrading Markovian bandits.

AI.tldr: This paper studies regret minimization in Markovian bandits with non-observable states, introducing "self-degrading Markovian bandits" where pure policies are asymptotically optimal, and proposes UCB-NOM which achieves near-logarithmic regret without state observability.
AI.motivation: Regret minimization in Markovian bandits typically assumes observable states, but many real-world applications involve hidden Markov states. The authors aim to understand whether non-observability fundamentally limits performance and to characterize when logarithmic regret is achievable under a "pure policy" benchmark.
AI.method: The authors generalize rested Markovian bandits to "self-degrading Markovian bandits," where pure policies are asymptotically optimal. They analyze lower bounds on regret for algorithms that switch arms rarely, then design UCB-NOM — an optimistic algorithm inspired by UCB that operates without state observability. They also analyze the algorithm's performance with and without prior knowledge (bias function bounds).
AI.result: (1) Without prior knowledge, regret for rare-switching algorithms scales as ω(log T). (2) UCB-NOM achieves nearly logarithmic regret despite this lower bound. (3) With prior knowledge of bias function bounds, UCB-NOM achieves O(log T) regret and O(√(T log T)) worst-case regret. All bounds are independent of the number of underlying Markov states.
AI.conclusion: Non-observability of states is only a mild inconvenience in self-degrading Markovian bandits. Logarithmic regret is achievable with appropriate prior knowledge, and UCB-NOM provides strong theoretical guarantees without dependence on state-space size.

title: From Bootstrapping to Sequence Modeling: A Unified Generative Framework for Personalized Landing-Page Modeling
comment: arXiv admin note: text overlap with arXiv:2507.23459
summary: Modern online platforms increasingly adopt multi-page architectures to accommodate diverse user needs. On these platforms, page navigation (the process of directing users to specific functional pages upon app entry) serves as a critical gateway that shapes user's first impression and significantly influences subsequent engagement. To optimize this process, Kuaishou formulated the task of Personalized Landing Page Modeling (PLPM) and proposed KLAN, a reinforcement learning framework built upon Conservative Q-Learning (CQL). However, CQL-based approaches suffer from two fundamental limitations: (1) the Markov assumption fails to capture the strong non-Markovian temporal dependencies inherent in real-world user behaviors, and (2) TD learning with bootstrapping incurs severe cumulative errors and credit assignment difficulties under delayed rewards, particularly in long-horizon settings where users enter the app multiple times daily. To address these limitations, we propose GLAN (Generative Landing-page Adaptive Navigator), a sequence modeling framework built on Decision Transformer to tackle PLPM from a unified global-local perspective. Specifically, GLAN incorporates two key modules. First, we design the L-RTG module that captures users' inter-day consumption dynamics to provide accurate global guidance for all page assignments within a day. Furthermore, we propose the HRM module that decomposes session-level feedback into fine-grained signals, enabling precise local supervision for each page assignment. Extensive online experiments conducted on the Kuaishou platform demonstrate the effectiveness of GLAN, achieving +0.158\% and +0.108\% improvements on Daily Active Users (DAU) and user Lifetime (LT) respectively.

AI.tldr: GLAN is a Decision Transformer-based framework for personalized landing page recommendation that replaces CQL-based RL to address non-Markovian dependencies and delayed reward issues. It uses a Long-term RTG (L-RTG) module for inter-day global guidance and a Hierarchical Reward Model (HRM) for fine-grained local supervision, achieving significant DAU and user Lifetime gains on Kuaishou.
AI.motivation: Existing CQL-based approaches (like KLAN) for Personalized Landing Page Modeling suffer from two key limitations: (1) the Markov assumption cannot capture non-Markovian temporal dependencies in real user behavior, and (2) TD learning with bootstrapping causes cumulative errors and credit assignment difficulties under delayed, long-horizon rewards. These shortcomings motivate a sequence modeling alternative.
AI.method: GLAN adopts a Decision Transformer architecture with two novel modules: (1) the L-RTG (Long-term Return-To-Go) module, which captures inter-day consumption dynamics to provide global guidance for within-day page assignments; and (2) the HRM (Hierarchical Reward Model) module, which decomposes session-level feedback into fine-grained reward signals for precise local supervision of each page assignment.
AI.result: Online A/B experiments on the Kuaishou platform show GLAN achieves +0.158% improvement on Daily Active Users (DAU) and +0.108% improvement on user Lifetime (LT).
AI.conclusion: Replacing CQL-based RL with a Decision Transformer framework that jointly models global (inter-day) and local (intra-day, session-level) reward signals effectively addresses the limitations of Markov assumptions and TD learning in long-horizon landing page optimization, yielding tangible business metric gains.

title: LLM-Assisted Model-Based GUI Testing for Vue.js Web Applications
summary: Vue.js is a popular framework for building modern web applications. As Vue.js functionality and tooling support grow, ensuring its reliability (through automated testing) is becoming increasingly important. Although model-based testing has been successfully used to automate graphical user interface (GUI) testing on other platforms, its application to Vue.js remains challenging: Transition candidates, which are spread across router configurations and single-file components (SFCs), must be concretized and normalized into an executable page transition graph (PTG) for testing. To address this, we propose the LLMVue framework, which uses a large language model (LLM) to generate a PTG from Vue.js source code. LLMVue infers component hierarchies and route transitions, merging them into a unified PTG across multiple SFCs. We evaluated LLMVue on a collection of ten open-source Vue.js projects from GitHub, using GPT-4o as the LLM backbone. The constructed graphs demonstrate high precision and recall, with low graph edit distance. LLMVue -guided testing also significantly improves the coverage and exploration efficiency, compared to a random exploration baseline (with the same time constraints). To the best of our knowledge, this is the first use of LLMs for model-based GUI testing of Vue.js applications using source-level PTG extraction.

AI.tldr: LLMVue leverages GPT-4o to automatically extract executable page transition graphs (PTGs) from Vue.js source code by inferring component hierarchies and route transitions, then uses these PTGs for model-based GUI testing. Evaluated on ten open-source Vue.js projects, the approach achieves high precision/recall and significantly outperforms random exploration in coverage and efficiency.
AI.motivation: Vue.js applications combine router configurations and single-file components (SFCs), making it challenging to concretize and normalize transition candidates into an executable page transition graph (PTG) for model-based testing. Existing model-based GUI testing approaches do not adequately address this extraction problem for Vue.js, motivating an LLM-based solution.
AI.method: The LLMVue framework uses a large language model (specifically GPT-4o) to analyze Vue.js source code, infer component hierarchies and route transitions across multiple SFCs, and merge them into a unified, executable page transition graph (PTG). This PTG then guides model-based GUI testing of the application.
AI.result: On ten open-source Vue.js GitHub projects, LLMVue-constructed PTGs achieved high precision and recall with low graph edit distance. LLMVue-guided testing significantly improved coverage and exploration efficiency compared to a random exploration baseline under identical time constraints.
AI.conclusion: This work represents the first application of LLMs to model-based GUI testing of Vue.js applications via source-level PTG extraction, demonstrating that LLMs can effectively bridge the gap between Vue.js source code and automated model-based testing.

title: GBC: Gradient-Based Connections for Optimizing Multi-Agent Systems
comment: 15 pages, 8 figures, accepted by SIGDIAL 2026 Long Papers
summary: Multi-agent systems (MAS) built on large language models (LLMs) provide a promising framework for solving complex tasks through role specialization and structured interaction. However, their performance is often limited by miscoordination and, more fundamentally, the lack of fine-grained credit assignment across agents. Existing approaches typically rely on coarse-grained feedback, making it difficult to identify which agents or interaction steps are responsible for errors. We propose Gradient-Based Connections (GBC), an approach for fine-grained attribution and optimization of multi-agent systems. GBC models a MAS as a computational graph and introduces gradient-based connection weights to quantify the influence of each agent's output on downstream agents at the token level. By constructing an attribution graph and propagating task-specific loss signals backward, our method enables precise identification of error sources and targeted prompt optimization. We further develop AgentChord, an efficient implementation that leverages prefix-based gradient computation. Experiments on MultiWOZ and τ-bench show that GBC improves multi-agent performance and outperforms strong single-agent and multi-agent baselines, and higher attribution quality is associated with greater optimization effectiveness. Code is available at: https://github.com/yxc-cyber/AgentChord.

AI.tldr: GBC introduces gradient-based credit assignment for multi-agent LLM systems by modeling interactions as a computational graph, enabling token-level attribution of errors and targeted prompt optimization, outperforming baselines on MultiWOZ and τ-bench.
AI.motivation: Multi-agent LLM systems suffer from miscoordination and lack fine-grained credit assignment — existing coarse-grained feedback makes it hard to pinpoint which agents or interaction steps cause errors, limiting optimization.
AI.method: GBC models the MAS as a computational graph with gradient-based connection weights that quantify each agent's token-level influence on downstream agents. It constructs an attribution graph, backpropagates task-specific loss signals, and identifies error sources for targeted prompt optimization. AgentChord implements this efficiently via prefix-based gradient computation.
AI.result: GBC improves multi-agent performance on MultiWOZ and τ-bench, outperforming both strong single-agent and multi-agent baselines. Higher attribution quality correlates with greater optimization effectiveness.
AI.conclusion: Fine-grained gradient-based credit assignment effectively addresses the miscoordination problem in LLM-based MAS, with attribution quality directly linked to downstream optimization gains.

title: Self-Verifying Measurement Records: Hash-Linked Evidence Graphs for Hardware Benchmarking
comment: 17 pages, 3 figures, 7 tables. Ancillary files (anc/) contain the full source code, the raw observations, the hash-linked evidence graph, and a SHA-256 manifest; the record audits offline with a standard-library script
summary: Performance numbers reported for hardware are accepted on trust: the reader cannot recompute them, the apparatus is gone, and the silicon itself can be silently wrong, with fleet studies reporting on the order of one core in a thousand returning incorrect arithmetic with no error raised. We make a reported hardware measurement a tamper-evident, independently checkable record. Every quantity in the text, a table, or a figure is bound, by its content hash, to the observation and the verification behind it; the whole is a hash-linked, append-only structure (a transparency log for measurement) that a verifier audits offline without trusting its producer. Matrix products are verified by a probabilistic identity (Freivalds) at O(k n^2) cost under a tolerance we derive from floating-point error analysis and calibrate to the device's own measured residual floor, so a wrong product is rejected with probability 1 - 2^(-k); quantities with no such identity carry an algebraic checksum and a measured reproducibility class. We then treat the check itself as a security object: a probe seed committed for offline reproducibility is an attack surface, and a probe-aware adversary can hide a corruption in the probe's null space, fooling even a quorum of bit-identical witnesses, while a Fiat-Shamir challenge derived from the claimed output closes this. Driving the device from an unprivileged tenant's reach, with a di/dt power virus and a thermal soak, neither moves the calibrated tolerance nor produces a silent error, placing the physical-fault threat at the rare defective part or the privileged attacker and marking the boundary at which the record must compose with a hardware root of trust. We demonstrate the construction across Blackwell and Hopper GPUs and report a residual-floor and reproducibility map by precision, size, and device.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a tamper-evident, independently verifiable record system for hardware performance measurements. It uses hash-linked append-only structures (transparency logs) to bind reported quantities to their underlying observations and verification proofs. Matrix products are verified via Freivalds' probabilistic identity with a calibrated floating-point tolerance, while other quantities carry algebraic checksums and reproducibility classes. The system addresses adversarial probe manipulation through Fiat-Shamir challenges and empirically demonstrates that physical stress (power viruses, thermal soak) neither shifts tolerance nor induces silent errors on Blackwell and Hopper GPUs.
AI.motivation: Hardware performance measurements are currently accepted on trust — readers cannot recompute them, hardware is ephemeral, and silicon itself can silently produce incorrect arithmetic (≈1 in 1000 cores return wrong results with no error). This creates a credibility crisis for empirical computer science. The authors seek to make hardware measurements tamper-evident and independently checkable so that reported results carry cryptographic guarantees of integrity.
AI.method: The system constructs a transparency log for measurements: every reported quantity is bound by content hash to its observation and verification, forming a hash-linked append-only structure auditable offline without trusting the producer. For matrix products, Freivalds' probabilistic identity provides O(k n²) verification with rejection probability 1−2⁻ᵏ, using a tolerance derived from floating-point error analysis calibrated to the device's own measured residual floor. Non-matrix quantities carry algebraic checksums and a measured reproducibility class. To counter probe-aware adversaries, the authors replace committed probe seeds (vulnerable to null-space hiding) with Fiat-Shamir challenges derived from the claimed output. Physical fault threats are tested using di/dt power viruses and thermal soak from an unprivileged tenant.
AI.result: The construction was demonstrated across Blackwell and Hopper GPUs, producing a residual-floor and reproducibility map by precision, size, and device. Neither the power virus nor thermal soak shifted the calibrated tolerance or produced silent errors, confining the physical-fault threat model to rare defective parts or privileged attackers.
AI.conclusion: Hardware measurements can be made tamper-evident and independently verifiable through cryptographic binding to verification proofs. The physical-fault attack surface is limited to rare defective silicon or privileged attackers, at which boundary the measurement record must compose with a hardware root of trust.

title: Supersede: Diagnosing and Training the Memory-Update Gap in LLM Agents
comment: 11 pages, 4 figures, 3 tables. Code, environment, model, and dataset: https://github.com/Vrin-cloud/supersede
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents operate over long, multi-session interactions in which facts change: a user moves, a price updates, a plan is revised. Acting correctly requires using the current value of a fact and discarding values that have been superseded. We isolate this ability on real conversational data and show that it is a distinct, unsolved failure. On the knowledge-update subset of LongMemEval, replacing an agent's full context with a bounded, self-maintained memory drops accuracy from 92% to 77% even on a frontier model (gpt-5.4), a gap that is statistically significant (paired McNemar p<0.005) and persists across model scale while full-context accuracy saturates near 92%. The bottleneck is therefore memory maintenance, not comprehension, and is not closed by a stronger model. We then ask whether this is merely an undersized memory, and find it is not: as the conversation grows 24x, accuracy falls further (from 68% to 28%), and granting the agent proportionally more memory yields no detectable recovery (28% to 28%, n=25). The failure scales with the length of the conversation, not the compression ratio. We release Supersede, an open reinforcement-learning environment (on the verifiers / prime-rl stack) that turns this measurement into a training signal: agents are rewarded for answering from the current value and penalized for stale ones. Finally, we close the loop and show the gap is trainable: GRPO fine-tuning a small open model (Qwen2.5-3B) on this environment nearly doubles its held-out supersession accuracy on real, unseen conversations (9.0% to 16.7%, a single run), along a monotonic checkpoint curve indicating the learned policy, not the harness, carries the gain. To our knowledge this is the first trainable environment whose reward targets temporal fact-currency, and the first evidence the supersession gap can be trained down, not only measured.

AI.tldr: LLM agents fail at supersession — discarding outdated facts for current ones — with accuracy dropping from 92% to 77% when using bounded memory instead of full context. The failure scales with conversation length, not compression ratio, and is not fixed by stronger models. The authors release Supersede, an RL environment targeting temporal fact-currency, and show GRPO fine-tuning nearly doubles supersession accuracy on a small open model.
AI.motivation: LLM agents in long, multi-session interactions must track changing facts (e.g., updated prices, revised plans) and use current values while discarding superseded ones. The authors demonstrate this is a distinct, unsolved failure mode that persists even in frontier models and is not addressed by scaling model size — framing it as a memory maintenance bottleneck rather than a comprehension problem.
AI.method: The authors (1) isolate supersession ability using the knowledge-update subset of LongMemEval on real conversational data; (2) compare full-context vs. bounded self-maintained memory conditions across model scales; (3) vary conversation length (24× growth) and memory allocation to test whether the failure is due to undersized memory or conversation length; (4) build Supersede, an open RL environment on the verifiers/prime-rl stack that rewards correct current-value answers and penalizes stale ones; and (5) fine-tune Qwen2.5-3B with GRPO on this environment and evaluate on held-out real conversations.
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Bounded memory drops accuracy from 92% to 77% (p<0.005, paired McNemar), with full-context accuracy saturating near 92% across model scales — the bottleneck is memory maintenance, not comprehension. (2) As conversation length grows 24×, accuracy falls from 68% to 28%; granting proportionally more memory yields no recovery (28%→28%), indicating failure scales with conversation length, not compression ratio. (3) GRPO fine-tuning on Supersede nearly doubles held-out supersession accuracy (9.0%→16.7%), with monotonic improvement across checkpoints.
AI.conclusion: Supersession — the ability to discard outdated facts and use current ones — is a distinct, measurable, and trainable capability gap in LLM agents. Stronger models alone do not close the gap, but targeted RL training on temporal fact-currency can. Supersede provides the first trainable environment for this skill, and the results constitute the first evidence that the supersession gap can be reduced through training.

title: Prism Transformer: Progressive Head Schedules for Hierarchical Attention Processing
summary: Multi-head attention conventionally partitions the hidden dimension equally across all heads at every layer, enforcing an identical representational subspace dimension (dh = dmodel/h) throughout the models depth. In this work, we identify this uniform allocation as a fundamental structural bottleneck: due to their restricted dimensional space, early-layer heads are unable to faithfully capture complex, high-dimensional contextual patterns.
