To resolve this, we introduce the Prism Transformer, a novel architectural paradigm that replaces the static, uniform head configuration with a progressive head schedule. By monotonically increasing the head count across layers, the Prism Transformer naturally establishes a local-to-global representational hierarchy: early layers leverage fewer, exceptionally wide heads to capture complex, local compositional patterns, while deep layers deploy many, narrow heads to decompose these patterns into specialized linguistic features. Crucially, this structural shift is parameter-neutral, compute-neutral, and introduces zero training or inference overhead, preserving identical weight matrices and FLOP budgets as the standard Transformer. Across three model scales (124M, 354M, and 757M), the Prism Transformer consistently outperforms uniform baselines, achieving consistent reductions in validation loss alongside consistent gains on downstream zero-shot benchmarks (including PIQA, HellaSwag, ARC-Easy, and WinoGrande). Our findings demonstrate that non-uniform subspace allocation unlocks latent capacity within the standard Transformer budget, enabling more effective use of model capacity.

AI.tldr: Standard Transformers allocate equal hidden dimension per attention head across all layers, creating a bottleneck where early layers lack sufficient representational capacity. The Prism Transformer replaces this with a progressive head schedule—fewer wide heads early, many narrow heads later—achieving better performance at zero additional cost.
AI.motivation: Uniform allocation of the hidden dimension across attention heads (d_h = d_model/h) at every layer forces early-layer heads to operate in a restricted subspace, preventing them from capturing complex, high-dimensional contextual patterns. This structural bottleneck limits representational capacity.
AI.method: The Prism Transformer replaces static, uniform head counts with a monotonically increasing head schedule across layers. Early layers use fewer, wider heads (larger d_h) to capture complex local compositional patterns; deeper layers use many narrow heads (smaller d_h) to decompose these into specialized linguistic features. This establishes a local-to-global representational hierarchy while being strictly parameter-neutral, compute-neutral, and introducing zero overhead.
AI.result: Across three model scales (124M, 354M, 757M), Prism Transformers consistently outperform uniform baselines in validation loss and on downstream zero-shot benchmarks including PIQA, HellaSwag, ARC-Easy, and WinoGrande.
AI.conclusion: Non-uniform subspace allocation unlocks latent capacity within the standard Transformer budget, enabling more effective use of model capacity without increasing parameters, FLOPs, or inference overhead.

title: MER-R1: Multimodal Emotion Reasoning via Slow-Fast Thinking Synergy
summary: We find that explicit reasoning does not necessarily translate into better multimodal emotion recognition (MER) accuracy, even though it makes predictions more interpretable. Specifically, for reasoning-based MLLMs, fast thinking by triggering direct answers often outperforms slow thinking after deliberative reasoning. Our empirical analyses show that fast thinking improves recall with broader and more confident predictions, whereas slow thinking favors precision through conservative filtering of incorrect categories. Building on these insights, we propose MER-R1, a reinforcement learning framework that turns slow-fast complementarity into explicit optimization. Dual-objective disentanglement separates recall and precision into two optimization signals, allowing them to be jointly optimized rather than traded off against each other. Slow-fast confidence calibration further aligns the final slow-thinking answer with fast-thinking intuition, strengthening correct emotions while suppressing incorrect ones. In this way, MER-R1 unifies the recall-oriented intuition of fast thinking with the precision-oriented selectivity of slow thinking. We further provide theoretical justification for this synergy, showing that it mitigates variance-induced interference during optimization. Extensive experiments on MER-UniBench and MME-Emotion show that MER-R1 achieves state-of-the-art performance and makes reasoning genuinely benefit emotion recognition.

AI.tldr: Slow (deliberative) thinking in MLLMs improves precision but hurts recall for emotion recognition; fast (intuitive) thinking does the opposite. MER-R1 uses reinforcement learning with dual-objective disentanglement and confidence calibration to jointly optimize both, achieving SOTA on MER benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Explicit reasoning in multimodal large language models (MLLMs) improves interpretability but paradoxically degrades multimodal emotion recognition (MER) accuracy — fast, direct answering often outperforms slow, deliberative reasoning. This reveals a recall-precision tradeoff that needs to be resolved for reasoning to genuinely benefit emotion recognition.
AI.method: MER-R1, a reinforcement learning framework with two key components: (1) Dual-objective disentanglement that separates recall and precision into distinct optimization signals for joint optimization, and (2) Slow-fast confidence calibration that aligns the slow-thinking answer with fast-thinking intuition to reinforce correct emotions and suppress incorrect ones. Theoretical justification shows this synergy mitigates variance-induced interference during optimization.
AI.result: MER-R1 achieves state-of-the-art performance on MER-UniBench and MME-Emotion benchmarks, demonstrating that reasoning can genuinely benefit emotion recognition when slow-fast complementarity is properly leveraged.
AI.conclusion: The slow-fast thinking dichotomy in MLLMs represents a fundamental recall-precision tradeoff in MER. By explicitly modeling and jointly optimizing these complementary signals through reinforcement learning with disentangled objectives and confidence calibration, reasoning becomes a genuine asset rather than a hindrance to emotion recognition accuracy.

title: An LLM-Powered Semantic Alignment Framework for Journal Recommendation
summary: Journal recommendation is an important task in scholarly information systems. Existing approaches typically rely on supervised learning models, manually engineered features, or historical interaction data, which may limit their generalizability and interpretability. We propose an LLM-powered semantic alignment framework that formulates journal recommendation as a semantic matching problem between manuscript content and journal scope descriptions. The framework enables large language models (LLMs) to infer journal suitability directly from article titles, abstracts, keywords, and candidate journal information without task-specific training. Experiments are conducted using DeepSeek-V3 on a dataset of 23,609 articles from 49 journals in statistics and related fields. The proposed framework achieves Top-3, Top-5, and Top-10 accuracies of 40.23\%, 53.67\%, and 70.05\%, respectively. Additional analyses show that incorporating reference information generally improves recommendation performance and that recommendations remain highly stable across repeated runs, with an average Top-5 Jaccard similarity of 84\%. The framework also generates interpretable reasoning outputs that provide insights into the recommendation process. These findings demonstrate the potential of LLMs as a training-free and scalable paradigm for journal recommendation and scholarly decision support.

AI.tldr: A training-free LLM framework matches manuscripts to journals via semantic alignment between article content and journal scope descriptions, achieving 53.67% Top-5 accuracy on 23,609 statistics articles while providing interpretable reasoning.
AI.motivation: Existing journal recommendation methods rely on supervised learning, handcrafted features, or historical interactions, which suffer from limited generalizability and interpretability. A more flexible, training-free paradigm is needed.
AI.method: An LLM-powered semantic alignment framework that casts journal recommendation as a semantic matching problem. LLMs (DeepSeek-V3) infer journal suitability directly from article titles, abstracts, keywords, and candidate journal scope descriptions without task-specific fine-tuning. Reference information is optionally incorporated for enhancement.
AI.result: Top-3, Top-5, and Top-10 accuracies of 40.23%, 53.67%, and 70.05% on 23,609 articles from 49 journals. Reference information boosts performance. Recommendations are highly stable (avg. 84% Top-5 Jaccard similarity across runs). The framework also produces interpretable reasoning outputs.
AI.conclusion: LLMs offer a viable, training-free, scalable paradigm for journal recommendation and scholarly decision support, combining competitive accuracy with interpretability and stability.

title: BashCoder-R1: Towards Robust and Explainable Bash Code Generation with Robustness-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization
summary: Bash scripts are the cornerstone of system administration and DevOps automation, where code quality directly impacts system stability and security. In automated Bash script generation using Large Language Models (LLMs), two interconnected failures emerge: unauditable "black box" reasoning and critical robustness vulnerabilities in generated code. To address both, we propose BashCoder-R1, a novel framework for robust and explainable Bash script generation. Our pipeline combines: (1) Continual Pre-training (CPT) to specialize the model on Bash paradigms; (2) Long Chain-of-Thought Supervised Fine-Tuning (L-CoT SFT) on expert-validated reasoning-and-code samples to emulate proactive risk-aware thinking; and (3) Robustness-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (R-GRPO), a reinforcement learning phase optimizing a weighted reward for syntax correctness, robustness (via shellcheck), and format correctness. We evaluate on BashBench, a new benchmark of 952 real-world tasks (773 single-line, 179 multi-line). BashCoder-R1 achieves SyntaxPass (100.00%/94.97%), RobustWarnRate (4.01%/16.47%), RobustPass (95.99%/79.33%), FuncRate (93.01%/93.85%), and FullRate (90.04%/73.18%) for single-line/multi-line tasks, outperforming the strongest baseline DeepSeek-V3.2 (Reasoning) by 37.82% and 20.18% in FullRate. Human evaluation on Functionality, Robustness, and Clarity further confirms BashCoder-R1 achieves the highest quality ratings.

AI.tldr: BashCoder-R1 is a novel framework for robust and explainable Bash script generation that combines continual pre-training, long chain-of-thought fine-tuning, and robustness-aware reinforcement learning (R-GRPO), achieving state-of-the-art results on the BashBench benchmark across syntax, robustness, functionality, and overall quality metrics.
AI.motivation: LLM-based Bash script generation suffers from two critical failures: (1) unauditable "black box" reasoning that undermines trust and explainability, and (2) robustness vulnerabilities in generated code that threaten system stability and security. Existing approaches fail to address both issues simultaneously.
AI.method: BashCoder-R1 employs a three-stage pipeline: (1) Continual Pre-training (CPT) to specialize the base model on Bash-specific paradigms; (2) Long Chain-of-Thought Supervised Fine-Tuning (L-CoT SFT) using expert-validated reasoning-and-code pairs to instill proactive risk-aware thinking; and (3) Robustness-Aware Group Relative Policy Optimization (R-GRPO), a reinforcement learning phase that optimizes a weighted reward combining syntax correctness, robustness (validated via shellcheck), and format correctness.
AI.result: On BashBench (952 tasks: 773 single-line, 179 multi-line), BashCoder-R1 achieves SyntaxPass (100.00%/94.97%), RobustWarnRate (4.01%/16.47%), RobustPass (95.99%/79.33%), FuncRate (93.01%/93.85%), and FullRate (90.04%/73.18%) for single-line/multi-line tasks respectively. It outperforms DeepSeek-V3.2 (Reasoning) by 37.82% (single-line) and 20.18% (multi-line) in FullRate. Human evaluation also confirms superior ratings on Functionality, Robustness, and Clarity.
AI.conclusion: The BashCoder-R1 framework effectively addresses both explainability and robustness in automated Bash script generation through its integrated training pipeline. The substantial improvements over strong baselines, validated by both automated metrics and human evaluation, demonstrate that incorporating expert reasoning traces and robustness-aware RL is a promising direction for producing safe, reliable code generation systems.

title: Triadic Werewolf: A Jester Role for Multi-Hop Theory of Mind in LLMs
summary: Theory-of-mind evaluations of large language models typically use dyadic social-deduction games, where every observable cue points to a single hidden side, so a model with strong language priors can score well without ever simulating opponents' incentives. We extend the Werewolf game with a Jester, a third faction whose utility on peer suspicion is inverted because it wins by being voted out, so optimal play requires reasoning across three opposing utility functions. Across 60 games on GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3.1, and Llama-3.3-70B with Jester self-learning on and off, the Jester wins 60-70% of games while Werewolves never exceed 20%, and GPT-4.1 wolves vote the Jester out on day 1 in 60-70% of games, a strictly self-defeating action. Self-learning helps DeepSeek and Llama but hurts GPT-4.1, with the cost landing on Villagers rather than Werewolves. Only DeepSeek learns the subtle strategy of looking suspicious without looking intentionally suspicious, and it gains the most from the loop. Triadic incentive structure exposes a layer of multi-agent reasoning that dyadic deduction games leave invisible.

AI.tldr: Adding a Jester (who wins by being voted out) to the Werewolf game exposes LLMs' failure to reason about inverted utility functions. GPT-4.1 wolves self-destruct by voting the Jester out immediately. Self-learning helps DeepSeek and Llama but harms GPT-4.1. Only DeepSeek learns to "look suspicious without looking intentionally suspicious." Triadic incentives reveal multi-agent reasoning gaps invisible in dyadic games.
AI.motivation: Standard theory-of-mind benchmarks for LLMs use dyadic social-deduction games (e.g., Werewolf with Villagers vs. Werewolves), where surface-level language cues correlate directly with hidden roles. This allows models with strong language priors to perform well without genuinely modeling opponents' incentive structures. The authors introduce a third faction (Jester) with an inverted utility function — winning by being eliminated — to test whether LLMs can reason about three-way opposing incentives, which dyadic setups cannot probe.
AI.method: The authors extend the Werewolf game with a Jester role whose victory condition is being voted out. They run 60 games across three LLMs (GPT-4.1, DeepSeek-V3.1, Llama-3.3-70B), with a self-learning loop on and off. In the self-learning condition, models reflect on past game transcripts to improve strategy. Win rates, voting patterns, and strategic behaviors are analyzed across roles and conditions.
AI.result: The Jester wins 60–70% of games while Werewolves never exceed 20%. GPT-4.1 werewolves vote the Jester out on Day 1 in 60–70% of games — a strictly self-defeating action (eliminating a player the wolves need alive to deflect suspicion). Self-learning helps DeepSeek and Llama improve but degrades GPT-4.1's performance, with the cost borne by Villagers. Only DeepSeek discovers the nuanced strategy of appearing suspicious without appearing intentionally suspicious, and it benefits most from self-learning.
AI.conclusion: Triadic incentive structures expose a layer of multi-agent reasoning that dyadic deduction games leave invisible. Current LLMs, particularly GPT-4.1, fail to model inverted utility functions and engage in self-defeating behaviors. Self-learning is not a universal remedy — it can harm performance when models cannot effectively extract useful strategic insights from experience. The Jester-augmented Werewolf game serves as a more rigorous benchmark for theory-of-mind capabilities in LLMs.

title: Agentic AI-Powered Re-Identification: An Emerging, Scalable Threat to Mobility Microdata Privacy
summary:
The widespread collection of fine-grained location data by commercial data brokers creates a re-identification risk that is not widely recognised by the public. While prior research has established that mobility traces are highly unique and that individuals can, in principle, be identified from a handful of spatio-temporal points, such attacks have historically required significant manual effort from skilled analysts, limiting their practical scale.
  In this feasibility study, we demonstrate in a real world setting that agentic AI fundamentally changes this threat model. We present an end-to-end pipeline in which large language model agents autonomously search the open web, cross-reference public records and social media, and resolve raw coordinate sequences to candidate identities - without human intervention. We evaluate the pipeline on a spatio-temporal dataset containing simulated location points anchored at and around true home and work addresses, focusing on a high-risk disclosure scenario. Our results demonstrate that, from spatio-temporal data and public sources alone, our agentic AI successfully re-identified 18 of the 25 re-identifiable individuals (72%) and 18 of 43 cases overall (41.9%).
  We discuss implications for Statistical Disclosure Control (SDC) practice and outline the near-future escalation that data custodians and regulators must anticipate. De facto anonymity - an implicit foundation of SDC practice - is shifting. Agentic AI strengthens the case that re-identification is reasonably likely by any means under the GDPR Recital-26 standard, at costs of minutes-and-dollars per target.

AI.tldr: This feasibility study demonstrates that agentic AI (LLM-powered autonomous agents) can re-identify individuals from raw location data at scale — successfully identifying 72% of re-identifiable targets — by autonomously cross-referencing spatio-temporal traces with public web data, fundamentally altering the re-identification threat model and challenging Statistical Disclosure Control assumptions.
AI.motivation: Commercial data brokers collect fine-grained location data at scale, creating a re-identification risk the public underestimates. While prior work showed mobility traces are unique and re-identification is theoretically possible, traditional attacks required skilled analysts and significant manual effort, limiting practical scalability. The authors investigate whether agentic AI (LLM agents) fundamentally changes this threat landscape by automating the entire re-identification pipeline.
AI.method: An end-to-end automated pipeline where LLM agents autonomously: (1) search the open web, (2) cross-reference public records and social media, and (3) resolve raw GPS coordinate sequences to candidate identities — all without human intervention. Evaluation used a spatio-temporal dataset with simulated location points anchored at/near true home and work addresses in a high-risk disclosure scenario, testing on 43 cases (25 of which were re-identifiable).
AI.result: The agentic AI pipeline successfully re-identified 18 of 25 re-identifiable individuals (72% precision on the re-identifiable subset) and 18 of 43 cases overall (41.9%). Re-identification costs were characterized as "minutes-and-dollars per target," demonstrating both effectiveness and economic feasibility at scale.
AI.conclusion: Agentic AI shifts the de facto anonymity assumption underlying Statistical Disclosure Control practice. The findings strengthen the case that re-identification is "reasonably likely by any means" under the GDPR Recital-26 standard. Data custodians and regulators must anticipate near-future escalation of this threat, as current SDC safeguards may be insufficient against automated LLM-driven adversaries.

title: The Context-Ready Transformer
summary: We introduce the context-ready transformer, a new recurrent neural network architecture built from a D-layer transformer block that pre-contextualizes each token before it enters the block. During left-to-right generation, a correction network combines the previous position's block output -- a cached summary of past context -- with the current token embedding, so the tokenenters the block already contextualized rather than as a raw embedding. At sequential inference, the correction chain makes the architecture a recurrent neural network. For training, we unroll the correction process K times over the full sequence, processing all positions in parallel at each step. A pretrained transformer can also be converted to a context-ready model by adding a zero-initialized correction FFN and fine-tuning. We evaluate across widths, depths, block sizes, and two datasets, with all comparisons against standard transformers, variants, and ablations. A D=5 model beats a 12-layer transformer while generating 1.7x faster on an A100. With K=10, a single-layermodel (D=1) beats a 6-layer transformer with a 2.6x inference speedup, and sequential inference matches parallel K=10 to within 0.01 PPL. The architecture benefits most from wide representations and long contexts. On a pointer-chasing task, D=1 trained with BPTT solves all 10 composition levels, while standard transformers exhibit staircase-like depth dependence.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the context-ready transformer, a recurrent architecture where a correction network pre-contextualizes each token before entering a transformer block. During left-to-right generation, it caches past context summaries, enabling fast sequential inference. A pretrained transformer can be converted via a zero-initialized correction FFN. A D=5 model outperforms a 12-layer transformer with 1.7× faster generation; a D=1 model beats a 6-layer transformer with 2.6× speedup.
AI.motivation: Standard transformers face a trade-off between depth (capacity) and inference speed during autoregressive generation. Deeper models are more powerful but slower at sequential inference. The authors aim to decouple representational capacity from inference latency by introducing recurrent-style context caching within the transformer block, enabling deep-capacity performance with shallow-block speed.
AI.method: The core mechanism is a correction network that, during left-to-right generation, takes the previous position's block output (a cached context summary) and the current token embedding, producing a context-aware input to the D-layer transformer block. This correction chain makes the architecture recurrent. Training uses a K-step unrolling procedure where the correction is applied iteratively across all positions in parallel. A pretrained standard transformer can be adapted by adding a zero-initialized correction FFN and fine-tuning.
AI.result: A D=5 context-ready model beats a 12-layer standard transformer while generating 1.7× faster on an A100. With K=10 correction steps, a single-layer (D=1) model surpasses a 6-layer transformer with 2.6× inference speedup. Sequential inference matches parallel K=10 within 0.01 PPL. Wide representations and long contexts yield the greatest benefits. On a pointer-chasing task, a D=1 model trained with BPTT solves all 10 composition levels, unlike standard transformers which show staircase-like depth dependence.
AI.conclusion: The context-ready transformer successfully trades depth for recurrent correction steps, achieving strong performance with fast sequential inference. It unifies parallel training with efficient recurrent generation, converts pretrained transformers, and excels on compositionally demanding tasks that typically require many layers.

title: Operator Learning for Cubic Nonlinear Schrödinger Equation on Periodic Domains
summary: We consider the cubic nonlinear Schrödinger (NLS) equation on two-dimensional flat tori with varying aspect ratios. In this formulation, the choice of aspect ratio governs the Fourier resonance structure, so rational and irrational geometries can exhibit different high-frequency cascade behaviors. We present a geometry-conditioned Fourier neural operator (FNO) for the cubic defocusing NLS equation, where the input consists of the real and imaginary parts of the solution together with the aspect-ratio parameter \(ω^2\). The model is trained to approximate the one-step solution operator and is evaluated on unseen trajectories generated from random-phase initial data using Fourier pseudospectral method. Our numerical experiments show that the learned operator captures the main solution dynamics on both tori and reproduces the distinct Sobolev norm behavior of the two geometries, with stronger \(H^2\)-growth on the rational torus and more constrained behavior on the irrational torus, consistent with the findings of \cite{hrabski2021energy}. We perform ablation studies to examine the roles of retained Fourier modes, activation functions, Fourier-layer depth, and explicit geometry conditioning. The results indicate that including $ω^2$ improves long-time predictive accuracy, especially for the rational geometry, and supports the use of geometry-aware neural operators for learning spectral-transfer phenomena in nonlinear dispersive partial differential equations.

AI.tldr: A geometry-conditioned Fourier neural operator (FNO) is proposed for the cubic defocusing NLS equation on 2D flat tori, where the aspect ratio ω² governs Fourier resonance and cascade behavior. The model captures distinct Sobolev growth patterns between rational and irrational tori, with explicit geometry conditioning improving long-time prediction accuracy.
AI.motivation: The cubic NLS equation on 2D tori exhibits qualitatively different high-frequency cascade dynamics depending on whether the aspect ratio is rational or irrational, due to changes in Fourier resonance structure. Standard neural operators lack awareness of this geometric parameter, motivating a geometry-conditioned approach that can generalize across both regimes and capture geometry-dependent spectral transfer phenomena.
AI.method: A Fourier neural operator is augmented with an explicit geometry-conditioning mechanism that receives the aspect-ratio parameter ω² alongside the real and imaginary parts of the solution. The model is trained to approximate the one-step solution operator using data generated via Fourier pseudospectral method from random-phase initial conditions. Ablation studies systematically vary retained Fourier modes, activation functions, Fourier-layer depth, and the presence of explicit ω² conditioning.
AI.result: The learned operator successfully captures the main solution dynamics on both rational and irrational tori. It reproduces the distinct Sobolev norm behavior: stronger H²-growth on the rational torus and more constrained growth on the irrational torus, consistent with Hrabski et al. (2021). Ablation results show that including ω² conditioning improves long-time predictive accuracy, particularly for the rational geometry.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-aware neural operators are effective for learning spectral-transfer phenomena in nonlinear dispersive PDEs. Explicit conditioning on the aspect ratio enables a single model to handle both rational and irrational geometries, capturing their qualitatively distinct energy cascade behaviors without requiring separate models for each regime.

title: ToE: A Hierarchical and Explainable Claim Verification Framework with Dynamic Multi-source Evidence Retrieval and Aggregation
summary: The rapid spread of fake news poses increasing threats to information ecosystems, especially as AI-generated misinformation under Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) poisoning allows adversarially crafted content to be systematically surfaced by retrieval systems, contaminating LLM reasoning. In this paper, we propose Tree of Evidence (ToE), a hierarchical evidence reasoning framework for automated fact-checking that models each claim as a dynamically expanding argument tree. ToE integrates a reinforcement learning-driven multi-source retrieval agent, an evidence evaluation agent, and an argument tree aggregation algorithm to iteratively decompose, retrieve, and verify claims through an explainable evidence chain. We further provide a theoretical analysis of the retrieval process, deriving a formal error bound that guarantees the learned policy converges to a neighborhood of the information-theoretically optimal policy. Experiments across multiple datasets and backbone LLMs demonstrate that ToE achieves improvements ranging from 4 to 24 percentage points over competitive baselines, with particularly pronounced gains on adversarially poisoned inputs.

AI.tldr: Tree of Evidence (ToE) is a hierarchical evidence reasoning framework for automated fact-checking that uses reinforcement learning-driven multi-source retrieval, evidence evaluation, and argument tree aggregation to decompose, retrieve, and verify claims. It achieves 4–24 pp improvements over baselines, especially against adversarially poisoned inputs, and provides theoretical convergence guarantees for the retrieval policy.
AI.motivation: Fake news and AI-generated misinformation under Generative Engine Optimization (GEO) poisoning enable adversarially crafted content to be surfaced by retrieval systems, contaminating LLM reasoning. Existing fact-checking methods lack robust, explainable, multi-step evidence reasoning capable of handling such adversarial contamination.
AI.method: ToE models each claim as a dynamically expanding argument tree. It comprises three components: (1) a reinforcement learning-driven multi-source retrieval agent that iteratively gathers evidence; (2) an evidence evaluation agent that assesses credibility; and (3) an argument tree aggregation algorithm that synthesizes an explainable evidence chain. A theoretical analysis derives a formal error bound showing the learned policy converges to a neighborhood of the information-theoretically optimal policy.
AI.result: Experiments across multiple datasets and backbone LLMs show ToE achieves improvements of 4 to 24 percentage points over competitive baselines, with particularly pronounced gains on adversarially poisoned inputs.
AI.conclusion: ToE provides a principled, explainable, and robust framework for automated fact-checking that effectively counters GEO-style adversarial poisoning through hierarchical evidence reasoning with formal convergence guarantees.

title: Listwise Explanation of Embedding-Based Rankings via Semantic Chunk Grouping
summary: Dense embedding rankers score documents through contextual sentence- and passage-level representations. Yet many listwise explanation methods still attribute rankings to isolated words. This feature-unit mismatch leaves word-level features too fragmented for dense semantic ranking. We introduce ChunkGroupSHAP, a listwise Shapley method that clusters semantically related chunks into shared cross-document features. Masking a group perturbs all documents with related evidence, attributing rankings at a granularity closer to dense representations while preserving the listwise setup. Our findings across MS MARCO, FinanceBench, AILACaseDocs, and FinQA with E5 rankers and BM25 show that the best explanation unit is setting-dependent: word features for lexical BM25, corpus-level groups for dense rankers, and query-local grouping for heterogeneous web retrieval. Feature units should thus follow both the ranker's representational granularity and the structure of the retrieved corpus.

AI.tldr: ChunkGroupSHAP introduces a listwise explanation method for dense retrieval rankers by clustering semantically related text chunks into cross-document feature groups, bridging the granularity mismatch between word-level attribution and passage-level dense representations. The best explanation unit depends on the ranker type and corpus structure.
AI.motivation: Existing listwise explanation methods for document ranking attribute importance to isolated words, but dense embedding rankers (e.g., E5) operate on sentence- and passage-level contextual representations. This feature-unit mismatch renders word-level features too fragmented and semantically incoherent for explaining dense neural rankers, motivating a coarser, semantically grouped explanation unit.
AI.method: The authors propose ChunkGroupSHAP, a listwise Shapley-value-based method that (1) clusters semantically related text chunks into shared cross-document feature groups using embedding similarity, and (2) perturbs these groups collectively during Shapley sampling, so masking a group removes related evidence across all documents. This preserves the listwise ranking setup while attributing importance at a granularity aligned with dense representations. The method is evaluated against word-level and sentence-level baselines across multiple corpora and ranker types.
AI.result: Experiments across MS MARCO, FinanceBench, AILACaseDocs, and FinQA using both E5 dense rankers and BM25 reveal that the optimal explanation unit is setting-dependent: word-level features work best for lexical BM25, corpus-level chunk groups work best for dense rankers on homogeneous corpora, and query-local grouping is most effective for heterogeneous web retrieval scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Feature units for ranker explanations should be chosen to match both the representational granularity of the underlying ranker and the structural characteristics of the retrieved corpus. ChunkGroupSHAP provides a principled way to adapt explanation granularity for dense retrieval settings.

title: UNICS: Multilingual Code Search via Unified Pseudocode and Contrastive Transfer Learning
comment: Accepted to the ACM International Conference on the Foundations of Software Engineering (FSE 2026). 24.pages
summary: While pre-trained models have achieved remarkable success in code search, their multilingual capabilities remain a major hurdle, plagued by data imbalance, cross-lingual semantic interference, and the loss of critical information from existing unified representations like Abstract Syntax Trees (ASTs) or Intermediate Representations (IRs). Furthermore, conventional contrastive learning strategies often rely on simplistic hard negative sampling while overlooking the potential of mining hard positives to learn code's intrinsic semantic invariance. To address these challenges, we introduce UNICS, a framework for multilingual code search built on a two-stage training strategy. In the first stage, UNICS is pre-trained on a novel dataset we constructed, which uses pseudo-code as a unified representation to learn a cross-lingual, algorithm-level logic that preserves full semantic fidelity. The second stage employs a multi-task transfer learning strategy that adapts this general knowledge to specific languages by decomposing code into semantic slices (e.g., API calls, function bodies) and incorporating tasks for hard positive mining and cross-lingual dynamic hard negative sampling. Experimental results demonstrate that UNICS achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple multilingual and cross-lingual benchmarks, showcasing superior generalization and performance balance, especially in zero-shot transfer tasks to low-resource languages.

AI.tldr: UNICS is a two-stage multilingual code search framework that uses pseudo-code as a unified representation during pre-training, followed by multi-task transfer learning with hard positive mining and cross-lingual dynamic hard negative sampling, achieving state-of-the-art results especially for low-resource languages.
AI.motivation: Existing pre-trained models for code search suffer from three key limitations: (1) data imbalance across programming languages, (2) cross-lingual semantic interference, and (3) information loss from unified representations like ASTs or IRs. Additionally, conventional contrastive learning relies on simplistic hard negative sampling while neglecting hard positive mining to capture intrinsic semantic invariance in code.
AI.method: UNICS employs a two-stage training strategy: Stage 1 pre-trains on a newly constructed pseudo-code dataset that serves as a unified, algorithm-level representation preserving full semantic fidelity across languages. Stage 2 uses multi-task transfer learning that adapts general knowledge to specific languages by decomposing code into semantic slices (API calls, function bodies, etc.) and incorporates hard positive mining alongside cross-lingual dynamic hard negative sampling.
AI.result: UNICS achieves state-of-the-art performance across multiple multilingual and cross-lingual benchmarks, demonstrating superior generalization and balanced performance, with particularly strong results in zero-shot transfer tasks targeting low-resource programming languages.
AI.conclusion: The two-stage approach of pseudo-code pre-training followed by semantic-slice-based multi-task transfer learning effectively addresses multilingual code search challenges, with hard positive mining proving to be a valuable complement to traditional hard negative sampling in contrastive learning for code representation.

title: Towards Value-Constrained Credit Assignment in Fully Delegated AI Cooperatives
summary: We propose a framework for reward allocation in fully delegated AI cooperatives where humans are represented by agents that contribute data and participate in model updates under heterogeneous value constraints. The key idea is to credit only those updates that remain admissible after screening them against each principal's value profile. We formulate value-conditioned gradient filtering, online marginal contribution signals, and cumulative revenue settlement within a traversal learning (TL) substrate. TL is especially attractive here because it performs decentralized backpropagation without the quality loss associated with aggregation-centric distributed learning and, we argue, offers a finer attribution substrate than FedAvg-style federated learning by preserving explicit traversal and gradient paths. The framework is positioned against data valuation, federated contribution estimation, personalized federated learning, and pluralistic alignment.

AI.tldr: Proposes a reward allocation framework for AI cooperatives where human-representing agents contribute data under heterogeneous value constraints. Uses value-conditioned gradient filtering and traversal learning (TL) for decentralized backpropagation with fine-grained contribution attribution and cumulative revenue settlement.
AI.motivation: Current distributed learning paradigms (e.g., FedAvg-style federated learning) lack fine-grained attribution mechanisms for reward allocation when agents have heterogeneous value constraints. There is a need for a framework that fairly credits contributions in fully delegated AI cooperatives while respecting each principal's value profile.
AI.method: The framework employs value-conditioned gradient filtering to screen updates against each principal's value profile, online marginal contribution signals for real-time attribution, and cumulative revenue settlement. These operate atop a traversal learning (TL) substrate, which enables decentralized backpropagation while preserving explicit traversal and gradient paths for finer attribution.
AI.result: The authors position TL as offering finer attribution than FedAvg-style federated learning by avoiding aggregation-centric quality loss and preserving explicit gradient paths. The framework is contextualized against data valuation, federated contribution estimation, personalized federated learning, and pluralistic alignment.
AI.conclusion: Traversal learning provides a superior substrate for reward allocation in AI cooperatives by enabling value-conditioned screening and fine-grained contribution tracking, addressing limitations of existing federated and distributed learning approaches.

title: Decoys Cannot Go Everywhere: Mapping the Deception Surface in MITRE ATT&CK
summary: Cyber deception research often assumes that a decoy can be placed wherever there is attacker behavior. This work tests that assumption across MITRE ATT&CK v18.1. We introduce a four-criterion rubric for infrastructure deception and apply it to all 250 ATT&CK techniques. The rubric evaluates whether a defender-controlled decoy can be placed, whether an attacker is likely to interact with it, what intelligence that interaction can yield, and whether the interaction reliably indicates malice. The resulting deception surface is sparse: only 80 techniques (32%) admit a decoy the attacker could plausibly reach. For the remaining 170 techniques, there is no defender-controlled asset in the attacker's path that can be fabricated as a decoy. Decoy placement across those 80 techniques falls into two patterns we call Sweep and Seek. In Sweep, the attacker moves broadly through assets in range and encounters the decoy as part of that activity. In Seek, the attacker looks for a specific kind of asset and interacts with a fabricated version of it. These patterns give a simple placement rule: a decoy must either sit on a sweep path or imitate a sought asset. We also show that decoys usually have useful intelligence potential, but whether an attacker interacts with them at all, and whether that interaction reliably indicates malice, both vary. We release the rubric, decision rules, and per-technique assessment as an auditable baseline for future deception research and deployment planning, and show that infrastructure decoys cannot be assumed to apply to all attacker behavior.

AI.tldr: The paper challenges the assumption that decoys can be placed for any attacker behavior. Applying a four-criterion rubric to all 250 MITRE ATT&CK v18.1 techniques, only 32% (80 techniques) admit plausible decoy placement. The resulting deception surface is sparse and falls into two patterns: Sweep (attacker encounters decoy while moving broadly) and Seek (attacker looks for a specific asset, finds a fabricated one).
AI.motivation: Cyber deception research implicitly assumes decoys can be deployed wherever attacker behavior exists. This work empirically tests that assumption, aiming to map the true "deception surface" — the subset of adversary techniques where defender-controlled decoys are actually feasible and meaningful.
AI.method: The authors construct a four-criterion rubric: (1) whether a defender-controlled decoy can be placed, (2) whether an attacker is likely to interact with it, (3) what intelligence that interaction yields, and (4) whether the interaction reliably indicates malice. This rubric is systematically applied to all 250 techniques in MITRE ATT&CK v18.1, yielding a per-technique auditable assessment.
AI.result: Only 80 out of 250 techniques (32%) admit a decoy an attacker could plausibly reach; the remaining 170 lack any defender-controlled asset in the attacker's path. Decoy placement across viable techniques follows two patterns: Sweep (broad movement across in-range assets) and Seek (targeted search for a specific asset type). Intelligence potential is generally high, but likelihood of interaction and reliability as a malice indicator both vary considerably.
AI.conclusion: Infrastructure decoys cannot be assumed to apply universally to all attacker behavior. The deception surface is sparse and structured around two simple placement rules: place a decoy on a sweep path or imitate a sought asset. The rubric and per-technique assessment are released as an auditable baseline for future deception research and operational planning.

title: EntMTP: Accelerating LLM Inference with Entropy Guided Multi Token Prediction
summary: Multi-token prediction has been shown to increase data density during training, improve downstream text-generation quality, and serves as the defacto approach for self-speculative decoding. Existing foundation and open source models that use MTP heads commit to a static tree-based attention topology throughout the entire generation sequence, meaning the speculation depth, and thus the compute required during verification, stays constant regardless of the context. This is fundamentally misaligned with the entropy patterns of natural language where low-entropy regions often support reliable multi-step drafting, while high-entropy regions require more conservative speculation. To address this, we propose Entropy-guided Multi-Token Prediction (EntMTP), a training-free scheduler that toggles between tree-based attention topologies from a set of task-specific pareto-optimal trees conditioned on a running estimate of local generation entropy. By matching speculation depth to context predictability, EntMTP maximizes expected accepted-token throughput across the full distribution of generated text without sacrificing generation quality. When evaluated across Humaneval, ShareGPT, GSM8k, and Litbench benchmarks, EntMTP consistently achieves a 1.15x speedup against Hydra and peak speedup of 1.36x against Medusa baselines respectively.

AI.tldr: EntMTP is a training-free scheduler that dynamically adjusts multi-token prediction tree depth based on local generation entropy, achieving 1.15x–1.36x speedups over Hydra and Medusa baselines without quality loss.
AI.motivation: Existing MTP models use a static tree-based attention topology with constant speculation depth, which is misaligned with natural language entropy patterns — low-entropy regions can support aggressive multi-step drafting while high-entropy regions require conservative speculation.
AI.method: EntMTP uses a running estimate of local generation entropy to dynamically toggle between a set of task-specific Pareto-optimal tree attention topologies, matching speculation depth to contextual predictability without any additional training.
AI.result: EntMTP achieves a 1.15x speedup against Hydra and a peak speedup of 1.36x against Medusa baselines across Humaneval, ShareGPT, GSM8k, and Litbench benchmarks, with no degradation in generation quality.
AI.conclusion: Entropy-guided dynamic topology scheduling effectively aligns MTP speculation depth with context predictability, yielding consistent throughput gains across diverse benchmarks while preserving output quality.

title: The Curse of Multiple Mediators: Hidden Interaction Effects in Activation Patching
summary: Activation patching is the primary tool in mechanistic interpretability. It attributes causal responsibility for a model behavior to each of its individual components by estimating its natural indirect effect (NIE). Re-deriving the activation patching estimand from causal mediation analysis, we find that the NIE does not solely capture the causal effect through the specific component. It also contains interaction effects (INT) that measure how much the component's causal effect itself depends on the state of other components in the model. A natural response may be to try to eliminate INT by adjusting the estimator or unit of analysis, but each of these potential remedies has predictable failure modes. We demonstrate these failure modes in the GPT-2 IOI circuit; components whose causal importance is conditional on the state of other components are either invisible or artificially inflated, and INT variance explains the previously documented instability of faithfulness scores. We prove that INT scales with the distance between clean and patched component activations, is negligible when the model is locally affine, and decomposes combinatorially into pairwise and higher-order group interactions. Despite its inevitability, INT is not a nuisance to be eliminated, but rather a diagnostic for interpretability studies. Its individual and group-level magnitude and sign signal when causal conclusions are prompt-dependent, and when greedy NIE-based component ranking will miss mechanisms only discoverable through combinatorial search.

AI.tldr: Activation patching (widely used in mechanistic interpretability) actually estimates the natural indirect effect (NIE) from causal mediation analysis, which includes not only the targeted component's causal effect but also interaction effects (INT) that depend on other components' states. The authors prove INT cannot be eliminated without failure modes, demonstrate these failures in GPT-2 IOI circuits, and argue INT should be embraced as a diagnostic tool rather than treated as a nuisance.
AI.motivation: Activation patching is the dominant method for attributing causal responsibility in mechanistic interpretability, yet the community has not rigorously examined what the estimator actually captures. The authors aim to clarify that the NIE estimand inherently includes interaction effects, reveal the failure modes of naive remedies, and reframe INT as valuable diagnostic information rather than unwanted noise.
AI.method: The authors re-derive the activation patching estimand from causal mediation analysis (Pearl, 2001), decomposing it into the pure natural indirect effect and interaction effects (INT). They prove INT scales with distance between clean/corrupted activations, becomes negligible under local linearity, and decomposes combinatorially into pairwise and higher-order interactions. Empirical verification uses the GPT-2 small IOI (Indirect Object Identification) circuit, demonstrating failure modes when INT is ignored and showing how INT explains instability in faithfulness scores.
AI.result: INT is shown to be theoretically inevitable: attempts to eliminate it via adjusted estimators or alternative units of analysis lead to predictable failure modes. In the GPT-2 IOI circuit, components whose causal importance is conditional on other components' states become invisible or artificially inflated. INT variance explains previously documented faithfulness-score instability. The combinatorial decomposition reveals pairwise and group-level interaction structure.
AI.conclusion: INT should not be treated as a nuisance to eliminate but as a diagnostic signal. Its magnitude and sign at individual and group levels indicate when causal conclusions are prompt-dependent and when greedy NIE-based component ranking will miss mechanisms requiring combinatorial search. This reframes activation patching from a tool yielding simple rankings to one that reveals interaction-dependent mechanisms.

title: Towards Reliable and Robust LLM Planning: Symbolic Feedback-Driven Iterative Self-Refinement Framework
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have attracted widespread attention from academia and industry, yet their deployment raises critical security concerns regarding robustness and reliability. Planning, a core component of intelligent behavior, remains challenging for LLMs, which often produce infeasible or incorrect solutions in long-horizon decision-making tasks due to inherent complexity. In this paper, we propose a symbolic feedback-driven iterative self-refinement framework to enhance the robustness and reliability of LLMs in long-horizon planning. Specifically, a natural language prompting mechanism is introduced to map logical symbols into natural language descriptions, enabling LLMs to better capture task constraints and semantics. We further design a symbolic verifier that identifies errors and converts them into corrective instructions interpretable by the LLM, thereby guiding self-refinement. In addition, we leverage a plan recognizer to infer goal reachability, facilitating more effective guidance toward desired goals. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently improves both feasibility and correctness in long-horizon planning tasks. This highlights its effectiveness in enhancing the reliability of LLM-based planning and potential to enable more trustworthy AI systems.

AI.tldr: Proposes a symbolic feedback-driven iterative self-refinement framework that uses natural language prompting, symbolic verification, and plan recognition to improve LLM robustness and reliability in long-horizon planning tasks.
AI.motivation: LLMs struggle with long-horizon planning, frequently producing infeasible or incorrect solutions. Existing approaches lack mechanisms to systematically detect errors and provide interpretable corrective feedback, creating a need for a framework that bridges symbolic reasoning with LLM-based planning to enhance reliability.
AI.method: A three-component iterative self-refinement framework: (1) a natural language prompting mechanism that maps logical symbols into natural language to improve LLM comprehension of task constraints and semantics; (2) a symbolic verifier that detects planning errors and generates corrective instructions interpretable by the LLM; and (3) a plan recognizer that infers goal reachability to steer the LLM toward desired goals. These components operate in a feedback loop enabling iterative refinement.
AI.result: The proposed framework consistently improves both feasibility and correctness metrics in long-horizon planning tasks, demonstrating enhanced robustness and reliability compared to baseline LLM planning approaches.
AI.conclusion: The symbolic feedback-driven self-refinement framework effectively enhances LLM-based planning reliability, offering a promising direction for building more trustworthy AI systems capable of complex, long-horizon decision-making.

title: Fast and Feasible: Permutation-based Constrained Reranking for Revenue Maximization
summary: Search and recommender systems have produced highly relevant search results. A natural next step in the development of such systems in e-commerce is to rerank these results to increase the platform's revenue from paid promotion products. However, maximizing revenue alone may degrade the user experience by reducing relevance or increasing fraud risk. To avoid this, we state the reranking problem as an integer linear program ($ILP$) that maximizes revenue subject to per-query constraints on other metrics, e.g., relevance. Since solving $ILP$ exactly for every query is slow for deployment to the online service, we propose a lightweight permutation-based reranking approximation algorithm PermR. At each step, the algorithm selects a pair of neighboring items and swaps them to either improve the objective or repair a violated constraint. We evaluate PermR across multiple categories of a large classified platform in offline and online settings. PermR achieves about 63\% of the ILP revenue improvement, within production latency limits, preserving all constraints. In a 14-day online A/B test over 56 million search queries, PermR increased revenue by $2$\%.

AI.tldr: PermR is a lightweight permutation-based reranking algorithm that approximates an integer linear program (ILP) to maximize e-commerce platform revenue while respecting per-query constraints on relevance and fraud risk. It achieves ~63% of optimal ILP revenue gains within production latency, delivering a 2% revenue increase in a 14-day A/B test over 56 million queries.
AI.motivation: E-commerce search and recommender systems must balance revenue maximization from paid promotions with user experience (relevance) and fraud risk. Exact ILP solutions are too slow for online deployment, necessitating a fast, approximate reranking method that respects multiple constraints.
AI.method: The authors formulate reranking as an integer linear program (ILP) maximizing revenue subject to per-query constraints. They propose PermR, a greedy approximation algorithm that iteratively selects and swaps neighboring item pairs in the ranked list, accepting swaps that improve the objective or repair constraint violations.
AI.result: PermR achieved ~63% of the ILP's revenue improvement within production latency limits while preserving all constraints. In a 14-day online A/B test across 56 million search queries on a large classifieds platform, PermR yielded a 2% revenue increase.
AI.conclusion: PermR provides a practical, deployable solution for revenue-aware reranking under multiple metric constraints, demonstrating that a lightweight greedy swap-based approximation can capture a majority of optimal ILP gains while meeting strict online serving requirements.

title: Reasoning Beyond Prediction: From Data-Driven to Causal Software Engineering
comment: Accepted for publication in Communications of the ACM
summary: Software engineering is an intellectually demanding, creative discipline that juggles a web of interdependent tasks to design, build, and assure the quality of increasingly complex systems. As our expectations from software soar - with demands spanning AI-driven products, pervasively distributed and cloud-native architectures, and deeply embedded cyber-physical environments - its complexity steadily increases. In response, a new wave of co-engineering methods and tools, fueled by deep learning, has emerged to augment the process, enhancing automation and decision support. Yet, these advances remain far from delivering the kind of intelligent support that modern software development demands. We call for a new paradigm of human-machine cooperation: one where machines don't just automate routine tasks or predict from learned patterns, but actively amplify engineers' reasoning through the lens of causation. As software becomes smarter, a smarter support is needed.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that current AI-augmented software engineering tools, based primarily on deep learning and pattern prediction, are insufficient. It calls for a new paradigm of human-machine cooperation where machines amplify engineers' reasoning through causal inference, rather than merely automating tasks.
AI.motivation: Software systems are growing in complexity — spanning AI-driven products, cloud-native architectures, and cyber-physical environments. Existing deep learning-based co-engineering tools still fall short of providing the truly intelligent decision support that modern software development requires.
AI.method: This is a position/vision paper that proposes shifting from correlation-based deep learning approaches toward a causation-centric human-machine cooperation paradigm. Rather than introducing a concrete algorithm, it advocates for machines that actively reason about cause-and-effect relationships to amplify engineers' cognitive capabilities.
AI.result: This paper does not present empirical results, as it is a vision statement articulating a research agenda for causation-driven intelligent support in software engineering.
AI.conclusion: As software becomes smarter, the tools supporting its development must similarly evolve. The authors call for a paradigm shift toward causation-based machine reasoning that genuinely augments human software engineers, rather than merely automating routine tasks or making statistical predictions.

title: Estimation--Prediction Tradeoff in Causal Probabilistic Temporal Graphs
summary: Temporal link prediction is usually evaluated by predictive performance on unseen edges, but in probabilistic temporal graphs this criterion can conflate model error with irreducible uncertainty. We study this issue by characterising an inherent estimation--prediction tradeoff in binary logistic models where regimes that maximise Fisher information and improve parameter recoverability are also those with the highest entropy, making individual predictions intrinsically harder even under perfect parameter recovery. We propose a probabilistic causal framework for generating temporal graphs with transient edges and known ground-truth causal structure, allowing temporal link prediction to be evaluated jointly with causal parameter recovery. For the proposed binary logistic parametrisation, we derive the Cramér--Rao bound and validate the tradeoff between parameter estimation error and irreducible predictive loss. Our results show that predictive accuracy alone may not reflect whether a model has learned the underlying causal mechanism, motivating benchmarks that distinguish reducible model error from intrinsic process uncertainty.

AI.tldr: Temporal link prediction faces a fundamental estimation-prediction tradeoff: parameter regimes optimal for estimation (maximizing Fisher information) coincide with high-entropy states that make individual predictions inherently uncertain. The authors introduce a probabilistic causal framework with known ground truth to jointly evaluate predictive accuracy and causal parameter recovery, using Cramér-Rao bounds to formalize the tradeoff.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluation of temporal link prediction via predictive accuracy on unseen edges conflates model error with irreducible uncertainty inherent to the probabilistic process. The authors aim to disentangle these two sources of error by investigating the relationship between parameter recoverability and predictive difficulty in binary logistic models for temporal graphs.
AI.method: The authors propose a probabilistic causal framework for generating temporal graphs with transient edges and known ground-truth causal structure. Under a binary logistic parametrization, they derive the Cramér-Rao bound to characterize parameter estimation limits and formally analyze the tradeoff between Fisher information (estimation quality) and entropy (predictive uncertainty). The framework enables joint evaluation of causal parameter recovery and link prediction performance.
AI.result: The derived Cramér-Rao bound validates a clear tradeoff: parameter regimes that maximize Fisher information (enabling better parameter recovery) correspond to higher entropy, making individual edge predictions intrinsically harder even with perfect parameter knowledge. Consequently, predictive accuracy alone fails to indicate whether a model has captured the underlying causal mechanism.
AI.conclusion: Temporal link prediction benchmarks should distinguish reducible model error from intrinsic process uncertainty. The proposed causal framework provides a principled way to jointly evaluate both aspects, motivating evaluation protocols that go beyond raw predictive accuracy to assess causal understanding of the generative process.

title: SHARD: cell-keyed residual splitting for alignment-resistant private dense retrieval
comment: arXiv admin note: text overlap with arXiv:2606.26373
summary:
Dense embeddings underpin semantic search and RAG, yet a leaked vector store hands much of the underlying text back to whoever holds it. The attacks that make this possible (few-shot alignment, zero-shot inversion, unsupervised cross-space translation) share one weakness: the protected store is a single global geometry that can be aligned to a known one. A secret global rotation, the usual lightweight defence, is no exception: orthogonal Procrustes recovers it once the attacker has about the subspace dimension in known pairs.
  We introduce Shard, a retrieval-preserving embedding transform that removes this weak axis. The centred embedding is split into a short public prefix (for stage-1 retrieval) and a private residual sharded into C cells under separate secret keys; the residual is reranked under CKKS, where the keys cancel and leave the inner product exact. A single parameter C runs the design from the global-linear baseline it replaces (C=1) to per-document micro-keys (C=N). Because the rerank is full-dimensional, Shard returns the raw-space nDCG@10 that half-SVD truncation gives up; and because the residual is keyed cell-locally, mapping it back to a common frame under a diffuse known-plaintext leak costs roughly C times more anchors (median 200 to 102,400 at C=256), for a few encrypted queries. The short public prefix leaks far less neighbour structure, and a micro-key limit drives the residual graph to zero with an unlinkable, renewable template. The barrier holds against learned, non-linear and unsupervised aligners, and where a matched-utility noise defence de-anonymises almost every probe, Shard de-anonymises none. We are plain about the limits: within a cell the keys cancel, a targeted attacker needs only about d_priv anchors, and an overlapping reference corpus still leaks through the prefix. Shard is an attack-aware geometric defence, not a cryptographic guarantee.

AI.tldr: Shard splits embeddings into a short public prefix and a private residual sharded into C cells under separate secret keys, using CKKS-based reranking to recover exact inner products while geometrically defeating embedding inversion attacks.
AI.motivation: Dense vector stores used in semantic search and RAG are vulnerable to inversion attacks that recover underlying text. Existing defences like secret global rotations are broken by orthogonal Procrustes alignment with few known pairs. A defence is needed that removes this "single global geometry" weak axis without sacrificing retrieval quality.
AI.method: Shard centres embeddings and splits each into: (1) a short public prefix for fast stage-1 retrieval, and (2) a private residual partitioned into C cells, each encrypted under an independent secret key. Stage-2 reranking uses CKKS homomorphic encryption where cell keys cancel, yielding exact inner products. The parameter C scales from C=1 (global-linear baseline) to C=N (per-document micro-keys).
AI.result: Shard matches raw-space nDCG@10 that half-SVD truncation loses. Inversion cost scales roughly linearly with C: median required anchors rise from 200 (C=1) to 102,400 (C=256). The public prefix leaks minimal neighbour structure; at the micro-key limit, the residual graph goes to zero. Shard defeats learned, non-linear, and unsupervised aligners, and where noise-based defences fail (de-anonymising nearly all probes), Shard de-anonymises none.
AI.conclusion: Shard is an attack-aware geometric defence that raises the cost of embedding inversion proportionally to the number of shards C, with modest encrypted-query overhead. It is not a cryptographic guarantee: within-cell attacks with ~d_priv anchors remain possible, and overlapping reference corpora still leak through the public prefix.

title: Ko-WideSearch: A Korean Breadth-Search Benchmark for Exhaustive Set Enumeration by Web Agents
summary: Web-agent benchmarks overwhelmingly measure depth -- pinning one obscure answer behind a chain of constraints -- while breadth, exhaustively enumerating a closed set and filling each item's attributes, is barely evaluated, especially outside English. Breadth is also hard to build: certifying that a gold set is complete and every cell correct is far costlier than checking a single answer. I introduce \textsc{Ko-WideSearch}, a Korean breadth-search benchmark built by an automated synthesize-and-verify pipeline. Each task names a set-parent entity -- a TV season, a dynasty, a league, an administrative region, an election -- and asks for its full membership plus a per-item attribute table, graded by Item-, Column-, and Row-F1. It spans 228 tables over 190 entities and sixteen categories across three difficulty tiers, set by two structural knobs I dial independently -- table width and a 2-D composite key -- so cross-product membership climbs from 0\% to 100\% across the tiers. A single normalization-aware comparator is shared between gold construction and grading, so stable date and count columns are not over-dropped on formatting alone. Across twenty web agents, the failure is consistent: agents recover the set but not the rows (e.g.\ Item-F1 92.8 against Row-F1 53.7), accuracy falls steadily as the knobs harden, and neither more search nor more spend closes the gap. Broken down by cell, the hard part is finding the right value, not formatting it: open-ended free-text cells fail most, while cells with a standard answer such as a date or a name usually come out right.

AI.tldr: Introduces Ko-WideSearch, a Korean-language benchmark for evaluating web agents on breadth-search tasks (exhaustively enumerating sets and attributes) rather than depth-search. Automated pipeline generates 228 tables across 190 entities. Evaluated 20 agents: they recover sets well but fail on row-level attributes; harder structural knobs worsen performance, and open-ended cells are the primary failure mode.
AI.motivation: Current web-agent benchmarks overwhelmingly measure depth (finding one answer behind a chain of constraints) while neglecting breadth (exhaustively enumerating a closed set with per-item attributes), especially in non-English languages. Building breadth benchmarks is costly because certifying completeness and correctness of a gold set is far harder than checking a single answer.
AI.method: An automated synthesize-and-verify pipeline constructs Ko-WideSearch with 228 tables over 190 entities across 16 categories and 3 difficulty tiers. Difficulty is controlled by two independent structural knobs: table width and a 2-D composite key, causing cross-product membership to vary from 0% to 100% across tiers. A single normalization-aware comparator handles both gold construction and grading to avoid penalizing formatting differences in dates and counts. Evaluation uses Item-F1, Column-F1, and Row-F1 metrics. Twenty web agents are tested.
AI.result: Agents consistently recover the set well (Item-F1 92.8) but fail on row-level attributes (Row-F1 53.7). Accuracy drops steadily as the difficulty knobs harden. Neither more search steps nor higher inference spend closes the gap. Cell-level analysis shows the hard part is finding the correct value, not formatting it: open-ended free-text cells fail most, while standardized cells (dates, names) are typically correct.
AI.conclusion: Breadth search is a distinct, underevaluated capability in web agents that current systems handle poorly. The gap between set recovery and row-level accuracy is persistent and structural, not overcome by scaling search or compute. Open-ended attribute retrieval remains the key bottleneck.

title: Boundary condition fidelity for bottom-hole pressure and CO2 plume prediction in geological carbon storage
summary: Accurate prediction of bottom-hole pressure (BHP) and CO2 plume migration is essential for safe geological carbon storage, yet practical simulations often rely on truncated domains where artificial boundaries distort pressure diffusion and CO2 saturation footprints. In this study, we evaluate how boundary-condition fidelity affects BHP and CO2 plume prediction by comparing ten reduced-domain boundary treatments against full-domain reference simulations in homogeneous and heterogeneous reservoirs. We test uniform pore-volume multipliers, transmissibility modifiers, corner-adjusted pore-volume corrections, layered corrections, and gradual modifiers using BHP RMSE, NRMSE, peak pressure deviation, and plume Intersection over Union (IoU) as performance metrics. Our results show that conserving corner pore volume is the most important requirement for truncated-domain modeling. We find that uniform treatments which neglect corner storage generate large pressure errors, with BHP RMSE of 362 to 382 psi in the homogeneous model and 250 to 304 psi in the heterogeneous model, and yield plume IoU values near 0.80 to 0.84, indicating roughly 16 to 20% of the combined plume area is misrepresented. Corner-adjusted scenarios substantially reduce pressure errors and raise plume IoU above 0.94, but we observe that transmissibility correction is not universally beneficial. In homogeneous reservoirs, uniform transmissibility adjustment improves pressure fidelity; in heterogeneous reservoirs, it can over-restrict flow across variable-permeability boundary faces, increasing BHP error and contracting the predicted plume. We find the gradual modifier with transmissibility correction provides the most consistent performance, achieving BHP NRMSE below 3.7% and plume IoU above 0.97 in both reservoir types.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates ten boundary-condition treatments for truncated-domain geological CO2 storage simulations, finding that corner pore-volume conservation is essential for accuracy, and that a gradual modifier with transmissibility correction achieves the most consistent BHP and plume predictions across homogeneous and heterogeneous reservoirs.
AI.motivation: Practical geological carbon storage simulations often use truncated domains where artificial boundaries distort pressure diffusion and CO2 saturation footprints. There is a need to systematically evaluate which boundary-condition treatments best preserve BHP and plume migration fidelity compared to full-domain reference simulations.
AI.method: The authors compare ten reduced-domain boundary treatments — including uniform pore-volume multipliers, transmissibility modifiers, corner-adjusted pore-volume corrections, layered corrections, and gradual modifiers — against full-domain reference simulations in both homogeneous and heterogeneous reservoirs. Performance is quantified using BHP RMSE, NRMSE, peak pressure deviation, and plume Intersection over Union (IoU).
AI.result: Corner pore-volume conservation is the single most important factor for truncated-domain accuracy. Uniform treatments neglecting corner storage produce large BHP errors (RMSE: 362–382 psi homogeneous; 250–304 psi heterogeneous) and plume IoU of 0.80–0.84 (~16–20% misrepresentation). Corner-adjusted scenarios reduce pressure errors and raise IoU above 0.94. Transmissibility correction is not universally beneficial — it helps in homogeneous reservoirs but can over-restrict flow in heterogeneous ones, increasing BHP error and contracting the plume. The gradual modifier with transmissibility correction yields BHP NRMSE below 3.7% and plume IoU above 0.97 in both reservoir types.
AI.conclusion: Conserving corner pore volume is the most critical requirement for truncated-domain CO2 storage modeling. The gradual modifier combined with transmissibility correction provides the most robust and consistent performance across reservoir types, achieving high fidelity in both pressure and plume predictions.

title: Understanding Rollout Error in Graph World Models
summary: World models are often used for planning by rolling learned dynamics forward. Many planning environments, however, are not vectors or images; they are graphs of agents, tools, skills, routes, and dependencies. In these settings, a local prediction error may stay local or spread through the graph, and the failure mode changes again when edges are predicted rather than fixed. This paper studies long-horizon rollout error in Graph World Models (GWMs). We formulate a unified fixed-edge and dynamic-edge GWM framework with action nodes for node-, edge-, and graph-level decisions. We develop graph-valued rollout bounds that separate topology-induced amplification from model-induced amplification, and we introduce a joint node-edge operator for dynamic-edge rollouts. Guided by the analysis, we propose Error-Aware GWM, which combines spectral regularization, rollout consistency, and critical-node weighting. Across synthetic topologies and heterogeneous agent-graph testbeds, rollout error and planning regret grow with horizon, dynamic-edge training is needed when structure evolves, and Error-Aware GWM prevents long-horizon divergence while preserving prediction accuracy. Real-world graph benchmarks clarify the scope of GWMs: they are most useful for dynamic graph rollout and agent planning, while specialized graph models remain strong on static or sparse prediction tasks.

AI.tldr: This paper formalizes Graph World Models (GWMs) for planning on graph-structured environments, analyzes how rollout errors propagate through topology, and proposes Error-Aware GWM with spectral regularization and critical-node weighting to prevent long-horizon divergence.
AI.motivation: World models typically assume vector or image states, but many planning domains involve graphs of agents, tools, and dependencies. In these settings, prediction errors can propagate non-locally through graph topology, and the problem worsens when edges are dynamic (predicted) rather than fixed. No prior work formally characterizes long-horizon rollout error in graph-structured world models.
AI.method: The authors (1) formulate a unified GWM framework with action nodes supporting node-, edge-, and graph-level decisions, encompassing both fixed-edge and dynamic-edge settings; (2) derive graph-valued rollout bounds that separate topology-induced amplification from model-induced amplification and introduce a joint node-edge operator for dynamic-edge rollouts; (3) propose Error-Aware GWM incorporating spectral regularization, rollout consistency, and critical-node weighting to mitigate error accumulation. Evaluation spans synthetic topologies, heterogeneous agent-graph testbeds, and real-world graph benchmarks.
AI.result: Rollout error and planning regret grow with horizon. Dynamic-edge training is necessary when graph structure evolves. Error-Aware GWM prevents long-horizon divergence while preserving prediction accuracy. GWMs prove most useful for dynamic graph rollout and agent planning; specialized graph models remain superior on static or sparse prediction tasks.
AI.conclusion: GWMs fill a distinct niche — dynamic graph rollout and agent planning — where topology-aware error mitigation is critical. The theoretical bounds and Error-Aware GWM architecture provide a principled foundation for learning and planning on graph-structured world models.

title: Evolution-Aware Regression Test Prioritization of ML-Enabled Systems Using Gradient-Based Behavior Vectors
comment: Accepted to the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
summary: The machine learning(ML) component of an ML-enabled system evolves through retraining, fine-tuning, and optimization, so previously valid test results may no longer hold. A single evolution step can worsen performance on some test cases while improving others, making regression test prioritization inherently directional. We present Gradient-based Behavior Vector-Parameter Delta(GBV-PD), the first approach to operationalize the behavior vector space for evolution-aware regression test prioritization. GBV-PD represents each test case as a gradient-based vector(GBV), a low-dimensional projection of its loss gradient under the original model. It then projects the observed parameter update of the evolved model onto the same PCA basis and uses the resulting alignment to estimate whether each test case's loss is likely to increase or decrease, without running the evolved model on test cases during prioritization. In an empirical study across classification and regression tasks, GBV-PD consistently outperformed non-directional baselines and remained competitive with a full-gradient reference, while offering better time and storage profiles for repeated updates via reusable GBV caching. These results show that behavior-space ideas can be operationalized into a practical and efficient mechanism for repeated-update regression testing of evolving ML-enabled systems.

AI.tldr: GBV-PD introduces a gradient-based behavior vector approach for evolution-aware regression test prioritization in ML systems, enabling directional prediction of test case performance changes without executing the evolved model, outperforming non-directional baselines while maintaining computational efficiency.
AI.motivation: ML-enabled systems evolve through retraining and fine-tuning, making previously valid test results unreliable. A single evolution step can simultaneously improve some test cases and degrade others, rendering regression test prioritization inherently directional. Existing approaches lack a practical mechanism to predict per-test-case loss directionality without re-executing the evolved model during prioritization.
