AI.method: GBV-PD represents each test case as a gradient-based vector (GBV)—a low-dimensional PCA projection of its loss gradient computed under the original model. When the model evolves, the parameter delta is projected onto the same PCA basis. The alignment between the GBV and the projected parameter delta estimates whether each test case's loss is likely to increase or decrease, enabling directional prioritization without running the evolved model on test cases. GBVs can be cached and reused across repeated updates.
AI.result: In an empirical study spanning classification and regression tasks, GBV-PD consistently outperformed non-directional baselines, remained competitive with a full-gradient reference method, and offered superior time and storage profiles for repeated updates due to reusable GBV caching.
AI.conclusion: Behavior-space ideas can be operationalized into a practical, efficient mechanism for repeated-update regression testing of evolving ML-enabled systems, with GBV-PD serving as a viable approach for directional regression test prioritization.

title: Agent-Native Immune System: Architecture, Taxonomy, and Engineering
summary: The transition from static chat bots to autonomous agents--equipped with persistent memory, tool-use protocols, and multi-agent collaboration--has fundamentally expanded the AI threat landscape. Current defense mechanisms, such as perimeter security and training-time alignment, remain external to the agent's active reasoning loop. Consequently, they fall short: a fully aligned agent remains highly vulnerable to runtime hijacking via memory poisoning, tool-chain manipulation, or multi-agent protocol attacks. To address this critical gap, we introduce the Agent-Native Immune System (ANIS), the first biologically inspired, endogenous defense architecture embedded directly within the agent's cognitive loop. Our framework presents four primary contributions. First, we design a six-layer Immune Tower (L0-L5), distinctly incorporating Barrier Immunity (L1) as a non-cognitive, physical-and-logical isolation layer. Second, we establish a unified taxonomy of Agent Viruses and Agent Vaccines, formalizing the critical distinction between superficial non-parametric defenses and robust parametric vaccines. Third, we conceptualize the Harness Triad--Meta, Self, and Auto--a self-monitoring, meta-cognitive automation backbone that drives Continual Immune Learning (CIL), enabling vaccines to dynamically adapt to novel threats. Finally, we establish a rigorous theoretical demarcation between model alignment and agent immunity: while alignment provides a static "constitutional" value foundation during training, ANIS serves as the dynamic "law enforcement" mechanism during runtime. We conclude by framing open challenges for the field, including immune protocol standardization, novel evaluation metrics such as the Autoimmunity Rate (false-positive intervention rate), and the co-evolutionary dynamics between pathogens and vaccines within collective intelligence ecosystems.

AI.tldr: ANIS is a biologically inspired, six-layer defense architecture embedded within an agent's cognitive loop, introducing agent viruses/vaccines, a self-monitoring Harness Triad for continual immune learning, and a theoretical distinction between static alignment (training) and dynamic immunity (runtime).
AI.motivation: Existing defenses like perimeter security and training-time alignment operate outside the agent's reasoning loop, leaving agents vulnerable to runtime attacks such as memory poisoning, tool-chain manipulation, and multi-agent protocol hijacking. A defense mechanism integrated directly into the agent's active cognitive process is needed.
AI.method: The authors propose ANIS, featuring: (1) a six-layer Immune Tower (L0–L5) with Barrier Immunity (L1) as a physical-logical isolation layer; (2) a unified taxonomy of Agent Viruses and parametric/non-parametric Agent Vaccines; (3) the Harness Triad (Meta, Self, Auto) enabling Continual Immune Learning (CIL) for dynamic vaccine adaptation; and (4) a theoretical framework distinguishing model alignment from agent immunity.
AI.result: The paper presents a conceptual architecture and theoretical framework rather than empirical results. Key contributions include the Immune Tower design, virus/vaccine taxonomy, the Harness Triad for meta-cognitive automation, and the alignment-vs-immunity distinction. Open challenges identified include immune protocol standardization, Autoimmunity Rate metrics, and pathogen-vaccine co-evolution dynamics.
AI.conclusion: ANIS redefines AI safety by shifting from external, static defenses to an endogenous, adaptive immune system operating at runtime. The framework frames alignment as a constitutional foundation and immunity as real-time law enforcement, calling for collective standardization and new evaluation paradigms in agent security.

title: AdvancedShelLM: A Stateful Multi-Agent LLM Honeypot for SSH Deception
summary: LLM-based SSH honeypots can generate believable interactions, but evaluations indicate they remain somewhat identifiable to determined attackers, indicating the need for a better scaffolding. We present a new LLM-based honeypot design that uses a multi-agent, multi-LLM architecture to address the limitations of the previous shelLM LLM honeypot. Our honeypot, called AdvancedShelLM, uses two LLM agents, a Manager and a Worker, that better understand the commands while reducing incorrect responses and increasing deception. It implements an advanced permanent filesystem, allowing many simultaneous attackers to see the same changing files for the first time. It was evaluated with: (i) unit tests for generative capabilities, (ii) an AI attacker (ARACNE) to assess realism and deception, (iii) human attackers to assess its deceptive capability, and (iv) an Internet deployment to evaluate deception in real-world attacks. In unit test results, AdvancedShelLM achieved a pass rate of up to 99.02%. The AI attacker ARACNE had issues making a decision if the system is honeypot or not, but showed slight bias towards saying honeypot, even for a real Ubuntu shell. With human attackers, AdvancedShelLM deceived more humans than Cowrie, but had similar results as shelLM. The Internet deployment showed concrete evidence that the output of AdvancedShelLM can influence the behaviour of real-life attackers.

AI.tldr: AdvancedShelLM is a multi-agent, multi-LLM SSH honeypot that improves upon shelLM by using Manager and Worker agents, a permanent shared filesystem, and achieves up to 99.02% pass rate on unit tests. It deceives human attackers comparably to shelLM and better than Cowrie, while real-world deployment shows it can influence attacker behavior.
AI.motivation: Prior LLM-based honeypots like shelLM generate believable SSH interactions but remain identifiable to determined attackers. A better scaffolding/architecture is needed to reduce incorrect responses, improve deception, and support realistic multi-attacker scenarios with a persistent filesystem.
AI.method: AdvancedShelLM employs a multi-agent, multi-LLM architecture with two agents: a Manager (interprets attacker commands) and a Worker (generates shell responses). It implements an advanced permanent filesystem enabling concurrent attackers to observe consistent, changing files. Evaluation uses four methods: (i) unit tests for generative capability, (ii) the ARACNE AI attacker for realism assessment, (iii) human attackers for deceptive capability, and (iv) an Internet deployment for real-world deception measurement.
AI.result: Unit tests: up to 99.02% pass rate. ARACNE AI attacker: struggled to classify the system definitively but showed slight honeypot bias, even against a real Ubuntu shell. Human attackers: AdvancedShelLM deceived more humans than Cowrie, with comparable results to shelLM. Internet deployment: demonstrated concrete evidence that AdvancedShelLM's output influences real attacker behavior.
AI.conclusion: The multi-agent, multi-LLM architecture with a permanent filesystem advances LLM-based honeypot design. While AdvancedShelLM matches or exceeds prior systems in deception metrics, the ARACNE results suggest distinguishing honeypots from real systems remains challenging even for AI attackers. The real-world deployment validates practical applicability.

title: Narrative-UFET: Narrative Generation for Ultra-Fine Entity Typing
summary: Ultra-fine entity typing (UFET) assigns highly specific types to entity mentions, but current approaches struggle with types in the long tail. We hypothesize that a key limitation is the reliance on sentence-level context, since disambiguating evidence is often spread across multiple sentences. Testing this has been difficult because all existing UFET resources are sentence-level. We present Narrative-UFET, a controlled extension of UFET in which each entity mention is paired with an automatically generated short, coherent narrative. Synthesizing narratives lets us isolate the effect of specific discourse properties. We experiment with two paired variants: one in which the entity's type is held constant across the narrative (Maintain) and one in which it shifts (Change). We show that narrative context yields consistent improvements on long-tail types over sentence-level baselines, with the Change variant providing the stronger signal. A comparison against naturally occurring contexts shows that synthetic narratives yield stronger gains, indicating that controlled discourse construction can surface signals that real text leaves implicit. Substantial room for improvement remains, suggesting open directions in both discourse modeling and narrative construction.

AI.tldr: Narrative-UFET introduces synthetic multi-sentence narratives to improve ultra-fine entity typing on long-tail types, demonstrating that discourse-level context (especially when entity types shift across sentences) provides stronger disambiguating signals than sentence-level baselines or naturally occurring text.
AI.motivation: Current UFET systems rely on sentence-level context, which is insufficient for disambiguating long-tail entity types whose evidence is often distributed across multiple sentences. Existing UFET benchmarks are exclusively sentence-level, making it impossible to test the value of broader discourse context.
AI.method: The authors create Narrative-UFET, augmenting UFET entity mentions with automatically generated short, coherent narratives. They design two controlled narrative variants: Maintain (entity type held constant across sentences) and Change (entity type shifts across the narrative). Synthetic narratives are compared against sentence-level baselines and naturally occurring multi-sentence contexts to isolate the effects of discourse properties.
AI.result: Narrative context consistently improves performance on long-tail types over sentence-level baselines, with the Change variant providing the stronger signal. Synthetic narratives yield larger gains than naturally occurring contexts, suggesting that controlled discourse construction surfaces signals that real text leaves implicit.
AI.conclusion: Discourse-level context benefits UFET, particularly for rare types. Controlled narrative synthesis is a promising direction, but substantial room for improvement remains, pointing to open challenges in discourse modeling and narrative construction.

title: Productionized Fairness Measurement Under Privacy Constraints
summary: Fairness measurements in the form of disaggregated evaluations often rely on demographic signals that are legally constrained or culturally sensitive. Race and ethnicity signals are among the more difficult signals to curate and use for this task. This paper presents Privacy-Preserving Probabilistic Race/Ethnicity Estimation (PPRE) as a method for enabling fairness measurements with respect to race/ethnicity for U.S.\ LinkedIn members in a privacy-preserving manner. PPRE applies privacy technologies (specifically: secure two-party computation, differential privacy, and additive homomorphic encryption) on top of two race/ethnicity demographic signal sources (the Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding estimator and a sparse golden survey set of self-reported demographics) to power a fairness measurement solution with respect to US-based race/ethnicity demographics. We detail its privacy guarantees and demonstrate its application on candidate- and viewer-side fairness measurements. We close with a transferable framework for institutions seeking to implement similar privacy-preserving measurement infrastructure.

AI.tldr: LinkedIn presents PPRE, a system combining secure two-party computation, differential privacy, and additive homomorphic encryption with BISG and sparse survey data to enable privacy-preserving race/ethnicity fairness measurements for U.S. members.
AI.motivation: Race and ethnicity signals are legally constrained and culturally sensitive, making them difficult to curate for disaggregated fairness evaluations. Organizations need a method to measure algorithmic fairness across demographic groups without directly accessing or storing protected attributes, thereby complying with privacy regulations and ethical constraints.
AI.method: PPRE layers three privacy technologies — secure two-party computation, differential privacy, and additive homomorphic encryption — atop two demographic signal sources: the Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding (BISG) estimator and a sparse golden set of self-reported survey data. This architecture enables race/ethnicity probability estimation without exposing individual-level demographic information.
AI.result: The system successfully powers fairness measurements on both candidate-side and viewer-side evaluations for U.S. LinkedIn members while maintaining formal privacy guarantees. The paper also provides a transferable framework for other institutions.
AI.conclusion: Privacy-preserving demographic inference for fairness measurement is technically feasible and operationally viable using a layered privacy architecture. The approach allows organizations to conduct responsible fairness audits without compromising member privacy or violating legal constraints on sensitive demographic data.

title: Grounded Iterative Language Planning: How Parameterized World Models Reduce Hallucination Propagation in LLM Agents
summary: World models for language agents come in two useful forms. An agent-based world model calls an LLM API and reasons flexibly in language, but its errors appear as hallucinated state changes that are hard to score with ordinary regression losses. A parameterized world model is a trained transition predictor; its errors are easier to measure with quantities such as NodeMSE, delta accuracy, and validity accuracy, but it is usually weaker as a standalone planner. We compare these two families on four graph-structured planning benchmarks and introduce operational hallucination metrics for the agent-based case. The comparison motivates \textbf{Grounded Iterative Language Planning} (GILP), which trains only a small parameterized backbone and combines it with API-based agent reasoning. The backbone supplies valid actions, predicted state deltas, risk, and value; the LLM drafts an action and imagined delta; and a consistency gate asks for revision when the two disagree. On real GPT-4o-mini calls, GILP reduces hallucinated-state rate from 0.176 to 0.035. In calibrated simulator ablations, it raises success from 0.668 to 0.838 while adding only ~22% extra LLM calls.

AI.tldr: GILP combines a small trained world model with LLM-based planning, using a consistency gate to reconcile disagreements, cutting hallucinated-state rate from 0.176 to 0.035 and boosting success from 0.668 to 0.838 with only ~22% more LLM calls.
AI.motivation: World models for language agents suffer from a trade-off: agent-based (LLM) models reason flexibly but produce hallucinated state changes that are hard to evaluate with regression losses, while parameterized (trained) world models have measurable errors but are weaker planners. The authors seek to unify the strengths of both.
AI.method: Grounded Iterative Language Planning (GILP) pairs a small parameterized backbone (providing valid actions, predicted state deltas, risk, and value) with an LLM agent (drafting actions and imagined deltas). A consistency gate triggers revision when the two disagree. Evaluated on four graph-structured planning benchmarks using both real GPT-4o-mini calls and calibrated simulator ablations.
AI.result: On real GPT-4o-mini calls, GILP reduces hallucinated-state rate from 0.176 to 0.035. In calibrated simulator ablations, success rate improves from 0.668 to 0.838, requiring only ~22% additional LLM calls.
AI.conclusion: Hybridizing a small parameterized world model with LLM-based reasoning via a consistency gate effectively mitigates hallucination in language-agent planning while largely preserving the flexibility of LLM reasoning, yielding substantial gains in both state accuracy and task success at modest computational overhead.

title: SBridge: Identifying Source-to-Binary Function Similarity via Cross-Domain Control Block Matching
summary: We present SBridge, a precise approach for identifying functions in binaries that are similar to the given source code functions. Identifying reused code in binaries is critical for security, particularly for detecting propagated vulnerabilities. Although binary-to-binary comparison is feasible, leveraging source code as the reference is more practical because source code is easier to collect and analyze directly without compilation. However, significant gaps between source and binary representations, including function inlining, create challenges in cross-domain function detection. Existing approaches primarily rely on string literals or structural similarities between entire functions, failing to capture detailed code behavior and generating many false alarms. SBridge addresses these limitations through a key innovation: control block-based function matching, which encapsulates essential functional features by segmenting functions into meaningful units such as conditionals and loops. Leveraging control blocks as a cross-domain representation, SBridge enables precise measurement of function similarity between source and binary code, effectively overcoming challenges posed by function inlining and stripped binaries. For evaluation, we collected 3,904 real-world C/C++ binaries from BinKit. In experiments identifying binary functions identical to input source functions, despite approximately 40% of binary functions being inlined, SBridge achieved 75.13% recall@1 and 80.98% recall@5, outperforming existing approaches, which achieved up to 43.31% recall@1 and 50.2% recall@

AI.tldr: SBridge introduces control block-based matching to identify binary functions similar to given source code, achieving 75.13% recall@1 and 80.98% recall@5 on 3,904 real-world binaries, significantly outperforming prior methods that reached only 43.31% recall@1.
AI.motivation: Detecting reused code in binaries is critical for security (e.g., finding propagated vulnerabilities). Source code is more practical as a reference than binary-to-binary comparison, but cross-domain (source-to-binary) function matching is challenging due to function inlining, stripped binaries, and representation gaps. Existing approaches relying on string literals or whole-function structural similarity fail to capture detailed behavior and produce many false alarms.
AI.method: SBridge proposes control block-based function matching. Functions are segmented into meaningful units — control blocks such as conditionals and loops — which serve as a cross-domain representation encapsulating essential functional features. Similarity between source and binary functions is then measured precisely using these control blocks, overcoming inlining and stripping challenges.
AI.result: Evaluated on 3,904 real-world C/C++ binaries from BinKit. Despite ~40% of binary functions being inlined, SBridge achieved 75.13% recall@1 and 80.98% recall@5, substantially outperforming existing approaches that reached at most 43.31% recall@1 and 50.2% recall@5.
AI.conclusion: Control block-based cross-domain matching is an effective approach for source-to-binary function identification, significantly improving recall over existing methods and handling challenging scenarios like function inlining and stripped binaries.

title: Democratic ICAI: Debating Our Way to Steering Principles from Preferences
comment: Accepeted to the ICLR 2026 HCAIR Workshop, 40 pages
summary: Preference-based alignment often struggles to capture the reasoning that underlies human judgments. Many evaluations rely on multiple interacting criteria, yet pairwise labels reveal only the final choice rather than the considerations that shape preferences. Inverse Constitutional AI (ICAI) improves interpretability in decision making by summarizing preferences into natural-language principles, but its single-pass explanations miss much of the nuance involved in complex decisions. We introduce Democratic ICAI, a novel approach that gathers multiple competing rationales through structured persona debate, offering a broader and more expressive account of the factors influencing each comparison. From these richer signals, we derive clearer and more comprehensive steering principles and use them to guide decision modeling through both LLM-based and decision-tree judges. Experiments on creative preference benchmarks, MuCE-Pref and LiTBench, across multiple creative task categories show that Democratic ICAI yields a more faithful preference structure. It improves average preference prediction across tasks relative to deliberative prompting and principle-based baselines, while producing constitutions that LLM annotators prefer.

AI.tldr: Democratic ICAI enhances interpretable preference alignment by using multi-persona debates to extract richer constitutional principles, improving preference prediction accuracy and constitution quality over single-pass methods.
AI.motivation: Existing preference-based alignment methods (including Inverse Constitutional AI) fail to capture the nuanced, multi-criteria reasoning behind human judgments. Single-pass explanations miss the complexity inherent in creative decision-making, where multiple competing rationales often interact.
AI.method: Democratic ICAI introduces structured persona debates to elicit multiple competing rationales for each preference comparison. These richer signals are then synthesized into clearer constitutional principles, which guide decision modeling via both LLM-based judges and interpretable decision-tree judges.
AI.result: Evaluated on creative preference benchmarks (MuCE-Pref, LiTBench) across multiple creative task categories, Democratic ICAI yields more faithful preference structures. It improves average preference prediction accuracy over deliberative prompting and principle-based baselines, and produces constitutions preferred by LLM annotators.
AI.conclusion: Democratic ICAI demonstrates that aggregating diverse rationales through debate yields constitutions that are both more faithful to human preferences and more interpretable, advancing the state of preference-based alignment for complex, subjective domains like creative evaluation.

title: Ghost Without Shell: Measuring Non-Interactive SSH Attacks on Honeypots
summary: Cyber deception research has focused on improving honeypot deception capabilities to increase attacker engagement and extend their interactions to collect more and better intelligence. For SSH honeypots, this relies on the assumption that attackers log in, open a shell, and type. We tested whether this still held by deploying eleven SSH honeypots that served both interactive and non-interactive session requests for fifteen days. We collected 177,622 authenticated sessions and validated our results against an independent Cowrie dataset over the same time window. We found that 99.23% of sessions were non-interactive. Interactive sessions account for only 0.10%. The same pattern held in the comparative third-party dataset used for evaluation. This finding is important because a honeypot that focuses on interactive shells or evaluates success based on session length and the number of commands can miss most authenticated attacks and draw the wrong conclusions about what attackers do after login.

AI.tldr: Analysis of 177,622 authenticated SSH honeypot sessions over 15 days reveals that 99.23% are non-interactive — only 0.10% involve actual shell interaction. This undermines the prevailing assumption that attackers log in, open a shell, and type commands, challenging how honeypot deception and engagement metrics are evaluated.
AI.motivation: Existing cyber deception research, especially for SSH honeypots, operates on the assumption that attackers engage interactively — logging in, obtaining a shell, and typing commands. Honeypot design and success metrics (session length, command count) are built around this assumption. The authors sought to empirically test whether this assumption still reflects real-world attacker behavior.
AI.method: Deployed eleven SSH honeypots over a 15-day period, configured to serve both interactive and non-interactive session requests. Collected 177,622 authenticated sessions. Classified sessions as interactive vs. non-interactive. Validated findings against an independent, contemporaneous Cowrie honeypot dataset as a comparative baseline.
AI.result: 99.23% of all authenticated sessions were non-interactive (e.g., automated scanning, file transfers, tunneling). Only 0.10% of sessions involved interactive shell activity. The same distribution pattern was confirmed in the independent Cowrie validation dataset, ruling out deployment-specific artifacts.
AI.conclusion: Honeypots that focus exclusively on interactive shells, or that evaluate engagement success via session duration and command counts, risk missing the vast majority of authenticated attack activity. This can lead to skewed threat intelligence and incorrect conclusions about post-login attacker behavior. Honeypot design and evaluation metrics must account for non-interactive sessions.

title: Masked Language Flow Models
summary: Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) promise fast, parallel language generation, but their reverse transition factorises across token positions -- an approximation that breaks down in the few-step sampling regime where parallel generation ought to provide the greatest efficiency gains. Flow Language Models (FLMs) sidestep this limitation by learning a continuous flow that transports noise toward clean sequences represented in Euclidean space, inducing a flow map that can be distilled for single-step generation. However, this makes complex tasks requiring multi-step reasoning problematic for FLMs, as FLMs are forced to decode every token during generation. To address this, we introduce Masked Language Flow Models (MLFMs), which incorporate masking into FLMs using a continuous stochastic interpolant to bridge partially masked and clean sequences. This design enables conditional generation via continuous flows and allows pretrained MDMs to be converted into MLFMs through a simple, lightweight adaptation. Leveraging this flexibility, we propose a novel sampler that alternates continuous denoising with the discrete unmasking of confident tokens to better support multi-step reasoning. We evaluate our approach on GSM8K and MT-Bench and find, for the first time, that flow-based language models can be scaled to solve downstream reasoning and instruction-following tasks.

AI.tldr: MLFMs integrate masking into flow language models via continuous stochastic interpolants, enabling a hybrid sampler that alternates continuous denoising with discrete unmasking for multi-step reasoning, and allowing MDMs to be converted into flow models through lightweight adaptation.
AI.motivation: Masked Diffusion Models (MDMs) suffer from a factorized reverse transition approximation that degrades in few-step sampling, while Flow Language Models (FLMs) struggle with multi-step reasoning tasks because they must decode all tokens simultaneously. The authors aim to combine the strengths of both paradigms.
AI.method: The authors propose Masked Language Flow Models (MLFMs), which use a continuous stochastic interpolant to bridge partially masked and clean sequences. This design supports conditional generation via continuous flows and enables conversion of pretrained MDMs into MLFMs through lightweight adaptation. They also introduce a novel sampler that alternates between continuous denoising steps and discrete unmasking of high-confidence tokens.
AI.result: Evaluations on GSM8K and MT-Bench demonstrate that flow-based language models can be scaled to solve downstream reasoning and instruction-following tasks for the first time.
AI.conclusion: MLFMs successfully bridge the gap between masked diffusion and flow-based language modeling, preserving the parallel generation speed of flows while enabling the iterative, conditional decoding needed for complex reasoning tasks.

title: Quantum Generative Diffusion Model for Real-World Time Series
summary: Generative models have achieved remarkable success in data synthesis, though recent advances driven by increasing model scale have introduced challenges in computational cost and efficiency. Quantum machine learning offers a promising alternative, representing complex data distributions using compact, highly expressive models. Here, we propose QDiffusion-TS, the first quantum generative diffusion model for time series synthesis, and validate it on the IQM quantum processor. The framework extends a classical diffusion architecture by replacing feed-forward components within the denoising transformer with quantum neural networks, yielding a hybrid quantum transformer that reduces the number of trainable parameters in each replaced component by nearly three orders of magnitude. Evaluated on financial time series from Apple and Amazon, the model generates synthetic data that more accurately reproduces the real distributions, reducing Wasserstein distance by approximately 44% relative to its classical counterpart across both datasets. In a downstream forecasting task, augmentation with the generated data improves predictive performance by up to 71% in RMSE over a baseline trained solely on real data. These results show that quantum enhanced architectures can consistently match and frequently surpass classical performance with substantially fewer parameters, establishing a practical framework towards more efficient and scalable data-driven generative modelling.

AI.tldr: First quantum generative diffusion model for time series synthesis, using a hybrid quantum-classical transformer that reduces parameters by ~1000x while improving data fidelity (44% lower Wasserstein distance) and downstream forecasting (up to 71% RMSE improvement).
AI.motivation: Classical generative models are scaling to enormous sizes with prohibitive computational costs. Quantum machine learning offers compact, highly expressive models that could achieve comparable or superior performance with far fewer parameters, yet no quantum diffusion model exists for time series synthesis.
AI.method: QDiffusion-TS replaces feed-forward layers in a classical denoising diffusion transformer with quantum neural networks (variational quantum circuits), creating a hybrid quantum-classical architecture. Evaluated on Apple and Amazon financial time series using the IQM quantum processor, with assessment via Wasserstein distance and downstream forecasting tasks.
AI.result: The hybrid quantum transformer reduced trainable parameters per component by nearly three orders of magnitude. Synthetic data reduced Wasserstein distance by ~44% versus classical counterparts on both datasets. Data augmentation improved RMSE in forecasting by up to 71% over a baseline trained only on real data.
AI.conclusion: Quantum-enhanced generative architectures can match or surpass classical performance with substantially fewer parameters, offering a practical path toward more efficient and scalable generative modeling.

title: ATOD: Annealed Turn-aware On-policy Distillation for Multi-turn Autonomous Agents
summary: Training small language-model agents for long-horizon interactive tasks requires both fast imitation and reward-driven improvement. On-policy distillation (OPD) provides dense teacher guidance and typically improves rapidly in the early stage, but its gains saturate once the student approaches the teacher, limiting the final performance ceiling. Reinforcement learning (RL) directly optimizes environment rewards and encourages exploratory improvement toward a higher reward-defined ceiling, but sparse and delayed feedback makes early-stage learning much less efficient than OPD. In this paper, we propose ATOD (Annealed Turn-aware On-policy Distillation), a hybrid online distillation algorithm that explicitly exploits this complementarity. (1) ATOD uses an annealed OPD-RL schedule: OPD dominates early training to approach teacher-level behavior, while RL is gradually strengthened to drive reward-based exploration. (2) ATOD introduces Turn-level Disagreement-Uncertainty Reweighting (T-DUR), which softly amplifies high-utility turns and improves dense supervision in long trajectories. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA show that ATOD consistently outperforms competing post-training baselines: across the three student sizes, ATOD improves average success rate by 3.03 points over OPD and 23.62 points over GRPO, while surpassing the corresponding teacher models by 2.16 points.

AI.tldr: ATOD combines on-policy distillation (OPD) and reinforcement learning (RL) in an annealed schedule with turn-level reweighting to train small language-model agents, achieving better sample efficiency early on and higher final performance than either method alone.
AI.motivation: Training small LM agents for long-horizon interactive tasks faces a trade-off: OPD provides dense supervision and fast early improvement but plateaus near teacher performance; RL explores beyond the teacher but suffers from sparse, delayed feedback early on. The complementarity between OPD's early efficiency and RL's higher ceiling is underexploited.
AI.method: ATOD (Annealed Turn-aware On-policy Distillation) has two key components: (1) an annealed OPD-RL schedule where OPD loss weight is high initially and gradually decays while RL loss weight increases, allowing a smooth transition from imitation to reward-driven exploration; (2) Turn-level Disagreement-Uncertainty Reweighting (T-DUR), which computes disagreement between student and teacher token distributions and epistemic uncertainty to softly upweight high-utility turns, improving the quality of dense supervision in long trajectories.
AI.result: On ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-QA, ATOD consistently outperforms OPD-only, RL-only (GRPO), and other post-training baselines. Across three student model sizes, ATOD improves average success rate by 3.03 points over OPD, 23.62 points over GRPO, and surpasses the teacher models by 2.16 points.
AI.conclusion: The annealed OPD-RL schedule with T-DUR effectively resolves the imitation-reinforcement trade-off, enabling small LM agents to both learn rapidly from teacher guidance and ultimately exceed the teacher's performance through reward-driven exploration.

title: The ARDoCo Tool Landscape: REST API, TraceView, and TraceViz for Architecture Traceability
comment: Accepted at ASE'26 Tools and Datasets
summary: Context and Problem. Software development produces interrelated artifacts like software architecture documentation (SAD), software architecture models (SAMs), and source code, whose relationships are essential for maintenance and consistency checking. However, automatically recovering links between these artifacts (traceability link recovery (TLR)) remains difficult to deploy in practice. Method and Aim. We present an accessible tool landscape for ARDoCo's TLR approaches: the ARDoCo REST API exposes four TLR pipelines (SAD-SAM, SAM-Code, SAD-Code, and SAD-SAM-Code) via HTTP endpoints with asynchronous execution and caching; TraceView is a browser-based frontend with a guided wizard and interactive multi-panel exploration of recovered links and inconsistencies; and TraceViz, which is a VS Code extension that overlays trace links directly onto documentation in the IDE. Results and Conclusion. All three components are publicly deployed and usable. A preliminary study for TraceViz's in-IDE visualization confirmed that it improves developer comprehension during software understanding tasks. The tool landscape makes state-of-the-art TLR accessible to architects, developers, and tool integrators. Video. We provide a screencast of our ARDoCo Tool Landscape and how it is used here: https://youtu.be/IOTEPZQ3tVs

AI.tldr: ARDoCo provides an accessible tool landscape for traceability link recovery (TLR) between software architecture documentation, models, and source code, comprising a REST API, a browser-based frontend (TraceView), and a VS Code extension (TraceViz). A preliminary study confirms in-IDE trace visualization improves developer comprehension.
AI.motivation: Automatically recovering traceability links between interrelated software artifacts (SAD, SAM, source code) remains difficult to deploy in practice, despite being essential for maintenance and consistency checking.
AI.method: The authors present three integrated components: (1) ARDoCo REST API exposing four TLR pipelines (SAD-SAM, SAM-Code, SAD-Code, SAD-SAM-Code) via HTTP with asynchronous execution and caching; (2) TraceView, a browser-based frontend with a guided wizard and interactive multi-panel exploration; and (3) TraceViz, a VS Code extension overlaying trace links directly onto documentation within the IDE.
AI.result: All three components are publicly deployed and usable. A preliminary study confirmed that TraceViz's in-IDE visualization improves developer comprehension during software understanding tasks.
AI.conclusion: The ARDoCo tool landscape successfully makes state-of-the-art TLR accessible to architects, developers, and tool integrators through multiple interfaces tailored to different usage contexts.

title: ToolPrivacyBench: Benchmarking Purpose-Bound Privacy in Tool-Using LLM Agents
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have increasingly moved from standalone text generation systems to agents that invoke external tools, access environments, and execute multi-step tasks. However, conventional function-calling benchmarks mainly evaluate task completion and API correctness, while privacy evaluation benchmarks typically focus on final responses or privacy judgments. Neither perspective captures purpose-bound information flow across an executed multi-tool trajectory. Motivated by this limitation in current agent evaluation, ToolPrivacyBench audits whether task-private atoms are routed only to authorized tools and downstream sinks, thereby evaluating both task completion and privacy over-disclosure during tool use. The benchmark contains 2,150 cases, including 1,150 fully synthetic privacy-sensitive business workflows and 1,000 cases adapted from existing multi-tool and function-calling benchmarks. Each case is represented by a policy knowledge base. After an agent executes against mock business backends, the evaluator compares recorded tool arguments and backend audit logs with this policy knowledge base. The evaluation covers nine widely used agents to characterize purpose-bound privacy over-disclosure. The results show that successful tool execution does not imply appropriate privacy disclosure: an agent may complete a task while transmitting unnecessary private information through intermediate tool calls. ToolPrivacyBench therefore formalizes a need-to-know disclosure boundary, under which each tool should receive only the information necessary for its stated purpose, and uses trajectory-level auditing to identify privacy over-disclosure in multi-tool workflows.

AI.tldr: ToolPrivacyBench is a benchmark auditing whether LLM agents unnecessarily disclose private information during multi-tool task execution, using trajectory-level analysis of 2,150 cases to reveal that successful task completion frequently coincides with privacy over-disclosure to unauthorized tools.
AI.motivation: Existing function-calling benchmarks only assess task completion/API correctness, while privacy benchmarks evaluate final outputs. Neither captures purpose-bound information flow — i.e., whether private data atoms are routed only to authorized tools and sinks — across an entire multi-step agent trajectory. This gap motivates a new evaluation paradigm.
AI.method: ToolPrivacyBench comprises 2,150 cases (1,150 synthetic privacy-sensitive business workflows + 1,000 adapted from existing benchmarks), each paired with a policy knowledge base specifying authorized information per tool. Agents execute tasks against mock business backends; an evaluator then compares recorded tool arguments and backend audit logs against the policy knowledge base to detect privacy over-disclosure. Nine widely-used agents are evaluated.
AI.result: Successful tool execution does not imply appropriate privacy disclosure — agents frequently complete tasks while transmitting unnecessary private information through intermediate tool calls. The benchmark quantifies this over-disclosure across nine agents.
AI.conclusion: ToolPrivacyBench formalizes a need-to-know disclosure boundary for multi-tool agent workflows, demonstrating that trajectory-level auditing is essential to identify privacy over-disclosure that conventional task-completion metrics miss.

title: Cross-Platform Chinese Offensive Comment Detection via Dual-Threshold Hard Example Mining
summary: Cross-platform deployment of offensive comment detection for Chinese social media suffers performance degradation. The paper proposes a dual-threshold hard mining method to address this. First, the clean-Chinese-base RoBERTa is finetuned on COLD to establish a binary baseline for fair comparison. Second, a three-class fine-labeled test set covering Weibo, Xiaohongshu, Tieba, and Zhihu is constructed, domain distances from the source are quantified using Jaccard and Proxy-A Distance, as well as the degradation bottleneck of the baseline under domain shift is systematically revealed. Herein, a dual threshold hard example mining strategy is proposed. High- and low-confidence error-prone samples are filtered from unlabeled corpora by prediction confidence. The model is secondarily finetuned under implicit contexts with merely a small set of manually labeled hard examples, realizing low-cost cross-platform domain adaptation. Experiments reveal significant performance gains of the optimized model across four platforms.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses cross-platform performance degradation in Chinese offensive comment detection by proposing a dual-threshold hard mining method that uses confidence-based filtering to select error-prone samples from unlabeled data, enabling low-cost domain adaptation with minimal manual labeling.
AI.motivation: Cross-platform deployment of Chinese offensive comment detection models suffers significant performance degradation due to domain shift. The authors aim to systematically quantify this degradation and develop a cost-effective domain adaptation strategy that minimizes manual labeling effort.
AI.method: 1) Fine-tune clean-Chinese-base RoBERTa on the COLD dataset as a binary classification baseline. 2) Construct a three-class fine-labeled test set spanning Weibo, Xiaohongshu, Tieba, and Zhihu; quantify domain distances using Jaccard similarity and Proxy-A Distance; systematically reveal degradation bottlenecks. 3) Propose a dual-threshold hard example mining strategy: filter high-confidence and low-confidence error-prone samples from unlabeled corpora based on prediction confidence, then secondary fine-tune the model using only a small set of manually labeled hard examples under implicit contexts.
AI.result: The optimized model achieved significant performance gains across all four platforms (Weibo, Xiaohongshu, Tieba, Zhihu) compared to the baseline.
AI.conclusion: The dual-threshold hard example mining strategy effectively enables low-cost cross-platform domain adaptation for Chinese offensive comment detection by targeting error-prone samples, substantially improving cross-platform robustness without requiring large-scale labeled data from each target domain.

title: hia-gat: A Heterogeneous Interaction-Aware Graph Attention Network For Frame-Level Traffic Conflict Risk Prediction On Freeways
summary: This paper formulates frame-level freeway risk assessment as a multi-agent scene graph-level binary classification problem, where each video or trajectory frame is labeled risky if any TTC- or PET-based conflict violates a specified severity threshold. We construct a relation-aware graph per frame with vehicles as nodes and two interaction types as edges: same-lane (longitudinal) and adjacent-lane (lateral), augmented with physics-informed edge features aligned to rear-end and lane-change conflict mechanisms. Building on a structured benchmarking suite of non-graph models and graph baselines, we propose HIA-GAT, a dual-stream heterogeneous graph attention network that processes longitudinal and lateral interactions through dedicated attention pathways and fuses them via a conflict-type-aware gating mechanism with event-level gate supervision derived from SSM conflict attribution. Experiments on the NGSIM I-80 and US-101 freeway datasets across nine TTC and PET threshold configurations show that HIA-GAT achieves the best average risk-ranking performance (AUC 0.835 on I-80 and 0.867 on US-101), with the largest gains on PET-only (lane-change) settings where relational structure is essential. Beyond accuracy, the learned gate provides interpretable per-vehicle attribution of dominant conflict type, supporting actionable, real-time freeway safety monitoring. We show that graph structure is critical for modeling lateral conflict risk, while longitudinal risk can often be captured by non-relational aggregation.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes HIA-GAT, a dual-stream heterogeneous graph attention network for frame-level freeway risk assessment that models vehicles as graph nodes with longitudinal (same-lane) and lateral (adjacent-lane) interactions as distinct edge types, using a gating mechanism to fuse both pathways with conflict-type supervision.
AI.motivation: Existing freeway risk assessment methods often rely on non-relational aggregation, which is insufficient for capturing lateral (lane-change) conflicts that depend on structured inter-vehicle relationships. The authors aim to demonstrate that graph-based relational modeling is essential for lateral conflict detection, while benchmarking against non-graph alternatives.
AI.method: Frame-level risk assessment is cast as binary classification on multi-agent scene graphs. Each frame's graph uses vehicles as nodes and two edge types — same-lane (longitudinal) and adjacent-lane (lateral) — with physics-informed edge features aligned to rear-end and lane-change conflict mechanisms. HIA-GAT processes each edge type through a dedicated graph attention pathway and fuses them via a conflict-type-aware gating mechanism. The gate is supervised at the event level using SSM (Surrogate Safety Measure) conflict attribution, providing interpretable per-vehicle dominant conflict type identification.
AI.result: On NGSIM I-80 and US-101 datasets across nine TTC/PET threshold configurations, HIA-GAT achieves the best average risk-ranking AUC (0.835 on I-80, 0.867 on US-101), with particularly strong gains on PET-only (lane-change) settings. Graph structure is shown to be critical for lateral conflict risk modeling, while longitudinal risk can often be captured by non-relational aggregation.
AI.conclusion: Relational graph structure is essential for modeling lateral (lane-change) conflict risk in freeway settings. The dual-stream heterogeneous attention architecture with supervised gating not only improves predictive performance but also provides interpretable conflict-type attribution, enabling actionable real-time safety monitoring.

title: NormAct: A Benchmark for Hidden Social Norm Compliance in Embodied Planning
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed as embodied planners in egocentric environments, where task success requires not only achieving instructed goals but also acting in socially appropriate ways. While explicit goals may render certain actions optimal, implicit social norms often impose hidden constraints. Existing evaluations typically focus on explicit goal achievement or direct norm knowledge, seldom assessing whether planners can infer and apply these hidden constraints within action sequences. We introduce NormAct, a benchmark for embodied social-norm interactions that evaluates plans on Goal Achievement, Norm Compliance, and overall Task Success. NormAct uniquely embeds hidden norms within ordinary tasks, testing whether models can realize them without explicit instruction. Experiments with state-of-the-art MLLMs (GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3 Pro) reveal a significant gap: models achieve explicit goals in 67.3\% of cases, but comply with hidden norms in only 26.4\%. Cue-condition experiments indicate that this gap stems not from a lack of general social knowledge, but from challenges in activating and grounding relevant norms in context. To address this, we propose NormPerceptor, a context-conditioned cue generator that infers scene-relevant norms prior to planning, increasing Task Success from 24.2\% to 46.7\%. Our results underscore the importance of enabling embodied agents to proactively detect hidden norms, ground them in visual evidence, and integrate them as action-planning constraints. Our benchmark is publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/Caleb196x/NormAct.

AI.tldr: NormAct is a benchmark evaluating embodied MLLMs on hidden social-norm compliance during planning. State-of-the-art models achieve 67.3% goal completion but only 26.4% norm compliance. The proposed NormPerceptor, a context-conditioned cue generator, boosts task success from 24.2% to 46.7% by inferring norms before planning.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of MLLMs as embodied planners focus on explicit goal achievement or direct norm knowledge but fail to assess whether models can infer and apply implicit/hidden social norms within action sequences. This gap is critical for real-world deployment where socially appropriate behavior is as important as task completion.
AI.method: The authors introduce NormAct, a benchmark embedding hidden social norms within ordinary egocentric tasks, evaluating on Goal Achievement, Norm Compliance, and overall Task Success. They test three SOTA MLLMs (GPT-5.4, Claude Opus 4.7, Gemini 3 Pro) and conduct cue-condition experiments to isolate the source of the norm-compliance gap. To address the gap, they propose NormPerceptor, a context-conditioned cue generator that infers scene-relevant norms from visual evidence prior to planning.
AI.result: SOTA MLLMs achieved 67.3% goal achievement but only 26.4% hidden-norm compliance, with overall Task Success at 24.2%. Cue-condition experiments revealed the gap stems from difficulty activating and grounding relevant norms in context, not from lack of social knowledge. NormPerceptor improved overall Task Success to 46.7%.
AI.conclusion: Embodied agents must proactively detect hidden norms, ground them in visual evidence, and integrate them as planning constraints. The substantial performance gap and the effectiveness of NormPerceptor demonstrate the importance of context-conditioned norm inference for socially competent embodied AI.

title: How Humans, Bots, and Agents Communicate About Vulnerabilities in Pull Requests
summary: Developers may reference vulnerabilities in pull request discussions through both explicit identifiers, such as CVEs or GHSAs, and implicit security-related language (e.g., "unauthorized access" or "SQL injection"). Prior work has primarily focused on explicit identifiers, potentially overlooking vulnerability discussions that lack formal references. Bots and coding agents are becoming more common in pull requests, raising new questions about how different accounts communicate about vulnerabilities. In this registered report, we describe our planned study of vulnerability communication in pull requests by humans, bots, and coding agents. Building on the AIDev-pop dataset, we analyze explicit vulnerability references and implicit security-related signals across pull request titles, descriptions, review comments, commit messages, and timeline discussions. We further investigate whether these references are associated with vulnerabilities introduced or fixed in the modified code and how they relate to pull request review activity and outcomes. This study contributes a large-scale empirical investigation of vulnerability communication practices in modern software development.

AI.tldr: This registered report outlines a planned large-scale empirical study of vulnerability communication in pull requests, examining both explicit references (CVEs, GHSAs) and implicit security-related language across PR discussions involving humans, bots, and coding agents, and linking these communications to code changes and review outcomes.
AI.motivation: Prior research has narrowly focused on explicit vulnerability identifiers (e.g., CVEs, GHSAs), potentially missing substantial vulnerability discussions conveyed through implicit security language (e.g., "SQL injection," "unauthorized access"). With the rise of bots and coding agents in pull requests, there is an open question about how different account types communicate vulnerabilities, necessitating a broader, more inclusive analysis.
AI.method: Building on the AIDev-pop dataset, the study will analyze vulnerability communication across PR titles, descriptions, review comments, commit messages, and timeline discussions. It will detect both explicit identifiers and implicit security-related signals, then investigate associations with vulnerabilities introduced or fixed in the modified code, as well as relationships with review activity and PR outcomes.
AI.result: As a registered report, results are not yet available; the paper details the planned methodology, research questions, and analysis framework for the forthcoming empirical investigation.
AI.conclusion: This study will provide the first large-scale empirical characterization of how vulnerabilities are communicated in pull requests by diverse contributors (humans, bots, coding agents), bridging the gap between explicit and implicit vulnerability discourse and their practical implications for code review.

title: GTI-mSEMP Framework : A Proposed Framework to Stimulate Malware Propagation with Inclusion of Attacker-Defender Strategy
summary: The rapid proliferation of automated, multi-vector malware threats poses a significant risk to heterogeneous, resource constrained cyber-physical networks. Conventional epidemiological models often treat security defenses as static parameters, failing to capture the strategic, asymmetric maneuvers between an attacker and a defender. To address the gap, this paper proposes a Game-Theory-Integrated Modified Multi- Wireless Sensor Epidemic Malware Propagation (GTI-mSEMP) framework. This paper analyzed and compared the operational trajectories of Susceptible (S) and Recovered (R) node populations across three different operational regimes: Balanced Matchup, Exploit Surge and Hardened Defense. Numerical simulation results capture the real-time transient dynamics of the network state variables, demonstrating how the epidemic curve shifts when either the defensive or offensive scaling vectors hold an efficiency advantage. The proposed mathematical and numerical framework provides a rigorous foundation that can be deployed in highly adversarial network environments to evaluate dynamic malware propagation and predict localized node population states.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes GTI-mSEMP, a game-theory-integrated epidemiological model for malware propagation in resource-constrained cyber-physical networks. It simulates three operational regimes — Balanced Matchup, Exploit Surge, and Hardened Defense — to capture attacker-defender dynamics and predict how epidemic curves shift under asymmetric efficiency advantages.
AI.motivation: Conventional epidemiological malware models treat security defenses as static parameters, failing to capture the strategic, asymmetric interplay between attackers and defenders in automated, multi-vector malware scenarios targeting heterogeneous, resource-constrained cyber-physical networks.
AI.method: The authors develop the Game-Theory-Integrated Modified Multi-Wireless Sensor Epidemic Malware Propagation (GTI-mSEMP) framework, which incorporates game-theoretic attacker-defender dynamics into an extended SIR compartmental model. Numerical simulations compare Susceptible (S) and Recovered (R) node population trajectories across three operational regimes: Balanced Matchup, Exploit Surge, and Hardened Defense.
AI.result: Simulations capture real-time transient dynamics of network state variables and demonstrate how the epidemic curve shifts depending on whether defensive or offensive scaling vectors hold an efficiency advantage across the three regimes.
AI.conclusion: The GTI-mSEMP framework provides a rigorous mathematical and numerical foundation for evaluating dynamic malware propagation and predicting localized node population states in highly adversarial network environments.

title: Yuvion LLM: An Adversarially-Aware Large Language Model for Content And AI Safety
summary: As large language models are increasingly deployed in real-world systems, safety failures can still lead to harmful outputs and dangerous misuse. We argue that the essence of safety is adversarial: many failures arise not from natural inputs alone, but from strategic attempts to evade model policies and safeguards. However, existing general-purpose model development largely overlook this adversarial nature, and often remain insufficient for realistic safety scenarios involving planning, tool use, and multi-step reasoning, causing measured safety performance to overestimate real deployment robustness. To address this gap, we present Yuvion LLM, a large language model built for adversarially robust content safety and broader AI safety. Yuvion LLM treats adversarial robustness and agentic capability as first-class objectives. Its pipeline combines adversarially aware data construction, knowledge-enhanced continued pretraining, and policy-grounded multi-task safety post-training, including risk-aware supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning-based policy optimization, together with safety-aware agentic reinforcement learning for tool use and multi-step reasoning in complex safety scenarios. We further introduce the Yuvion LLM RiskEval (YLRE), a collection of 93 benchmarks across four evaluation categories, covering diverse open and internal evaluations with a focus on safety, adversarial robustness, and real-world capability requirements. Across these evaluations, Yuvion LLM demonstrates clear advantages on safety-focused benchmarks and particularly strong robustness under adversarial conditions, while maintaining solid overall capability. Notably, Yuvion-8B outperforms most state-of-the-art baselines, including substantially larger models such as GPT-5.4 and Qwen3-MAX, on several safety tasks.

AI.tldr: Yuvion LLM is a language model designed for adversarial safety robustness, combining adversarial data construction, safety-focused pretraining/post-training, and agentic RL. It introduces the YLRE benchmark suite (93 evaluations) and demonstrates that Yuvion-8B outperforms much larger models like GPT-5.4 and Qwen3-MAX on safety tasks under adversarial conditions.
AI.motivation: Current LLM development overlooks the adversarial nature of real-world safety failures, where strategic users attempt to circumvent safeguards. Existing models are insufficient for realistic safety scenarios involving planning, tool use, and multi-step reasoning, leading to overestimated safety performance in deployment.
AI.method: Yuvion LLM's pipeline includes: (1) adversarially aware data construction, (2) knowledge-enhanced continued pretraining, (3) policy-grounded multi-task safety post-training (risk-aware SFT + RL-based policy optimization), and (4) safety-aware agentic RL for tool use and multi-step reasoning. The YLRE evaluation suite comprises 93 benchmarks across four categories covering safety, adversarial robustness, and real-world capabilities.
AI.result: Yuvion LLM shows clear advantages on safety benchmarks with strong robustness under adversarial conditions while maintaining overall capability. Yuvion-8B outperforms most state-of-the-art baselines, including substantially larger models like GPT-5.4 and Qwen3-MAX, on several safety tasks.
AI.conclusion: Treating adversarial robustness and agentic capability as first-class objectives is critical for real-world LLM safety. Yuvion LLM demonstrates that a relatively small model (8B parameters) can surpass much larger counterparts on safety-critical tasks when trained with adversarially grounded methods.

title: PEBS: Per-rater Empirical-Bayes Shrinkage for RLHF Reward-Model Calibration
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Pluralistic Alignment. Code: https://github.com/deadsmash07/pebs-pluralistic
summary: Reward models for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) pool preferences across thousands of annotators and fit one global affine calibrator, collapsing raters with systematically different rating-scale offsets and slopes into a single average-rater fit that does not match any individual annotator. PEBS is a per-rater empirical-Bayes shrinkage estimator: it fits per-rater affine calibrators on a held-out slice of each annotator's ratings and applies Morris-James-Stein empirical-Bayes shrinkage toward the population mean, in closed form and without retraining the reward model. On PRISM, PEBS reduces within-user held-out RMSE by 8.58% over the pooled population-slope baseline. The procedure replicates on PluriHarms harm ratings (Qwen-2.5 base, in-family) with a +9.66% RMSE reduction over the same population-slope baseline. PEBS is a closed-form post-hoc estimator for annotator-specific affine calibration in RLHF reward modeling; it leaves the reward base model unchanged and estimates only the rater-level map used at inference time for new ratings.

AI.tldr: PEBS introduces a per-rater empirical-Bayes shrinkage estimator for RLHF reward models, fitting individual affine calibrators and applying Morris-James-Stein shrinkage toward the population mean, achieving ~8-10% RMSE reduction without retraining the base reward model.
AI.motivation: Standard RLHF reward modeling pools preferences across diverse annotators into a single global affine calibrator, ignoring systematic inter-rater differences in rating-scale offsets and slopes. This produces an "average-rater" fit that matches no individual annotator, degrading per-user predictive accuracy.
AI.method: PEBS fits per-rater affine calibrators on a held-out slice of each annotator's ratings, then applies Morris-James-Stein empirical-Bayes shrinkage toward the population mean. This is a closed-form, post-hoc procedure requiring no reward model retraining — only the rater-level map is estimated for inference-time use.
AI.result: On the PRISM dataset, PEBS reduces within-user held-out RMSE by 8.58% over the pooled population-slope baseline. The method replicates on PluriHarms harm ratings (Qwen-2.5 base, in-family) with a 9.66% RMSE reduction over the same baseline.
AI.conclusion: PEBS provides an effective, computationally lightweight solution for personalizing RLHF reward models to individual annotators without modifying the base model, offering consistent improvements across datasets and base models.

title: Verifiable Geometry Problem Solving: Solver-Driven Autoformalization and Theorem Proposing
summary: Geometry Problem Solving have increasingly adopt the neuro-symbolic paradigm, combining neural intuition with symbolic rigor. However, current frameworks suffer from severe bottlenecks in two core stages: autoformalization, which treats multimodal translation as a static task decoupled from downstream solver compatibility, and theorem prediction, where solvers frequently hit a deductive impasse due to fixed rule libraries. To address these, we propose SD-GPS, a solver-driven framework that treats the symbolic solver as an execution oracle throughout both formalization and deduction. First, Solver-Driven Autoformalization unifies supervised formal-language adaptation and solvability-guided reinforcement learning into a single module built on QwenVL3-2B, making executability the central training signal. Second, Verified Theorem Proposing introduces an impasse-aware agent that proposes local auxiliary lemmas from current proof states, ensuring soundness by filtering all proposals through symbolic verification. Empirical evaluations on Geometry3K and PGPS9K demonstrate that SD-GPS consistently outperforms existing MLLM, neural, and neuro-symbolic methods across standard completion, multiple-choice, and cross-modal reference regimes, proving that closing the loop between multimodal perception and symbolic execution significantly improves geometric reasoning, offering profound insights into how neural agents can be grounded by formal systems to achieve verifiable problem-solving capabilities.

AI.tldr: SD-GPS is a solver-driven neuro-symbolic framework for geometry problem solving that integrates solver feedback into both autoformalization (via supervised adaptation + solvability-guided RL on QwenVL3-2B) and theorem prediction (via an impasse-aware agent that proposes soundness-verified auxiliary lemmas), outperforming existing methods on Geometry3K and PGPS9K.
AI.motivation: Current neuro-symbolic geometry solvers suffer from two critical bottlenecks: (1) autoformalization treats multimodal translation as a static task, decoupled from whether the output is actually executable by the downstream solver; (2) theorem prediction relies on fixed rule libraries, causing solvers to frequently hit deductive impasses. The authors aim to close the loop between multimodal perception and symbolic execution.
AI.method: SD-GPS uses the symbolic solver as an execution oracle throughout. It consists of two components: (1) Solver-Driven Autoformalization, which unifies supervised formal-language adaptation with solvability-guided reinforcement learning into a single module based on QwenVL3-2B, using executability as the central training signal; (2) Verified Theorem Proposing, an impasse-aware agent that generates local auxiliary lemmas from current proof states and filters all proposals through symbolic verification to guarantee soundness.
AI.result: Empirical evaluations on Geometry3K and PGPS9K show that SD-GPS consistently outperforms existing MLLM, neural, and neuro-symbolic methods across standard completion, multiple-choice, and cross-modal reference regimes.
AI.conclusion: Closing the loop between multimodal perception and symbolic execution significantly improves geometric reasoning. The work demonstrates how neural agents can be grounded by formal systems to achieve verifiable problem-solving capabilities.

title: CrossLangFuzzer: Differential Testing of Cross-Language JVM Compilers
summary: Modern JVM software increasingly integrates multiple programming languages, such as Java, Kotlin, Groovy, and Scala, within a single application. Supporting such interoperability requires JVM compilers to perform cross-language compilation while reconciling subtle semantic differences across language boundaries. Errors in this process can lead to critical miscompilations, yet existing compiler testing techniques focus exclusively on isolated, singlelanguage compilation. To address this gap, we present CrossLangFuzzer, the first differential testing framework for cross-language JVM compilation. CrossLangFuzzer leverages the Kotlin compiler's unified intermediate representation (IR) to synthesize cross-language test programs. It further applies seven mutation operators to diversify generated test programs and improve bug-finding capability. Evaluated on the latest versions of five major JVM compilers, CrossLangFuzzer uncovered 32 confirmed bugs, including 15 in Kotlin, 4 in Groovy, 7 in Scala 3, 2 in Scala 2, and 4 in Java. CrossLangFuzzer is open-source at https://github.com/XYZboom/CrossLangFuzzer

AI.tldr: CrossLangFuzzer is a differential testing framework that synthesizes cross-language JVM test programs using Kotlin's unified IR and seven mutation operators, uncovering 32 confirmed bugs across five major JVM compilers (Kotlin, Groovy, Scala 3, Scala 2, Java).
AI.motivation: Modern JVM applications increasingly mix multiple languages (Java, Kotlin, Groovy, Scala), requiring compilers to handle cross-language compilation with subtle semantic differences. Existing compiler testing techniques only target single-language compilation, leaving a critical gap in detecting cross-language miscompilations.
AI.method: CrossLangFuzzer is a differential testing framework that: (1) leverages the Kotlin compiler's unified intermediate representation (IR) to synthesize cross-language test programs spanning multiple JVM languages; and (2) applies seven mutation operators to diversify generated test programs and enhance bug-finding capability.
AI.result: Evaluated on five major JVM compilers' latest versions, CrossLangFuzzer found 32 confirmed bugs: 15 in Kotlin, 4 in Groovy, 7 in Scala 3, 2 in Scala 2, and 4 in Java.
AI.conclusion: CrossLangFuzzer demonstrates the effectiveness of differential testing for cross-language JVM compilation, revealing that interoperability bugs are prevalent across major JVM compilers. The tool is open-source, enabling further research and practical adoption.

title: Robust Harmful Features Under Jailbreak Attacks: Mechanistic Evidence from Attention Head Specialization in Large Language Models
comment: 323 pages, 19 figures. Accepted at ICML 2026 as a Oral presentation
summary: Jailbreak attacks bypass LLM safety alignment, yet their mechanisms remain poorly understood. We provide evidence that attacks do not comprehensively eliminate safety features, but instead selectively suppress specific attention heads. We identify two functionally differentiated types: Adversarially Compromised Heads (ACHs) concentrated in early layers, which are suppressed under attacks, and Safety-Aligned Heads (SAHs) in mid-layers, which maintain robust activations even when attacks succeed. Ablation studies support the causal role of ACHs and the contribution of SAHs to robust activations: suppressing a small number of ACHs is sufficient to induce jailbreak-like behavior on normally refused inputs, while removing SAHs substantially weakens mid-layer safety activations. Token-level attribution further shows that ACH suppression is driven specifically by attack-template tokens, providing a mechanistic account of why attacks can bypass refusal decisions through ACH suppression while leaving internal safety signals sustained by SAHs -- a phenomenon we term Robust Harmful Features. To validate the practical significance of this robustness, we show that simply reading these persistent activations -- without any training -- yields competitive aggregate detection performance with strong adversarial robustness.

AI.tldr: Jailbreak attacks don't fully eliminate LLM safety features but selectively suppress specific early-layer "Adversarially Compromised Heads" (ACHs), while mid-layer "Safety-Aligned Heads" (SAHs) retain robust harmful-content activations. Attack-template tokens drive ACH suppression, enabling bypass of refusal despite persistent internal safety signals — a phenomenon dubbed Robust Harmful Features — which can be exploited for training-free jailbreak detection.
AI.motivation: The mechanistic basis of jailbreak attacks on LLM safety alignment is poorly understood. This work aims to uncover how attacks circumvent refusal at the level of individual attention heads, moving beyond behavioral observations to a causal, mechanistic account.
AI.method: The authors analyze attention head activations across layers under jailbreak attacks, identifying two functional head types: ACHs (early layers, suppressed under attack) and SAHs (mid-layers, robustly activated). Causal roles are tested via ablation (suppressing ACHs induces jailbreak-like behavior; removing SAHs weakens safety activations). Token-level attribution links ACH suppression to attack-template tokens. Detection performance is evaluated by reading SAH activations directly without training.
AI.result: Suppressing a small number of ACHs suffices to induce jailbreak-like behavior on normally refused inputs. SAH removal substantially weakens mid-layer safety activations. Attack-template tokens specifically drive ACH suppression, leaving SAH-mediated safety signals intact (Robust Harmful Features). Reading these persistent activations yields competitive jailbreak detection with strong adversarial robustness — without any training.
AI.conclusion: Jailbreak attacks operate via selective, token-driven suppression of early-layer ACHs rather than wholesale safety elimination. Persistent safety signals in mid-layer SAHs represent Robust Harmful Features that can be directly leveraged for practical, training-free, adversarially robust detection.

title: When Search Agents Should Ask: DiscoBench for Clarification-Aware Deep Search
summary: Search agents powered by large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to solve complex information-seeking tasks, requiring multi-step retrieval and reasoning to fulfill user goals. However, existing benchmarks often assume that user queries are complete and explicit, overlooking the fact that real-world search requests are frequently vague, underspecified, or even factually incorrect. In deep search scenarios, such ambiguity can propagate along multi-step reasoning chains and lead agents toward incorrect search trajectories. To address this gap, we introduce DiscoBench, a benchmark for clarification-aware deep search, designed to evaluate whether search agents can proactively identify ambiguity, ask effective clarification questions, and recover correct reasoning paths through user interaction. DiscoBench contains 211 samples and 463 ambiguity instances across 11 real-world domains, covering four ambiguity types. We further design a user simulator for multi-turn interaction and evaluate model performance from four perspectives: task utility, ambiguity detection, interaction strategy, and cost efficiency. Experiments on representative LLMs show that ambiguity detection and effective clarification are distinct capabilities, and that repeatedly searching instead of asking for clarification often performs worse than direct guessing, highlighting a critical gap between retrieval ability and interactive problem-solving in current search agents.

AI.tldr: DiscoBench is a benchmark evaluating whether LLM-based search agents can detect ambiguity in underspecified queries, ask clarifying questions, and recover correct reasoning paths through user interaction, revealing a critical gap between retrieval ability and interactive problem-solving.
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks assume user queries are complete and explicit, but real-world search requests are often vague, underspecified, or factually incorrect. In deep search scenarios, ambiguity propagates through multi-step reasoning chains, leading agents to incorrect trajectories. No benchmark currently evaluates whether agents can proactively identify and resolve ambiguity through clarification.
AI.method: The authors introduce DiscoBench with 211 samples and 463 ambiguity instances across 11 domains, covering four ambiguity types. They design a user simulator for multi-turn interaction and evaluate models along four dimensions: task utility, ambiguity detection, interaction strategy, and cost efficiency. Representative LLMs are tested for their ability to detect ambiguity and ask effective clarification questions.
AI.result: Ambiguity detection and effective clarification are distinct capabilities. Repeatedly searching instead of asking for clarification often performs worse than direct guessing, demonstrating that strong retrieval does not imply strong interactive problem-solving.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM-based search agents exhibit a significant gap between retrieval proficiency and the ability to engage in clarification-driven, interactive problem-solving. DiscoBench provides a structured framework to measure and improve this capability.

title: Retroactive Advantage Correction: Closed-Form V-Trace Bias Correction for Delay-Aware RLHF
comment: Accepted at the ICML 2026 Workshop on Reinforcement Learning from World Feedback (RLxF). Code: https://github.com/deadsmash07/rac-rlxf-code
summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) in production does not always have a synchronous reward signal. Code-execution verifiers, slow judge ensembles, and queued human review can return several gradient steps after the rollout that produced them, breaking the synchronous-reward assumption underlying standard PPO. We address this gap with Retroactive Advantage Correction (RAC): each pending slow completion is queued, aged through a non-negative kernel, and reinjected as a clipped residual into the next optimiser step's advantage. We prove that under an unbiased clipped importance ratio, the cumulative RAC correction is exactly unbiased when the effective delay kernel reinjects all of its mass, and carries a bias linear in the unreinjected fraction otherwise; at the no-delay identity kernel it reduces to V-trace. On a tabular Markov decision process (MDP) proof-of-concept, RAC reduces the closed-form policy bias by up to 47.9x at the two-slow-channel configuration, beating wait-for-slow at lower wall-clock cost. RAC integrates with PPO and GRPO through a two-line reward-manager patch.

AI.tldr: RAC addresses RLHF with asynchronous rewards by queuing delayed feedback, aging it through a non-negative kernel, and reinjecting it as a clipped residual advantage correction — proving unbiasedness under full mass reinjection and achieving up to 47.9× bias reduction over baselines.
AI.motivation: Standard PPO and similar RLHF algorithms assume synchronous reward signals, but production systems often involve asynchronous feedback from code-execution verifiers, slow judge ensembles, or queued human review — where rewards arrive several gradient steps after the rollout. This breaks the synchronous-reward assumption, creating a gap that existing methods do not adequately address.
AI.method: The authors propose Retroactive Advantage Correction (RAC): each pending slow reward completion is queued, aged through a non-negative delay kernel, and reinjected as a clipped residual into the advantage estimate at the next optimizer step. RAC generalizes V-trace (recovered under the no-delay identity kernel) and provides unbiased cumulative correction when the kernel reinjects all mass, with bias linear in the unreinjected fraction otherwise. Integration with PPO and GRPO requires only a two-line reward-manager patch.
