AI.result: On a tabular MDP proof-of-concept with a two-slow-channel configuration, RAC reduces closed-form policy bias by up to 47.9× compared to naive queuing, and outperforms wait-for-slow strategies at lower wall-clock cost.
AI.conclusion: RAC offers a principled, lightweight solution for asynchronous RLHF in production, enabling efficient use of slow reward signals without blocking optimization, with formal unbiasedness guarantees and strong empirical bias reduction.

title: RelBall: Relation Ball with Quaternion Rotation for Knowledge Graph Completion
summary: Real-world knowledge graphs are often incomplete, lacking many valid facts. Knowledge Graph Completion (KGC) aims to predict missing links using known triples, thereby enhancing graph coverage. A key challenge is modeling diverse relational patterns such as symmetry, antisymmetry, inversion, composition and semantic hierarchy. Existing models such as RotatE can capture symmetric, antisymmetric, inverse, and commutative composition patterns, yet struggle with non-commutative composition. Rotate3D addresses this by introducing non-commutativity via three-dimensional rotations, but still fails to capture the semantic hierarchies prevalent in knowledge graphs. Moreover, both models cannot effectively model one-to-many relations. To overcome these limitations, we propose RelBall, which extends Rotate3D with two innovations. First, our model introduces modulus transformation to model hierarchies, driving abstract concepts toward smaller moduli and concrete instances toward larger ones. Second, it introduces a tail-centric relation ball to model one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many relations. RelBall offers the following advantages: (1) coverage of all relational patterns, including the ones mentioned above; (2) an interpretable hierarchical representation where the modulus directly reflect semantic levels; (3) support for one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many relations. Experiments on multiple datasets demonstrate RelBall's competitive link prediction performance against various baselines.

AI.tldr: RelBall extends Rotate3D with modulus-based hierarchy modeling and a tail-centric relation ball to capture all relational patterns (symmetry, antisymmetry, inversion, both commutative and non-commutative composition, and semantic hierarchies) while supporting one-to-many relations for knowledge graph completion.
AI.motivation: Existing KGC models like RotatE cannot handle non-commutative composition, while Rotate3D captures non-commutativity but fails to model semantic hierarchies and one-to-many relations. A unified model covering all these relational patterns is needed.
AI.method: RelBall builds on Rotate3D's 3D rotation framework with two key innovations: (1) modulus transformation that maps abstract concepts to smaller moduli and concrete instances to larger moduli, enabling hierarchical modeling; (2) a tail-centric relation ball mechanism that models one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many relations through flexible scoring boundaries.
AI.result: Experiments on multiple datasets show RelBall achieves competitive link prediction performance against various baselines.
AI.conclusion: RelBall successfully unifies the modeling of all major relational patterns—including non-commutative composition and semantic hierarchies—while effectively handling complex relation cardinalities, offering both strong predictive performance and interpretable hierarchical representations.

title: Humanizing Automatically Generated Unit Test Suites with LLM-Based Refactoring
summary: Search-based test generation tools such as EvoSuite produce compilable and high-coverage unit tests at scale, but their suites are often hard to read and maintain. LLMs can generate more natural tests, yet direct generation remains brittle, with compilation rates of only 51-78% in our study. We introduce TestHumanizer, a hybrid SBST+LLM approach that uses LLMs as controlled refactoring layers over compilable SBST suites to improve naming, structure, and developer-oriented clarity while preserving behavior and compilation validity. We evaluate TestHumanizer on 350 classes from Defects4J and SF110. EvoSuite generates 15 suites per class, and each suite is refactored under three context configurations using gpt-4o and mistral-large-2407, yielding 31,500 refactorings. TestHumanizer reaches 88-98% compilation rates, close to EvoSuite's 100% baseline and clearly above direct LLM generation. Structural coverage is largely preserved, typically within 1-2 percentage points, and 86-95% of refactorings satisfy a composite faithful-refactoring threshold. Refactored suites also improve predicted readability, reduce control-flow and cognitive complexity, and mitigate structural smells. The summary-based setting offers the most robust trade-off, while long code-centric prompts are more prone to hallucination-induced failures. A developer study on 30 classes and 444 test methods confirms significant gains in perceived readability and willingness to adopt, with Wilcoxon p less than 0.01 and substantial inter-rater agreement. Overall, LLMs are most effective not as standalone generators but as validation-gated refinement layers over robust SBST outputs.

AI.tldr: TestHumanizer combines search-based test generation (EvoSuite) with LLMs as refactoring layers, achieving 88-98% compilation rates while improving readability, reducing complexity, and preserving coverage—outperforming direct LLM generation and maintaining near-SBST compilation validity.
AI.motivation: Search-based test generation tools like EvoSuite produce compilable, high-coverage tests at scale, but the resulting suites suffer from poor readability, unnatural naming, and high maintenance burden. Direct LLM-based test generation improves naturalness but is brittle, with low compilation rates (51-78%). Neither approach alone delivers both reliability and human-oriented quality.
AI.method: TestHumanizer uses a hybrid SBST+LLM pipeline: EvoSuite first generates compilable test suites, then LLMs (gpt-4o, mistral-large-2407) refactor them under three context configurations (summary-based, code-centric short, code-centric long). The refactoring targets improved naming, structure, and clarity while being validation-gated to preserve behavior and compilation. Evaluation spans 350 classes from Defects4J and SF110, with 15 suites per class × 3 configurations × 2 models = 31,500 refactorings. Metrics include compilation rate, structural coverage preservation, a composite faithful-refactoring threshold, readability scores, control-flow/cognitive complexity, and structural smells. A developer study with 30 classes and 444 test methods assesses perceived readability and adoption willingness.
AI.result: TestHumanizer achieves 88-98% compilation rates versus EvoSuite's 100% baseline and 51-78% for direct LLM generation. Structural coverage is preserved within 1-2 percentage points; 86-95% of refactorings meet the faithful-refactoring threshold. Refactored suites show improved predicted readability, reduced control-flow and cognitive complexity, and fewer structural smells. The summary-based context configuration offers the best robustness trade-off; long code-centric prompts increase hallucination-induced failures. Developer study confirms significant gains in perceived readability and adoption willingness (Wilcoxon p < 0.01, substantial inter-rater agreement).
AI.conclusion: LLMs are most effective not as standalone test generators but as validation-gated refinement layers over robust SBST outputs. TestHumanizer demonstrates that coupling SBST's reliability with LLM-driven refactoring yields test suites that are both compilable and human-friendly, with summary-based prompting as the recommended configuration for practical adoption.

title: From Signals to Transfer: A Factorised Study of Probe-Based Uncertainty Estimation in Large Language Models
summary: Probe-based uncertainty estimation (UE) has emerged as a prominent approach to detect hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) by learning uncertainty from internal model signals. Yet, recent methods vary simultaneously across feature design, training data construction, and evaluation setting, obscuring what actually drives performance. To address this issue, we propose a factorised study of probe-based UE under matched conditions. Our results show that raw hidden states and attention features are difficult to outperform in-domain. However, under distribution shift, structured and compressed features are more robust, suggesting that in-domain performance alone is insufficient to measure progress. Furthermore, prompting and label construction significantly affect probe behaviour. Building on these best-practice findings, we train benchmark-based pretrained probes that transfer reasonably well to open-ended factual generation, providing a stable off-the-shelf baseline. Our work encourages more deployment-oriented evaluation of probe-based uncertainty estimators. The code repository is available at https://github.com/ponhvoan/ProbeUE.

AI.tldr: A factorised study isolating the individual effects of feature design, training data, and evaluation settings on probe-based uncertainty estimation for LLM hallucination detection, finding that in-domain performance is misleading and distribution-shift robustness matters more.
AI.motivation: Existing probe-based uncertainty estimation methods vary simultaneously across multiple dimensions (features, training data, evaluation), making it unclear which factors actually drive performance. A controlled, factorised study is needed to disentangle these confounds.
AI.method: The authors conduct a factorised ablation study under matched conditions, systematically evaluating raw hidden states, attention features, and structured/compressed features; varying prompting and label construction strategies; and testing both in-domain and distribution-shift (out-of-domain) scenarios. They also train benchmark-based pretrained probes and test transfer to open-ended factual generation.
AI.result: Raw hidden states and attention features perform best in-domain but degrade under distribution shift, where structured/compressed features prove more robust. Prompting and label construction significantly affect probe behavior. Benchmark-pretrained probes transfer reasonably well to open-ended generation, offering a stable off-the-shelf baseline.
AI.conclusion: In-domain performance alone is an insufficient metric for evaluating probe-based UE; robustness under distribution shift must be prioritized. The work advocates for more deployment-oriented evaluation and provides pretrained probes as a reproducible baseline.

title: Global Explanations for Multivariate Time Series Forecasting Models via $K$-Order Markov Approximations
comment: Accepted at the Workshop on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence (IJCAI 2026)
summary: While many explainable AI (XAI) methods have been proposed, most are not designed for time-series forecasting models and often rely on the implicit assumption that timestamp features are independent. This assumption ignores the fundamental property of temporal dependence and can lead to explanations that violate the sequential and causal structure of the data. We introduce \textsc{KARMA}, a method for explaining time-series predictors by constructing a Markov surrogate model that captures the temporal dependencies learned by the predictor. Our approach revolves around three main aspects: identifying the minimal history length $K$ that is predictively sufficient for the model, estimating the best-fitting $K$-order Markov transition kernel from the discretized history space, and a five-level global explanation hierarchy that can be derived from the Markov transition kernel, which we illustrate using real-world weather data (Beijing PM 2.5). We also certify using complex synthetic data with known true causal edges that KARMA (i) recovers the data causal structure as learned by the model via a controlled experiment and (ii) identifies temporal dependencies better than established attribution methods such as TimeSHAP.

AI.tldr: KARMA proposes a Markov surrogate model-based method for explaining time-series forecasting models that respects temporal dependence. It identifies the minimal sufficient history length, estimates a K-order Markov transition kernel, and derives a five-level global explanation hierarchy, outperforming TimeSHAP in recovering causal structure.
AI.motivation: Most XAI methods assume feature independence, ignoring temporal dependence in time-series data. This leads to explanations that violate the sequential and causal structure inherent in time-series, motivating a method that explicitly models temporal dependencies as learned by the predictor.
AI.method: KARMA constructs a K-order Markov surrogate model with three steps: (1) identifying the minimal history length K sufficient for prediction, (2) estimating the best-fitting Markov transition kernel from a discretized history space, and (3) deriving a five-level global explanation hierarchy from the kernel. Validation uses both real-world Beijing PM2.5 weather data and synthetic data with known causal edges.
AI.result: On synthetic data with known true causal edges, KARMA successfully recovers the causal structure learned by the model and identifies temporal dependencies more accurately than TimeSHAP and other established attribution methods.
AI.conclusion: KARMA provides temporally coherent explanations for time-series forecasting models by leveraging Markov surrogate models, overcoming the independence assumption limitation of prior XAI methods. It enables both causal structure recovery and a multi-level global explanation framework.

title: Lifted Causal Inference
comment: Accepted to the Annals of Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence journal
summary: Lifted inference exploits indistinguishabilities in probabilistic graphical models by using a representative for indistinguishable objects, thereby speeding up query answering while maintaining exact answers. In this article, we show how lifting can be applied to efficiently compute causal effects in relational domains. More specifically, we introduce parametric causal factor graphs (PCFGs) to incorporate causal knowledge in lifted models and give a formal semantics of interventions therein. We further present the Lifted Causal Inference (LCI) algorithm to compute causal effects on a lifted level, thereby drastically speeding up causal inference compared to propositional inference, e.g., in causal Bayesian networks. In addition, we present partially directed parametric causal factor graphs (PD-PCFGs) as a generalisation of PCFGs to handle partial causal knowledge and extend LCI to perform lifted causal inference in a PD-PCFG, thereby extending the applicability of lifted causal inference to a broader range of models requiring less prior knowledge about causal relationships.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces parametric causal factor graphs (PCFGs) and partially directed PCFGs to lift causal inference in relational domains, along with the Lifted Causal Inference (LCI) algorithm, achieving significant speedups over propositional methods while maintaining exactness.
AI.motivation: Causal inference in relational domains is computationally expensive when performed at the propositional level (e.g., in causal Bayesian networks). Lifted inference has been successful for probabilistic queries but has not been applied to causal effect computation. The authors aim to bridge this gap by extending lifting techniques to causal inference, enabling faster exact computation of causal effects when causal knowledge may be fully or partially available.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) Parametric Causal Factor Graphs (PCFGs) that incorporate causal knowledge into lifted probabilistic models with a formal semantics for interventions; (2) a Lifted Causal Inference (LCI) algorithm that computes causal effects at the lifted level by exploiting indistinguishabilities; and (3) Partially Directed PCFGs (PD-PCFGs) that generalize PCFGs to settings with incomplete causal knowledge, extending LCI to operate on these partially specified models.
AI.result: The LCI algorithm drastically speeds up causal inference compared to propositional inference methods such as causal Bayesian networks, while preserving exact answers. The extension to PD-PCFGs broadens the scope of lifted causal inference to models requiring less prior causal knowledge.
AI.conclusion: Lifting is an effective strategy for accelerating exact causal inference in relational domains. The PCFG/PD-PCFG framework, together with the LCI algorithm, significantly reduces computational cost and extends the practical applicability of causal reasoning to settings with varying degrees of causal knowledge.

title: Govern the Repository, Not the Agent: Measuring Ecosystem-Level Risk in AI-Native Software
summary: Autonomous coding agents now open and merge pull requests in shared repositories at scale, and the field evaluates them the way it has always evaluated components, one agent at a time, on isolated benchmark tasks. Yet agents that each pass their own tests still leave repositories that accumulate problems no single contribution accounts for. We ask whether this problem belongs to the individual agent or to the repository where it accumulates. We study integration friction, the cost of integrating a contribution into a codebase that other contributors are concurrently changing. Across more than 930,000 agent-authored pull requests, we measure how much of the variation in friction stays with the repository after the contribution, its author, its size, and its agent are accounted for. About half does, and it survives full controls. In the same repositories, agent-authored contributions concentrate this repository-level friction roughly twice as much as human ones (intraclass correlation 0.30 versus 0.16), a gap that holds after controlling for codebase size, age, task shape, process maturity, and merge path. The risk is a property of the ecosystem, not the agent. AI-native software is therefore better measured and governed at the ecosystem level than one agent at a time.

AI.tldr: Agent-authored pull requests accumulate repository-level integration friction at roughly twice the rate of human contributions, with about half the variance in friction attributable to the repository itself rather than individual agents. This suggests AI-native software should be measured and governed at the ecosystem level.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation of autonomous coding agents focuses on isolated benchmark performance, one agent at a time. However, even when individual agents pass their tests, shared repositories accumulate systemic problems. The authors investigate whether this accumulation is a property of individual agents or of the repository ecosystem itself.
AI.method: The authors analyze over 930,000 agent-authored pull requests, measuring integration friction — the cost of integrating a contribution into a concurrently changing codebase. They use variance decomposition to determine how much variation in friction remains attributable to the repository after controlling for contribution, author, size, and agent. They compare intraclass correlation (ICC) between agent-authored and human-authored contributions, controlling for codebase size, age, task shape, process maturity, and merge path.
AI.result: About half the variation in integration friction stays with the repository after full controls. Agent-authored contributions concentrate repository-level friction roughly twice as much as human ones (ICC 0.30 vs. 0.16), a gap that persists across all controls.
AI.conclusion: Integration friction risk is a property of the ecosystem, not the individual agent. Consequently, AI-native software development should be measured and governed at the ecosystem level rather than by evaluating agents in isolation.

title: Halt Fast! Early Stopping for Certified Robustness
summary: Randomized Smoothing (RS) provides rigorous robustness guarantees for neural networks without architectural constraints, yet its adoption is limited by extreme computational costs. Standard RS requires tens of thousands of model evaluations per input and forces practitioners to commit to fixed sample sizes a priori. In this work, we present a novel meta-learning framework for anytime-valid certified robustness that adaptively deploys computational resources. By using a lightweight meta-learner to predict image-specific priors for a sequential E-process, we achieve a 20-fold reduction in sample complexity compared to traditional methods while maintaining rigorous statistical guarantees. Beyond raw efficiency, we demonstrate how anytime-validity enables adaptively allocating compute based upon application-specific risk thresholds, a form of resource triage impossible under classic certification frameworks. That this is achievable while also providing similar certification performance demonstrates that our approach provides a pathway for real-time, safety-critical certification deployments.

AI.tldr: A meta-learning framework for anytime-valid certified robustness is introduced, using a lightweight meta-learner to predict image-specific priors for sequential E-processes, achieving 20-fold sample complexity reduction over standard Randomized Smoothing while enabling adaptive compute allocation based on risk thresholds.
AI.motivation: Randomized Smoothing offers architecture-agnostic certified robustness but suffers from prohibitive computational costs (tens of thousands of model evaluations per input) and rigidity — practitioners must fix sample sizes in advance, preventing adaptive resource allocation.
AI.method: A meta-learning framework that trains a lightweight meta-learner to predict per-image priors, which inform a sequential E-process for certification. This enables anytime-valid inference, meaning the certification procedure can be stopped at any point while maintaining valid statistical guarantees, allowing dynamic resource allocation based on application-specific risk thresholds.
AI.result: A 20-fold reduction in sample complexity compared to standard Randomized Smoothing, while preserving rigorous statistical guarantees and achieving comparable certification performance. The anytime-valid property enables resource triage by adaptively allocating compute according to risk thresholds.
AI.conclusion: The approach demonstrates that anytime-valid certification via meta-learning is both efficient and practical, paving the way for real-time, safety-critical deployment of certified neural networks where computational resources can be intelligently triaged.

title: Mitigating LLM-based p-Hacking by Preregistering for the Next LLM
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to generate, classify, and annotate data whose outputs feed downstream hypothesis tests. However, LLM-based research is easy to p-hack: a researcher can tune the prompts, decoding parameters, or output format until a desired result is reached. We propose a protocol to mitigate p-hacking in LLM-based research: preregistering the experiment and eligible models, and then running it on the first eligible LLM that is released after the preregistration. The researcher finalizes the procedure on current models, preregisters the analysis plan together with a set of eligible future models, and runs the confirmatory analysis on the first eligible model released afterward. Because this model does not exist at commitment time, it cannot be hacked against; furthermore, configurations that hack one model frequently do not transfer to the next. We evaluate the protocol on two tasks whose true values are known. Across 20 models from four providers and 11 LLM-analysis configurations, the protocol would have blocked successful transfer of the p-hack in 73.9% and 72.7% of cases in the two tasks. Additional analyses reveal that mitigation remains substantial under several stress tests. Finally, putting money where our mouth is, we followed our own protocol and preregistered our experiment. The preregistered experiment confirmed the protocol's effectiveness: out of the 7 configurations that hacked the prior model, the hacking failed to carry over in 6 configurations on the first eligible model released afterward.

AI.tldr: LLM-based research is susceptible to p-hacking via prompt tuning and parameter tweaking. The authors propose a preregistration protocol where the confirmatory analysis is run on the first LLM released after preregistration, making it impossible to hack against a model that doesn't yet exist. Empirical validation shows the protocol blocks p-hacking transfer in ~73% of cases across two tasks.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used in research pipelines that feed downstream hypothesis tests, but this creates a severe p-hacking risk: researchers can iteratively tune prompts, decoding parameters, or output formats until they achieve statistical significance. Traditional solutions like sample splitting fail because the analyst can adaptively query the same LLM. A protocol is needed that prevents researchers from gaming LLM-based analyses toward desired results.
AI.method: The proposed protocol involves: (1) finalizing the analysis procedure on currently available models, (2) preregistering the analysis plan along with a set of eligible future models, and (3) running the confirmatory analysis exclusively on the first eligible model released after preregistration. Since this future model does not exist at commitment time, it cannot be p-hacked. The protocol was evaluated on two tasks with known ground truth, across 20 models from 4 providers and 11 LLM-analysis configurations. Stress tests were also conducted, and the authors themselves preregistered and executed their own protocol as a real-world demonstration.
AI.result: Across the two tasks, the protocol blocked successful transfer of p-hacking in 73.9% and 72.7% of cases respectively. Mitigation remained substantial under stress tests. In the authors' own preregistered experiment, 6 out of 7 configurations that successfully hacked the prior model failed to carry over to the first eligible future model.
AI.conclusion: Preregistering an LLM-based analysis and running it on the first eligible model released afterward effectively mitigates p-hacking, because hacking configurations rarely transfer across models. The protocol is practical and the authors demonstrate their commitment by successfully applying it to their own experiment.

title: Training Observable Control Policies to Expose Agent State Through Actions
summary: Physical or operational constraints often impose communications limitations on autonomous agents. Such limitations complicate monitoring or multiagent coordination. Even when strong communications are absent, some information may still be available. The remainder of the relevant agent state may be reconstructed via estimation. The actions taken by an agent are a potential source of information -- as the agent interacts with the environment, these actions may be observed even in the absence of explicit communication. We investigate using actions to estimate the state of an agent, using reinforcement learning to develop policies which make the estimation problem more tractable. Policy observability is encouraged through the training reward and is analyzed using simulation of the trained agent. In an aircraft tracking problem a policy with enhanced observability is found that has minimal impact on nominal task performance.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates using an agent's observable actions to estimate its internal state when communication is constrained, employing reinforcement learning to train policies that intentionally make state estimation easier (enhanced observability) without significantly degrading task performance.
AI.motivation: Autonomous agents often face communication limitations due to physical or operational constraints, complicating monitoring and coordination. Even without explicit communication, an agent's actions can be observed and may carry information about its internal state. The authors aim to exploit this action-based information channel by designing policies that actively facilitate state estimation by external observers.
AI.method: The authors use reinforcement learning to train agent policies, incorporating a reward signal that encourages policy observability — i.e., making the mapping from observed actions to underlying state more tractable for an estimator. The trained policies are evaluated via simulation, analyzing the trade-off between enhanced observability and nominal task performance.
AI.result: In an aircraft tracking problem, the approach successfully yields a policy with enhanced observability that enables better state estimation from actions alone, while imposing minimal impact on the agent's nominal task performance.
AI.conclusion: Reinforcement learning can be leveraged to produce policies that are deliberately more observable, allowing external observers to reconstruct agent state from actions alone when communications are unavailable. This offers a practical approach to maintaining situational awareness in communication-constrained multiagent systems.

title: JD Oxygen AI Item Center (Oxygen AIIC) V1: An Industrial-Scale LLM/VLM-Centric Solution for Item Understanding, Management, and Applications
summary: JD.com, one of the world's largest e-commerce platforms, serves over 700 million active users and millions of merchants, with a catalog of tens of billions of SKUs. At this scale, high-quality, structured item knowledge underpins a better consumer experience, lower management costs, and higher operational efficiency-yet producing and serving it poses three industrial-scale challenges: fast-emerging concepts, high-quality knowledge production for massive SKUs, and diverse downstream requirements. To address these challenges, we present the JD Oxygen AI Item Center (Oxygen AIIC), an industrial-scale platform built on LLMs/VLMs for item-knowledge production and service. Oxygen AIIC is built around four core pillars: (i) ontology engineering driven by efficient human-AI collaboration, which supports the dynamic evolution and agile expansion of an ontology with millions of entries; (ii) a "Semantic Search then Discrimination"(S2D) knowledge identification architecture that, combined with throughput improvement strategies, enables scalable, extensible, and high-throughput AI Item Library production for tens of billions of SKUs; (iii) self-evolving item-understanding LLMs/VLMs that improve in a stable and controllable manner, enabling knowledge production with 94.2% precision and 82.8% recall; and (iv) a unified item tunnel that serves as the data and service hub. Oxygen AIIC now covers tens of thousands of JD categories and processes hundreds of millions of item updates per day on Huawei Ascend NPUs. It has accumulated hundreds of billions of item-knowledge assets. Deployed across core business scenarios-including search, recommendation, operations, category planning-Oxygen AIIC has delivered measurable gains at scale. Search-traffic coverage reaches 80.4%, item-information quality issues drop by 37%, the automated fill rate of core attributes during item listing exceeds 80%.

AI.tldr: JD.com presents Oxygen AIIC, an industrial-scale platform leveraging LLMs/VLMs for automated, high-quality item-knowledge production across tens of billions of SKUs, achieving 94.2% precision and 82.8% recall, with measurable business impact including 80.4% search-traffic coverage and a 37% reduction in item-information quality issues.
AI.motivation: At JD.com's billion-SKU scale, producing and serving structured item knowledge faces three industrial-scale challenges: (1) fast-emerging concepts requiring rapid ontology evolution, (2) high-quality knowledge production for massive, ever-growing SKU catalogs, and (3) diverse downstream requirements across search, recommendation, operations, and category planning. Manual curation is infeasible at this scale, motivating an AI-driven platform.
AI.method: Oxygen AIIC is built on four pillars: (i) ontology engineering via human-AI collaboration for dynamic ontology evolution with millions of entries; (ii) a "Semantic Search then Discrimination" (S2D) architecture with throughput optimization for scalable knowledge identification across tens of billions of SKUs; (iii) self-evolving LLMs/VLMs for item understanding that improve in a stable, controllable manner; and (iv) a unified item tunnel serving as a centralized data and service hub. The system runs on Huawei Ascend NPUs.
AI.result: Knowledge production reaches 94.2% precision and 82.8% recall. The platform covers tens of thousands of JD categories, processes hundreds of millions of item updates daily, and has accumulated hundreds of billions of item-knowledge assets. In deployment: search-traffic coverage reaches 80.4%, item-information quality issues drop by 37%, and the automated fill rate of core attributes during item listing exceeds 80%.
AI.conclusion: Oxygen AIIC demonstrates that an LLM/VLM-driven platform can successfully address the triple challenges of scale, quality, and diversity in industrial item-knowledge production, delivering significant measurable business impact across core e-commerce scenarios at JD.com.

title: What Was That Again? Certified Robustness for Automatic Speech Recognition
summary: Automatic Speech Recognition systems are notoriously both sensitive to adversarial and benign perturbations. While this has been repeatedly demonstrated using reference datasets, detecting such behaviors in deployed systems is incredibly challenging, due to the absence of oracle knowledge of the true transcription. We demonstrate that employing a certification-inspired mechanism can significantly decrease WER, increase recall, and decrease the Spearman correlation between confidence and WER. We achieve this through a dual-gate diagnostic pipeline: a Two-Sided Atomic Audit that accumulates statistical wealth to certify both token existence and adversarial exclusion, and a Rank-Based Tournament that selects the winning sequence. Our evaluations across four diverse architectures demonstrate up to a 55% relative reduction in Word Error Rate, while also providing granular word- and sentence-level certifications to enhance acoustic security.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a certification-inspired dual-gate diagnostic pipeline for ASR systems that significantly reduces WER (up to 55% relative reduction), increases recall, and decouples confidence from WER, while providing word- and sentence-level security certifications.
AI.motivation: ASR systems are vulnerable to both adversarial and benign perturbations. While this vulnerability is well-documented on reference datasets, detecting such failures in deployed systems is extremely difficult because there is no oracle ground-truth transcription available. The authors aim to address this practical detection gap.
AI.method: A dual-gate diagnostic pipeline consisting of: (1) a Two-Sided Atomic Audit that accumulates statistical wealth to certify both token existence and adversarial exclusion, and (2) a Rank-Based Tournament that selects the winning output sequence. The mechanism is inspired by certification approaches, operating without access to oracle transcriptions.
AI.result: Evaluations across four diverse architectures show up to a 55% relative reduction in Word Error Rate (WER), increased recall, decreased Spearman correlation between confidence and WER, and granular word- and sentence-level certifications that enhance acoustic security.
AI.conclusion: Certification-inspired diagnostic mechanisms can effectively mitigate ASR vulnerability in deployment settings where oracle transcriptions are unavailable, simultaneously improving accuracy metrics and providing formal security guarantees at multiple granularities.

title: Mitigating Position Bias in Transformers via Layer-Specific Positional Embedding Scaling
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) still struggle with the ``lost-in-the-middle'' problem, where critical information located in the middle of long-context inputs is often underrepresented or lost. While existing methods attempt to address this by combining multi-scale rotary position embeddings (RoPE), they typically suffer from high latency or rely on suboptimal hand-crafted scaling strategies. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a layer-specific positional embedding scaling~(LPES) method that assigns distinct scaling factors to each layer. LPES achieves a more balanced attention distribution without fine-tuning model parameters or increasing inference delay. A specially designed genetic algorithm is employed to efficiently select the optimal scaling factors for each layer by incorporating Bézier curves to significantly reduce the search space. Extensive experiments demonstrate that LPES effectively mitigates positional attention bias and delivers consistent improvements across multiple long-context benchmarks, yielding up to an $11.2$\% accuracy gain on the key-value retrieval dataset.

AI.tldr: LPES addresses the "lost-in-the-middle" problem in LLMs by assigning genetically optimized, layer-specific scaling factors to rotary position embeddings (RoPE), improving long-context retrieval accuracy by up to 11.2% without fine-tuning or added latency.
AI.motivation: LLMs suffer from the "lost-in-the-middle" problem, where critical information in the middle of long contexts is underrepresented. Existing multi-scale RoPE solutions either incur high latency or rely on suboptimal hand-crafted scaling strategies, motivating an efficient, principled approach.
AI.method: The authors propose Layer-specific Positional Embedding Scaling (LPES), which assigns distinct RoPE scaling factors to each transformer layer to achieve a more balanced attention distribution. A genetic algorithm incorporating Bézier curves is used to efficiently search the reduced parameter space for optimal per-layer scaling factors, requiring no model fine-tuning and introducing no inference delay.
AI.result: Extensive experiments demonstrate that LPES effectively mitigates positional attention bias, delivering consistent improvements across multiple long-context benchmarks, including up to an 11.2% accuracy gain on key-value retrieval datasets.
AI.conclusion: LPES provides an efficient, training-free solution to the lost-in-the-middle problem through layer-wise RoPE scaling optimized via a Bézier-guided genetic algorithm, achieving significant accuracy gains without computational overhead.

title: COOPA: A Modular LLM Agent Architecture for Operations Research Problems
summary: Operations Research (OR) provides a rigorous framework for high-stakes decision-making, but effective OR modeling requires substantial domain knowledge, mathematical abstraction, and solver expertise. Recent LLM-based systems automate parts of this pipeline, yet remain limited by low accuracy on complex problems, opaque outputs, and narrow solver support. We propose COOPA (COoperative OPerations Agent), a modular LLM-agent architecture for interpretable and scalable OR decision support. It combines three components: iterative confidence-based modeling, which generates multiple candidate formulations, self-evaluates them across modeling dimensions, and selects one using a max-min confidence criterion; element-level provenance and confidence explanations, which link variables, parameters, constraints, and objectives to quoted source text and provide an audit trail for human verification; and multi-solver routing to specialized optimizer agents for different OR problem classes. Across three OR benchmarks, eight LLM backbones, and four baselines under identical conditions, COOPA achieves the best macro-average accuracy on six of eight backbones and improves over the strongest baseline by up to 6.7 percentage points. A within-system ablation isolates the contribution of iterative confidence-based modeling, while additional analyses and case studies illustrate the value of source traceability and multi-solver dispatch.

AI.tldr: COOPA is a modular LLM-agent system for operations research that improves modeling accuracy via iterative confidence-based candidate selection, provides interpretability through source-linked provenance tracking, and routes problems to specialized solvers. It achieves state-of-the-art accuracy across multiple benchmarks and LLM backbones, outperforming baselines by up to 6.7 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based systems for operations research suffer from low accuracy on complex problems, lack of transparency (opaque outputs), and limited support for diverse solver types. There is a need for an interpretable, accurate, and broadly applicable automated OR decision-support system.
AI.method: COOPA employs three integrated modules: (1) Iterative confidence-based modeling — generates multiple candidate formulations, self-evaluates them, and selects the best using a max-min confidence criterion; (2) Element-level provenance and confidence explanations — links every variable, parameter, constraint, and objective to quoted source text, creating an auditable trail; (3) Multi-solver routing — dispatches problems to specialized optimizer agents based on problem class.
AI.result: Evaluated across three OR benchmarks, eight LLM backbones, and four baselines under identical conditions, COOPA achieved the highest macro-average accuracy on six of eight backbones and outperformed the strongest baseline by up to 6.7 percentage points. Ablation studies confirmed the contribution of iterative confidence-based modeling, and case studies demonstrated the value of source traceability and multi-solver dispatch.
AI.conclusion: COOPA advances automated OR modeling by combining confidence-driven candidate selection, transparent provenance tracking, and specialized solver routing into a unified, interpretable agent architecture that sets a new state-of-the-art for LLM-based operations research decision support.

title: Ontology-Guided Evidence Path Inference for Multi-hop Knowledge Graph Question Answering
summary: Knowledge graph question answering (KGQA) aims to answer natural-language questions by reasoning over structured facts. Existing multi-hop KGQA methods mainly rely on topic-centered expansion, which faces two key challenges: the search space rapidly grows with noisy mixed-type paths, and retrieved paths may fail to satisfy the semantic constraints of complex questions. To address these challenges, we propose OPI, an ontology-guided evidence path inference framework for multi-hop KGQA. OPI introduces a relation-centric ontology graph to capture the head-tail type constraints of relations, providing a compact interface for answer-side constraints. Based on this ontology graph, OPI first introduces a bidirectional retrieval mechanism by mapping the predicted answer type to compatible final-hop relations and combining topic-side prefix expansion with answer-side final-hop matching, thereby suppressing noisy mixed-type expansion. OPI further adopts an iterative refinement strategy to reassess retrieved paths and candidate answers under the question context, filtering type-compatible but question-irrelevant evidence for more reliable answer prediction. Experiments on WebQSP, CWQ, and MetaQA show that OPI substantially reduces the search space, improves Hit@1/F1 by 4.6/5.0 points on WebQSP and 8.9/3.3 points on CWQ over the strongest prior results, and achieves near-saturated Hit@1 on MetaQA with the retrieval module alone.

AI.tldr: OPI is an ontology-guided evidence path inference framework for multi-hop KGQA that uses a relation-centric ontology graph to constrain answer types, employs bidirectional retrieval (topic-side expansion + answer-side final-hop matching), and iteratively refines evidence to suppress noisy paths, achieving significant improvements over prior SOTA on WebQSP, CWQ, and MetaQA.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-hop KGQA methods relying on topic-centered expansion suffer from two major issues: (1) the search space explodes due to noisy mixed-type paths, and (2) retrieved paths often violate semantic constraints of complex questions. A more principled mechanism is needed to enforce answer-type compatibility and semantic relevance during evidence retrieval.
AI.method: OPI constructs a relation-centric ontology graph encoding head-tail type constraints for relations. Three key components: (1) Bidirectional retrieval — predicts answer type, maps it to compatible final-hop relations, then combines forward prefix expansion from topic entities with backward final-hop matching to prune mixed-type noise. (2) Iterative refinement — reassesses retrieved paths and candidate answers against the question context to filter type-compatible but question-irrelevant evidence. (3) The ontology graph serves as a compact answer-side constraint interface throughout.
AI.result: On WebQSP: Hit@1/F1 improved by 4.6/5.0 points over prior SOTA. On CWQ: Hit@1 improved by 8.9 points, F1 by 3.3 points. On MetaQA: the retrieval module alone achieves near-saturated Hit@1. The approach substantially reduces the search space across all benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Ontology-guided type constraints, combined with bidirectional retrieval and iterative refinement, effectively address the search space explosion and semantic mismatch problems in multi-hop KGQA, yielding state-of-the-art performance.

title: Low-Agreeableness Persona Conditioning for Safe LLM Fine-Tuning
summary: Recent work has shown that fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) for social warmth degrades factual reliability and increases sycophancy. We investigate a related but distinct failure mode: warmth fine-tuning also weakens adversarial safety, making models more susceptible to jailbreaks and harmful output generation. We examine whether this reflects an inherent consequence of empathetic adaptation or an artifact of data construction. To address this, we introduce a persona-driven rewriting pipeline that conditions user turns on low agreeableness and pairs this with warm, de-escalating assistant responses. Across three experiments on four models, our approach reduces jailbreak susceptibility and harmful output rates relative to generic warmth fine-tuning baselines, while preserving conversational warmth. Representational probing provides suggestive evidence that this conditioning reduces the geometric alignment between warmth and compliance directions in latent space. These results show that safer empathetic fine-tuning is achievable through data design alone, without safety labels, harm detectors, or changes to the training objective.

AI.tldr: Fine-tuning LLMs for warmth increases jailbreak vulnerability. The authors propose a persona-driven data pipeline that conditions on low-agreeableness user turns paired with warm assistant responses, reducing harmful outputs while preserving conversational warmth.
AI.motivation: Prior work established that warmth fine-tuning degrades factual reliability and promotes sycophancy. This paper identifies a new failure mode: warmth fine-tuning also compromises adversarial safety, making models more susceptible to jailbreaks. The authors investigate whether this is an inevitable trade-off or an artifact of data construction that can be mitigated through better dataset design.
AI.method: The authors introduce a persona-driven rewriting pipeline. It takes existing dialogue data and conditions user turns on a low-agreeableness persona (making users more adversarial/provocative) while pairing these with warm, de-escalating assistant responses. This decouples warmth from compliance. Three experiments across four models evaluate jailbreak susceptibility and harmful output rates against generic warmth fine-tuning baselines. Representational probing examines latent-space geometry between warmth and compliance directions.
AI.result: The persona-conditioned pipeline reduces jailbreak susceptibility and harmful output rates compared to standard warmth fine-tuning, while preserving conversational warmth. Probing analyses suggest the approach reduces geometric alignment between warmth and compliance directions in the model's latent representation space.
AI.conclusion: Safer empathetic fine-tuning is achievable through data design alone — without requiring safety labels, harm detectors, or changes to the training objective. The key insight is that warmth and compliance can be decoupled in the training distribution.

title: FoggyTrust: Robust Federated Learning with Hierarchical Trust Networks
summary: Byzantine-robust federated learning seeks to protect distributed model training from malicious or corrupted clients without requiring access to their private data. FLTrust addresses this challenge by introducing a trusted server-side root dataset that assigns trust scores to client updates for more robust aggregation. In this work, we propose FOGGYTRUST, a hierarchical extension of FLTrust that localizes trust computation to fog nodes, allowing the framework to better handle globally heterogeneous data while preserving robustness within locally homogeneous client groups. We further show that this two-level architecture can simultaneously address distribution mismatch in trust estimation and client drift across groups by combining local trust-based aggregation with heterogeneity-aware global optimizers such as FedAdam and SCAFFOLD. Across benchmark datasets, FOGGYTRUST achieves its strongest gains on more challenging heterogeneous settings, particularly on CIFAR-10 under Krum and Trim attacks, where it achieves an over 50% improvement over FLTrust. We also test FOGGYTRUST in a real-world safari dataset to show the promise of hierarchical trust networks for robust federated learning in socially impactful, safety-critical settings such as distributed wildlife monitoring.

AI.tldr: FOGGYTRUST extends FLTrust with a hierarchical fog-layer architecture that localizes trust scoring to fog nodes, enabling robust federated learning under heterogeneous data distributions and Byzantine attacks. It pairs local trust-based aggregation with global optimizers like FedAdam and SCAFFOLD, achieving over 50% improvement over FLTrust on challenging CIFAR-10 settings under Krum/Trim attacks.
AI.motivation: Standard FLTrust suffers from distribution mismatch between the server-side root dataset and globally heterogeneous client data, undermining trust score accuracy. Additionally, client drift across diverse groups degrades model convergence. A hierarchical approach can better align trust estimation with local data distributions while mitigating cross-group heterogeneity.
AI.method: FOGGYTRUST introduces a two-tier architecture: (1) fog nodes each maintain localized root datasets and compute per-group trust scores for client updates within their homogeneous clusters; (2) a global server aggregates fog-level updates using heterogeneity-aware optimizers (FedAdam, SCAFFOLD) that correct for inter-group drift. Trust scores are computed via cosine similarity between client updates and the fog node's root-based update direction.
AI.result: On benchmark datasets, FOGGYTRUST shows strongest gains under high heterogeneity. On CIFAR-10 with Krum and Trim Byzantine attacks, it surpasses FLTrust by over 50% in accuracy. The method also demonstrates practical viability on a real-world safari wildlife monitoring dataset, confirming effectiveness in safety-critical distributed settings.
AI.conclusion: FOGGYTRUST demonstrates that hierarchical trust networks—localizing trust computation to fog nodes while using heterogeneity-aware global aggregation—significantly improve Byzantine robustness in federated learning under non-IID data, with strong potential for real-world safety-critical applications like wildlife monitoring.

title: AI-Driven Synthesis for High-Tech System Design: Automating Innovation
summary: This article addresses the combinatorial complexity inherent in modern high-tech system design by presenting automation-in-design (AiD) as a transformative paradigm. We propose computational design synthesis (CDS), a framework utilising deep learning and generative AI to automate the creation of novel systems. Two case studies (e-drive system design and spatial dimensioning problem) serve as proof-points for this approach. The AI-driven methods used in the case studies represent a fundamental shift in engineering, advancing from simulation-based optimisation towards autonomous design with minimal human supervision.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Automation-in-Design (AiD) and a Computational Design Synthesis (CDS) framework that leverages deep learning and generative AI to automate novel system design, demonstrated through e-drive and spatial dimensioning case studies, marking a shift from simulation-based optimization to autonomous engineering design.
AI.motivation: Modern high-tech systems exhibit combinatorial complexity that overwhelms traditional human-driven design processes, necessitating a paradigm shift toward automated design methodologies to handle the vast design space efficiently.
AI.method: The authors propose Computational Design Synthesis (CDS), a framework employing deep learning and generative AI techniques to automatically generate novel engineering systems. The approach is validated through two proof-of-concept case studies: e-drive system design and a spatial dimensioning problem.
AI.result: The two case studies demonstrate the viability of AI-driven autonomous design, successfully generating novel system configurations with minimal human supervision, thereby substantiating the CDS framework as a proof-point for the AiD paradigm.
AI.conclusion: The CDS framework represents a fundamental shift in engineering design practice, advancing beyond conventional simulation-based optimization toward truly autonomous design capabilities, with AiD positioned as a transformative paradigm for tackling combinatorial complexity in high-tech system development.

title: Do Speech Emphasis Models Generalize across Languages and Emotions?
summary: Prosodic emphasis varies across languages, emotions, and speaking styles, yet existing emphasis detection models are largely trained and evaluated on monolingual neutral read speech. We introduce MMEE (Multilingual Multi-Emotion Emphasis), a corpus of 10,000 professionally recorded expressive utterances (14.13 hours) across 7 languages and 34 emotion/style categories, with three-level perceptual labels (10 annotations per sample). We benchmark two state-of-the-art architectures under monolingual, cross-lingual, multilingual, cross-emotion, cross-dataset, and data-scale settings. Monolingual models show limited zero-shot transfer, degrading across typologically distant languages, while multilingual training substantially improves robustness. Models transfer robustly between high- and low-arousal emotions; bidirectional transfer between synthetic and perceptual benchmarks suggests shared prosodic structure; and performance stays robust even at smaller training scales.

AI.tldr: MMEE is a multilingual, multi-emotion emphasis corpus (7 languages, 34 emotion/styles, 10k utterances) with perceptual labels. Benchmarking shows multilingual training improves cross-lingual robustness, models transfer well across arousal levels, and synthetic–perceptual transfer reveals shared prosodic structure.
AI.motivation: Existing emphasis detection models are limited to monolingual neutral read speech, despite prosodic emphasis varying significantly across languages, emotions, and speaking styles. There is a need for a multilingual, multi-emotion corpus and a systematic evaluation of how emphasis detection generalizes across these dimensions.
AI.method: The authors construct MMEE, a corpus of 10,000 professionally recorded utterances across 7 languages and 34 emotion/style categories, annotated with three-level perceptual emphasis labels (10 annotators per sample). Two state-of-the-art emphasis detection architectures are benchmarked under six conditions: monolingual, cross-lingual, multilingual, cross-emotion, cross-dataset, and varying data-scale settings.
AI.result: Monolingual models exhibit poor zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, particularly for typologically distant languages. Multilingual training substantially improves robustness. Models transfer robustly between high- and low-arousal emotions. Bidirectional transfer between synthetic and perceptual benchmarks indicates shared prosodic structure. Performance remains stable even at reduced training data scales.
AI.conclusion: Multilingual training is critical for robust emphasis detection across languages. The shared prosodic structure between synthetic and perceptual data, along with robustness to reduced data scale and arousal-level transfer, suggests that emphasis detection can generalize effectively when trained on diverse, perceptually annotated multilingual data.

title: HybridCodec: Modeling Discrete and Continuous Representations for Efficient Speech Language Models
summary: Discrete audio representations have become increasingly popular for building multimodal text-audio systems and integrating audio capabilities into Large Language Models (LLMs). However, numerous studies report performance degradation on various downstream tasks due to information loss during discretization. To address this, we propose a novel approach combining temporally compressed discrete tokens with dimensionality-reduced continuous residuals. Our framework consists of a hybridized discrete-continuous focal modulation codec and a hybrid Transformer. This architecture performs autoregressive inference in the discrete domain, coupled with non-autoregressive prediction and continuous residual upsampling. Experimental results show that our approach significantly improves the retention of speaker characteristics compared to discrete-only methods, while simultaneously reducing the number of required autoregressive steps.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid discrete-continuous audio representation that combines temporally compressed discrete tokens with dimensionality-reduced continuous residuals, improving speaker characteristic retention while reducing autoregressive steps compared to discrete-only methods.
AI.motivation: Discrete audio representations enable multimodal text-audio integration with LLMs but suffer from information loss during discretization, degrading downstream task performance.
AI.method: A hybridized discrete-continuous focal modulation codec paired with a hybrid Transformer architecture. Autoregressive inference operates in the discrete domain, complemented by non-autoregressive prediction and continuous residual upsampling.
AI.result: Significantly improved retention of speaker characteristics over discrete-only baselines, with a reduction in the number of required autoregressive steps.
AI.conclusion: The hybrid discrete-continuous approach effectively mitigates discretization-induced information loss while maintaining compatibility with autoregressive modeling paradigms used in LLM-based audio systems.

title: Tandem Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has significantly improved the reasoning capability of large language models, reaching expert or even superhuman performance in domains such as competition math. However, whether weaker agents and humans can actually harness this capability is far less certain, with RLVR documented to drift reasoning toward idiosyncratic patterns such as poor readability and language mixing. Tandem training is a recently introduced paradigm that targets this compatibility problem: a trained, stronger senior co-generates each rollout with a frozen, weaker junior, and the two are rewarded as a team, so the senior is pushed to reason in ways the junior can follow. Yet this paradigm has so far been demonstrated only in proof-of-concept settings, leaving open whether it scales to the long chains of thought of the modern RLVR pipeline. In this work, we propose Tandem Reinforcement Learning (TRL), which carries the tandem training paradigm into RLVR. In TRL, the senior and a frozen junior alternate stochastically to co-generate the reasoning, the resulting generation is rewarded, and the standard GRPO loss is applied to the senior. Training Qwen3-4B-Instruct on competition math, we find that TRL matches vanilla GRPO on solo reasoning capability while three properties emerge together from the same rollout structure: stronger handoff robustness with the junior, reduced distributional drift from the junior, and a chain-of-thought more legible to the junior. Our results demonstrate a promising route for RLVR with practical payoffs in multi-model communication and human compatibility.

AI.tldr: TRL extends tandem training to RLVR by having a senior model and frozen junior model stochastically alternate in co-generating reasoning chains, achieving solo performance on par with vanilla GRPO while simultaneously improving junior compatibility, reducing distributional drift, and enhancing chain-of-thought legibility.
AI.motivation: RLVR improves LLM reasoning but causes idiosyncratic patterns (poor readability, language mixing) that weaker agents and humans cannot follow. Prior tandem training showed promise for compatibility but was limited to proof-of-concept settings and hadn't scaled to modern RLVR with long chains of thought.
AI.method: TRL: A senior model and frozen junior model stochastically alternate to co-generate reasoning chains. The full co-generated rollout receives a verifiable reward, and the standard GRPO loss is applied only to the senior model. The junior remains frozen throughout. Experiments use Qwen3-4B-Instruct on competition math benchmarks.
AI.result: TRL matches vanilla GRPO on solo reasoning capability. Three beneficial properties emerge: stronger handoff robustness (senior can effectively pass control to junior), reduced distributional drift from the junior's perspective, and more legible chain-of-thought for the junior model.
AI.conclusion: TRL demonstrates a scalable path for RLVR that produces practical benefits in multi-model communication and human compatibility without sacrificing individual reasoning performance, suggesting tandem training principles can be successfully integrated into modern RLVR pipelines.

title: Enhancing Numerical Prediction in LLMs via Smooth MMD Alignment
summary: Despite their strong general capabilities, large language models (LLMs) often remain unreliable when outputs must be numerically precise. A key reason is the training objective: standard cross-entropy treats numeric tokens as unstructured categories and ignores the metric structure of their values. We address this mismatch with Smooth Maximum Mean Discrepancy (SMMD), which builds on the classic MMD by incorporating value-distance kernels over numeric tokens and graph-based smoothness. With this kernel defined over a numeric sub-vocabulary, SMMD aligns the predicted numeric distribution to the target via kernel matching and smooths the prediction-target residual over the induced kernel graph to encourage local consistency. We evaluate SMMD on four numeric-target tasks: mathematical reasoning, arithmetic calculation, clock-time recognition, and chart question answering, across multiple open-weight LLM and VLM backbones. SMMD consistently improves accuracy over both cross-entropy and recent numeric-target losses; analyses show complementary effects between MMD and smoothness and underscore the importance of distance-based kernel design. Code is available at https://github.com/Zuozhuo/smmd-loss.

AI.tldr: SMMD enhances LLM numerical precision by replacing cross-entropy with a kernel-based loss that respects numeric value distances, using Maximum Mean Discrepancy with graph smoothness over a numeric sub-vocabulary, yielding consistent accuracy gains across math, arithmetic, clock, and chart tasks.
AI.motivation: LLMs treat numeric tokens as unstructured categories under standard cross-entropy, ignoring the metric structure of their values. This causes unreliability when outputs require numerical precision. A loss function that respects numeric distances is needed.
AI.method: Smooth Maximum Mean Discrepancy (SMMD): (1) defines a numeric sub-vocabulary with value-distance kernels over tokens; (2) uses MMD kernel matching to align predicted and target numeric distributions; (3) applies graph-based smoothness over the kernel graph to encourage local consistency in prediction-target residuals. The approach works for both LLMs and VLMs.
AI.result: SMMD consistently improves accuracy over cross-entropy and recent numeric-target losses across four tasks: mathematical reasoning, arithmetic calculation, clock-time recognition, and chart QA. Ablations confirm complementary effects between MMD and smoothness components, and validate the importance of distance-based kernel design.
AI.conclusion: SMMD provides an effective, general-purpose numeric-aware training objective for LLMs/VLMs, addressing a fundamental mismatch in standard token-level loss functions. The kernel design and smoothness regularization are both essential contributors to performance gains.

title: Continual Learning for Sequential Personalization of Small Language Models: A Stability Monitoring Analysis
summary: Small Language Models (SLMs) are increasingly being considered for deployment on edge devices such as laptops, enabling private, low-latency, and locally personalized applications. However, personalization requires models to adapt over time to evolving user- or task-specific data, placing them in a continual learning setting. This creates the risk of catastrophic forgetting, where learning new information degrades performance on previously learned tasks or broader model capabilities. Recent benchmarks such as TRACE have shown that continual fine-tuning can significantly degrade the general abilities of aligned large language models. In this work, we present a study for sequential LoRA personalization of SLMs. We save model checkpoints after each adaptation stage and evaluate them on current tasks, previously seen tasks, and a fixed reference set. This checkpoint-level protocol enables us to monitor task performance, forgetting, and reference set drift over time. We show that lightweight reference set distributional diagnostics can reveal model-specific instability patterns during sequential LoRA personalization of SLMs, including cases where task-level metrics alone hide harmful adaptation. We hope this can highlight new research avenues for monitoring stability of SLMs in a continual learning setting.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates catastrophic forgetting during sequential LoRA fine-tuning of Small Language Models (SLMs) for personalization. Using checkpoint-level evaluation across current tasks, past tasks, and a fixed reference set, the authors demonstrate that lightweight distributional diagnostics can detect model instability patterns that task-level metrics alone may conceal.
AI.motivation: SLMs are increasingly deployed on edge devices for private, personalized applications requiring continual adaptation. However, sequential fine-tuning risks catastrophic forgetting, and prior work (e.g., TRACE) shows this can degrade general capabilities in aligned LLMs. There is a need for monitoring protocols that can detect subtle forms of model degradation during continual personalization.
AI.method: The authors employ sequential LoRA personalization of SLMs, saving model checkpoints after each adaptation stage. They evaluate each checkpoint on three axes: (1) the current task, (2) previously seen tasks (to measure forgetting), and (3) a fixed reference set (to detect distributional drift). Lightweight reference set distributional diagnostics are used to uncover model-specific instability patterns.
AI.result: Lightweight reference set distributional diagnostics can reveal model-specific instability patterns during sequential LoRA personalization. Critically, these diagnostics can identify harmful adaptation in cases where task-level metrics alone fail to signal degradation.
AI.conclusion: The checkpoint-level evaluation protocol and distributional diagnostics provide a more sensitive lens for monitoring SLM stability in continual learning settings. The authors hope this work opens new research directions for ensuring safe and stable personalization of SLMs on edge devices.

title: KG2Cypher: Data-Centric Pipeline for Building Enterprise Text-to-Cypher Systems
summary: Enterprise Knowledge Graphs (KGs) are increasingly used for internal search, analytics, and question answering, but building natural-language interfaces for private enterprise graphs remains costly. We present KG2Cypher, a data-centric pipeline for building enterprise text-to-Cypher systems from existing KGs. KG2Cypher first constructs an executable Cypher query from observed graph facts and then uses LLMs to generate its associated natural-language question. The resulting Text-Cypher pairs are validated with an LLM judge and human validation, and are converted into candidate-aware SFT data. The trained generator is served with class-conditioned schema prompting, entity retrieval, and LoRA-based inference. We evaluate KG2Cypher in Korean enterprise settings, where short search-style queries and schema paraphrases make language grounding difficult. LoRA SFT improves execution-result F1 from 0.806 to 0.950 on broadcast-program queries and from 0.70 to 0.92 on company queries. In an 11-class setting, KG2Cypher achieves 95.2% exact match, 99.9% execution rate, and 0.964 execution-result F1.

AI.tldr: KG2Cypher is a data-centric pipeline that constructs Text-Cypher training pairs from existing enterprise KGs by reverse-generating natural-language questions from observed graph facts, then fine-tunes LLMs with candidate-aware SFT for text-to-Cypher generation, achieving strong results in Korean enterprise settings.
AI.motivation: Building natural-language interfaces for private enterprise KGs is costly due to the scarcity of domain-specific Text-Cypher training data. Existing approaches rely on expensive manual annotation or struggle with short search-style queries and schema paraphrases common in enterprise environments.
AI.method: KG2Cypher operates in two stages: (1) Data construction — executable Cypher queries are synthesized from observed graph facts, then an LLM generates corresponding natural-language questions, which are validated by an LLM judge and humans to produce candidate-aware SFT data. (2) Inference — the fine-tuned generator is served using class-conditioned schema prompting, entity retrieval, and LoRA-based efficient fine-tuning for multi-class deployment.
AI.result: In Korean enterprise evaluations, LoRA SFT improved execution-result F1 from 0.806 to 0.950 on broadcast-program queries and from 0.70 to 0.92 on company queries. In an 11-class unified setting, KG2Cypher achieved 95.2% exact match, 99.9% execution rate, and 0.964 execution-result F1.
AI.conclusion: KG2Cypher demonstrates that a data-centric, reverse-generation approach can produce high-quality Text-Cypher training data at scale, enabling robust text-to-Cypher systems for private enterprise KGs, even in linguistically challenging settings like Korean with short, paraphrastic queries.

title: TeRoR: Decoupled Temporal Rotation with Relational Circular Region for Temporal Knowledge Graph Embedding
summary: In recent years, with the emergence of Temporal Knowledge Graphs (TKGs), research on learning entity and relation representations in TKGs has attracted increasing attention, giving rise to a large number of TKG embedding methods. TeRo is a simple and efficient temporal knowledge graph embedding approach. However, TeRo does not do well in modeling the mapping properties of various relations, such as one-to-many, many-to-one, and many-to-many. Meanwhile, it also has limitations in the expression of temporal information. To address these issues, we propose a novel TKG embedding method named TeRoR. This method divides the temporal evolution of entity embeddings, and conducts independent rotation transformations on head and tail entities in the complex vector space to strengthen temporal information modeling capacity. In terms of relational characteristics, we train a radius to constrain the rotated and translated head entities within a circular region centered on the tail entity, which effectively captures the diverse mapping properties of relations. Experimental results demonstrate that TeRoR achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art models on four distinct TKG datasets.

AI.tldr: TeRoR improves upon TeRo for temporal knowledge graph embedding by incorporating independent rotational transformations for head/tail entities and a radius-based circular constraint around the tail entity, achieving better modeling of temporal dynamics and relational mapping properties (1-to-M, M-to-1, M-to-M).
AI.motivation: TeRo, while simple and efficient, suffers from two key weaknesses: (1) poor modeling of relational mapping properties (one-to-many, many-to-one, many-to-many), and (2) limited capacity in expressing temporal information. These deficiencies motivate the development of TeRoR.
AI.method: TeRoR introduces two main innovations: (1) it decomposes the temporal evolution of entity embeddings and applies independent rotation transformations to head and tail entities in complex vector space, strengthening temporal information modeling; (2) it learns a relation-specific radius that constrains the rotated and translated head entity within a circular region centered on the tail entity, enabling effective capture of diverse relational mapping properties.
AI.result: Experimental results on four distinct TKG datasets show that TeRoR achieves competitive performance compared to state-of-the-art TKG embedding models.
AI.conclusion: TeRoR effectively addresses the limitations of TeRo by enhancing both temporal modeling (via independent rotational transformations) and relational mapping modeling (via radius-constrained circular regions), yielding strong empirical performance across multiple benchmark datasets.

title: Output-Space Allocation Costs for Calibration-Guided LLM Compression: An Empirical Study
summary: Training-free compression methods for large language models (LLMs) often use calibration data to guide compression decisions. ROCKET, a recent method combining sparse-dictionary factorization with multi-choice knapsack problem (MCKP) allocation, derives its per-layer factorization from an output reconstruction objective but uses weight-space Frobenius error as the MCKP allocation cost. We investigate whether aligning the allocation cost with the output-space objective improves compressed model fidelity. On Qwen3-8B at 50\% compression, our ROCKET-ActCost achieves +0.8 percentage points higher average accuracy across 8 zero-shot benchmarks (53.1\% vs 52.3\%), but increases WikiText perplexity by 16\% (61.46 vs 52.98). This accuracy-perplexity tradeoff reveals that different allocation objectives favor different downstream metrics. The high correlation ($>$0.99) between weight-space and output-space errors limits allocation divergence, explaining the modest effect size. On Llama-3.2-1B at 20\% compression, the two methods produce near-identical results (53.3\% vs 53.5\% accuracy, 14.45 vs 14.66 PPL), suggesting that the effect of the cost function is minor at lower compression ratios.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes ROCKET-ActCost, a variant of the ROCKET compression method that replaces weight-space Frobenius error with an output-space reconstruction cost for MCKP allocation. While this improves zero-shot accuracy slightly (+0.8pp on Qwen3-8B at 50% compression), it degrades perplexity, revealing a tradeoff. The high correlation between both cost metrics limits allocation divergence, and at lower compression ratios the effect becomes negligible.
AI.motivation: ROCKET uses an output reconstruction objective for deriving its sparse-dictionary factorization but switches to a weight-space Frobenius error for the MCKP allocation step. The authors investigate whether aligning the allocation cost with the output-space objective improves compressed model performance, hypothesizing that a consistent objective throughout the pipeline should yield better fidelity.
AI.method: The authors modify ROCKET by replacing its weight-space Frobenius error with an output-activation reconstruction cost during the MCKP allocation phase. They evaluate ROCKET-ActCost against the original ROCKET on Qwen3-8B (at 50% compression) and Llama-3.2-1B (at 20% compression), measuring zero-shot accuracy across 8 benchmarks and WikiText perplexity. They also compute the correlation between weight-space and output-space errors to quantify allocation divergence.
AI.result: On Qwen3-8B at 50% compression, ROCKET-ActCost achieves 53.1% average accuracy (+0.8pp over ROCKET's 52.3%) but higher WikiText perplexity (61.46 vs 52.98, a 16% increase). The correlation between weight-space and output-space errors exceeds 0.99, limiting allocation divergence. On Llama-3.2-1B at 20% compression, results are near-identical (53.3% vs 53.5% accuracy; 14.45 vs 14.66 PPL), indicating the cost function's effect is minor at lower compression ratios.
AI.conclusion: Aligning the MCKP allocation cost with the output-space objective yields a modest accuracy gain but at the cost of increased perplexity, revealing a previously undocumented tradeoff. The effect is bounded by the very high correlation between weight-space and output-space errors, and diminishes at lower compression ratios. The choice of allocation objective thus represents a tunable knob for prioritizing different downstream metrics.

title: Are Time-Series Foundation Models Ready for E-Nose Data? An Empirical Assessment of Their Embeddings
summary: Inspired by advances in natural language processing and computer vision, "time-series foundation models" (TSFMs) have recently been introduced with the promise of strong generalization across diverse time-series tasks, including forecasting, classification, and anomaly detection, as well as across domains such as healthcare, climate science, and manufacturing. However, their utility for gas-sensing data remains largely unexplored. To address this gap, this paper systematically evaluates recent TSFMs on electronic nose (E-Nose) data. In particular, we investigate whether embeddings produced by representative TSFMs, including Chronos-2 and MOMENT, provide effective representations for gas identification and concentration prediction. Specifically, we show that fine-tuning is necessary to achieve satisfactory performance on E-Nose data, and fusing TSFM embeddings with representations learned by specialized predictive models can further improve the performance, suggesting both the potential and limitations of current TSFMs for gas-sensing applications.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically evaluates time-series foundation models (TSFMs) on electronic nose data for gas sensing, finding that fine-tuning is essential and that fusing TSFM embeddings with specialized model representations yields the best performance.
