AI.motivation: TSFMs have shown strong generalization across domains, but their utility for gas-sensing data remains unexplored. This gap motivates a systematic evaluation of TSFMs on E-Nose data.
AI.method: The authors evaluate representative TSFMs (Chronos-2 and MOMENT) on E-Nose data for gas identification and concentration prediction, comparing raw TSFM embeddings, fine-tuned models, and fusion of TSFM embeddings with specialized predictive model representations.
AI.result: Fine-tuning is necessary for satisfactory performance; fusing TSFM embeddings with representations from specialized models further improves gas identification and concentration prediction accuracy.
AI.conclusion: Current TSFMs show both potential and limitations for gas-sensing applications — they require fine-tuning and benefit from hybrid fusion approaches rather than working out-of-the-box.

title: SHIFT: Gate-Modulated Activation Steering for Knowledge Conflict Mitigation in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) enhances LLMs by incorporating external knowledge to support response generation. However, conflicts between retrieved context and parametric knowledge have emerged as a critical challenge in RAG systems. To mitigate such conflicts, numerous studies have attempted to identify and edit knowledge-related internal neurons, aiming to improve the ability of LLMs to rely on contextual evidence during generation. However, these neuron-level approaches may introduce unintended cascading effects that compromise the general capabilities of LLMs, as the modified neurons are often entangled with broader model behaviors and functionalities. In this paper, we introduce SHIFT, a novel framework that reformulates neuron-level modification as learnable gate modulation, allowing LLMs to adaptively regulate internal activations for knowledge conflict resolution. Technically, our SHIFT equips LLMs with a lightweight gate module and optimizes fewer than 0.01% trainable parameters while keeping the backbone model frozen. During generation, the gate module adjusts the model's internal representations to adaptively leverage contextual and parametric knowledge. Extensive experiments on six datasets validate the effectiveness of our SHIFT in comparison with various competing baselines. All datasets and code are available at https://github.com/OpenBMB/SHIFT.

AI.tldr: SHIFT proposes a parameter-efficient framework that resolves knowledge conflicts in RAG systems by using learnable gate modulation instead of directly editing neurons, preserving general LLM capabilities while adaptively balancing contextual and parametric knowledge.
AI.motivation: In RAG systems, conflicts between retrieved context and the LLM's internal parametric knowledge pose a significant challenge. Existing neuron-editing methods risk unintended cascading effects that degrade general model capabilities, motivating a need for a less invasive, more targeted approach to knowledge conflict resolution.
AI.method: SHIFT reformulates neuron-level modification as learnable gate modulation. A lightweight gate module (fewer than 0.01% trainable parameters) is added to a frozen backbone LLM. During generation, the gate module adaptively adjusts internal representations, allowing the model to flexibly leverage either contextual or parametric knowledge as needed.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across six datasets demonstrate that SHIFT outperforms various competing baselines in resolving knowledge conflicts within RAG systems.
AI.conclusion: SHIFT provides an effective and parameter-efficient solution for knowledge conflict resolution in RAG, avoiding the pitfalls of direct neuron editing. Code and datasets are publicly available.

title: Textual Belief States for World Models: Identifiable Representation Learning Under Strict Mediation
summary: World models in partially observed environments rely on latent representations that summarize interaction history, but in many modern LLM-based architectures predictive performance fails to reflect representation quality due to history bypass, rendering the latent state unidentifiable. Strict latent state mediation, requiring predictions to depend only on the latent state and action, is a classical principle that resolves this, but enforcing it in text-based settings is an open challenge: textual latent states are discrete and non-differentiable, precluding variational training, and expressive LLM decoders readily ignore the bottleneck. We show how to make strict mediation work in the text domain. We formalize why it is necessary, showing that strict mediation makes representation quality empirically testable while history-leaky architectures break this connection. We then introduce textual latent states, which are discrete, interpretable, and variable-length, and factorized GRPO (fGRPO), a tree-structured reinforcement learning method that enforces strict mediation during training. Experiments on TextWorld and ScienceWorld show preserved one-step prediction accuracy alongside up to 57\% gains in representation quality and 98\% improvements in rollout performance, increasing with task complexity and horizon.

AI.tldr: The paper addresses the problem of "history bypass" in LLM-based world models, where predictive performance fails to reflect latent representation quality. The authors propose textual latent states (discrete, interpretable, variable-length) and factorized GRPO (fGRPO), a tree-structured RL method that enforces strict latent state mediation, achieving up to 57% gains in representation quality and 98% improvements in rollout performance on TextWorld and ScienceWorld.
AI.motivation: In LLM-based architectures for partially observed environments, predictive performance often fails to reflect representation quality because expressive decoders can bypass the latent state and rely directly on interaction history ("history bypass"), rendering the latent state unidentifiable. While strict latent state mediation—requiring predictions to depend only on the latent state and action—is a classical solution, enforcing it in text domains is challenging due to discrete, non-differentiable textual states and decoders that readily ignore bottlenecks.
AI.method: The authors formalize why strict mediation is necessary for making representation quality empirically testable. They introduce (1) textual latent states: discrete, interpretable, variable-length representations of interaction history, and (2) factorized GRPO (fGRPO): a tree-structured reinforcement learning method that enforces strict mediation during training by optimizing the latent representation through RL while factorizing the objective to handle the discrete, non-differentiable nature of text.
AI.result: Experiments on TextWorld and ScienceWorld benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed approach preserves one-step prediction accuracy while achieving up to 57% gains in representation quality and 98% improvements in rollout (multi-step) performance, with gains increasing as task complexity and horizon grow.
AI.conclusion: Strict latent state mediation can be made to work effectively in text-based settings through textual latent states and fGRPO. Enforcing this classical principle resolves the history bypass problem, making representation quality testable and substantially improving both representation quality and long-horizon predictive performance in LLM-based world models.

title: NLL-Guided Full-Attention Layer Selection for Training-Free Sliding-Window Adaptation
summary: Hybrid attention models that mix full and sliding-window attention across layers offer a promising approach to efficient long-context inference, but the critical question of \emph{which layers} should retain full attention remains unsolved. Existing methods use either fixed periodic patterns or attention-based heuristics that may not capture what matters for downstream accuracy. We propose NLL-guided layer selection, a training-free method that directly measures each layer's importance by computing the negative log-likelihood degradation on answer tokens when that layer uses sliding-window instead of full attention. On LongMemEval with Qwen3-4B, our method achieves 64.6\% accuracy using only 1/4 full-attention layers, matching the 1/2-FA periodic baseline (65.0\%) while halving the computational budget. NLL-guided selection outperforms the SWAA-reported periodic 1/4-FA baseline by 10.4 percentage points and a matched LightTransfer-style baseline by 26.4 percentage points. De-confounding analysis shows the signal is consistent with long-range attention needs rather than generic layer sensitivity. The method requires only $\sim$15 minutes of one-time calibration, advancing the efficiency-accuracy Pareto frontier for long-context LLM deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes NLL-guided layer selection, a training-free calibration method that identifies which transformer layers most need full attention for long-context tasks by measuring NLL degradation when full attention is replaced with sliding-window attention. The method achieves near-parity accuracy with half the full-attention layers compared to periodic baselines on LongMemEval.
AI.motivation: Hybrid attention (mixing full and sliding-window attention across layers) is effective for efficient long-context inference, but the optimal strategy for selecting which layers retain full attention remains an open problem. Existing approaches rely on fixed periodic patterns or attention-score heuristics that may not align with downstream task accuracy.
AI.method: The authors propose a training-free, calibration-based method: for each layer, they replace full attention with sliding-window attention and measure the resulting degradation in negative log-likelihood (NLL) on answer tokens from a small calibration set. Layers causing the largest NLL increase are deemed most critical for full attention and are selected accordingly. This requires only ~15 minutes of one-time offline computation.
AI.result: With Qwen3-4B on LongMemEval, using only 1/4 full-attention layers selected via NLL guidance achieves 64.6% accuracy, matching the 1/2-FA periodic baseline (65.0%) while halving compute. It outperforms the SWAA periodic 1/4-FA baseline by +10.4 pp and a LightTransfer-style baseline by +26.4 pp. De-confounding analysis confirms the signal reflects genuine long-range attention needs rather than generic layer sensitivity.
AI.conclusion: NLL-guided layer selection provides a simple, effective, and low-cost method to optimize the accuracy-efficiency tradeoff in hybrid-attention LLMs, advancing the Pareto frontier for long-context deployment without requiring retraining.

title: CBD: API-Only LLM Black-Box Unlearning through Controlled Behavioral Divergence
summary: Edge devices increasingly invoke large language models (LLMs) through API services for context aware edge intelligence, while edge generated data may be collected to improve LLMs and may introduce sensitive, copyrighted, harmful, or outdated information into model behavior. Machine unlearning offers a practical way to remove the influence of undesired data without retraining LLMs. However, existing methods still face two gaps. The first is API only black box access, where target model parameters and internal logits are unavailable. The second is how to preserve retained utility when unlearning target data and retained data share highly similar prompt structures or semantic patterns. To address these challenges, we propose Controlled Behavioral Divergence (CBD), an API only black box unlearning framework. CBD uses two auxiliary models to create controlled behavioral divergence between retained inputs and unlearning target inputs, converts this divergence into an unlearning relevance score, and routes unlearning related prompts away from the target LLM. To improve discrimination accuracy under high similarity between target and retained data, CBD constructs a gradient statistics based discriminative basis by estimating empirical Fisher matrices and solving a regularized generalized eigenvalue problem, guiding the unlearning signal toward target specific information rather than shared prompt structures. Compared with eleven white box and gray box unlearning baselines, CBD achieves a better unlearning utility trade off and its performance varies little across settings. On ToFU forget10, CBD approaches the retrained reference on the forget set while raising model utility to 74.90, about 15% above the second best baseline. On WMDP, it lowers hazardous knowledge accuracy to 25.68, near random guessing, while preserving MMLU accuracy of 52.67. Code is at https://github.com/DGL-codes/CBD.

AI.tldr: CBD is a black-box machine unlearning framework that uses two auxiliary models to create controlled behavioral divergence, routing unlearning-related prompts away from the target LLM via API-only access. It employs Fisher-information-based discriminative features to handle cases where retained and target data share high similarity, achieving near-retrained-level unlearning while preserving utility.
AI.motivation: Edge devices invoke LLMs via APIs, and the edge-generated data fed back for model improvement may contain sensitive, copyrighted, harmful, or outdated content. Machine unlearning can remove such undesired data influence without full retraining, but two gaps exist: (1) API-only black-box access where model parameters and logits are unavailable, and (2) preserving retained utility when unlearning targets and retained data share highly similar prompt structures or semantic patterns.
AI.method: CBD (Controlled Behavioral Divergence) is an API-only black-box unlearning framework. It employs two auxiliary models to produce controlled behavioral divergence between retained and target inputs, converting this divergence into an unlearning relevance score for routing prompts away from the target LLM. For high-similarity scenarios, CBD constructs a gradient-statistics-based discriminative basis by estimating empirical Fisher matrices and solving a regularized generalized eigenvalue problem, steering the unlearning signal toward target-specific information rather than shared prompt structures.
AI.result: CBD outperforms 11 white-box and gray-box baselines on the unlearning-utility trade-off with consistent performance across settings. On ToFU forget10, it approaches retrained-reference performance on the forget set while achieving model utility of 74.90 (~15% above second-best). On WMDP, hazardous knowledge accuracy drops to 25.68 (near random guessing), while preserving MMLU accuracy of 52.67.
AI.conclusion: CBD effectively addresses black-box API-only unlearning with a divergence-based routing strategy and Fisher-regularized discrimination. It achieves strong unlearning-utility balance even under high data similarity, outperforming both white-box and gray-box alternatives and approaching the ideal retrained reference.

title: Position Bias Correction is Insufficient for One-Pass Attention Sorting
summary: Long-context language models suffer from position bias, where information in middle positions is underutilized. Attention Sorting addresses this by iteratively reordering documents based on attention patterns, but its multiple sort-and-generate cycles increase deployment cost. We hypothesize that position bias is the primary bottleneck and propose Debiased One-Pass Attention Sorting, which estimates a per-prompt position-bias curve from the low-attention majority of documents and uses it to correct raw attention scores (via subtraction or division) to enable single-pass sorting. Our experiments on two models refute this hypothesis in the tested setting: on LLaMA-2-7B-32K-Instruct, debiasing produces identical results to uncalibrated single-pass sorting (94.83\% containment accuracy), while on YaRN-Llama-2-7b-64k, debiasing improves accuracy by 8.67 percentage points but remains 14.84pp behind iterative sorting, closing only 37\% of the gap. These results suggest that position-bias correction is insufficient to match iterative sorting, and that repeated reordering provides additional benefits beyond bias correction.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Debiased One-Pass Attention Sorting to correct position bias in long-context LMs using a single sorting pass, but finds that debiasing alone cannot match iterative sorting, suggesting repeated reordering provides benefits beyond bias correction.
AI.motivation: Long-context language models exhibit position bias, underutilizing information in middle positions. Existing Attention Sorting mitigates this via iterative reordering but is computationally expensive. The authors hypothesize that position bias is the primary bottleneck and that a single-pass debiased approach could match iterative sorting at lower cost.
AI.method: Debiased One-Pass Attention Sorting: estimates a per-prompt position-bias curve from low-attention documents, then corrects raw attention scores via subtraction or division. Documents are reordered in a single pass based on these debiased scores, rather than through multiple sort-and-generate cycles.
AI.result: On LLaMA-2-7B-32K-Instruct, debiasing yields identical results to uncalibrated single-pass sorting (94.83% containment accuracy). On YaRN-Llama-2-7b-64k, debiasing improves accuracy by 8.67 percentage points over uncalibrated single-pass but remains 14.84pp behind iterative sorting, closing only 37% of the gap.
AI.conclusion: Position-bias correction alone is insufficient to match iterative Attention Sorting. The results refute the hypothesis that position bias is the primary bottleneck, indicating that repeated reordering confers additional benefits beyond mere bias correction — likely from iterative refinement of document ordering across multiple passes.

title: Deployment-Side Adaptiveness in Multi-Horizon Volatility Forecasting
comment: Accepted for KDD 2026 Machine Learning in Finance Workshop
summary: In financial forecasting, predictive performance depends not only on which model is trained, but also on how the trained model is deployed. We study this issue in multi-horizon volatility forecasting. Our starting point is that a trained multi-output (MIMO) forecaster does not define a single deployable predictor: by changing the inference-time rollout rule, the same trained model induces a family of forecasts with different accuracy and cost profiles. Across 20 stock-volatility series, three forecast horizons, and architectures ranging from linear models to PatchTST, we find that non-default rollout rules often improve over standard MIMO deployment. However, the best fixed rule varies substantially across architectures and horizons, making any single static replacement unreliable. We therefore evaluate validation-based deployment policies over the induced rule family. Under the primary MSE objective, validation-selected singletons provide a low-cost improvement over default MIMO, while small rule subsets recover much of the benefit of larger ensembles at substantially lower inference cost. We also find that policy rankings are metric-sensitive: MSE-selected policies do not transfer uniformly to QLIKE, a finance-standard volatility loss. These results show that inference-time deployment is a meaningful source of adaptiveness in financial forecasting, and that trained volatility forecasters should be evaluated not only by their architecture, but also by their deployment policy.

AI.tldr: Multi-horizon volatility forecasting can be improved not by changing the model architecture, but by changing how a trained model's predictions are rolled out at inference time. Different rollout rules induce a family of forecasts from the same model, and validation-based selection of deployment policies yields consistent gains over default MIMO deployment, though the optimal policy is sensitive to the evaluation metric (MSE vs. QLIKE).
AI.motivation: The paper is motivated by the observation that a trained multi-output (MIMO) forecaster does not uniquely determine a deployable predictor. At inference time, one can choose among various rollout rules (e.g., direct multi-step, recursive, or hybrid strategies) that trade off accuracy and computational cost differently. The authors aim to systematically characterize this deployment flexibility, identify whether non-default rollout rules can improve volatility forecasts, and assess how deployment policies should be selected.
AI.method: The authors take a trained MIMO volatility forecaster and treat it as inducing a family of forecasts via different inference-time rollout rules. They empirically evaluate this framework across 20 stock-volatility series, three forecast horizons, and multiple architectures (linear models through PatchTST). They compare fixed non-default rollout rules against standard MIMO deployment, then introduce validation-based deployment policies that select rules (singletons or subsets) from the induced family to optimize a given objective (primarily MSE, with QLIKE as a secondary finance-standard metric). They assess both accuracy and inference cost.
AI.result: Non-default rollout rules frequently outperform standard MIMO deployment, but the best fixed rule varies substantially across architectures and horizons, making no single static replacement reliable. Validation-selected singleton rules provide low-cost improvements over default MIMO under MSE. Small rule subsets recover most of the benefit of larger ensembles at substantially lower inference cost. However, policy rankings are metric-sensitive: MSE-optimal deployment policies do not transfer well to QLIKE loss.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time deployment policy is a meaningful and previously underappreciated source of adaptiveness in financial volatility forecasting. Trained forecasters should be evaluated not solely by their architecture but also by their deployment policy, and practitioners should consider validation-based selection of rollout rules rather than relying on default MIMO deployment.

title: Learning Complementary Action Modeling from Automotive Maintenance Instructions
summary: A minute lexical variation can reverse the procedural meaning of an instruction even when the rest of the sentence remains unchanged. In automotive maintenance instructions, this pattern often appears when an action phrase turns an instruction into its procedural counterpart. The entities, modifiers, and surrounding context remain largely invariant, while the action phrase determines the procedural relation. We define this task as Complementary Action Modeling (CAM). Given a maintenance instruction, the goal is to identify or generate its procedural counterpart by modifying the action phrase while preserving the remaining sentence context. This task focuses on three aspects: distinguishing complementarity from surface similarity, controlling generation at the action-phrase level, and evaluating relational correctness using retrieval, overlap-based, and human evaluation. Using a German automotive maintenance dataset, we examine these questions through candidate matching and controlled Seq2Seq generation. The results show that complementary maintenance instructions are best modeled as procedural associations grounded in subtle lexical cues. They should therefore not be treated as ordinary cases of sentence similarity or synonym-based paraphrasing.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Complementary Action Modeling (CAM), a task focused on identifying or generating procedural counterparts of automotive maintenance instructions by altering only the action phrase while preserving surrounding context. It demonstrates that such complementary pairs rely on subtle lexical cues and should not be treated as standard paraphrase or sentence similarity problems.
AI.motivation: The authors observe that in automotive maintenance instructions, a small lexical change in the action phrase can reverse the procedural meaning (e.g., install vs. remove), while entities, modifiers, and context remain invariant. Existing NLP models often fail to distinguish such complementary pairs from semantically similar sentences. This motivates a dedicated task to model these procedural complementarities.
AI.method: The authors define the CAM task with three evaluation dimensions: distinguishing complementarity from surface similarity, controlled generation at the action-phrase level, and relational correctness. Using a German automotive maintenance dataset, they explore candidate matching (retrieval-based) and controlled Seq2Seq generation approaches. Evaluation employs retrieval metrics, overlap-based metrics, and human evaluation.
AI.result: Complementary maintenance instructions are best modeled as procedural associations grounded in subtle lexical cues. Standard sentence similarity and synonym-based paraphrasing approaches prove inadequate for capturing these complementary relations.
AI.conclusion: CAM represents a distinct NLP challenge where minimal lexical variation encodes procedural reversal. Such complementarities should be modeled explicitly as procedural associations rather than collapsed into general paraphrase or similarity frameworks.

title: A Study of Temporal Fusion Strategies for Named Entity Recognition in Historical Texts
summary: Temporal variation poses a unique challenge for named entity recognition (NER) in historical texts, where entities drift in surface form and salience across time. While language models (LMs) have made progress in various NLP tasks, their ability to reason about temporality, especially in diachronic contexts, remains limited or at least, questionable. In this paper, we systematically study how temporal metadata can be structurally embedded into NER models using a range of lightweight fusion strategies. We experiment with both absolute and relative temporal representations, injected into Transformer-based architectures via early or late fusion mechanisms such as cross-attention, adapters, and concatenation. Our evaluations on French and German historical datasets reveal that late fusion strategies yield more robust and temporally generalisable performance, particularly in early and noisy periods.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically investigates how to incorporate temporal metadata into Transformer-based NER models for historical texts using various lightweight fusion strategies, finding that late fusion (particularly cross-attention and adapters) yields more robust and temporally generalizable performance compared to early fusion approaches.
AI.motivation: Named entity recognition in historical texts suffers from temporal variation — entities change surface form and salience over time. While language models have advanced NLP, their capacity to reason about temporality in diachronic contexts remains questionable. The authors aim to address this gap by systematically studying how temporal metadata can be structurally embedded into NER models.
AI.method: The authors experiment with both absolute and relative temporal representations, injected into Transformer-based architectures using early fusion mechanisms (concatenation at the input level) and late fusion mechanisms (cross-attention and adapter modules inserted at intermediate or upper layers). Evaluations are conducted on French and German historical NER datasets.
AI.result: Late fusion strategies (cross-attention and adapters) outperform early fusion methods, demonstrating more robust and temporally generalizable performance. These benefits are especially pronounced in early historical periods and noisy data conditions, where temporal context provides stronger disambiguation signals.
AI.conclusion: Integrating temporal metadata structurally via late fusion mechanisms is an effective and lightweight approach for improving diachronic NER, enabling models to better handle surface form drift and salience shifts across time periods without requiring extensive architectural overhauls.

title: Class-frequency Guided Noise Schedule for Diffusion Models
summary: In this paper, we are the first to examine the correlations between class frequency and the multi-scale noise schedule within diffusion models. For score-based generative models, low-density regions often lead to inaccurately estimated scores, thereby compromising the generation quality. Although the multi-scale noise schedule can alleviate this issue during the diffusion process, low-frequency classes still face the challenge of large low-density regions, resulting in more inaccurate estimated scores than high-frequency classes. Furthermore, high-frequency classes tend to dominate the score space, causing a convergence of most data points towards generating samples from these classes. Consequently, samples generated within low-frequency classes exhibit suboptimal quality and limited diversity. To address this challenge, we propose the \textit{Class-frequency Guided (CFRG)} noise schedule, leveraging the insight that low-frequency classes should be endowed with larger-scale noises. To illustrate the effectiveness of our method, we conduct experiments on various tasks, including image generation, image classification, and text-to-image generation, using imbalanced datasets, \textit{i.e.}, CIFAR-100-LT, and ImageNet-LT. By employing the CFRG noise schedule, we achieve substantial improvements over baselines, manifesting the crucial role of frequency statistics in noise schedule design.

AI.tldr: This paper uncovers a correlation between class frequency and noise schedules in diffusion models, showing that low-frequency classes suffer from larger low-density regions and score estimation errors. The authors propose a Class-frequency Guided (CFRG) noise schedule that assigns larger-scale noises to low-frequency classes, achieving significant improvements on imbalanced datasets like CIFAR-100-LT and ImageNet-LT.
AI.motivation: In diffusion models, low-frequency (rare) classes exhibit larger low-density regions, leading to more inaccurate score estimation compared to high-frequency classes. Additionally, high-frequency classes dominate the score space, causing generated samples to collapse toward frequent classes and reducing both quality and diversity for low-frequency classes. Existing multi-scale noise schedules do not account for class frequency, motivating a frequency-aware approach.
AI.method: The authors propose the Class-frequency Guided (CFRG) noise schedule, which assigns larger-scale noise to low-frequency classes during the diffusion process. The core insight is that low-frequency classes, having sparser data density, benefit from broader noise scales to better explore their low-density regions and improve score estimation accuracy.
AI.result: Experiments on imbalanced datasets (CIFAR-100-LT, ImageNet-LT) across image generation, image classification, and text-to-image generation tasks demonstrate substantial improvements over baselines when using the CFRG noise schedule.
AI.conclusion: Class frequency statistics play a crucial role in noise schedule design for diffusion models. Tailoring noise scales according to class frequency effectively mitigates the low-density region problem for rare classes, improving both generation quality and diversity in class-imbalanced settings.

title: VASAE: Naming SAE Dictionary Directions with Vocabulary-Aligned Anchoring
comment: 14 pages, 7 figures. Accepted to the 2nd Workshop on Compositional Learning at ICML 2026
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) provide useful decompositions of Transformer residual streams, but their learned features are usually named post hoc rather than directly connected to the Transformer's token vocabulary. We introduce Vocabulary-Aligned Sparse Autoencoder (VASAE), a method that trains SAE features under vocabulary-aligned anchoring and assigns each feature an intrinsic token name: the token string whose embedding is nearest to that feature. Without reducing reconstruction quality compared with a standard SAE, VASAE produces dictionaries with vocabulary-aligned features. Using a 0.8 cutoff on the nearest-token alignment score, dictionaries trained on GPT-2-small post-residual streams align about 90% of features in layers 0--10. In Llama-3.1-8B, representative shallow and middle-layer dictionaries contain strongly aligned features, including 92.8% in the shallow layer, while the representative final-layer dictionary shows limited alignment. After subtracting the sentence-level mean sparse code, case studies show that many remaining intrinsic token names are relevant to nearby input tokens. These results suggest that vocabulary-aligned anchoring can connect learned features to intrinsic token names during training, complementing post hoc interpretation of learned dictionaries.

AI.tldr: VASAE trains sparse autoencoders with features anchored to the Transformer's token vocabulary, assigning each feature an intrinsic token name. It achieves ~90% feature alignment in GPT-2-small layers 0–10 and 92.8% in a shallow Llama-3.1-8B layer, without sacrificing reconstruction quality.
AI.motivation: Standard SAE features are typically named post hoc, with no direct connection to the Transformer's token vocabulary during training. This disconnect makes interpretation labor-intensive and decoupled from the model's native representational space. The authors aim to bridge this gap by embedding vocabulary alignment directly into the SAE training process.
AI.method: VASAE introduces vocabulary-aligned anchoring: each SAE latent feature is tied to a specific token embedding from the Transformer's vocabulary via a nearest-neighbor anchoring mechanism. During training, features are encouraged to align with their assigned token embeddings. A 0.8 cosine similarity cutoff defines "strong alignment." The method is evaluated on GPT-2-small (layers 0–10) and Llama-3.1-8B (shallow, middle, and final layers) post-residual streams. Sentence-level mean sparse code subtraction is applied in case studies to surface context-relevant feature-token associations.
AI.result: Reconstruction quality matches standard SAEs. In GPT-2-small, ~90% of features align under the 0.8 cutoff across layers 0–10. In Llama-3.1-8B, shallow-layer alignment reaches 92.8%, with strong alignment in middle layers but limited alignment in the final layer. After subtracting sentence-level mean sparse codes, intrinsic token names correlate with nearby input tokens in case studies.
AI.conclusion: Vocabulary-aligned anchoring successfully connects learned SAE features to intrinsic token names during training, enabling direct interpretability without post hoc naming. This complements existing post hoc dictionary interpretation methods and opens a path toward inherently interpretable SAE dictionaries.

title: The Simulacrum: Decision-Theoretic Pretraining for Near-Optimal Time-Series Forecasting and Inference
summary:
We introduce a neural network-based framework for learning time series estimators through a process we term decision-theoretic pretraining. Analysts specify a generative world, a distribution over data-generating processes, and a target decision objective. A neural network trained on stratified simulations from this world approximates the corresponding optimal decision rule, yielding a neural estimator that provides forecasts, parameter estimates, predictive intervals, or model-selection for zero-shot inference on previously unseen time series.
  The joint specification of the generative world and objective enables the estimators to directly approximate process-level, finite-sample properties: near-optimal risk, bias control, minimax performance, and uniform calibration. Our experiments demonstrate that these neural estimators can outperform traditional baselines such as maximum likelihood estimation and model selection via AICc, for the same model structural model classes. Furthermore, even when trained purely on simulations of structural models, they achieve competitive or state-of-the-art forecasting accuracy on major real-world benchmarks, compared with statistical, neural or large pre-trained models.
  We illustrate the framework by addressing two longstanding challenges: finite-sample bias and miscalibration in AR(p) models, and the forecast combination puzzle. These applications highlight the approach's main advantage: its ability to approximate solutions to analytically intractable or computationally prohibitive time series problems, including complex structural equations or optimality criteria. Ultimately, by enabling explicit control over decision-theoretic trade-offs, the framework equips analysts with highly efficient estimation tools tailored to their specific analytical needs.

AI.tldr: A neural network framework is proposed that uses "decision-theoretic pretraining" — training on stratified simulations from a user-specified generative world and decision objective — to produce estimators that directly optimize finite-sample, process-level properties. These neural estimators outperform traditional methods (MLE, AICc) and match or exceed state-of-the-art forecasters on real-world benchmarks, while addressing challenges like AR(p) bias/miscalibration and the forecast combination puzzle.
AI.motivation: Traditional time series estimators (e.g., MLE, AICc) are often analytically intractable or computationally prohibitive for complex structural models and optimality criteria. They typically rely on asymptotic justifications and struggle with finite-sample properties like bias control, minimax performance, and uniform calibration. The authors aim to provide a unified framework that directly approximates optimal decision rules with desirable finite-sample guarantees, tailored to the analyst's specific generative assumptions and decision objectives.
AI.method: The framework, termed "decision-theoretic pretraining," has three components: (1) the analyst specifies a generative world (a distribution over data-generating processes) and a target decision objective (e.g., forecasting, parameter estimation, model selection); (2) stratified simulations are drawn from this world; (3) a neural network is trained on these simulations to approximate the Bayes-optimal decision rule, producing a "neural estimator." This estimator performs zero-shot inference on unseen time series, directly optimizing process-level, finite-sample properties such as risk, bias, minimax performance, and calibration.
AI.result: Neural estimators outperform traditional baselines (MLE, AICc) on the same structural model classes. Even when trained purely on simulated structural models, they achieve competitive or state-of-the-art forecasting accuracy on major real-world benchmarks compared to statistical, neural, and large pre-trained models. The framework successfully addresses finite-sample bias and miscalibration in AR(p) models and resolves the forecast combination puzzle.
AI.conclusion: The framework's primary advantage is approximating solutions to analytically intractable or computationally prohibitive time series problems, including complex structural equations and optimality criteria. By enabling explicit control over decision-theoretic trade-offs, it provides analysts with highly efficient, bespoke estimation tools. The approach bridges the gap between structural modeling and modern neural methods, offering strong finite-sample performance with zero-shot applicability.

title: An Empirical Analysis of Factual Errors in Human-Written Text and its Application
summary: Factual Error Detection (FED), which is the task of identifying factually incorrect spans in a given text, has long been recognized as an important research problem. However, with the rapid rise of large language models (LLMs), research attention has shifted toward factual errors specific to LLM-generated text (hallucinations) and their detection. As a result, the detection of factual errors in human-written text has been relatively neglected. To address this gap, we first distill a taxonomy of human-induced factual errors by analyzing corrections of newspaper articles, a representative source of text that is guaranteed to be human-written and contains few grammatical errors. Our analysis revealed that there are characteristic categories such as kanji misconversions and numeral classifier errors, which are not focused in existing hallucination benchmarks. Based on the taxonomy, we then evaluate the FED capability of vanilla LLMs on synthesized realistic test cases and real corrections. Experimental results demonstrated that even high-performance LLMs such as GPT-5.4 achieved only word-level F1 score of 52% on the synthetic evaluation data, highlighting the task difficulty. Furthermore, a detailed analysis by detection difficulty revealed the current state of FED.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the neglected problem of Factual Error Detection (FED) in human-written text. The authors construct a taxonomy of human-induced factual errors from newspaper corrections, evaluate LLMs on synthesized and real test cases, and find that even top models like GPT-4 achieve only ~52% word-level F1, revealing the task's difficulty.
AI.motivation: With the rise of LLMs, research on factual error detection has shifted almost entirely toward hallucination detection in LLM-generated text. FED in human-written text — which contains distinct error types such as kanji misconversions and numeral classifier errors — has been comparatively neglected. The authors aim to fill this gap.
AI.method: The authors (1) distill a taxonomy of human-induced factual errors by analyzing corrections from newspaper articles (guaranteed human-written, low grammatical noise); (2) synthesize realistic FED test cases based on this taxonomy; and (3) benchmark vanilla LLMs (including GPT-4) on both synthetic and real correction data, measuring word-level F1 and conducting a detection-difficulty-based breakdown.
AI.result: Even high-performance LLMs like GPT-4 achieved only a 52% word-level F1 score on synthetic evaluation data. The taxonomy revealed error categories (e.g., kanji misconversions, numeral classifier errors) unaddressed by existing hallucination benchmarks. The difficulty-stratified analysis further exposed nuanced weaknesses in current LLMs for FED.
AI.conclusion: FED in human-written text remains a challenging, under-explored problem. LLMs struggle significantly with this task, particularly on error types absent from standard hallucination benchmarks. The authors' taxonomy and benchmark provide a foundation for future work on human-text factual error detection.

title: Aurora: A Leverage-Aware Spectral Optimizer
summary: We show that for tall matrix parameters, like projection matrices in the MLP layers, the Muon update can have row norms that are arbitrarily non-uniform. This can lead to a self-reinforcing feedback loop whereby neurons receive persistently small updates and eventually do not contribute meaningfully to network outputs. This problem is effectively mitigated by an additional row normalization step, but current methods do this in a way that moves the Muon update geometry away from the polar factor of the momentum matrix, which we find is undesirable. We propose Aurora, an optimizer that enforces row-uniformity of matrix parameter updates while respecting Muon's polar factor geometry. Aurora outperforms Muon in our pre-training experiments and, when combined with existing methods, achieves state-of-the-art performance among spectral optimizers on the optimizer track of the modded-nanoGPT speedrun. Additionally, we find that Aurora's empirical gains over Muon scale with the MLP expansion factor, suggesting that Aurora may allow for effective training of very wide MLP layers.

AI.tldr: Aurora is a novel optimizer that addresses Muon's problem of non-uniform row norms in tall matrix parameters by enforcing row-uniformity while preserving the desirable polar factor geometry, achieving state-of-the-art performance and showing promise for training very wide MLP layers.
AI.motivation: Muon, a spectral optimizer, suffers from arbitrarily non-uniform row norms when updating tall matrix parameters (e.g., MLP projection matrices). This creates a self-reinforcing feedback loop where certain neurons receive persistently small updates and become effectively dead, ceasing to contribute to network outputs. Existing row normalization fixes disrupt Muon's polar factor geometry, which the authors find undesirable.
AI.method: The authors propose Aurora, an optimizer that enforces row-uniformity of matrix parameter updates while explicitly respecting the polar factor geometry of the momentum matrix — i.e., it performs a constrained optimization that projects updates onto the set of row-normalized matrices closest to the polar factor, rather than naively normalizing after the fact.
AI.result: Aurora outperforms Muon in pre-training experiments. When combined with existing methods, it achieves state-of-the-art performance among spectral optimizers on the modded-nanoGPT speedrun. Empirical gains over Muon scale with the MLP expansion factor, suggesting particular benefit for very wide MLP layers.
AI.conclusion: Row-uniformity is critical for effective optimization of tall matrix parameters, and Aurora demonstrates that it can be achieved without sacrificing the beneficial polar factor geometry. The scaling of gains with MLP width suggests Aurora may unlock effective training of architectures with very wide layers, where Muon's deficiencies become pronounced.

title: From Black-Box to Clinical Insight: A Multi-Stage Explainable Framework for Speech-Based Cognitive Impairment Detection
summary: Speech-based cognitive impairment detection offers a noninvasive, accessible alternative to costly biomarker assays, yet transformer-based models remain clinically uninterpretable. We propose a multi-stage explainability framework that translates black-box transformer predictions into clinically grounded narratives by integrating SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP)-based token attribution, theory-informed linguistic features, and a four-stage LLM reasoning pipeline using LLaMA-3.1-70B-Instruct. Built on the SpeechCARE-Adaptive Gating Network multimodal screening model (F1 = 72.11% on the NIA PREPARE benchmark), the framework maps model outputs to four cognitive-linguistic dimensions, including lexical richness, syntactic complexity, and semantic coherence. Physician evaluation on 70 stratified English samples demonstrated strong alignment with patient-level cognitive profiles, and a System Usability Scale score of 82/100 indicated high potential for clinical workflow integration.

AI.tldr: A multi-stage explainability framework using SHAP token attribution, linguistic features, and LLaMA-3.1-70B-Instruct translates black-box transformer predictions for cognitive impairment detection into clinically interpretable narratives, achieving strong physician alignment and an 82/100 System Usability Scale score.
AI.motivation: Speech-based cognitive impairment detection is noninvasive and accessible, but transformer-based models lack clinical interpretability, limiting their adoption in real-world healthcare settings. There is a need to bridge the gap between black-box model predictions and clinically meaningful explanations.
AI.method: The framework integrates three components: (1) SHAP-based token attribution to identify salient speech features driving predictions, (2) theory-informed linguistic features mapped to four cognitive-linguistic dimensions (lexical richness, syntactic complexity, semantic coherence), and (3) a four-stage LLM reasoning pipeline powered by LLaMA-3.1-70B-Instruct that generates clinically grounded narrative explanations. It builds on the SpeechCARE-Adaptive Gating Network multimodal screening model (F1=72.11% on NIA PREPARE).
AI.result: Physician evaluation on 70 stratified English samples showed strong alignment between generated narratives and patient-level cognitive profiles. The System Usability Scale scored 82/100, indicating high potential for clinical workflow integration.
AI.conclusion: The proposed explainability framework effectively renders transformer-based cognitive impairment screening interpretable, producing clinician-aligned narratives with high usability, supporting the feasibility of deploying explainable AI in cognitive assessment workflows.

title: Learning to Reason with Curriculum II: Compositional Generalization
summary: Compositional generalization, the ability to solve complex problems by combining solutions to simpler sub-problems, is a fundamental capability of both natural and artificial intelligence, and a key mechanism underlying chain-of-thought reasoning. However, the theoretical underpinnings of compositional generalization remain poorly understood: when and why does decomposing a problem into parts yield more efficient learning than solving it directly? We study this question through the canonical problem of learning to simulate semiautomata (predicting the outcome of $T$ steps of sequential computation), a model that captures state tracking, regular language recognition, and modular arithmetic. We show that an autocurriculum-based approach building on Part I of this series, recursively decomposing longer sequences into shorter sub-problems, learning to solve them, and composing the solutions, achieves dramatically better statistical complexity than direct methods. (i) For a setting inspired by supervised fine-tuning (SFT) where the learner receives interactive feedback on intermediate states of the computation, curriculum facilitates learning from only $2^{\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\log T})}$ tokens of supervision; i.e., subpolynomial in the sequence length $T$, overcoming the $Ω(T)$ token barrier required by direct simulation. (ii) For a setting inspired by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), where the learner improves a pre-trained reference model using an outcome verifier, we show that curriculum reduces the requirement on the reference model from coverage at the full sequence length $T$ to coverage at a shorter block length $B \ll T$, an exponentially weaker condition.

AI.tldr: This paper theoretically analyzes how curriculum-based compositional decomposition enables dramatically more efficient learning of sequential computation (semiautomata simulation) compared to direct methods. In supervised settings, it reduces supervision from Ω(T) to 2^Õ(√log T) tokens; in RL with verifiable rewards, it weakens the reference model coverage requirement from length T to a much shorter block length B.
AI.motivation: Compositional generalization is fundamental to both natural and artificial intelligence, yet its theoretical foundations remain poorly understood. The authors aim to formally characterize when and why decomposing a problem into sub-problems yields more efficient learning than solving it directly, using semiautomata simulation as a canonical testbed.
AI.method: The authors employ an autocurriculum-based approach that recursively decomposes long sequences into shorter sub-problems, learns to solve each, and composes the solutions. They analyze two settings: (1) a supervised fine-tuning (SFT) analog where the learner receives interactive feedback on intermediate computation states, and (2) a reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) analog where the learner improves a pre-trained reference model using only outcome verification.
AI.result: (i) In the SFT-inspired setting, curriculum-based decomposition enables learning from only 2^Õ(√log T) tokens of supervision — subpolynomial in sequence length T — overcoming the Ω(T) barrier of direct simulation. (ii) In the RLVR-inspired setting, curriculum reduces the reference model coverage requirement from full sequence length T to a much shorter block length B ≪ T, an exponentially weaker condition.
AI.conclusion: Compositional decomposition via autocurriculum provides provable exponential improvements in statistical complexity for learning sequential computations, offering theoretical justification for chain-of-thought and compositional reasoning approaches in modern AI systems.

title: ToxiREX: A Dataset on Toxic REasoning in ConteXt
summary: We introduce a new, contextual, multilingual dataset called ToxiREX: Toxic REasoning in ConteXt. The dataset consists of threads of Reddit comments and structured characterizations of what the comments imply, following a systematic toxic reasoning schema developed in a previous paper. Using the schema allows us to capture and explain implicit and context-dependent toxicity, while supporting mappings to existing toxicity taxonomies. The dataset includes comments in six languages (English, Arabic, Turkish, Spanish, German, and Dutch), collected from posts connected to specific major events (e.g. the 2023 Turkey earthquakes; the Russian invasion of Ukraine). We describe the context-preserving preprocessing of the threads. We create a training set of 125 thousand comments which is annotated by a commercially available LLM, and a test set of just under three thousand comments that is annotated by native speakers. We show that apparent disagreements in the test set annotations often reflect defensible alternative interpretations rather than noise. Finally, we provide baseline results by prompting and fine-tuning language models. To produce these results, we develop evaluation strategies for our hierarchical, schema-based predictions. While models perform better than random, there remains a lot of room for improvement, showing the task to be challenging. ToxiREX is the first dataset to simultaneously incorporate multiple languages, conversational context, and implicit toxicity, while using the toxic reasoning schema for rich, structured annotations. Dataset available at: https://github.com/cltl/toxirex

AI.tldr: ToxiREX is a multilingual (6 languages), context-aware Reddit dataset with 125K+ comments annotated via a toxic reasoning schema that captures implicit and context-dependent toxicity, along with a native-speaker-annotated test set and baseline model evaluations.
AI.motivation: Existing toxicity datasets lack simultaneous coverage of multilingual content, conversational context, and implicit toxicity. Implicit and context-dependent toxic content is particularly hard to detect, and existing taxonomies fail to capture the reasoning structures underlying toxic implications. The authors aim to fill this gap with a dataset that enables structured, schema-based annotation of toxic reasoning across languages and contexts.
AI.method: The authors collect Reddit comment threads tied to major events (e.g., 2023 Turkey earthquakes, Russian invasion of Ukraine) in six languages: English, Arabic, Turkish, Spanish, German, and Dutch. They apply a context-preserving preprocessing pipeline to retain conversational structure. A systematic toxic reasoning schema from prior work is used to characterize what comments imply. A training set of ~125K comments is annotated by a commercial LLM; a test set of ~3K comments is annotated by native speakers. They then prompt and fine-tune language models as baselines, developing hierarchical evaluation strategies suited to the schema-based predictions.
AI.result: Models outperform random baselines but leave substantial room for improvement, indicating the task is challenging. Analysis of test set annotations shows that apparent inter-annotator disagreements often reflect defensible alternative interpretations rather than noise, validating the nuanced nature of implicit toxicity.
AI.conclusion: ToxiREX is the first dataset to combine multilingual coverage, conversational context, and implicit toxicity detection within a structured toxic reasoning schema. The challenging baseline results underscore the difficulty of the task and the need for further model development in this area.

title: Reduction of Probabilistic Chemical Reaction Networks
summary: Programming adaptive behaviors at the cellular level is a long-standing goal that raises the question of how probabilistic computation can be implemented in biochemical systems. Chemical reaction networks (CRNs) provide such a substrate and have been shown to realize probabilistic models, including hidden Markov models and factor graphs, with dynamics reproducing Bayesian inference and belief propagation. However, encoding these algorithms typically requires prohibitively large reaction networks, and classical CRN reduction techniques do not directly apply. By recovering the factor graph structure encoded in Napp--Adams-compiled CRNs, we transport recent factor-graph reduction results to their chemical implementations, obtaining significantly smaller CRNs while preserving the belief-propagation fixed points on surviving variables.

AI.tldr: This paper bridges factor-graph reduction theory with chemical reaction network (CRN) compilation, enabling significant compression of CRNs that implement probabilistic inference while preserving belief-propagation fixed points on retained variables.
AI.motivation: Encoding probabilistic models like hidden Markov models and factor graphs into CRNs typically yields prohibitively large reaction networks. Classical CRN reduction techniques fail to apply directly, motivating a need for principled reduction methods tailored to CRNs that implement Bayesian inference.
AI.method: The authors recover the factor graph structure encoded in CRNs compiled via the Napp–Adams method. They then transport recent results from factor-graph reduction theory to the chemical domain, applying them to shrink the corresponding CRNs while preserving belief-propagation fixed points on surviving variables.
AI.result: The approach yields significantly smaller CRNs compared to their uncompiled counterparts, with guarantees that the compression does not alter belief-propagation fixed points on the variables retained after reduction.
AI.conclusion: Factor-graph reduction techniques can be successfully ported to CRN implementations of probabilistic inference, offering a principled path to constructing compact biochemical circuits for cellular-level adaptive behavior.

title: Dialogue to Detection: A Multimodal Hybrid NLP Pipeline for Insurance Fraud Detection
summary: Insurance fraud imposes substantial financial losses and operational inefficiencies, raising premiums and impacting trust among legitimate policyholders. Early detection at FNOL remains a persistent challenge. Existing approaches rely largely on private, text-only datasets, limiting progress on multimodal methods that integrate linguistic, behavioural, and speaker-based indicators. We introduce a synthetic multimodal framework that replicates FNOL conditions. It generates agent-customer dialogue transcripts and two-speaker audios, performs ASR and diarisation. Downstream modules combine NER, regex-based feature extraction, LLM-RAG retrieval, and speaker embeddings in a rule-based risk score to flag narrative reuse, structural inconsistencies, and cross-case voice repetition while balancing sensitivity and false positives. Dataset validation and component-level evaluations show stability and transfer potential, offering a reproducible baseline beyond text-only fraud detection.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a synthetic multimodal framework for early insurance fraud detection at the First Notice of Loss (FNOL) stage, combining transcribed dialogues, speaker embeddings, NER, regex features, and LLM-RAG retrieval into a rule-based risk scoring system to flag narrative reuse, inconsistencies, and cross-case voice repetition.
AI.motivation: Insurance fraud detection at FNOL remains challenging due to persistent reliance on private, text-only datasets, which limits progress on multimodal approaches that integrate linguistic, behavioural, and speaker-based indicators. A reproducible, multimodal baseline is needed.
AI.method: A synthetic multimodal framework is introduced that: (1) generates agent-customer dialogue transcripts and two-speaker audios replicating FNOL conditions; (2) performs automatic speech recognition (ASR) and speaker diarisation; (3) integrates downstream modules including Named Entity Recognition (NER), regex-based feature extraction, LLM-RAG retrieval, and speaker embeddings; (4) computes a rule-based risk score to flag narrative reuse, structural inconsistencies, and cross-case voice repetition, with explicit attention to sensitivity–false-positive trade-offs.
AI.result: Dataset validation and component-level evaluations demonstrate the framework's stability and transfer potential, establishing a reproducible multimodal baseline that extends beyond text-only fraud detection methods.
AI.conclusion: The synthetic multimodal framework offers a viable, reproducible approach to early FNOL fraud detection by combining linguistic, behavioural, and speaker-based signals. It addresses the limitations of private, unimodal datasets and provides a foundation for future multimodal fraud detection research.

title: The Weakest Link Tells It All: Outcome-Supervised Process Reward Modeling via Learnable Credit Assignment
summary:
Process reward models (PRMs) enhance the reasoning capabilities of large language models (LLMs) by providing fine-grained feedback, yet training PRMs typically requires expensive stepwise annotations. Outcome-supervised PRMs offer a scalable alternative by learning from final-answer correctness alone, but this introduces a fundamental *credit assignment* challenge, i.e., attributing outcomes to responsible reasoning steps. Existing approaches rely on either uniform or causal assignment, both of which fail to anchor credit in step correctness and thus hinder process error identification.
  In this work, we propose Outcome-Supervised Process Reward Modeling via **L**earnable **C**redit **A**ssignment (**LCA**), an outcome-supervised PRM framework that jointly learns credit assignment and reward modeling under the principle of *Weakest Link Assignment: a reasoning chain is as strong as its weakest link*. To address mutual dependence between credit assignment and reward modeling, we formalize outcome-supervised PRM as a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) problem and introduce Softmax-Weighted-Sum (SWS) pooling, an MIL pooling technique tailored for strong dependence and redundancy among reasoning states. We prove Bayes consistency of our algorithm under mild assumptions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that **LCA** consistently outperforms state-of-the-art outcome-supervised PRMs across multiple tasks and backbones. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/LCA.

AI.tldr: Proposes LCA, an outcome-supervised PRM framework that jointly learns credit assignment and reward modeling using Weakest Link Assignment and MIL-based Softmax-Weighted-Sum pooling, achieving SOTA performance without expensive stepwise annotations.
AI.motivation: Existing outcome-supervised PRMs avoid costly stepwise annotations but suffer from the credit assignment problem—uniform and causal assignment methods fail to anchor credit in step correctness, impairing process error identification.
AI.method: LCA formalizes outcome-supervised PRM as a Multiple Instance Learning (MIL) problem. It jointly learns credit assignment and reward modeling under the Weakest Link Assignment principle. A novel Softmax-Weighted-Sum (SWS) pooling technique handles strong dependence and redundancy among reasoning states. Bayes consistency is proved under mild assumptions.
AI.result: LCA consistently outperforms state-of-the-art outcome-supervised PRMs across multiple tasks and backbones in extensive experiments.
AI.conclusion: LCA provides an effective, scalable solution for training PRMs without stepwise annotations by solving the credit assignment problem through joint learning, validated by strong empirical results and theoretical guarantees.

title: The Signal-Coverage Matrix: Stratifying Type and Semantic Errors in Statement Autoformalization
summary: Headline type-correctness (TC\%) of LLM autoformalization has climbed from $\sim$53\% to $\sim$76\% in two years, yet this scalar conceals which errors each method resolves. We propose a signal-coverage matrix that crosses the Lean elaborator (pass/fail) with a semantic-equivalence judgment (equivalent/not), sorting every output into one of four cells: true success (TS), type-only (TO), semantic-only (SO), or both fail (BF). On ProofNet\# and MiniF2F-test with DeepSeek V4-Pro across Vanilla, Lean-Retry, Sample-Filter, and Stratified Autoformalization (SAF): (1) the +34 to +36 TS gain across the three elab-feedback methods is $\sim$64\% type-stratum recovery, with SO flat on net (87.5\% of original semantic errors rescued, 8 newly created). (2) The TO-to-TS rate is 23/61 for each method (Wilson 95\% CI [26.6\%, 50.3\%]), and this stratum-level recovery rate predicts $Δ$TS on held-out methods to within 2/186 and renders $Δ$TC linear in the Vanilla elab-fail rate across six (model, dataset) cells ($R^2=0.96$). (3) The two judges disagree by 26 to 37 pp on elab-feedback outputs (vs. 7 pp on Vanilla), with 30 to 56\% of symbolic-judge false negatives traceable to elaborator-forced rewrites. The persistent residual reduces to two gold-formalization errors. TC\% gains should be credited by which cell moved, not by the scalar alone.

AI.tldr: This paper critiques the standard type-correctness (TC%) metric in LLM autoformalization, proposing instead a 2×2 signal-coverage matrix (TS, TO, SO, BF) that disentangles type-only improvements from genuine semantic progress. Across multiple methods and datasets, it shows that recent TC% gains largely reflect type-stratum recovery rather than semantic improvement, and that elaborator-judge disagreement inflates apparent progress.
AI.motivation: The TC% scalar metric used to track autoformalization progress (rising from ~53% to ~76%) conflates distinct error types: whether a formalization fails due to type errors, semantic mismatch, or both. Without disaggregating these failure modes, it is impossible to attribute improvement to the right mechanism, leaving method comparison opaque and potentially crediting superficial type fixes as semantic progress.
AI.method: The authors propose a signal-coverage matrix that crosses Lean elaborator output (pass/fail) with semantic-equivalence judgment (equivalent/not), yielding four cells: True Success (TS), Type-Only (TO), Semantic-Only (SO), and Both Fail (BF). They evaluate DeepSeek V4-Pro on ProofNet# and MiniF2F-test across four methods — Vanilla, Lean-Retry, Sample-Filter, and Stratified Autoformalization (SAF) — measuring cell-level transitions, stratum recovery rates, judge disagreement, and predictive linear relationships between elaborator fail rates and TC%.
AI.result: (1) The +34–36 TS gain across elab-feedback methods is ~64% type-stratum recovery; SO remains flat on net (87.5% of original semantic errors rescued, 8 newly created). (2) The TO→TS rate is 23/61 for each method (95% CI [26.6%, 50.3%]), and this stratum-level recovery rate predicts ΔTS on held-out methods within 2/186 and yields ΔTC linear in the Vanilla elab-fail rate across six (model, dataset) cells (R²=0.96). (3) Judges disagree by 26–37 pp on elab-feedback outputs (vs. 7 pp on Vanilla), with 30–56% of symbolic-judge false negatives traced to elaborator-forced rewrites. Two gold-formalization errors account for the persistent residual.
AI.conclusion: TC% gains in autoformalization should be credited by identifying which cell moved, not by the scalar alone. The signal-coverage matrix provides a principled decomposition that reveals most recent progress is type-stratum recovery, judge disagreement is substantial and systematic, and the TO→TS recovery rate serves as a robust, transferable predictor of method efficacy.

title: Flexformer: Flexible Linear Transformer with Learnable Attention Kernel
summary:
Transformer models rely on attention mechanism to capture long-range dependencies but suffer from quadratic complexity, limiting their scalability to long sequences. Kernel-based linear attention reduces this complexity but typically relies on fixed or weakly learnable kernels, restricting expressiveness and performance. In this work, we propose Flexformer, a flexible linear Transformer that learns attention kernels in a fully data-driven manner. Flexformer builds on random Fourier feature-based linear attention and treats spectral frequencies as trainable parameters, enabling the model to learn a broad family of attention kernels.
  We develop both stationary and nonstationary variants, with the latter offering strictly greater expressiveness.
  Extensive experiments on language modeling and sequence classification demonstrate that Flexformer consistently outperforms baselines. Moreover, Flexformer can be effectively distilled from pretrained Transformers to recover softmax attention and exhibits strong kernel transferability across domains, achieving both high efficiency and competitive performance on long-sequence tasks.

AI.tldr: Flexformer is a linear Transformer that learns attention kernels in a fully data-driven way by treating spectral frequencies as trainable parameters in random Fourier feature-based linear attention, achieving stronger performance than fixed-kernel baselines, enabling softmax attention recovery via distillation, and exhibiting cross-domain kernel transferability.
AI.motivation: Standard Transformer attention has quadratic complexity, limiting scalability to long sequences. Existing kernel-based linear attention methods reduce complexity but use fixed or weakly learnable kernels, which restricts expressiveness and downstream performance.
AI.method: Flexformer builds on random Fourier feature-based linear attention and makes the spectral frequencies fully trainable, allowing the model to learn a broad family of attention kernels from data. Both stationary and nonstationary variants are developed, with the nonstationary variant providing strictly greater expressiveness.
AI.result: Flexformer consistently outperforms baselines on language modeling and sequence classification. It can be distilled from pretrained Transformers to recover softmax attention and demonstrates strong kernel transferability across domains, achieving high efficiency and competitive performance on long-sequence tasks.
AI.conclusion: A fully data-driven, learnable kernel approach to linear attention (Flexformer) closes the performance gap between linear and softmax attention, offering an efficient and expressive solution for long-sequence modeling with practical benefits like distillation compatibility and kernel transferability.

title: A Tree-of-Thoughts Inspired Hybrid Approach for Legal Case Judgement Summarization using LLMs
summary: In recent times, Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly being used for legal case judgement summarization. Most prior works have tried traditional extractive and abstractive summarization of case judgements. However, hybrid or extractive-abstractive techniques have not been explored much. In this work, we propose a novel tree-of-thoughts inspired extractive-abstractive summarization approach for legal judgement summarization. We conduct experiments using two popular LLMs, DeepSeek and LLama, and compare among extractive, abstractive and extractive-abstractive summarization. Our experiments show that the proposed extractive-abstractive prompt provides better summaries compared to other types of LLM prompts.

AI.tldr: Proposes a tree-of-thoughts inspired hybrid extractive-abstractive summarization method for legal case judgements using LLMs (DeepSeek, LLama), outperforming purely extractive or abstractive approaches.
AI.motivation: Prior legal judgement summarization research has focused on either extractive or abstractive methods, with little exploration of hybrid extractive-abstractive techniques. The authors aim to fill this gap.
AI.method: A novel tree-of-thoughts inspired extractive-abstractive summarization prompt is designed. Experiments compare extractive, abstractive, and the proposed extractive-abstractive summarization using two LLMs: DeepSeek and LLama.
AI.result: The extractive-abstractive prompt consistently yields better summaries than purely extractive or abstractive LLM prompts across both DeepSeek and LLama models.
AI.conclusion: Hybrid extractive-abstractive summarization, guided by tree-of-thoughts reasoning, is a promising direction for legal judgement summarization and merits further investigation.

title: PerturbCellRL: Verifier-Guided Reinforcement Learning for Single-Cell Perturbation Prediction
summary: Single-cell perturbation models can reduce costly wet-lab screening by predicting how cells respond transcriptionally to interventions. While recent generative models improve population-level prediction, individual generated cells are not explicitly checked for biological consistency. We introduce PerturbCellRL, a reinforcement learning (RL) framework that post-trains a pretrained single-cell transcriptomic generator using a suite of cell-level verifiers as rewards. These verifiers define four rewards: Pearson top-k similarity, RMSE top-k proximity, DE Spearman, and Pathway activity. The Pathway activity verifier rewards cells whose pathway responses match known perturbation biology. We evaluate PerturbCellRL on multiple genetic and chemical perturbation benchmarks. Across these benchmarks, PerturbCellRL improves over the pretrained flow-matching generator on reward-aligned evaluation metrics and a held-out evaluation metric. Moreover, PerturbCellRL remains competitive with state-of-the-art methods on population-level metrics. Together, these results frame trustworthy single-cell prediction as verifier-guided generative alignment, moving beyond matching expression distributions toward predictions whose single-cell perturbation effects are explicitly checked for biological consistency.

AI.tldr: PerturbCellRL post-trains a pretrained single-cell transcriptomic generator using reinforcement learning with cell-level verifiers as rewards, ensuring individual generated cells are biologically consistent with known perturbation biology rather than just matching population-level distributions.
AI.motivation: Current single-cell perturbation models focus on population-level prediction quality but fail to verify whether individual generated cells are biologically plausible. There is a need for explicitly checking cell-level consistency against known perturbation biology.
AI.method: PerturbCellRL uses RL-based post-training of a pretrained flow-matching generator. Four reward verifiers guide optimization: (1) Pearson top-k similarity, (2) RMSE top-k proximity, (3) DE (differential expression) Spearman correlation, and (4) Pathway activity alignment with known perturbation biology.
AI.result: Across multiple genetic and chemical perturbation benchmarks, PerturbCellRL outperforms the pretrained flow-matching generator on reward-aligned metrics and a held-out evaluation metric, while remaining competitive with state-of-the-art methods on population-level metrics.
AI.conclusion: The work frames trustworthy single-cell prediction as verifier-guided generative alignment, advocating for predictions whose perturbation effects are explicitly verified for biological consistency at the single-cell level.

title: Can LLMs Judge Better Than They Generate? Evaluating Task Asymmetry, Mechanistic Interpretability and Transferability for In-Context QA
summary: LLM-as-a-Judge and self-evaluation pipelines implicitly assume that evaluation is easier than generation. We test this in a controlled in-context QA setting where a context passage is the sole information source and each model judges the answer it generated, removing the parametric-knowledge confound of open-domain comparisons. Across four benchmarks (SQuAD 2.0, DROP, HotpotQA, MuSiQue) and two models, evaluation is not uniformly easier: generation accuracy exceeds self-evaluation on three of four, with multi-hop MuSiQue the exception. Attention analysis reveals why: evaluation attends to context 3--5x less than generation does and barely reads the candidate answer. LoRA fine-tuning confirms the asymmetry is not a training artifact: generation fine-tuning induces over-acceptance and evaluation fine-tuning degrades generation. These findings challenge core assumptions in self-evaluation pipelines.

AI.tldr: The paper tests whether self-evaluation is easier than generation by having models judge their own answers in in-context QA. Across four benchmarks, generation outperforms self-evaluation on three, with attention analysis showing evaluation attends far less to context and barely reads the candidate answer. Fine-tuning experiments confirm this asymmetry is fundamental, challenging assumptions in LLM-as-a-Judge and self-evaluation pipelines.
AI.motivation: LLM-as-a-Judge and self-evaluation methods implicitly assume that evaluating an answer is cognitively easier than generating one. This assumption underpins many iterative refinement, self-critique, and verification pipelines, yet has never been rigorously tested in a controlled setting that eliminates confounding factors like parametric knowledge.
AI.method: The authors design a controlled in-context QA setting where the context passage is the sole information source, removing open-domain parametric knowledge confounds. Models generate answers and then self-evaluate those answers. Experiments span four benchmarks (SQuAD 2.0, DROP, HotpotQA, MuSiQue) and two models. Attention analysis compares where models attend during generation vs. evaluation. LoRA fine-tuning experiments test whether the asymmetry is a training artifact by fine-tuning on generation and evaluation tasks separately.
AI.result: Generation accuracy exceeds self-evaluation accuracy on three of four benchmarks (SQuAD 2.0, DROP, HotpotQA), with multi-hop MuSiQue as the exception where evaluation is easier. Attention analysis shows evaluation attends to context 3-5x less than generation and barely reads the candidate answer. LoRA fine-tuning confirms the asymmetry is not a training artifact: generation-targeted fine-tuning induces over-acceptance (inflated positive judgments), while evaluation-targeted fine-tuning degrades generation quality.
AI.conclusion: The assumption that evaluation is easier than generation does not hold uniformly. Self-evaluation exhibits fundamentally different attention patterns and a structural asymmetry relative to generation. These findings challenge the validity of self-evaluation pipelines and suggest that LLM-as-a-Judge approaches may require architectural or procedural redesign to ensure reliable self-assessment.

title: Layerwise Progressive Freezing: A Training Scaffold for Depth-Scalable Binary Networks
comment: arXiv admin note: substantial text overlap with arXiv:2601.22660
summary: Training binary neural networks (BNNs) from scratch is dominated by the straight-through estimator (STE), whose forward/backward mismatch produces severe accuracy degradation as networks deepen. We study an orthogonal axis: when and where binarization is enforced during training. We introduce StoMPP (Stochastic Masked Partial Progressive Binarization), which gradually replaces clipped weights and activations with their hard binary counterparts layer by layer from input to output, using stochastic partial masks with soft refresh. StoMPP delivers two complementary benefits. As a standalone training rule, it provides a fully STE-free procedure that improves over vanilla STE with gains that grow with depth (ResNet-50 BNN: +18.0/+13.5/+3.8 on CIFAR-10/100/ImageNet), and the pattern holds across ResNet-18/34/50, MobileNetV2, and BERT fine-tuning.
