Composed with surrogate gradients by applying STE only to frozen entries, it reaches +27.1/+19.8/+17.7 over vanilla STE on the same setting. Underlying both regimes is a single mechanistic finding: progression order is decisive. Forward layerwise progression prevents depth collapse, reverse progression collapses to near-chance, and binary-weight networks (without binary activations) are insensitive to order. We trace this asymmetry to activation-induced gradient blockades: a committed binary activation severs gradient flow upstream, and ordering controls when these blockades form. To isolate the progression's contribution from any benefit conferred by STE, we conduct all ablations in the STE-free regime; the resulting characterization (schedule, refresh, ordering, dynamics) thus reflects the progression itself rather than its interaction with surrogate gradients.

AI.tldr: StoMPP introduces a STE-free training method for BNNs that progressively binarizes layers from input to output using stochastic partial masks, preventing depth collapse. Forward progression order is critical—reverse order fails. Combined with STE on frozen entries, it achieves up to +27.1% on CIFAR-10 over vanilla STE.
AI.motivation: The straight-through estimator (STE) used in training binary neural networks suffers from a forward/backward mismatch that causes severe accuracy degradation as network depth increases. The authors investigate an orthogonal dimension: the timing and ordering of binarization enforcement during training, aiming to eliminate reliance on STE entirely.
AI.method: StoMPP (Stochastic Masked Partial Progressive Binarization) gradually replaces clipped weights and activations with hard binary counterparts layer-by-layer from input to output. It uses stochastic partial masks with soft refresh, meaning each layer transitions progressively rather than all at once. The core mechanism: forward layerwise progression prevents activation-induced gradient blockades, where committed binary activations sever upstream gradient flow. Ablations are conducted entirely STE-free to isolate the progression's contribution.
AI.result: As a standalone STE-free method, StoMPP improves over vanilla STE: ResNet-50 BNN gains +18.0/+13.5/+3.8 on CIFAR-10/100/ImageNet. Combined with STE applied only to frozen entries: +27.1/+19.8/+17.7. The pattern holds across ResNet-18/34/50, MobileNetV2, and BERT. Reverse progression collapses to near-chance accuracy; binary-weight-only networks are insensitive to order.
AI.conclusion: Progression order is decisive for deep BNN training. Forward layerwise binarization prevents the gradient blockades caused by binary activations that sever upstream gradient flow. StoMPP provides an STE-free alternative that scales with depth, and its benefits compound when modestly combined with STE on frozen entries.

title: MultiHashFormer: Hash-based Generative Language Models
summary: Language models (LMs) represent tokens using embedding matrices that scale linearly with the vocabulary size. To constrain the parameter footprint, prior work proposes hashing many tokens into a single vector within encoder-only models. While this offers parameter efficiency, many-to-one collisions prevent its use in causal LMs. In this paper, we propose MultiHashFormer, a new framework that allows hash-based autoregression. Each token is represented as a unique hash signature, a short sequence of discrete hash IDs, generated by multiple independent hash functions. A Hash Encoder compresses this signature into a single latent vector for processing by a Transformer decoder. Then, a Hash Decoder generates the hash signature of the next token, which is then mapped back to text. We evaluate our approach at the 100M, 1B and 3B parameter scales, demonstrating that MultiHashFormer consistently outperforms standard Transformer LMs across multiple benchmarks. Furthermore, we show that our model handles multilingual vocabulary expansion with a constant parameter footprint without any modifications.

AI.tldr: MultiHashFormer replaces token embeddings with multi-hash signatures to decouple parameter count from vocabulary size, enabling hash-based autoregressive language modeling that outperforms standard Transformers at 100M–3B scales while supporting constant-footprint multilingual vocabulary expansion.
AI.motivation: Standard language models scale embedding matrices linearly with vocabulary size, creating a large parameter footprint. Prior hashing-based approaches (many-to-one collisions) work only for encoder-only models and fail for causal/autoregressive LMs because collisions prevent unambiguous next-token prediction. The authors aim to achieve parameter-efficient autoregressive modeling via hashing.
AI.method: MultiHashFormer assigns each token a unique hash signature — a short sequence of discrete hash IDs from multiple independent hash functions. A Hash Encoder compresses the signature into a single latent vector for the Transformer decoder. A Hash Decoder then autoregressively predicts the next token's hash signature, which is mapped back to text via a hash-to-token lookup.
AI.result: MultiHashFormer consistently outperforms standard Transformer LMs across multiple benchmarks at 100M, 1B, and 3B parameter scales. The model also handles multilingual vocabulary expansion with a constant parameter footprint without requiring any architectural modifications.
AI.conclusion: Hash-based autoregressive language modeling is viable and parameter-efficient. MultiHashFormer decouples model size from vocabulary size, offering a practical path to scaling LMs to large vocabularies (including multilingual settings) without inflating embedding parameters, while maintaining or exceeding standard Transformer performance.

title: RS-Diffuser: Risk-Sensitive Diffusion Planning with Distributional Value Guidance
summary: Offline reinforcement learning enables policy learning from fixed datasets without additional environment interaction, making it appealing for safety-critical applications where online exploration is costly or unsafe. Diffusion-based decision-making methods have recently achieved strong performance in offline RL by modeling rich, multimodal trajectory distributions. However, existing diffusion planners are typically risk-neutral and therefore may overlook rare but catastrophic outcomes that are crucial in real-world deployment. In this work, we propose RS-Diffuser, a risk-sensitive offline diffusion planning framework that combines diffusion-based trajectory generation with distributional value critics. RS-Diffuser learns a diffusion planner over future state trajectories, a separate inverse dynamics model for action decoding, and a Monte Carlo distributional critic that estimates the full return distribution of candidate plans through quantile regression. At sampling time, we incorporate a risk-sensitive guidance signal into the denoising process, using gradients computed from tail-aware objectives such as Conditional Value at Risk to steer generation toward desired risk profiles. As a result, a single trained model can flexibly produce risk-averse, risk-neutral, or risk-seeking behaviors by changing only the inference-time risk parameter. Extensive experiments on risk-sensitive D4RL and risky robot navigation benchmarks demonstrate that RS-Diffuser achieves state-of-the-art performance, improving both overall return and worst-case robustness while reducing safety violations.

AI.tldr: RS-Diffuser is a risk-sensitive offline RL framework that combines diffusion-based trajectory generation with distributional value critics, enabling flexible risk-averse, risk-neutral, or risk-seeking behaviors at inference time by simply adjusting a risk parameter.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion-based offline RL planners are risk-neutral and fail to account for rare but catastrophic outcomes, which is problematic for safety-critical real-world deployment where worst-case robustness matters.
AI.method: RS-Diffuser integrates three components: (1) a diffusion planner over future state trajectories, (2) an inverse dynamics model for action decoding, and (3) a Monte Carlo distributional critic using quantile regression to estimate the full return distribution. At sampling time, risk-sensitive guidance via tail-aware objectives like Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) is injected into the denoising process through gradient-based steering.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on risk-sensitive D4RL and risky robot navigation benchmarks show state-of-the-art performance, with improvements in overall return, worst-case robustness, and reduction in safety violations.
AI.conclusion: RS-Diffuser demonstrates that incorporating risk sensitivity into diffusion planning yields a unified, flexible framework capable of adapting to diverse risk preferences without retraining, advancing the applicability of offline RL in safety-critical domains.

title: Mechanism-Driven Monitors for Preemptive Detection of LLM Training Instability
summary: Frontier large language model training consumes massive accelerator fleets and long wall-clock computation, making stability failures costly when they occur. After a numerical or a hyperparameter fault has already destabilized the training dynamics, it may continue for thousands of steps while loss and gradient norms still appear normal. We study mechanism-driven detection of training instability by deriving internal monitors from the functional role of each critical module and from the earliest computational sites where failures are expected to produce measurable signatures. For low-precision flash attention, we monitor the spectral entropy of a QK bilinear decomposition, whose first-order term becomes abnormal before the loss fully collapses. For MoE routers, we derive indicators from their role in expert selection. Our fault-injection experiments on low-precision attention, large learning-rate, and combined faults show that these signals provide distinct signatures for different failures, triggering thousands of steps before loss divergence.

AI.tldr: Proposes mechanism-driven stability monitors for LLM training that detect failures (e.g., low-precision attention collapse, MoE routing faults) thousands of steps before loss divergence, using spectral entropy of QK decomposition and expert-selection indicators.
AI.motivation: Training frontier LLMs requires massive compute; stability failures that go undetected for thousands of steps are extremely costly. Current reliance on loss and gradient norms is insufficient, as these metrics can appear normal long after destabilization begins.
AI.method: Derives internal monitors from the functional role of each critical module and the earliest computational sites where failures produce measurable signatures: (1) for low-precision flash attention, monitors spectral entropy of a QK bilinear decomposition whose first-order term becomes abnormal pre-collapse; (2) for MoE routers, derives indicators from expert-selection behavior. Validates via fault-injection experiments on low-precision attention faults, large learning-rate faults, and combined faults.
AI.result: The proposed mechanism-driven signals provide distinct signatures for different failure types and trigger thousands of training steps before loss divergence occurs, substantially earlier than standard loss/gradient-norm monitoring.
AI.conclusion: Mechanism-driven internal monitoring enables early, interpretable detection of training instabilities, offering a practical path to reducing wasted computation in large-scale LLM training by catching failures well before they manifest in the loss.

title: Difference of Convex Programming in the Wasserstein Space with Applications to MMD Optimization
summary: Optimizing functionals over the space of probability measures is now ubiquitous in machine learning. A widely used approach is to perform the optimization directly over the Wasserstein space, but many objective functionals of practical interest are non-convex along Wasserstein geodesics, making the analysis of standard first-order methods challenging. In this work, we study a class of objectives over the Wasserstein space that admit a difference-of-convex (DC) decomposition and we lift the classical convex-concave procedure (CCCP) to this setting. Under smoothness and strong convexity assumptions on the convex components of the decomposition, we prove almost stationarity along the iterates of the resulting algorithm. Our main focus is on the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) and the Energy Distance (ED) functionals, for which we develop explicit Wasserstein DC decompositions, and establish local convergence of the scheme under mild assumptions. Empirically, we show that well-chosen DC decompositions yield faster and more stable convergence than Wasserstein gradient descent on these MMD objectives.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the classical convex-concave procedure (CCCP) to optimization over Wasserstein space for objectives admitting a difference-of-convex (DC) decomposition. The authors prove almost stationarity of iterates under smoothness/strong convexity assumptions, derive explicit DC decompositions for Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) and Energy Distance (ED), and demonstrate faster, more stable convergence than Wasserstein gradient descent.
AI.motivation: Many practically important objective functionals over probability measure spaces are non-convex along Wasserstein geodesics, which breaks standard convex optimization guarantees and complicates first-order method analysis in Wasserstein gradient descent.
AI.method: The authors (1) lift the classical CCCP algorithm to the Wasserstein space setting; (2) prove that under smoothness and strong convexity of the convex DC components, the iterates achieve almost stationarity; (3) derive explicit Wasserstein DC decompositions for MMD and ED functionals; and (4) empirically evaluate convergence against Wasserstein gradient descent.
AI.result: Theoretically, almost stationarity is guaranteed for the lifted CCCP under standard regularity conditions. Empirically, appropriately chosen DC decompositions lead to faster and more stable convergence on MMD objectives compared to standard Wasserstein gradient descent.
AI.conclusion: The Wasserstein CCCP framework provides a principled approach for optimizing a broad class of DC-decomposable functionals over probability measure spaces, with MMD and ED as key motivating examples where the method outperforms Wasserstein gradient descent.

title: From Tokens to States: LLMs as a Special Case of World Models and the Continuous Path Beyond
summary: The AI community has framed the relationship between large language models (LLMs) and world models as a dichotomy: LLMs predict tokens; world models simulate reality. Yann LeCun argues in 2022 that reaching general intelligence requires abandoning autoregressive token prediction in favour of latent-space architectures. This framing is unnecessarily binary. Two claims will be defended. First, LLMs are a degenerate special case of world models: the state space is the set of all token sequences, the only action is appending one token, and world models are therefore a strict generalisation of LLMs, not a replacement. Second, there is a natural continuous spectrum from NTP to JEPA, with multi-token prediction, future-summary prediction, and next-latent prediction as intermediate stations already populated by current research. Moving along this spectrum relaxes the LLM constraints one by one. It also progressively surrenders the two practical advantages that make LLMs trainable at scale: internet-scale self-supervised data, and a transformer architecture co-designed for discrete token prediction. Both are examined as open research questions: the data question (the cliff from self-supervised text to instrumented action-labelled environments) and the architecture question (whether the transformer generalises to continuous-state prediction, or whether a new primitive is needed).

AI.tldr: The paper argues that LLMs and world models are not opposing paradigms but exist on a continuous spectrum, with LLMs being a degenerate special case of world models. It maps intermediate architectures (multi-token prediction, future-summary prediction, next-latent prediction) along this spectrum and identifies two open challenges: the data cliff from self-supervised text to action-labelled environments, and whether transformers generalize to continuous-state prediction.
AI.motivation: To challenge the false dichotomy between autoregressive LLMs and latent-space world models (exemplified by LeCun's 2022 JEPA proposal), and to reframe the relationship as one of generalization rather than replacement, thereby clarifying the research landscape between these extremes.
AI.method: Conceptual/philosophical analysis: (1) Formal demonstration that LLMs satisfy the definition of world models under degenerate constraints — state space = token sequences, action = single-token append. (2) Construction of a spectrum ordering architectures by progressively relaxing these constraints: next-token prediction → multi-token prediction → future-summary prediction → next-latent prediction → full world models/JEPA. Each intermediate station is grounded in existing research. (3) Identification and analysis of two practical barriers that emerge along this spectrum.
AI.result: Two main claims are defended: (1) World models strictly generalize LLMs — autoregressive token prediction is world modeling with maximally constrained state and action spaces. (2) The NTP-to-JEPA spectrum is populated by real intermediate architectures, each relaxing one constraint. However, moving rightward surrenders LLMs' two key advantages: internet-scale self-supervised text data and the transformer's co-adaptation to discrete tokens, posing open questions about data acquisition and architectural suitability for continuous-state prediction.
AI.conclusion: The LLM-vs-world-model dichotomy is a false binary. Progress toward general intelligence can be understood as gradual relaxation of LLM constraints along a spectrum, but doing so requires solving two hard problems: sourcing rich action-labelled data beyond self-supervised text, and determining whether transformers or novel primitives are needed for continuous latent-state prediction.

title: NormGuard: Reward-Preserving Norm Constraints in Flow-Matching Reinforcement Learning
summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training improves the reward alignment of flow-based generators, but often degrades perceptual quality in ways that are not captured by the reward proxy. We identify a simple structural signature of this drift: across three post-training methods (NFT, AWM, DPO), RL fine-tuning inflates the per-step velocity norm $\|v_θ\|$ by $5\%$ to $15\%$ relative to the reference. A form of norm inflation has been studied in classifier-free guidance (CFG), where rescaling the velocity back to a reference norm at inference time can mitigate the resulting artifacts. However, this inference-time correction does not transfer cleanly to RL: rescaling $v_θ$ to match $\|v_{\text{ref}}\|$ at inference time neither improves reward nor fixes the quality degradation, because the inflation is co-adapted into the model weights. Furthermore, an adjoint sensitivity analysis shows that velocity magnitude rescaling carries no coherent first-order reward signal at the batch level, indicating that suppressing norm inflation is unlikely to remove a consistently reward-carrying component. Since inference-time renormalization fails while norm suppression carries no reward cost, training-time intervention is the appropriate strategy. Together, these findings motivate \methodname, a hinge penalty that activates only when $\|v_θ\|$ exceeds $\|v_{\text{ref}}\|$ and composes additively with any velocity-local base loss. Across two base models, three post-training methods, and two reward proxies, \methodname consistently improves MLLM-judged image quality and forensic realism while preserving reward, with gains that amplify under few-step inference and are not explained by early stopping.

AI.tldr: RL fine-tuning of flow-based generators increases per-step velocity norm, degrading perceptual quality. Inference-time rescaling fails because inflation is co-adapted into weights. The authors propose a hinge penalty on velocity norm that activates only when exceeding the reference norm, improving quality while preserving reward across multiple methods and models.
AI.motivation: RL post-training of flow-based generative models improves reward alignment but degrades perceptual quality in ways not captured by the reward proxy. Existing inference-time corrections (like CFG rescaling) fail for RL because the velocity norm inflation is embedded in model weights. A training-time solution is needed.
AI.method: The authors first characterize the problem: RL fine-tuning inflates per-step velocity norm ||v_θ|| by 5–15% across NFT, AWM, and DPO methods. They show inference-time rescaling to match ||v_ref|| fails because norm inflation is co-adapted into weights, and adjoint sensitivity analysis reveals no coherent first-order reward signal from magnitude rescaling. They then propose a hinge penalty that activates only when ||v_θ|| exceeds ||v_ref||, composed additively with any velocity-local base loss.
AI.result: The proposed hinge penalty consistently improves MLLM-judged image quality and forensic realism while preserving reward across two base models, three post-training methods, and two reward proxies. Gains amplify under few-step inference and are not attributable to early stopping.
AI.conclusion: Since inference-time renormalization fails and norm suppression carries no reward cost, training-time intervention via the hinge penalty is the correct strategy. The method is lightweight, plug-and-play, and effective across diverse RL post-training setups.

title: Cognitive Episodes in LLM Reasoning Traces Enable Interpretable Human Item Difficulty Prediction
summary: Predicting human item difficulty is central to educational assessment, where reliable estimates support fairness and effective test construction. Existing methods often depend on costly human calibration or item-level textual representations, providing limited evidence about the cognitive processes that make items difficult. We argue that difficulty should be viewed not only as a property of item text, but also as an observable consequence of the problem-solving burden an item induces. Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) offer scalable process evidence through reasoning traces, but such evidence must be structured to support interpretable modeling. To this end, we introduce Epi2Diff (Episode to Difficulty), a framework that maps LRM reasoning traces into cognitively grounded episode sequences. These episodes group trace segments into functional problem-solving states, enabling difficulty to be modeled through reasoning scale, effort allocation, and state transitions. Epi2Diff extracts compact episode-dynamic features and combines them with semantic item representations for human difficulty prediction. Experiments on four real-world human difficulty datasets show that Epi2Diff consistently outperforms strong baselines, including fine-tuned small language models, LLM in-context learning, and supervised LLM adaptation. On SAT-derived classification benchmarks, Epi2Diff achieves an 8.1% average relative gain over supervised LLM fine-tuning baselines. Further analyses show that harder items induce more effortful, iterative, and implementation-centered episode dynamics, rather than merely longer responses. These results demonstrate that cognitive episodes in LRM reasoning traces provide a predictive and interpretable process representation for human item difficulty, offering a new lens for educational measurement with reasoning models.

AI.tldr: Epi2Diff maps Large Reasoning Model (LRM) traces into cognitive episodes—functional problem-solving states—and uses resulting episode dynamics (scale, effort allocation, state transitions) combined with semantic features to predict human item difficulty, outperforming strong baselines on four datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing difficulty prediction methods rely on costly human calibration or static item text, failing to capture the cognitive processes that actually make items difficult. LRMs provide process evidence via reasoning traces, but lack structured, interpretable representations for modeling difficulty.
AI.method: Epi2Diff segments LRM reasoning traces into cognitively-grounded episode sequences representing functional problem-solving states. It extracts compact episode-dynamic features (reasoning scale, effort allocation, state transitions) and combines them with semantic item representations for downstream human difficulty prediction via supervised learning.
AI.result: Epi2Diff consistently outperforms fine-tuned small LMs, LLM in-context learning, and supervised LLM adaptation baselines across four real-world datasets. On SAT-derived classification benchmarks, it achieves an 8.1% average relative gain over supervised LLM fine-tuning. Analyses show harder items exhibit more effortful, iterative, implementation-centered episode dynamics rather than merely longer responses.
AI.conclusion: Cognitive episodes extracted from LRM reasoning traces provide predictive and interpretable process representations for human item difficulty, offering a new lens for educational measurement that leverages reasoning models' observable problem-solving behavior.

title: Accelerating Hierarchical Sparse Predictive Coding with Hybrid Amortized Inference
summary: Hierarchical predictive coding provides an interpretable framework for perception as error-driven inference in multi-layer generative models, while sparse coding imposes parsimonious latent representations through explicit sparsity constraints. Their combination yields hierarchical sparse predictive coding models with appealing computational and neuroscientific properties, but practical use is often limited by the cost of iterative latent inference. In such models, each input may require many recurrent refinement steps before a useful sparse representation is obtained, and this burden becomes more severe as the hierarchy deepens. We study this bottleneck by holding the hierarchical sparse energy fixed and varying the inference procedure. The comparison includes four schemes: classical iterative inference based on ISTA, an accelerated MFISTA reference, structurally informed amortized inference using a LISTA-style bottom-up encoder adapted to the hierarchical model, and a hybrid method in which this fast amortized initialization is followed by a small number of corrective energy-based refinement steps. Under this shared objective, we measure reconstruction quality, sparsity, latency, and stability on static image benchmarks. The results show that a shallow LISTA-style initializer plus short corrective recurrence improves over pure amortization while remaining much faster than long iterative inference.

AI.tldr: This paper examines inference speed bottlenecks in hierarchical sparse predictive coding models by comparing four inference schemes under a shared energy objective: classical ISTA, accelerated MFISTA, amortized LISTA-style encoder, and a hybrid amortized+recurrence approach. The hybrid method—combining a shallow LISTA initializer with few corrective steps—achieves superior speed-accuracy trade-off over pure amortization while being substantially faster than full iterative inference.
AI.motivation: Hierarchical sparse predictive coding models combine interpretable error-driven inference with parsimonious representations, but practical adoption is hindered by costly iterative latent inference—each input requires many recurrent refinement steps, and this cost worsens with deeper hierarchies. The authors aim to systematically study this inference bottleneck by evaluating alternative inference procedures under a fixed hierarchical sparse energy.
AI.method: The authors fix a hierarchical sparse predictive coding energy and compare four inference procedures: (1) classical iterative inference via ISTA, (2) accelerated MFISTA as a reference, (3) structurally informed amortized inference using a LISTA-style bottom-up encoder adapted for the hierarchical model, and (4) a hybrid method that initializes with fast amortized encoding then applies a small number of corrective energy-based refinement steps. Evaluation is conducted on static image benchmarks measuring reconstruction quality, sparsity, latency, and stability.
AI.result: Under the shared energy objective, the hybrid approach—a shallow LISTA-style initializer followed by short corrective recurrence—outperforms pure amortization in reconstruction quality and sparsity while remaining significantly faster than full iterative inference (ISTA/MFISTA). This demonstrates a favorable speed-accuracy-latency trade-off.
AI.conclusion: Combining amortized inference with a small number of energy-based refinement steps offers a practical solution to the inference bottleneck in hierarchical sparse predictive coding, preserving the benefits of both approaches: the speed of learned feedforward initialization and the accuracy of iterative correction.

title: Vision-Default, Prior-Override: Causal Mechanisms of Perception-Knowledge Conflict in Vision-Language Models
summary: Vision-language models must reconcile visual evidence with memorized world knowledge when the two conflict. How they resolve this conflict shapes the reliability of multimodal systems, yet prior work characterizes it behaviorally without a component-level causal account. We combine activation patching across three granularities (residual stream, attention heads, and MLP sublayers) with model-component ablation studies and mechanistic analysis. Across three VLM families, we find that visual grounding emerges by default, whereas prior grounding depends on a small set of causally necessary attention heads (2.5-4.8%) concentrated in the second half of the network. These heads enable answers from stored world knowledge (e.g., "red" for a strawberry) despite conflicting visual input. Ablating them flips predictions from knowledge-grounded to visually grounded answers in 68-96% of cases under prior-knowledge prompts, but changes only 0.8-7.5% of visually grounded predictions, establishing an asymmetric causal structure. The identified heads decompose into routing heads, which modulate information flow, and writing heads, which directly project answer tokens into the residual stream. This structure is consistent across model families and scales, revealing a sparse causal circuit underlying perception-knowledge conflict in VLMs.

AI.tldr: This paper uses activation patching and ablation to identify a sparse set of attention heads (2.5–4.8%) in the second half of VLMs that causally mediate prior-knowledge grounding. These heads decompose into routing and writing subtypes and, when ablated, flip knowledge-grounded predictions to visually grounded ones in 68–96% of cases, revealing an asymmetric causal circuit for perception-knowledge conflict resolution.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models (VLMs) face a core tension between visual evidence and memorized world knowledge. Prior work describes this conflict behaviorally but lacks a component-level causal account of which model mechanisms resolve it. Understanding this is critical for the reliability and interpretability of multimodal systems.
AI.method: The authors apply activation patching at three granularities (residual stream, attention heads, MLP sublayers), combined with model-component ablation studies and mechanistic analysis, across three VLM families. They isolate causally necessary attention heads for prior-knowledge grounding, then further decompose them into routing heads (modulating information flow) and writing heads (projecting answer tokens into the residual stream).
AI.result: (1) Visual grounding is the default behavior; prior-knowledge grounding depends on only 2.5–4.8% of attention heads concentrated in the network's second half. (2) Ablating these heads flips knowledge-grounded predictions to visually grounded ones in 68–96% of cases under prior-knowledge prompts, but affects visually grounded predictions in only 0.8–7.5% of cases, demonstrating asymmetry. (3) The identified heads decompose functionally into routing heads and writing heads. (4) This sparse causal circuit is consistent across model families and scales.
AI.conclusion: VLMs resolve perception-knowledge conflicts via a sparse, interpretable causal circuit of attention heads that can be cleanly ablated to shift model behavior toward visual grounding. This circuit is structurally consistent across architectures and scales, offering both mechanistic insight and a practical lever for controlling multimodal model reliability.

title: Pepti-drift: Toxicity-Repulsive Drifting for Antigen-Conditioned Discrete Peptide Generation
summary: Peptides are a promising therapeutic modality that combine the chemical tunability of small molecules with the target specificity of macromolecular therapeutics. However, designing antigen-specific binding peptides while avoiding toxicity remains a major challenge for therapeutic peptide discovery. Here, we present Pepti-drift, a toxicity-aware latent refinement framework that generates peptide candidates through a single antigen-conditioned drift step. In a peptide embedding space, Pepti-drift learns to attract generated peptide latents toward antigen-matched binding peptides while repelling them from toxicity-associated regions. This is challenging because binding-promoting physicochemical features often overlap with toxicity-associated features in peptide representation space. To address this, we introduce a warm-up strategy to stabilize this competing objective by first learning binding-oriented attraction and then increasing toxicity repulsion.

AI.tldr: Pepti-drift is a latent refinement framework that generates antigen-specific binding peptides using a single drift step, while simultaneously repelling candidates from toxicity-associated regions in embedding space via a warm-up training strategy.
AI.motivation: Designing therapeutic peptides that bind specifically to targets while avoiding toxicity is difficult because the physicochemical features that promote binding often overlap with those associated with toxicity, making joint optimization challenging.
AI.method: Pepti-drift operates in a peptide latent embedding space, performing antigen-conditioned diffusion/drift. It learns to attract generated peptide latents toward antigen-matched binding peptides while repelling them from toxicity-associated regions. A warm-up strategy is introduced that first learns binding-oriented attraction, then progressively increases toxicity repulsion to stabilize the competing objectives.
AI.result: The paper presents the Pepti-drift framework architecture and the warm-up training strategy. (Specific quantitative results — such as binding affinity improvements, toxicity reduction metrics, or benchmark comparisons — are not detailed in the provided abstract.)
AI.conclusion: Pepti-drift offers a principled approach to navigate the binding-toxicity trade-off in therapeutic peptide design by jointly modeling both objectives in latent space with a stabilized training procedure.

title: USAD: Uncertainty-aware Statistical Adversarial Detection
summary: Statistical adversarial detection (SAD) treats detection as a two-sample test. Given a reference set of clean examples (CEs) and a batch of queries, potentially containing an unknown mixture of CEs and adversarial examples (AEs), SAD decides whether the query distribution drifts away from the CE distribution while controlling the false-alarm rate. Existing SAD-based methods mainly use maximum mean discrepancy (MMD) to measure the distributional discrepancy. However, MMD's distributional properties limit its ability to capture characteristic uncertainty patterns of AEs that are crucial for detection: AEs typically exhibit abnormal feature spread (i.e., global uncertainty) and instability under perturbations (i.e., local uncertainty). To close the gap, we propose Uncertainty-aware Statistical Adversarial Detection (USAD), which explicitly captures these uncertainty patterns with two new statistics: (1) Variance Discrepancy (VD), which measures the difference in feature spread between AEs and CEs to capture global uncertainty differences. (2) Perturbation-based Covariance Discrepancy (PCD), which compares feature covariance under Gaussian perturbations to capture local uncertainty differences. By aggregating VD and PCD, USAD achieves superior detection performances over baseline methods against various adversarial attacks, highlighting the importance of considering characteristic behaviors of AEs for effective SAD. Our code is available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/USAD.

AI.tldr: USAD enhances statistical adversarial detection by introducing Variance Discrepancy (VD) and Perturbation-based Covariance Discrepancy (PCD) to capture global and local uncertainty patterns of adversarial examples, outperforming MMD-based SAD methods.
AI.motivation: Existing SAD methods rely on MMD, which fails to capture two characteristic uncertainty patterns of adversarial examples: abnormal feature spread (global uncertainty) and instability under perturbations (local uncertainty). This limits detection effectiveness.
AI.method: USAD introduces two new statistics: (1) Variance Discrepancy (VD) to measure differences in feature spread between clean and adversarial examples (global uncertainty), and (2) Perturbation-based Covariance Discrepancy (PCD) to compare feature covariance under Gaussian perturbations (local uncertainty). These are aggregated for the final detection decision.
AI.result: USAD achieves superior detection performance over baseline SAD methods against various adversarial attacks.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling characteristic uncertainty behaviors of adversarial examples — global feature spread and local perturbation instability — is crucial for effective statistical adversarial detection.

title: WattLayer: Get Layers Right to Estimate Inference Energy of Neural Networks
summary: The widespread adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has led to increasing concerns about energy consumption, yet there is a lack of standardized methodologies to accurately estimate AI inference energy consumption, particularly across various tasks and architectures. In this study, we propose a task independent, layer-wise energy estimation model for AI architectures. Our model is evaluated on a large dataset of more than 100,000 layers for 295 neural network architectures across 3 widely-used tasks and 3 distinct hardware platforms. Our approach achieves a median error of 19.6%, outperforming state-of-the-art methods. We further show that layer-wise decomposition generalize to new tasks without complete retraining, by leveraging shared layers across architectures. It offer tools, insights and a precise methodology to empower stakeholders in designing energy-efficient AI systems.

AI.tldr: A layer-wise, task-independent energy estimation model for AI inference is proposed, evaluated on 100K+ layers across 295 architectures, 3 tasks, and 3 hardware platforms, achieving a median error of 19.6% and outperforming existing methods.
AI.motivation: Despite growing concerns over AI energy consumption, there is a lack of standardized, accurate methodologies for estimating inference energy across diverse tasks, architectures, and hardware platforms.
AI.method: The authors propose a task-independent, layer-wise energy estimation model that decomposes neural network architectures into individual layers to predict inference energy consumption. The model leverages shared layers across architectures to generalize to new tasks without full retraining.
AI.result: Evaluated on a dataset of over 100,000 layers from 295 architectures across 3 tasks and 3 hardware platforms, the model achieves a median estimation error of 19.6%, surpassing state-of-the-art methods.
AI.conclusion: Layer-wise decomposition enables accurate, generalizable energy estimation across tasks and hardware. The methodology provides practical tools and insights for stakeholders to design more energy-efficient AI systems.

title: Applicability of memorization indicators for early spotting of overfitting while recalibrating sEMG-decoders on low sample sizes
summary: Deep learning models for surface electromyography (sEMG) can benefit substantially from subject-specific (re-)calibration, since no sufficiently large and diverse datasets are available to train fully generic decoders. However, for user acceptance, the number of repetitions that can realistically be collected during calibration is severely limited, which increases the risk of overfitting and, in extreme cases, can even degrade performance compared to the uncalibrated model. Classical overfitting indicators such as validation performance and regularization with early stopping are difficult to apply in this low-sample regime, as they require additional held-out data that is rarely available in practical calibration scenarios. In this work, we investigate a recently proposed class of memorization indicators based solely on the activation statistics of rectified linear units (ReLU) in deep neural networks, which can be computed directly from training data without any extra validation set. We conduct a transferlearning experiment on a benchmark sEMG dataset, where a convolutional neural network is first pre-trained on multiple subjects and subsequently fine-tuned on individual users using only a small number of repetitions. During calibration, we monitor both decoding performance and the activation behaviour of the last hidden layer. Our results provide first evidence that decreases in test accuracy during fine-tuning are ac companied by characteristic changes in activation rates, indicating that activation-based memorization indicators are a promising tool for early spotting of unsuccessful learning in low-sample sEMG calibration settings.

AI.tldr: This paper explores using ReLU activation statistics as memorization indicators to detect overfitting during subject-specific fine-tuning of sEMG decoders when only very limited calibration data is available, finding that drops in test accuracy correlate with characteristic changes in activation rates.
AI.motivation: Subject-specific calibration of sEMG deep learning models is essential but constrained by very few training repetitions, creating a high overfitting risk. Classical overfitting detection methods (validation performance, early stopping) require held-out data that is impractical in real-world calibration. A data-only indicator of unsuccessful learning is needed.
AI.method: A CNN is pre-trained on multiple subjects for sEMG decoding, then fine-tuned per individual with few repetitions. During fine-tuning, the authors monitor both decoding accuracy and ReLU activation statistics (specifically activation rates) in the last hidden layer, using a recently proposed class of memorization indicators that require only training data.
AI.result: Decreases in test accuracy during fine-tuning are accompanied by characteristic changes in ReLU activation rates, providing first evidence that activation-based memorization indicators can signal unsuccessful learning in low-sample sEMG calibration.
AI.conclusion: Activation-based memorization indicators are a promising, practical tool for early spotting of overfitting in low-sample sEMG calibration without requiring held-out validation data.

title: GNBAN: Graph Neural Basis Attention Networks for Long-Horizon Forecasting over Large Entity Sets
summary: Demand forecasting at the bottom of a retail hierarchy requires predicting tens of thousands of correlated long-horizon series across products, stores, and regions. Modern systems must scale across massive catalogs, capture shared demand dynamics, and remain interpretable enough to be trusted. Classical statistical methods need a separate model per series and are hard to manage at scale; deep autoregressive models struggle as the joint state grows to tens of thousands of dimensions; and recent graph-based forecasters, while capturing cross-entity dependencies, often produce opaque long-horizon forecasts. We propose GNBAN (Graph Neural Basis Attention Network), an end-to-end architecture combining heterogeneous graph representation learning with an interpretable basis-decomposition head. Retail data are represented directly as a heterogeneous graph derived from the relational schema, so a single model serves the entire catalog. Rather than predicting the horizon directly, GNBAN decomposes each forecast into trend, seasonal, and generic components. Its key innovation is a per-basis attention mechanism: each basis function keeps its own learnable query and retrieves information independently from the entity's historical neighborhood, letting different bases specialize to distinct temporal patterns while preserving interpretability. On two large-scale benchmarks, M5 Walmart and Favorita Grocery Sales, evaluated under matched protocols, GNBAN improves volume-weighted WRMSSE by roughly 4-5% over a matched graph baseline. Qualitative analysis shows the learned decomposition exposes trend, seasonal, and residual demand drivers without post-hoc explanation methods. These results demonstrate that scalable relational forecasting and interpretable forecast decomposition can be achieved together in a unified graph-based framework.

AI.tldr: GNBAN is a graph neural network for large-scale retail demand forecasting that uses a heterogeneous graph to model the entire product catalog and decomposes forecasts into interpretable trend, seasonal, and generic components via a per-basis attention mechanism, achieving 4–5% WRMSSE improvement over graph baselines on M5 and Favorita benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Retail demand forecasting at scale faces three challenges: (1) classical per-series statistical models don't scale; (2) deep autoregressive models struggle with high-dimensional joint states (tens of thousands of dimensions); (3) recent graph-based forecasters capture cross-entity dependencies but produce opaque long-horizon forecasts. There is a need for a single, scalable, interpretable model that captures shared dynamics across the entire catalog.
AI.method: GNBAN combines heterogeneous graph representation learning with an interpretable basis-decomposition head. The retail relational schema is directly modeled as a heterogeneous graph, enabling a single model for the entire catalog. Instead of direct horizon prediction, forecasts are decomposed into trend, seasonal, and generic components. The key innovation is a per-basis attention mechanism: each basis function has its own learnable query and independently retrieves information from the entity's historical neighborhood, allowing different bases to specialize to distinct temporal patterns while maintaining interpretability.
AI.result: On M5 Walmart and Favorita Grocery Sales benchmarks under matched protocols, GNBAN improves volume-weighted WRMSSE by approximately 4–5% over a matched graph baseline. Qualitative analysis shows the learned decomposition naturally exposes trend, seasonal, and residual demand drivers without post-hoc explanation methods.
AI.conclusion: Scalable relational forecasting and interpretable forecast decomposition can be achieved together in a unified graph-based framework, as demonstrated by GNBAN's performance and interpretability on large-scale retail benchmarks.

title: FlexMoE: One-for-All Nested Intra-Expert Pruning for MoE Language Models
summary: Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) language models scale model ability with sparsely activated experts, making this architecture a standard recipe for modern large models. However, sparse activation does not remove the deployment burden of storing and serving all experts, and the available deployment budget can vary substantially across devices, users, and workloads. Existing MoE compression methods are still largely fixed-budget, typically optimizing one compressed endpoint at each chosen target budget. We study a different setting: converting a large pretrained MoE LLM into a nested family of deployable subnetworks across budgets. Our method first ranks expert FFN channels by their importance, then lets each expert learn a discrete action to prune its channels. By gradually increasing cost pressure, a single action-training run exports a series of action masks from high to low budgets, each of which identifies a reliable smaller subnetwork nested in the ranked base model. Moreover, we use a single recovery fine-tune at a mid pruning budget (40%) to recover degraded model quality and transfer the recovered model to other unseen budgets. Overall, our framework surpasses recent MoE compression baselines. Specifically, on Qwen2-57B-A14B, our method retains ~99.8% of base performance while pruning 50% of routed expert parameters even without fine-tuning. For deployment, our pruned subnetworks deliver real memory reduction and throughput gains, and further support realtime online budget switching with kernel-level co-design.

AI.tldr: Presents a method to convert a pretrained MoE LLM into a nested family of subnetworks across deployment budgets via ranked channel importance, discrete action learning for pruning, and progressive cost pressure, enabling real-time budget switching with strong performance retention (~99.8% at 50% pruning on Qwen2-57B-A14B).
AI.motivation: MoE models still require storing and serving all experts despite sparse activation, and deployment budgets vary widely across devices and workloads. Existing compression methods are fixed-budget, producing a single compressed model per target, which is inflexible for dynamic deployment scenarios.
AI.method: The method ranks expert FFN channels by importance, then trains each expert to learn a discrete pruning action via a single training run under gradually increasing cost pressure. This produces a series of action masks from high to low budgets, identifying nested subnetworks. A single recovery fine-tune at a mid budget (40%) restores quality and transfers to other unseen budgets.
AI.result: On Qwen2-57B-A14B, retains ~99.8% of base performance while pruning 50% of routed expert parameters without fine-tuning. Pruned subnetworks deliver real memory reduction and throughput gains, and support real-time online budget switching via kernel-level co-design.
AI.conclusion: The proposed nested subnetwork framework surpasses existing MoE compression baselines, offering a flexible, one-shot solution for multi-budget deployment with minimal quality degradation and practical runtime benefits.

title: A Comparison of Fusion Techniques for Multi-Modal Human Activity Recognition on the HARMES Dataset
summary: Recent advances in Human Activity Recognition (HAR) from wearable sensors have shown that multi-modal deep learning models consistently outperform their uni-modal counterparts. Modalities can include IMUs, RGB cameras, audio signals, and others. One important aspect of multi-modal deep learning is the sensor fusion approach we apply. Over recent years, multiple fusion paradigms have been proposed for multi-modal HAR. However, to the best of our knowledge, no head-to-head comparison of these paradigms exists on a common multi-modal HAR benchmark dataset. To address this research gap, we systematically compare seven state-of-the-art sensor fusion methods on the recently released HARMES dataset, which comprises 61 hours of fully labeled IMU, audio, and ambient humidity data. The chosen dataset focuses on 15 household and personal hygiene activities of daily living (ADLs). By applying the seven different fusion techniques to a state-of-the-art multi-modal model architecture, we show that Gated Multi-modal Fusion achieves the highest macro F1-score (0.82), surpassing the concatenation-based late fusion HARMES paper baseline of 0.76 by +6pp under leave-one-participant-out evaluation. All code used in our experiments is made publicly available on GitHub.

AI.tldr: This paper systematically benchmarks seven sensor fusion paradigms for multi-modal Human Activity Recognition (HAR) on the HARMES dataset (IMU, audio, humidity). Gated Multi-modal Fusion achieves the best macro F1-score of 0.82, outperforming the concatenation-based late fusion baseline by +6 percentage points.
AI.motivation: Despite the proliferation of sensor fusion approaches in multi-modal HAR, no head-to-head comparison of these paradigms exists on a common benchmark dataset, making it difficult to assess their relative merits under controlled conditions.
AI.method: Seven state-of-the-art sensor fusion methods (including concatenation-based late fusion, gated fusion, and others) are implemented within a shared multi-modal deep learning architecture and evaluated on the HARMES dataset (61 hours of labeled IMU, audio, and ambient humidity data covering 15 household/personal hygiene ADLs) using leave-one-participant-out cross-validation.
AI.result: Gated Multi-modal Fusion achieves the highest macro F1-score of 0.82, surpassing the concatenation-based late fusion baseline (0.76) by +6 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: Gated Multi-modal Fusion is the most effective fusion paradigm among those tested for multi-modal HAR on this dataset. The authors release all code publicly to facilitate reproducibility and further benchmarking.

title: Towards Automating Scientific Review with Google's Paper Assistant Tool
summary:
Artificial intelligence is driving a revolution in scientific discovery, accelerating everything from hypothesis generation to mathematical theorem proving. However, this rapid acceleration is creating a systemic challenge: traditional human peer review cannot scale to match the influx of AI-assisted science. Ultimately, to resolve this tension, we must also deploy AI to accelerate the verification and review process itself. To frame the discussion around this transition, we propose a taxonomy consisting of four progressive levels of AI-human collaboration in scientific evaluation, and discuss various trade-offs involved with each.
  As a step toward this future, we introduce the Paper Assistant Tool (PAT), an agentic AI framework built for deep scientific review and verification. PAT ingests full scientific manuscripts and produces a comprehensive evaluation, checking theoretical results, validating experiments, suggesting improvements, and identifying potential flaws. By utilizing inference scaling techniques, PAT is able to identify deeper issues than a single model call alone, achieving a 34% improvement over zero-shot recall on mathematical errors in the SPOT benchmark. Pilot deployments of PAT as a pre-submission tool for authors at two major Computer Science conferences -- STOC and ICML -- demonstrate its ability to identify critical errors and suggest substantive improvements to research papers. By catching errors early, PAT eases the cognitive burden placed on referees, while preserving their control over the outcomes of the review process.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a four-level taxonomy for AI-human collaboration in scientific peer review and introduces PAT (Paper Assistant Tool), an agentic AI framework that performs deep review of scientific manuscripts. PAT uses inference scaling techniques to catch errors beyond single-model calls, achieving 34% improvement on the SPOT benchmark. Pilot deployments at STOC and ICML show PAT can identify critical errors and suggest improvements, easing reviewer burden while preserving human control.
AI.motivation: AI is accelerating scientific discovery, but traditional human peer review cannot scale to match the growing influx of AI-assisted science. This creates a systemic bottleneck where verification lags behind generation, motivating the need for AI-assisted review mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors propose a four-level taxonomy of AI-human collaboration in scientific evaluation (from fully human to fully automated). They then introduce PAT, an agentic AI framework that ingests full manuscripts and performs comprehensive evaluation — checking theoretical results, validating experiments, suggesting improvements, and identifying flaws. PAT employs inference scaling techniques (multiple model calls and deeper reasoning) rather than single-pass zero-shot evaluation.
AI.result: PAT achieved a 34% improvement over zero-shot recall on mathematical error detection in the SPOT benchmark. Pilot deployments at STOC and ICML conferences demonstrated PAT's ability to identify critical errors and suggest substantive improvements to research papers during pre-submission.
AI.conclusion: AI-assisted review tools like PAT can help resolve the scalability crisis in peer review by catching errors early in the submission process, reducing cognitive burden on human referees while keeping them in control of final decisions.

title: TA-SparseMG: Trend-Aware Sparse Forecasting via Multi-Scale Gating for Long-Term Time Series
summary: Long-term time series forecasting finds extensive applications in domains such as power demand, traffic flow, meteorological observation, and renewable energy dispatch. Forecasting dynamically varying long-term time series poses inherent challenges, including statistical nonstationarity, local high-frequency disturbances, and coupled cross-period dependencies, which make it difficult for lightweight models to balance parameter efficiency and forecasting performance. To address this issue, this study presents TA-SparseMG, a lightweight cross-period forecasting model built on SparseTSF's sparse cross-period modeling framework. It incorporates three key modules: a trend-aware reversible instance normalization module, a scale-adaptive gated denoising module, and a multiscale gated-attention MLP forecasting module. The trend-aware normalization module captures input-window statistics and calibrates forecast-window distributions, effectively mitigating distribution shift. The scale-adaptive gated denoising module performs feature smoothing and residual suppression before period rearrangement, thereby reducing interference from high-frequency perturbations. The multiscale gated attention prediction module strengthens the prediction head's adaptive representational capacity via conditional gating and feature modulation. Extensive experiments across multiple LTSF benchmarks demonstrate that the proposed TA-SparseMG consistently achieves superior, stable performance. Ablation studies confirm that each module independently improves distribution adaptation, input robustness, and cross-period feature mapping capability.

AI.tldr: TA-SparseMG is a lightweight long-term time series forecasting model that extends SparseTSF with three modules — trend-aware normalization, scale-adaptive gated denoising, and multiscale gated-attention MLP — to address nonstationarity, high-frequency disturbances, and cross-period dependencies, achieving superior performance on LTSF benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Long-term time series forecasting faces three core challenges: statistical nonstationarity (distribution shift), local high-frequency disturbances, and coupled cross-period dependencies. Existing lightweight models struggle to balance parameter efficiency with forecasting performance under these conditions.
AI.method: TA-SparseMG builds on the SparseTSF sparse cross-period modeling framework and adds three modules: (1) a trend-aware reversible instance normalization module that captures input-window statistics to calibrate forecast-window distributions, mitigating distribution shift; (2) a scale-adaptive gated denoising module that performs feature smoothing and residual suppression before period rearrangement to reduce high-frequency perturbations; (3) a multiscale gated-attention MLP forecasting module that enhances the prediction head's adaptive capacity via conditional gating and feature modulation.
AI.result: Extensive experiments across multiple LTSF benchmarks show that TA-SparseMG consistently achieves superior and stable performance. Ablation studies confirm that each module independently contributes to distribution adaptation, input robustness, and cross-period feature mapping.
AI.conclusion: The three proposed modules — trend-aware normalization, scale-adaptive gated denoising, and multiscale gated-attention MLP — each provide independent improvements, and their integration yields a lightweight yet high-performing model for long-term time series forecasting.

title: Graph Dimensionality Reduction for Contextual Bandits: Structure-Specific Regret Bounds under Approximate Smoothness and Noisy Eigenspaces
summary: Contextual bandits with graph-structured arms arise in recommendation, citation retrieval, and social advertising, where arms connected on a graph tend to share reward signal. Standard dimensionality reduction ignores this structure, inflating exploration cost by a factor of $d/k$. We propose GraphDR-LinUCB, which projects arm features onto the graph's low-frequency spectral subspace and runs linear UCB in the resulting $k$-dimensional space. We prove the first $\wtO(k\sqrt{T})$ regret bound for spectral-projection-based contextual bandits, reducing dimension dependence from $d$ to $k$; a perturbation argument extends this to noisy graphs, with an explicit penalty for reward-smoothness mismatch and graph-estimation error. Our central theoretical finding is that the high-frequency reward component need not incur a worst-case linear-in-$T$ penalty: its actual cost depends on its realized impact along the played path, not on its total energy. A simple spectral comparison between subspaces ($Γ_k$) predicts which reducer wins on a given dataset, correctly calling five of six real-dataset outcomes without any fitted threshold. Across a synthetic benchmark and six real datasets (MovieLens, Amazon, LastFM, ogbn-arxiv, MIND), GraphDR-LinUCB reduces cumulative regret by $15\times$ over full-dimensional LinUCB and outperforms competing graph-aware methods on five of six; the single failure is precisely where the graph's spectral subspace is misaligned with the reward.

AI.tldr: GraphDR-LinUCB projects contextual bandit arms onto a graph's low-frequency spectral subspace, achieving a $\widetilde{O}(k\sqrt{T})$ regret bound that breaks the $d$-dimensional dependence. High-frequency reward components incur cost only through realized play, not total energy. Across synthetic and six real-world benchmarks, it reduces regret by up to 15× over standard LinUCB and outperforms graph-aware baselines on five of six datasets.
AI.motivation: Standard contextual bandit algorithms operate in the full $d$-dimensional feature space, yielding regret that scales with $d$. In many applications (recommendation, citation retrieval, social advertising), arms are linked by a known graph whose edges encode reward similarity. Ignoring this graph structure inflates exploration cost by a factor of $d/k$, where $k \ll d$ is the effective dimension of the reward signal. Existing graph-aware methods lack rigorous regret guarantees that decouple dimension dependence from $d$.
AI.method: GraphDR-LinUCB applies spectral projection to arm features: it projects features onto the $k$-dimensional subspace spanned by the graph Laplacian's lowest-frequency eigenvectors, then runs standard LinUCB in this reduced space. The theoretical analysis uses a decomposition of the reward into low-frequency (smooth) and high-frequency (non-smooth) components. A perturbation argument extends guarantees to noisy graphs, with explicit penalties for reward-smoothness mismatch and graph-estimation error. A spectral subspace alignment metric $\Gamma_k$ is introduced to predict which dimensionality reduction method will perform better on a given dataset.
AI.result: The paper proves the first $\widetilde{O}(k\sqrt{T})$ regret bound for spectral-projection-based contextual bandits. The central finding is that high-frequency reward components do not incur a worst-case linear-in-$T$ penalty; their cost depends on realized impact along the played trajectory. The $\Gamma_k$ metric correctly predicts winner on five of six real datasets without fitted thresholds. Empirically, GraphDR-LinUCB reduces cumulative regret by up to 15× versus full-dimensional LinUCB and beats competing graph-aware methods on five of six real datasets; the sole failure occurs when the graph's spectral subspace is misaligned with the reward.
AI.conclusion: Spectral graph projection is a principled and theoretically grounded approach to dimensionality reduction in contextual bandits, effectively reducing regret dimension dependence from $d$ to $k$. The $\Gamma_k$ metric provides a practical, assumption-free diagnostic for method selection. The work opens questions about adaptive subspace selection and extensions to time-varying graphs.

title: Two-Stage Fine-Tuning for Protein Sequence Generation with Targeted Amino-Acid Composition
summary: Protein language models are standard priors for biological sequence generation, but steering them toward explicit distributional design targets remains largely unexplored. We study a constrained protein generation problem in which sequences must match a desired amino-acid (AA) composition profile while preserving plausible sequence statistics and diversity. The motivating application is synthetic feed protein design, where the AA composition of dietary proteins directly determines their nutritional value. We propose a two-stage pipeline in which domain-adaptive fine-tuning (FT) on an in-domain protein dataset is followed by iterative reward-weighted FT via reinforcement learning (RL) anchored against the FT model as a frozen reference. We evaluate the pipeline on two AA compositions and find that FT brings the average composition close to the target, while the subsequent RL enforces specific sequence constraints that FT alone cannot satisfy. We additionally evaluate the design choices of the proposed composition reward term against two baselines and an ablated variant, isolate the contribution of each training stage, and verify that AA composition alignment is achieved without degrading sequence quality.

AI.tldr: A two-stage pipeline combining domain-adaptive fine-tuning with iterative reward-weighted reinforcement learning is proposed to steer protein language models toward generating sequences that match target amino-acid composition profiles while preserving sequence quality and diversity, motivated by synthetic feed protein design.
AI.motivation: Protein language models excel at generating plausible sequences but lack mechanisms to enforce explicit compositional constraints. The motivating use case is synthetic feed protein design, where the nutritional value of dietary proteins is directly determined by their amino-acid composition profile, necessitating methods that can steer generative models toward specific AA distributional targets.
AI.method: A two-stage pipeline: (1) domain-adaptive fine-tuning (FT) on an in-domain protein dataset to bring average composition near the target, followed by (2) iterative reward-weighted FT via reinforcement learning (RL), using the FT model as a frozen reference (anchoring) to enforce specific sequence-level compositional constraints. The authors also evaluate design choices for the composition reward term against baselines and an ablated variant.
AI.result: FT alone brings average AA composition close to the target but cannot satisfy specific sequence-level constraints. The subsequent RL stage successfully enforces these constraints. AA composition alignment is achieved without degrading sequence quality. Ablation studies isolate each stage's contribution and validate the proposed reward design.
AI.conclusion: The proposed two-stage FT+RL pipeline effectively steers protein language models toward desired amino-acid composition targets while maintaining sequence plausibility and diversity, demonstrating a viable approach for constrained protein sequence generation in nutritional applications.

title: RECAST: Model Reconstruction via Counterfactual-Aware Wasserstein Geometry under Limited Data
comment: Accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: Counterfactual explanations (CFs) help understand machine learning models by identifying minimal input changes that would lead to alternative model outcomes. Recent work demonstrates their utility for reconstructing black-box models, enabling third-party auditing of opaque decision systems for fairness and accountability. Still, CF-based reconstruction may suffer from decision boundary shifts, overfitting, and restrictive assumptions requiring online query access to target platforms. We propose REconstruction via Counterfactual-Aware waSserstein opTimization (RECAST) under limited data and restricted access, a behavioral surrogate model based on Wasserstein barycentric prototypes. Our approach addresses decision boundary shifts by incorporating CFs as informative, though less representative, samples for both classes, maintaining high surrogate fidelity in low-sample regimes without requiring online access during reconstruction. To enhance fairness auditing, our method enables systematic group fairness diagnostics. Experiments on real-world datasets and various setups show that RECAST effectively achieves high fidelity and query efficiency, as well as stable results even when the access is limited and noisy.

AI.tldr: RECAST is a surrogate model reconstruction method that uses counterfactual explanations and Wasserstein barycentric prototypes to audit black-box models under limited data and restricted access, achieving high fidelity without online queries while enabling group fairness diagnostics.
AI.motivation: Existing CF-based black-box model reconstruction methods suffer from decision boundary shifts, overfitting, and require online query access to target platforms. There is a need for a method that works under limited data and restricted/no online access while maintaining surrogate fidelity and supporting fairness auditing.
AI.method: RECAST uses Wasserstein barycentric prototypes informed by counterfactual explanations. CFs are incorporated as informative samples for both classes (original and counterfactual outcomes), constructing a behavioral surrogate model without requiring online access during reconstruction. The Wasserstein barycenter framework handles distributional alignment, mitigating decision boundary shifts even in low-sample regimes.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that RECAST achieves high surrogate fidelity, query efficiency, and stable reconstruction performance even under limited and noisy access conditions.
AI.conclusion: RECAST provides an effective approach for black-box model reconstruction and auditing, enabling systematic group fairness diagnostics while overcoming the limitations of prior CF-based methods regarding data scarcity, boundary shifts, and access restrictions.

title: Dual-Learning based Penalized Multi-Align Clustering for Multi-View Incomplete and Disorderly Data
summary:
Multimodal feature fusion can effectively capture complex patterns in real-world data by integrating complementary information from different modalities. However, in many applications, such as boiler combustion monitoring, equipment failure, inconsistent sensor sampling frequencies, and network delays often cause missing modalities and temporal asynchrony. These issues lead to incomplete and disorderly multimodal data. To address them, previous studies have proposed several data fusion methods that align cluster centers before fusion. However, these methods have two key limitations. First, they cannot guarantee accurate sample-level alignment of data pairs. Second, they do not address significant discrepancies in data sizes across different classes, which may affect subsequent fusion performance.
  To address these problems, we propose a dual-learning based penalized multi-align clustering model, named DLPMAC. The dual-learning mechanism enables the model to learn prior knowledge from each modality, including semantic and structural information. This helps preserve semantic consistency and structural similarity across modalities at both local and global levels. In addition, the penalized multi-align module performs multi-to-multi data alignment through a penalty mechanism. It allows one sample to form data pairs with different samples from other modalities, thereby improving data-pair alignment accuracy. The penalty mechanism also prevents data aggregation, avoiding the case where excessive samples are linked to a single sample. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of DLPMAC in addressing data alignment and fusion challenges from both sampling and clustering perspectives.

AI.tldr: DLPMAC is a dual-learning penalized multi-align clustering model that addresses missing modalities and temporal asynchrony in multimodal data fusion by learning semantic/structural priors from each modality and using a penalty mechanism for accurate sample-level multi-to-multi alignment without data aggregation.
AI.motivation: Real-world multimodal applications (e.g., boiler combustion monitoring) suffer from missing modalities and temporal asynchrony due to sensor failures and network delays. Existing cluster-center alignment methods fail to guarantee accurate sample-level alignment and cannot handle significant inter-class data size discrepancies, motivating a more robust alignment approach.
AI.method: DLPMAC employs: (1) a dual-learning mechanism that extracts prior semantic and structural knowledge from each modality to preserve cross-modal consistency at local and global levels; (2) a penalized multi-align module that performs multi-to-multi data alignment, allowing each sample to pair with multiple samples from other modalities via a penalty mechanism that prevents excessive many-to-one linking (data aggregation).
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate DLPMAC's effectiveness in addressing data alignment and fusion challenges from both sampling and clustering perspectives.
AI.conclusion: DLPMAC overcomes the limitations of existing cluster-center alignment methods by enabling accurate sample-level multi-to-multi alignment with a penalty mechanism, while dual-learning preserves cross-modal semantic consistency. The model proves effective for incomplete and asynchronous multimodal data fusion tasks.

title: Benchmarking on Tasks That Matter: Dataset Selection for Preserving Model Rankings
comment: Accepted to the 32nd ACM SIGKDD Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining (KDD 2026)
summary:
Benchmarks of machine learning models often include many datasets, making evaluation expensive. For efficiency, it is preferable to perform evaluations on small, representative datasets instead. The selection of such subsets typically relies on heuristics and is rarely analyzed for the robustness of the resulting model rankings.
  We introduce a framework to perform the task of selecting datasets subsets with an evaluation of how different selection strategies preserve the global model rankings. Our framework includes bootstrap aggregation, which provides valid confidence intervals, allowing a principled comparison of selection strategies. We consider clustering, design criteria (A/D-optimality), random baselines, and greedy farthest-first (FAFI). For the latter, we derive upper bounds on selection quality in terms of ranking errors as a function of the number of selected datasets.
  Empirically, in time series classification (TSC, 112 datasets) and in a supplementary natural language processing benchmark derived from MTEB (57 tasks), several selection strategies improve rank preservation compared with random subsets, including simple FAFI. In contrast, in recommender systems (30 datasets), the improvement of strategies over random selection is small and typically statistically insignificant. For TSC, our best-performing strategy achieves a Spearman correlation of 0.95 with the full benchmark model rankings using only five selected datasets. Additional experiments indicate that the effectiveness of selection approaches depends on both the quality of dataset representations and the scale of the benchmarking regime.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a principled framework for selecting small, representative dataset subsets from large benchmarks while preserving model rankings. Using bootstrap aggregation for valid confidence intervals, it compares strategies like clustering, design criteria, and farthest-first traversal. Experiments on time series classification (112 datasets), NLP (57 tasks), and recommender systems (30 datasets) show that farthest-first and other strategies significantly outperform random selection in preserving rankings for TSC and NLP, but gains are minimal for recommender systems.
AI.motivation: Full benchmarking across many datasets is computationally expensive. While practitioners often use heuristic-based subsets to reduce costs, there is little systematic analysis of how these subset selection strategies affect the robustness and preservation of global model rankings. The authors aim to fill this gap with a rigorous, statistically grounded evaluation framework.
AI.method: The framework evaluates subset selection strategies by measuring rank preservation (e.g., Spearman correlation) between rankings from the subset and the full benchmark. Key components: (1) bootstrap aggregation to produce valid confidence intervals for principled strategy comparison; (2) several strategies compared — clustering, A/D-optimal design criteria, random baselines, and greedy farthest-first (FAFI); (3) theoretical upper bounds on FAFI's ranking error as a function of the number of selected datasets.
AI.result: In TSC (112 datasets), the best strategy achieves Spearman correlation of 0.95 with full rankings using only 5 datasets. In NLP (MTEB-derived, 57 tasks), several strategies improve over random subsets. However, in recommender systems (30 datasets), improvements over random selection are small and statistically insignificant. Effectiveness depends on dataset representation quality and the scale of the benchmarking regime.
AI.conclusion: Strategic subset selection can substantially reduce benchmarking costs while preserving model rankings, particularly for larger benchmarks with good dataset representations. FAFI is a simple yet effective strategy. However, gains are domain-dependent — smaller benchmarks may not benefit significantly. The bootstrap-based framework provides a statistically rigorous way to evaluate and compare selection strategies.

title: OperatorSHAP: Fast and Accurate Shapley Value Estimation for Neural Operators
summary: Understanding model predictions is essential for physical applications, where outputs often inform safety-critical decisions, such as structural load assessment, weather warnings, and clinical diagnosis. Shapley values satisfy many desirable properties as an attribution method, but their computational cost during inference hinders their practical use. Current amortized explainers, such as FastSHAP, are limited to homogeneous inputs, which is problematic for physical applications where data often comes from irregular grids and geometries. We introduce OperatorSHAP, a grid-agnostic attribution method and training procedure that allows us to train FastSHAP-like explainers for neural operators.
