We establish a theoretical framework for attributions in function space, connecting to Aumann-Shapley values. We further show that OperatorSHAP's explanations are consistent with state-of-the-art discrete Shapley values across resolutions and transfer across grid sizes without retraining.

AI.tldr: OperatorSHAP introduces a grid-agnostic attribution method for neural operators, enabling efficient Shapley-value-based explanations for physical applications with irregular grids, while maintaining consistency across resolutions and transferability without retraining.
AI.motivation: Shapley values are theoretically attractive for interpreting model predictions in safety-critical physical applications, but are computationally prohibitive at inference time. Existing amortized explainers like FastSHAP only handle homogeneous (regular-grid) inputs, yet physical data frequently resides on irregular grids and geometries (e.g., unstructured meshes, point clouds). This gap motivates a grid-agnostic amortized explainer for neural operators.
AI.method: OperatorSHAP extends FastSHAP to neural operators by defining attributions in function space rather than on fixed discrete grids. The method trains an amortized explainer that directly outputs Shapley-value-style attributions for operator predictions. The authors establish a theoretical connection between their function-space attributions and Aumann-Shapley values, providing a principled foundation. The training procedure is grid-agnostic, allowing the explainer to handle inputs on arbitrary discretizations.
AI.result: OperatorSHAP explanations are consistent with state-of-the-art discrete Shapley values across varying resolutions. The method transfers across different grid sizes without requiring retraining, demonstrating its resolution independence and practical utility for physical simulation settings where mesh refinement may change between training and deployment.
AI.conclusion: OperatorSHAP enables efficient, grid-agnostic attribution for neural operators, bridging the gap between amortized Shapley-value explanation and physical applications on irregular geometries, with strong theoretical grounding and empirical validation of cross-resolution consistency.

title: Fair Classification with Efficient and Post-hoc Controllable Fairness-Accuracy Trade-off
summary: Post-hoc controllability of fair machine learning models, the ability to control the trade-off between fairness and accuracy after training, is valuable for practical deployment. Existing post-processing methods provide such post-hoc controllability but often suffer from significant accuracy degradation, whereas in-processing methods achieve efficient trade-offs but require computationally expensive retraining for each change in trade-off ratio. To achieve both post-hoc controllability and efficient trade-offs, we propose a novel fair classification algorithm that learns effective feature representations to improve the trade-off efficiency of post-processing fair classifiers, by a gradient-based optimization approach. Experimental results on real-world datasets demonstrate that our method achieves trade-off efficiency comparable to, or even surpassing, in-processing methods, without requiring any retraining.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a fair classification algorithm that learns feature representations via gradient-based optimization, enabling post-hoc fairness-accuracy trade-off control without retraining. It achieves trade-off efficiency matching or exceeding in-processing methods while maintaining the flexibility of post-processing approaches.
AI.motivation: Existing post-processing methods offer post-hoc controllability (adjusting fairness-accuracy trade-off after training) but degrade accuracy significantly. In-processing methods achieve efficient trade-offs but require costly retraining for each trade-off ratio change. The goal is to unify both advantages: post-hoc controllability and efficient trade-offs, without retraining.
AI.method: A gradient-based optimization approach that learns effective feature representations to enhance the trade-off efficiency of post-processing fair classifiers. The learned representations are designed to improve the downstream post-processing fairness intervention.
AI.result: Experimental results on real-world datasets show that the proposed method achieves trade-off efficiency comparable to or surpassing in-processing methods, without any retraining.
AI.conclusion: The method successfully combines the post-hoc controllability of post-processing with the trade-off efficiency of in-processing approaches, offering a practical solution for fair ML deployment where trade-off ratios may need frequent adjustment.

title: When One Adapter Speaks for Many: Discovering Low-Rank Redundancy in Continual Fine-Tuning
summary: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard tool for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models. When applied sequentially across tasks in Continual Learning (CL), the standard assumption is that each new task requires a dedicated low-rank adapter. In this work, we challenge this assumption empirically and structurally. We show that task-specific LoRA adapters in CL exhibit significant low-rank redundancy: the subspaces spanned by adapters trained on different tasks substantially overlap, and in many cases earlier adapters can faithfully represent later tasks. Building on this observation, we propose LiteLoRA, a plug-and-play gating mechanism that learns at train time whether to recruit a new adapter or reuse existing low-rank representations. Our method reduces the number of active adapters by 20-70% while matching or exceeding state-of-the-art performance on standard CL benchmarks, revealing that structural redundancy is pervasive and that selective learning is sufficient to achieve stability without sacrificing plasticity.

AI.tldr: LoRA adapters across sequential tasks in continual learning exhibit substantial low-rank overlap. The authors propose LiteLoRA, a gating mechanism that selectively reuses existing adapters instead of always training new ones, reducing adapter count by 20–70% without sacrificing performance.
AI.motivation: Standard continual learning with LoRA assumes each new task requires a dedicated adapter, but this may be wasteful. The authors investigate whether task-specific LoRA adapters are truly distinct or whether structural redundancy can be exploited for more efficient continual learning.
AI.method: The paper first empirically demonstrates low-rank redundancy by measuring subspace overlap between adapters trained on different tasks. It then introduces LiteLoRA, a plug-and-play gating mechanism that learns at training time whether to recruit a new low-rank adapter or reuse an existing one, enabling selective adapter allocation.
AI.result: LiteLoRA reduces the number of active adapters by 20–70% while matching or exceeding state-of-the-art performance on standard continual learning benchmarks, demonstrating that selective reuse preserves both stability and plasticity.
AI.conclusion: Structural redundancy among task-specific LoRA adapters is pervasive in continual learning. Selective adapter reuse via learned gating is sufficient to achieve strong performance, challenging the default assumption that each task requires an independent adapter.

title: Dangerous Liaisons of Convex Learning and Non-Affine Aggregation
summary: Last-iterate convergence and generalization guarantees in first-order convex learning hinge on the monotonicity of the update operator. While linear averaging preserves the monotonicity of gradient updates, this property is often violated when gradients are aggregated non-affinely, as in modern pipelines enforcing constraints like adaptivity, privacy, robustness or fairness. Whether it is possible to design non-affine aggregation rules that maintain monotonicity has remained an open question. We answer this question negatively: we prove that the monotonicity of aggregated gradients is preserved if and only if the aggregation rule is positively affine. Consequently, non-affine aggregation prevents steady convergence and substantially degrade algorithmic stability. We quantify these drawbacks and propose a path forward by identifying sufficient conditions under which monotonicity can be restored. Our results provide a unified theoretical framework explaining the disparate failure modes observed in modern learning systems.

AI.tldr: Monotonicity of gradient aggregation is preserved if and only if the aggregation rule is positively affine. Non-affine aggregation (as in adaptive, private, robust, or fair learning) inevitably breaks monotonicity, causing degraded convergence and stability. The authors provide a unified framework quantifying these drawbacks and identifying conditions to restore monotonicity.
AI.motivation: Modern learning pipelines increasingly use non-affine gradient aggregation (e.g., for adaptivity, differential privacy, robustness, or fairness constraints), but whether such aggregation can preserve the monotonicity property crucial for last-iterate convergence and generalization has remained an open question.
AI.method: The authors prove a necessary and sufficient condition (positive affinity) for preserving monotonicity under aggregation, and theoretically quantify the convergence and stability degradation caused by non-affine aggregation. They also derive sufficient conditions under which monotonicity can be restored.
AI.result: Monotonicity of aggregated gradients is preserved if and only if the aggregation rule is positively affine — a negative answer to the open question. Non-affine aggregation prevents steady convergence and substantially degrades algorithmic stability. Sufficient restoration conditions are identified.
AI.conclusion: The negative result provides a unified theoretical explanation for disparate failure modes in modern learning systems that use non-affine aggregation, and the restoration conditions offer a path forward for designing better algorithms.

title: Beyond Sparse Supervision: Diffusion-Guided Learning for Few-Shot Graph Fraud Detection
summary: Graph-based fraud detection is essential for safeguarding large-scale transaction systems, where undetected anomalies may lead to substantial financial losses and security risks. Real-world fraud graphs pose two coupled challenges: sparse and imbalanced supervision, where verified fraudulent labels are scarce and heavily skewed toward benign accounts, and representation dilution, where spatial message passing may oversmooth camouflaged anomalies while spectral filters may suppress fraud-relevant mid- and high-frequency irregularities. To address these challenges, we propose ADC-GNN, short for Attention-guided Diffusion-Contrastive Graph Neural Network, a unified framework that combines diffusion-guided feature augmentation, contrastive representation learning, and multi-hop spectral attention for few-shot graph fraud detection. The diffusion component is formulated as a feature-space denoising augmentation mechanism rather than a full topology-generative graph diffusion model: it constructs noise-perturbed node-feature views under a cosine schedule and uses contrastive learning to stabilize node representations across perturbations. The spectral attention module further adaptively emphasizes fraud-relevant hop-level and relation-level cues. We evaluate ADC-GNN primarily on three public benchmarks and additionally report a proprietary real-world telecom transaction dataset with approximately 60,000 records as a private case study. Under the 1% training setting, ADC-GNN achieves consistent improvements over original graph fraud baselines and four protocol-consistent recent graph anomaly/fraud baselines on the public benchmarks. Additional analyses on split stability, training ratios, oversampling alternatives, module-level ablations, diffusion schedules, and runtime and memory-consumption comparisons further characterize the effective operating regime of ADC-GNN.

AI.tldr: ADC-GNN is a unified framework for few-shot graph fraud detection that combines diffusion-guided feature augmentation, contrastive representation learning, and multi-hop spectral attention to address sparse/imbalanced supervision and representation dilution in fraud graphs.
AI.motivation: Real-world fraud graphs suffer from two coupled challenges: (1) sparse and imbalanced supervision, where fraudulent labels are scarce and skewed toward benign accounts; (2) representation dilution, where spatial message passing oversmooths camouflaged anomalies and spectral filters suppress fraud-relevant mid/high-frequency irregularities. Existing methods fail to address both simultaneously.
AI.method: ADC-GNN integrates three components: (1) a diffusion module that performs feature-space denoising augmentation (not full graph diffusion) by constructing noise-perturbed node-feature views under a cosine schedule, stabilized via contrastive learning; (2) contrastive representation learning across perturbed views; and (3) a multi-hop spectral attention module that adaptively emphasizes fraud-relevant cues at different hop levels and relation types.
AI.result: Under the 1% training setting on three public benchmarks and one proprietary telecom dataset (~60,000 records), ADC-GNN achieves consistent improvements over original graph fraud baselines and four protocol-consistent recent graph anomaly/fraud baselines. Analyses cover split stability, training ratios, oversampling alternatives, ablation studies, diffusion schedules, and runtime/memory comparisons.
AI.conclusion: ADC-GNN provides an effective operating regime for few-shot graph fraud detection by jointly mitigating supervision scarcity and representation dilution through its diffusion-contrastive-spectral design, validated across public and proprietary benchmarks.

title: MixTTA: Low-Rank Cross-Channel Mixing for Reliable Test-Time Adaptation
comment: To be published in the 19th European Conference on Computer Vision -- ECCV 2026
summary: Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) methods commonly update the affine parameters of normalization layers to adapt deployed models under distribution shifts. However, per-channel affine parameters perform axis-aligned scaling and shifting, making them geometrically incapable of correcting cross-channel structural changes induced by distribution shift. To address this limitation, we propose MixTTA, a lightweight plug-in module that equips normalization layers with a low-rank cross-channel transformation, enabling inter-channel mixing at each layer. To ensure that the low-rank branch captures only cross-channel interactions, we also propose Decoupling Projection that enforces strict separation from the diagonal affine path, along with Spectral Projection that prevents rank-1 collapse under non-stationary test streams. MixTTA can be seamlessly integrated into any existing normalization-based TTA method. Experiments in both standard and wild TTA settings show consistent improvements over strong baselines while mitigating adaptation failure under challenging conditions. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/delta6189/MixTTA.

AI.tldr: MixTTA introduces a lightweight low-rank cross-channel transformation into normalization layers to overcome the geometric limitation of per-channel affine parameters in test-time adaptation, with decoupling and spectral projections to ensure robust adaptation under distribution shifts.
AI.motivation: Existing TTA methods only update per-channel affine parameters (axis-aligned scaling and shifting), which are geometrically incapable of correcting cross-channel structural changes caused by distribution shift. This fundamentally limits adaptation performance.
AI.method: MixTTA is a plug-in module that adds a low-rank cross-channel transformation branch to normalization layers. It includes: (1) Decoupling Projection to strictly separate the low-rank branch from the diagonal affine path, ensuring it captures only cross-channel interactions; (2) Spectral Projection to prevent rank-1 collapse under non-stationary test streams. The module integrates seamlessly into any normalization-based TTA method.
AI.result: Experiments in both standard and wild TTA settings demonstrate consistent improvements over strong baselines, with mitigated adaptation failure under challenging conditions.
AI.conclusion: Enabling inter-channel mixing via a lightweight low-rank module effectively addresses a fundamental geometric limitation of existing normalization-based TTA methods, yielding robust improvements across diverse adaptation scenarios.

title: Autoencoder Architectures for Athlete Performance Scoring from Wearable Telemetry
comment: 6 pages, 3 figures, submitted to SPA 2026 Conference https://spaconference.org.pl/
summary: Wearable devices produce large, high dimensional training logs for everyday runners, and interpretation rather than data collection is now the limiting step. This paper evaluates five dimensionality reduction models, three autoencoder variants, PCA, and a Variational Autoencoder, on their ability to compress nine sensor runner profiles into a single scalar performance indicator, the latent score. Because the setting is fully unsupervised, model quality is assessed along two complementary axes: reconstruction error (Mean Squared Error) and latent score interpretability, measured via Spearman and Kendall rank correlations, Mutual Information, and Permutation Importance. These are combined into a composite selection criterion that prevents selecting models on reconstruction accuracy alone. Feature rankings from the four metrics are aggregated via a modified Borda count, and their stability is confirmed by bootstrap validation. A two feature linear baseline is included to anchor the comparison. Deep autoencoder achieved the lowest reconstruction error and the highest composite score. Once the PCA hidden layers were widened, the deeper variants became closely competitive with Deep AE on the composite criterion, indicating that the limiting factor was hidden layer capacity rather than the one dimensional bottleneck. Running pace, aerobic decoupling, and average heart rate emerged as the dominant latent score drivers across all models and resampling runs, consistent with established physiology.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates five dimensionality reduction models (three autoencoder variants, PCA, and a Variational Autoencoder) on their ability to compress nine-sensor runner profiles into a single latent performance score, using a composite criterion that balances reconstruction error with latent interpretability. Deep autoencoders perform best, with running pace, aerobic decoupling, and average heart rate emerging as the dominant latent drivers.
AI.motivation: Wearable devices generate large, high-dimensional training logs for everyday runners, but the bottleneck has shifted from data collection to interpretation. There is a need for unsupervised methods that can distill multivariate sensor data into a single, interpretable performance indicator without relying on labeled outcomes.
AI.method: Five dimensionality reduction models are compared: three autoencoder variants (including a deep AE), PCA, and a Variational Autoencoder (VAE). All compress nine sensor-derived runner profiles into a one-dimensional latent score. Since the setting is unsupervised, model quality is assessed along two axes: (1) reconstruction error via Mean Squared Error, and (2) latent score interpretability via Spearman and Kendall rank correlations, Mutual Information, and Permutation Importance. These metrics are combined into a composite selection criterion. Feature rankings are aggregated using a modified Borda count with bootstrap validation for stability. A two-feature linear baseline anchors the comparison.
AI.result: The deep autoencoder achieved the lowest reconstruction error and the highest composite score. When PCA hidden layers were widened, deeper PCA variants became closely competitive with the deep AE on the composite criterion, suggesting that hidden layer capacity—not the one-dimensional bottleneck—was the limiting factor. Running pace, aerobic decoupling, and average heart rate consistently emerged as the dominant latent score drivers across all models and resampling runs.
AI.conclusion: Deep autoencoders are effective for unsupervised compression of multivariate runner data into a single interpretable latent score. The composite selection criterion prevents over-reliance on reconstruction accuracy alone. The consistent identification of running pace, aerobic decoupling, and average heart rate as key drivers aligns with established exercise physiology, validating the approach's real-world interpretability.

title: Regularized Reward-Punishment Reinforcement Learning
summary: We propose KL-Coupled Policy Regularization (KCPR), a policy coordination framework for Reward-Punishment Reinforcement Learning (RPRL). Based on KCPR, we derive KL-Coupled Soft Optimality (KCSO) and develop its deep realization, klDMP. Unlike existing RPRL approaches that optimize reward-seeking and punishment-related policies largely independently, KCPR enables direct interactions between companion policies by treating each as a dynamically learned prior for the other. KCSO yields coupled soft-optimal policies and KL-regularized Bellman operators, allowing reward and punishment information to jointly influence value propagation. To improve learning stability, we introduce a companion-prior softening mechanism and evaluate separate replay-buffer designs for balancing reward- and punishment-related experience. Experiments in grid-world and Gazebo robotic navigation tasks demonstrate that klDMP improves safety and learning stability while maintaining competitive task performance compared with DQN, SQL and softDMP. These results suggest that policy-level coordination provides an effective mechanism for integrating multiple behavioral objectives and may serve as a useful design principle for reinforcement learning systems with interacting motivational processes.

AI.tldr: KL-Coupled Policy Regularization (KCPR) enables reward-seeking and punishment-avoidance policies to interact as mutual priors in RL, yielding coupled soft-optimal policies (KCSO) and improved safety/performance trade-offs in navigation tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing Reward-Punishment Reinforcement Learning (RPRL) methods optimize reward-seeking and punishment-related policies largely independently, missing opportunities for synergistic information sharing. The authors aim to create a framework where these companion policies directly interact to jointly influence learning, thereby improving safety without sacrificing task performance.
AI.method: KCPR treats each companion policy as a dynamically learned KL-divergence prior for the other, deriving KL-Coupled Soft Optimality (KCSO) with coupled soft-optimal policies and KL-regularized Bellman operators. The deep realization, klDMP, incorporates a companion-prior softening mechanism for stability and evaluates separate replay-buffer designs. Experiments span grid-world and Gazebo robotic navigation tasks, benchmarking against DQN, SQL, and softDMP.
AI.result: klDMP demonstrates improved safety and learning stability while maintaining competitive task performance compared to DQN, SQL, and softDMP in both grid-world and Gazebo robotic navigation experiments.
AI.conclusion: Policy-level coordination via mutual KL-regularization is an effective mechanism for integrating multiple behavioral objectives. KCPR/KCSO may serve as a general design principle for RL systems with interacting motivational processes (e.g., reward and punishment).

title: Recovering Sharp Conductivity Features in the Finite-Data Calderón Problem with Physics-Informed Neural Networks
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have recently emerged as a promising framework for addressing the Calderón inverse problem from limited boundary data. In this work, we revisit neural Calderón inversion by introducing multiscale boundary excitations based on randomized wavelet functions and investigating the role of Fourier-feature encoding (FFE) for representing sharp conductivity variations. We propose a physics-informed reconstruction framework that represents the unknown conductivity and the associated family of electric potentials with separate neural networks conditioned on the applied boundary excitations. The governing elliptic PDE is enforced through physics-informed residuals, while finite Dirichlet-to-Neumann (DtN) data are incorporated through boundary losses. Using synthetic data from a finite-difference forward solver, we evaluate the method on conductivity fields with inclusions, sharp interfaces, smooth profiles, and heterogeneous media. Results show that the framework recovers dominant conductivity structures from finite boundary measurements with relative errors between $3\%-12\%$ approximately. We show that FFE improves the reconstruction of localized sharp features, particularly for inclusions and interfaces, but are not universally optimal, with raw-coordinate networks performing competitively for smoother fields. These results highlight coordinate representations and boundary excitation design as key factors in neural Calderón inversion.

AI.tldr: This paper revisits the Calderón inverse problem using physics-informed neural networks (PINNs), proposing a framework with multiscale randomized wavelet boundary excitations and Fourier-feature encoding (FFE) to reconstruct conductivity fields from limited boundary data. FFE improves sharp feature recovery, while raw-coordinate networks suffice for smooth fields.
AI.motivation: The Calderón inverse problem — recovering internal conductivity from boundary measurements — is ill-posed and challenging with limited data. While PINNs offer promise, key design choices such as boundary excitation strategy and network architecture (particularly for representing sharp conductivity variations) remain underexplored. The authors aim to systematically investigate these factors.
AI.method: The framework uses two neural networks: one for the unknown conductivity field and one for the family of electric potentials, conditioned on boundary excitations. Multiscale randomized wavelet functions generate the boundary excitations. Physics-informed residuals enforce the governing elliptic PDE, and boundary losses incorporate finite Dirichlet-to-Neumann (DtN) data. Both Fourier-feature encoding (FFE) and raw-coordinate MLPs are tested for representing the conductivity. Synthetic data from a finite-difference solver is used for evaluation across diverse conductivity fields (inclusions, sharp interfaces, smooth profiles, heterogeneous media).
AI.result: The framework achieves relative reconstruction errors of approximately 3%–12% from finite boundary measurements. FFE substantially improves reconstruction of localized sharp features (inclusions, interfaces) but is not universally optimal; raw-coordinate networks perform competitively on smoother conductivity fields.
AI.conclusion: Coordinate representation choice and boundary excitation design are critical factors in neural Calderón inversion. FFE offers benefits for sharp features but is not a one-size-fits-all solution, suggesting that architecture should be tailored to the expected conductivity profile characteristics.

title: CPAgents: Agentic Composite Phenotype Generation for Cardiac Disease Association
summary: Identifying robust associations between cardiac imaging phenotypes and clinical diseases is fundamental to population-scale cardiovascular research and reliable risk stratification. However, current phenome-wide association studies rely on pre-defined, single-variable phenotypes or expert-crafted features, which limits their ability to capture clinically meaningful non-linear effects and cross-phenotype interactions. To address this, we propose CPAgents, an iterative phenotype-Composition framework for cardiovascular Phenome-wide association study (PheWAS) that automatically constructs and validates interpretable composite phenotypes (e.g., polynomial, ratio, and interaction forms) from base imaging features. Specifically, our system coordinates three agents: (i) an Analyst that identifies statistical pathologies and nominates candidate transformations; (ii) a Proposer that generates constrained, medically and statistically motivated expressions under numerical safety rules; and (iii) a Verifier that evaluates candidates using multi-stage criteria and produces transparent evidence trails for accepted phenotypes. Evaluated on a population-scale cardiac imaging cohort, the discovered composite phenotypes markedly improve disease discrimination: across 72 classifier-disease-metric combinations, our variants achieve the top rank in 56 cases versus 18 for baselines, with gains observed across all nine clinical disease categories. Our framework yields compact, clinically interpretable phenotype formulas with transparent evidence trails, enabling scalable discovery of stronger phenotype-disease associations beyond expert-driven feature selection.

AI.tldr: CPAgents is a multi-agent framework that automatically discovers interpretable composite cardiac imaging phenotypes (polynomial, ratio, interaction forms) for phenome-wide association studies, outperforming conventional single-variable phenotypes across 72 classifier-disease-metric combinations.
AI.motivation: Current PheWAS approaches rely on pre-defined single-variable phenotypes or handcrafted features, missing clinically meaningful non-linear effects and cross-phenotype interactions that could yield stronger phenotype-disease associations.
AI.method: A three-agent iterative system: (i) Analyst — identifies statistical pathologies and nominates candidate transformations; (ii) Proposer — generates constrained, medically and statistically motivated composite phenotype expressions under numerical safety rules; (iii) Verifier — evaluates candidates via multi-stage criteria and produces transparent evidence trails.
AI.result: Composite phenotypes achieved top rank in 56 of 72 classifier-disease-metric combinations (vs. 18 for baselines), with improvements across all nine clinical disease categories in a population-scale cardiac imaging cohort.
AI.conclusion: CPAgents enables scalable, automated discovery of compact, clinically interpretable phenotype formulas with transparent evidence trails, yielding stronger phenotype-disease associations than expert-driven feature selection alone.

title: LLawCo: Learning Laws of Cooperation for Modeling Embodied Multi-Agent Behavior
summary: Embodied agents operating in decentralized and partially observable environments have attracted growing attention in recent years. However, existing large language model (LLM)-based agents often exhibit behaviors that are misaligned with their partners or inconsistent with the environment state, leading to inefficient cooperation and poor task success. To address this challenge, we propose a novel framework, Learning Laws of Cooperation (LLawCo), that enables embodied agents to autonomously align with both their partners and task objectives. Our framework allows agents to reflect on past failures to extract misaligned behavioral patterns, which are used to derive high-level behavioral laws, such as "Talk when necessary" and "Wait for partner." These laws are explicitly incorporated into the agents' chains of thought via supervised fine-tuning, aligning their reasoning with task requirements and the behavior of other agents. To evaluate our approach, we introduce PARTNR-Dialog, a large-scale multi-agent communicative and cooperative planning benchmark built on the PARTNR environment. Experiments on existing tasks and our new benchmark demonstrate significant improvements in cooperative efficiency and task success rates. Across four backbone LLMs, our method achieves average success rate improvements of 4.5% on the PARTNR-Dialog benchmark and 6.8% on the TDW-MAT benchmark over state-of-the-art open-source communicative agent frameworks. See the LLawCo project page for details: https://www.merl.com/research/highlights/LLawCo

AI.tldr: LLawCo is a framework that enables embodied agents to learn high-level behavioral laws from past failures via reflection, then incorporates these laws into chain-of-thought reasoning through supervised fine-tuning, significantly improving cooperative efficiency and task success in decentralized, partially observable multi-agent environments.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM-based embodied agents in decentralized, partially observable environments exhibit behaviors misaligned with partners or inconsistent with environment state, causing inefficient cooperation and poor task success. The authors aim to solve this misalignment problem by enabling agents to autonomously derive and internalize cooperative behavioral principles.
AI.method: LLawCo works in two stages: (1) Reflection — agents analyze past failure trajectories to extract misaligned behavioral patterns and derive high-level behavioral laws (e.g., "Talk when necessary," "Wait for partner"). (2) Alignment — these laws are explicitly incorporated into the agents' chain-of-thought reasoning via supervised fine-tuning, ensuring reasoning aligns with task requirements and partner behavior. The authors also introduce PARTNR-Dialog, a new large-scale multi-agent communicative and cooperative planning benchmark built on the PARTNR environment.
AI.result: LLawCo achieves average success rate improvements of 4.5% on PARTNR-Dialog and 6.8% on TDW-MAT over state-of-the-art open-source communicative agent frameworks, evaluated across four backbone LLMs.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly deriving and integrating high-level behavioral laws into LLM-based agents' reasoning processes through reflection and fine-tuning is an effective approach for improving multi-agent cooperation in embodied, partially observable environments.

title: The Remittance Blueprint: Data-driven Intelligence for Sri Lanka
summary: This study analyzes Sri Lankan migration and remittances over 32 years (1994-2025). Using a 384-month harmonized dataset, we apply exploratory data analysis, stationarity corrected time-series modeling (ADF, Johansen, VAR/VECM), and supervised learning. Results reveal remittance inflows are primarily driven by external macroeconomic variables, specifically exchange rate dynamics and global oil prices, rather than domestic indicators. Impulse response analysis confirms the asymmetric impact of currency depreciation and oil price shocks. Predictively, multivariate machine learning models outperform traditional univariate approaches; Ridge Regression achieves a 73.8% accuracy improvement over SARIMA (Annualized RMSE: USD 494.8 Mn). The optimized framework projects 2026 remittances at USD 9,001 million under stable conditions. These findings highlight the structural dependence of remittances on global economies, emphasizing the need for robust exchange rate policies, skilled migration, and formal financial channels to enhance long-term economic resilience.

AI.tldr: A 32-year analysis of Sri Lankan remittances (1994–2025) finds that external factors—exchange rates and oil prices—drive inflows more than domestic variables. Machine learning models (notably Ridge Regression) outperform traditional time-series methods, achieving a 73.8% accuracy gain, and project 2026 remittances at ~USD 9 billion.
AI.motivation: To understand the structural drivers of Sri Lankan remittance inflows and improve predictive accuracy by moving beyond conventional univariate time-series models, given remittances' critical role in the nation's economic resilience.
AI.method: A harmonized 384-month dataset (1994–2025) was analyzed using exploratory data analysis, stationarity-corrected time-series modeling (ADF tests, Johansen cointegration, VAR/VECM frameworks), impulse response functions, and supervised machine learning models (including Ridge Regression and SARIMA as a baseline).
AI.result: Remittance inflows are predominantly driven by external macroeconomic variables (exchange rate dynamics, global oil prices) rather than domestic indicators. Impulse response analysis confirms asymmetric effects of currency depreciation and oil price shocks. Ridge Regression achieved a 73.8% accuracy improvement over SARIMA (Annualized RMSE: USD 494.8 Mn). The model projects 2026 remittances at USD 9,001 million under stable conditions.
AI.conclusion: Sri Lanka's remittance inflows exhibit structural dependence on global economic conditions. Policymakers should prioritize robust exchange rate policies, promote skilled migration pathways, and strengthen formal financial channels to bolster long-term economic resilience.

title: COCOLogic-V2: Identifying Logical Inconsistencies via Truly Hard-Negatives
summary: While interpretable models such as concept bottleneck models (CBMs) and program synthesis methods enable verification of model decisions, their evaluation is typically limited to simple tasks, leaving complex reasoning on real-world images largely unexplored. We introduce COCOLogic-V2, an object-centric dataset for visual inductive reasoning on real-world images covering a broad subset of first-order logic. By categorizing samples into positive variants, near-boundary (NB), and far-from-boundary (FB) negatives, COCOLogic-V2 enables fine-grained diagnosis of model accountability. Our evaluations show that models tend to separate positive and FB samples well but fail on NB samples, while perceptual noise and large rule-induced search spaces pose additional challenges in few-shot settings. Together, these results highlight that visual inductive reasoning remains an open challenge and COCOLogic-V2 provides a concrete foundation for advancing methods in this direction.

AI.tldr: COCOLogic-V2 is an object-centric dataset for visual inductive reasoning on real-world images, covering first-order logic with fine-grained sample categorization (positive, near-boundary, and far-from-boundary negatives). Evaluations reveal that current models fail on near-boundary samples, and perceptual noise plus large search spaces pose significant challenges in few-shot settings.
AI.motivation: Existing interpretable models (CBMs, program synthesis) are mostly evaluated on simple tasks, leaving visual inductive reasoning on real-world images underexplored. There is a need for a dataset that enables fine-grained diagnosis of model accountability in complex reasoning scenarios.
AI.method: The authors construct COCOLogic-V2, an object-centric dataset built on real-world images (from COCO), covering a broad subset of first-order logic. Samples are categorized into three types: positive variants, near-boundary (NB) negatives, and far-from-boundary (FB) negatives. This categorization enables fine-grained evaluation of model behavior. Models are tested in standard and few-shot settings to assess reasoning under perceptual noise and rule-induced search space constraints.
AI.result: Models separate positive and far-from-boundary samples well but consistently fail on near-boundary negatives. Perceptual noise and the large rule-induced search space further degrade performance in few-shot settings. These findings indicate that visual inductive reasoning remains largely unsolved.
AI.conclusion: Visual inductive reasoning on real-world images remains an open challenge. COCOLogic-V2 provides a solid benchmark for advancing interpretable, accountable models capable of complex logical reasoning over visual inputs.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Network with Transfer Learning for State Estimation in Lithium-Ion Batteries using the Single Particle Model with Electrolyte
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for solving nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs), including battery electrochemical models. They typically en-force conservation laws within the loss function to ensure physically consistent solutions. Tradi-tional numerical methods such as finite difference, finite volume, and finite element techniques, re-ly on discretization and can be computationally expensive for nonlinear systems. To address this challenge, PINNs offer improved scalability, particularly for reduced-order models like the single particle model with electrolyte (SPMe). The SPMe describes lithium-ion battery dynamics through coupled diffusion, transport, reaction kinetics, and voltage equations. Despite these advantages, training SPMe-based PINNs from scratch for different battery chemistries or operating conditions is demanding and often leads to slow convergence. To overcome this limitation, this work introduces a transfer learning framework for SPMe-PINNs. The model is first pretrained to learn general elec-trochemical dynamics and then adapted to a target battery by transferring weights, freezing se-lected layers, and fine tuning the remaining parameters, including estimating key electrochemical variables. Validation using PyBaMM demonstrates accurate voltage prediction, indicating that the proposed approach preserves electrochemical consistency while reducing training time and ena-bling efficient generalization across batteries.

AI.tldr: A transfer learning framework is proposed for physics-informed neural networks applied to the single particle model with electrolyte (SPMe), enabling pretraining on general electrochemical dynamics and rapid fine-tuning to specific battery chemistries, thereby reducing training time while maintaining accuracy.
AI.motivation: Training SPMe-based PINNs from scratch for each new battery chemistry or operating condition is computationally demanding and suffers from slow convergence. A more efficient approach is needed to generalize across different batteries without retraining entirely.
AI.method: A transfer learning framework where the SPMe-PINN is first pretrained to capture general electrochemical dynamics (coupled diffusion, transport, reaction kinetics, voltage). Weights are then transferred to a target battery, selected layers are frozen, and the remaining parameters are fine-tuned — including estimation of key electrochemical variables. Validation is performed against PyBaMM simulations.
AI.result: The proposed approach achieves accurate voltage prediction validated against PyBaMM, preserves electrochemical consistency, reduces training time, and enables efficient generalization across different battery chemistries and operating conditions.
AI.conclusion: Transfer learning effectively addresses the retraining bottleneck in SPMe-PINNs, offering a practical pathway for rapid deployment of PINN-based battery models across diverse chemistries while maintaining physical fidelity and reducing computational cost.

title: Disentangling Continuous-Time Latent Dynamics: Identifiability of Latent SDEs via Diffusion Shifts
summary: Causal representation learning for time series has developed strong identifiability results in discrete-time latent causal models, but identifiability in continuous-time latent stochastic differential equation (SDE) models remains largely open. We address this gap using environment-induced shifts in diffusion covariance. We study additive-noise latent SDEs observed through an unknown nonlinear diffeomorphism, with shared drift but environment-specific diffusion covariance. We show that two diagonal diffusion regimes with pairwise distinct coordinate-wise variance ratios identify the latent coordinates up to permutation and scaling, without any sparsity assumption on the drift. We first prove this result for linear Ornstein--Uhlenbeck systems and then extend it to general additive-noise latent SDEs. Under mild smoothness, the instantaneous drift-Jacobian causal graph is identifiable up to the same permutation. We propose a two-stage estimator for latent disentanglement and optional graph recovery; experiments on synthetic systems confirm the predicted identifiability boundary, and an application to Hardanger Bridge monitoring data illustrates the approach on real sensor trajectories.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes identifiability results for continuous-time latent SDE models using environment-induced shifts in diffusion covariance. It proves that two environments with distinct diagonal diffusion ratios can identify latent coordinates up to permutation and scaling, and extends this to recover the drift-Jacobian causal graph, with a practical two-stage estimator validated on synthetic and real bridge monitoring data.
AI.motivation: While causal representation learning for discrete-time time series has achieved strong identifiability guarantees, identifiability in continuous-time latent stochastic differential equation (SDE) models remains largely unexplored. Closing this gap is critical for real-world dynamical systems that evolve continuously, such as sensor networks and physical processes.
AI.method: The authors study additive-noise latent SDEs observed through an unknown nonlinear diffeomorphism, where the drift function is shared across environments but the diffusion covariance is environment-specific. The key insight leverages two environments with diagonal diffusion matrices whose coordinate-wise variance ratios are pairwise distinct. They first prove identifiability (up to permutation and scaling) for linear Ornstein–Uhlenbeck systems, then extend the result to general additive-noise latent SDEs using local linearization. A two-stage estimator is proposed: the first stage uses contrastive learning across environments to disentangle latent coordinates, and the second stage optionally recovers the instantaneous drift-Jacobian causal graph.
AI.result: The theoretical analysis shows that two diagonal diffusion regimes with pairwise distinct variance ratios suffice to identify latent coordinates up to permutation and scaling, without requiring sparsity assumptions on the drift. Under mild smoothness conditions, the drift-Jacobian causal graph is also identifiable up to the same permutation. Synthetic experiments confirm the predicted identifiability boundary, and a real-world application to Hardanger Bridge monitoring data demonstrates practical utility on sensor trajectories.
AI.conclusion: Environment-induced diffusion shifts provide a principled pathway to identifiability in continuous-time latent causal models. The work bridges discrete-time causal representation learning with continuous-time SDE models, opening avenues for causal discovery in real-world dynamical systems with continuous-time observations.

title: How Width and Data Shape Generalization Scaling Laws in Quadratic Neural Networks
summary: Understanding how performance scales jointly with model size and data is a central problem in modern machine learning. Existing theoretical works on scaling laws typically describe generalization as a function of data or compute, often in fixed-feature or infinite-width regimes and for online SGD. Here, we instead study how generalization scales with the number of trainable parameters and the number of samples in a feature-learning model. We analyze $\ell_2$-regularized empirical test error minimization in a quadratic two-layer network in a finite-sample setting with structured data. This setting allows for an explicit characterization of the generalization error as a function of the number of samples, model width, and regularization. Our results reveal a phase diagram with distinct scaling regimes as the number of parameters varies. In particular, the generalization error follows data-dependent power laws controlled by the spectral structure of the target. We further characterize the transitions between regimes, including the onset of interpolation, and their impact on generalization.

AI.tldr: This paper studies how generalization error scales with both the number of trainable parameters and the number of samples in a feature-learning quadratic two-layer network with ℓ2 regularization. It derives an explicit characterization of test error and reveals a phase diagram with distinct scaling regimes governed by the spectral structure of the target, including transitions between regimes and the onset of interpolation.
AI.motivation: Existing theoretical works on scaling laws typically describe generalization as a function of data or compute, often restricted to fixed-feature or infinite-width regimes and online SGD. The authors aim to go beyond these limitations by jointly studying how generalization scales with both model size (trainable parameters) and dataset size in a feature-learning setting, where the model actively learns representations from data.
AI.method: The authors analyze ℓ2-regularized empirical test error minimization in a quadratic two-layer neural network under a finite-sample setting with structured data. This tractable setting enables an explicit analytical characterization of the generalization error as a function of the number of samples (n), model width (p), and the regularization parameter (λ). The analysis leverages the spectral structure of the target to derive scaling behaviors.
AI.result: The analysis yields a phase diagram with distinct scaling regimes as the number of parameters varies. Generalization error follows data-dependent power laws governed by the spectral structure of the target function. The authors characterize transitions between these regimes, including the onset of interpolation (where training error becomes zero), and analyze how these transitions impact generalization performance.
AI.conclusion: Generalization scaling laws in feature-learning models are richer than those predicted by fixed-feature or infinite-width theories. The scaling behavior depends critically on the interplay between model width, sample size, regularization, and the spectral properties of the target, giving rise to distinct phases and transitions that prior frameworks could not capture.

title: Parameter Efficient Hybrid Transformer (PEHT) for Network Traffic Prediction via Dynamic Urban Congestion Integration
summary: Accurate network traffic prediction is a critical element for efficient resource allocation in dynamic urban cellular networks. However, prediction remains challenging because network demand is influenced by complex mobility patterns, congestion dynamics, and heterogeneous user behavior. This paper introduces the Parameter-Efficient Hybrid Transformer (PEHT), a network traffic prediction framework that integrates urban mobility and congestion information into a Transformer-based architecture. PEHT separates primary network communication features from secondary urban mobility features and incorporates Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) into the Transformer encoder to reduce the number of trainable parameters while maintaining high predictive accuracy. A multimodal fusion strategy then injects external mobility and congestion features into the decoder to improve traffic forecasting. Experiments on the Telecom Italia Milan dataset and multiple synthetic congestion scenarios show that PEHT outperforms state-of-the-art baselines in terms of RMSE, MAE, and $R^2$. The implementation is available in the GitHub repository.

AI.tldr: PEHT is a parameter-efficient Transformer for urban cellular network traffic prediction that integrates mobility and congestion data via LoRA adaptation and multimodal fusion, outperforming baselines on the Telecom Italia Milan dataset.
AI.motivation: Urban cellular network traffic prediction is challenging due to complex mobility patterns, congestion dynamics, and heterogeneous user behavior. Existing models struggle to efficiently incorporate external contextual factors (mobility, congestion) while maintaining parameter efficiency.
AI.method: PEHT separates primary network communication features from secondary urban mobility features. It applies Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) to the Transformer encoder to reduce trainable parameters while preserving accuracy. A multimodal fusion strategy injects external mobility and congestion features into the decoder for improved forecasting.
AI.result: PEHT outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on the Telecom Italia Milan dataset and multiple synthetic congestion scenarios, achieving superior RMSE, MAE, and R² scores.
AI.conclusion: Integrating urban mobility and congestion information into a parameter-efficient Transformer architecture significantly improves cellular traffic prediction accuracy while maintaining computational efficiency. Code is publicly available on GitHub.

title: VGB for Masked Diffusion Model: Efficient Test-time Scaling for Reward Satisfaction and Sample Editing
summary: Inference-time scaling is a promising paradigm to improve generative models, especially when outputs must satisfy structural constraints or optimize downstream rewards. We consider Masked Diffusion Model (MDM) and introduce MDM-VGB, a discrete diffusion sampler that augments unmasking generation with theoretically principled reward-guided remasking. Inspired by the recent success of the classical Jerrum-Sinclair backtracking Markov chain in reward-tilted generation, MDM-VGB extends the backtracking random walk from a fixed prefix tree to a masked-state graph, allowing tokens to be unmasked and remasked at arbitrary positions. The resulting sampler favors unmasking and remasking moves that lead to higher-value partial configurations, enabling both effective high-reward generation and efficient repair of low-reward samples. We prove that MDM-VGB is robust to process-verifier noise and achieves quadratic complexity, while popular test-time heuristics such as best-of-$N$ can incur exponential complexity due to error accumulation. Our theoretical findings are corroborated by strong empirical performance, particularly on popular constraint-satisfaction and scientific benchmarks such as Sudoku and QM9.

AI.tldr: MDM-VGB introduces a reward-guided discrete diffusion sampler for Masked Diffusion Models that extends Jerrum-Sinclair backtracking to masked-state graphs, enabling efficient high-reward generation and low-reward sample repair with quadratic complexity, outperforming exponential-cost heuristics like best-of-N on benchmarks such as Sudoku and QM9.
AI.motivation: Inference-time scaling is promising for improving generative models under structural constraints or downstream reward optimization. Existing test-time heuristics (e.g., best-of-N) can incur exponential complexity due to error accumulation, motivating a principled, efficient alternative for reward-guided generation with discrete diffusion models.
AI.method: MDM-VGB extends the Jerrum-Sinclair backtracking Markov chain from fixed prefix trees to masked-state graphs in Masked Diffusion Models. It allows tokens to be unmasked and remasked at arbitrary positions, with a sampler that favors moves leading to higher-value partial configurations. The method is theoretically proven robust to process-verifier noise and achieves O(n²) complexity.
AI.result: MDM-VGB achieves quadratic complexity while avoiding the exponential complexity of best-of-N heuristics. It demonstrates strong empirical performance on constraint-satisfaction and scientific benchmarks, notably Sudoku and the QM9 molecular dataset.
AI.conclusion: MDM-VGB provides a theoretically grounded, efficient framework for reward-guided inference in Masked Diffusion Models, bridging classical Markov chain theory with modern generative modeling and outperforming popular heuristic baselines.
